Product sense and taste

Foundations › Product Thinking and Product Sense. How practised judgement is constructed, where it is load-bearing, and where it quietly fails.

1. Two decisions in the same fortnight

On Tuesday, 22 September 2026, two days after a fourteen-day experiment closed, Malini Raghunath sat in Manzar Picture Labs' Bengaluru office with a result she had expected and a recommendation she did not accept. Manzar sells a consumer photography application — camera, editor, subscription at ₹299 a month. In the month to 31 August it drew 6,40,000 installs, of which 2,24,000 completed a first edit, 56,000 began the seven-day trial and 10,080 converted to paid: ₹30,13,920 of first-month subscription revenue. The experiment tested one change, making Mukammal Portrait, a one-tap generative enhancement, the camera screen's default rather than a choice. Nishad Virkar, the growth lead in Indore, wanted it shipped before the festival season. Mitali Dongre, who leads design from Kochi, had written four words in the review document: "it flatters the wrong thing." Narendra Shenvi, the chief executive, wanted the activation number up before a November investor conversation. Malini had nine days, until Thursday, 1 October.

On Wednesday, 23 September 2026, in Pune, Nirav Satpute faced a different shape of decision. Mistri Service Forge sells field-service software to appliance and air-conditioning manufacturers, plus a diagnostic dongle technicians plug into the equipment. Thirty-eight enterprise accounts produced ₹28.5 crore of annual recurring revenue; the largest, Mandovi Climate Industries, contributed ₹4.2 crore, or 14.7 per cent, and renewed on 31 March 2027. Mandovi wanted a configurable workflow builder so each of its six regions could define its own job stages. Manjula Kaikini, who runs field-operations research from Coimbatore, wanted an offline mode instead: 18.5 per cent of jobs across the installed base were recorded hours late for want of a signal. Niyati Gadgil, who owns enterprise success from Ahmedabad, thought refusing Mandovi reckless. Sprint planning was twelve days away, on Monday, 5 October.

Both decisions turn on the same faculty, and in both the decider had formed a view in under two minutes. What follows asks what that view consists of and when it deserves trust.

TypeConsumer, AI-native, subscriptionEnterprise, hardware plus software
Scale6,40,000 installs a month38 accounts; 11,400 technicians
Revenue basis₹299 per subscriber per month₹28.5 crore annual recurring
DecisionGenerative enhancement as default?Workflow builder, or offline mode?
Decision dateThursday, 1 October 2026Monday, 5 October 2026
Cost of errorReversible in a week22 engineer-months; a year

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Product sense is the capacity to judge, quickly and with articulable reasons, whether a proposed change serves a real user and a viable business. Taste is the narrower faculty applied to quality: which of two defensible options is better made, more coherent with what the product already is, and less likely to be regretted. The definition that survives scrutiny is that taste is fast, internalised deconstruction, calibrated by outcomes: the content is the set of questions a beginner asks slowly, the expert no longer asks them aloud, and a confident feeling never scored against reality is preference, not taste.

The idea exists to solve a scheduling problem: decisions arrive faster than evidence can be manufactured, and Manzar changes something on the camera screen most weeks. The practice crystallised in the consumer software and design studios of the 1990s and 2000s, and took its respectability from an argument settled elsewhere: Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein concluded that intuition is trustworthy where the environment offers regularities to learn and feedback is prompt. That is a testable claim about domains, not a compliment to individuals. Three schools now disagree, about propositions rather than emphasis.

No synthesis reconciles them. What they share is narrow: all three accept that the judgement must be stated before the data arrives, so the data can disconfirm it.

3. Mechanics, including the steps left implicit

The teaching form of deconstruction has six slots — user, job, promise, business model, key metric, biggest assumption. A competent practitioner fills them. An expert then performs five operations almost never written down.

First, the counterfactual split. Divide the affected population into those who would have acted anyway and those whose behaviour the change alters; costs fall on the whole population, benefits only on the second group. Second, ledger location. Every number belongs to somebody's accounts, and "whose profit and loss does this land in?" separates value created from value captured.

Third, rate-chain compounding. A funnel is a product of rates, so an intervention's effect on the terminal outcome is the product of its effects on each stage. This is where Malini's two-minute judgement did its work. In the control arm, 60,000 installs produced 21,000 first edits (35.0 per cent), 5,250 trials (25.0 per cent of first edits) and 945 conversions (18.0 per cent of trials). In the treatment arm the same 60,000 installs produced 27,600 first edits (46.0 per cent), 5,520 trials (20.0 per cent) and 828 conversions (15.0 per cent). The stage ratios are 46/35 = 1.3143, 20/25 = 0.80 and 15/18 = 0.8333; their product is 0.8762, and 828 ÷ 945 is 0.8762 exactly. The eleven-point activation gain was not offset but multiplied away.

The formalism yields a rule a practitioner can carry in the head. For terminal conversion to hold, the activation ratio must be at least 1 ÷ (0.80 × 0.8333) = 1.50, so activation would have to reach 35.0 × 1.50 = 52.5 per cent, not 46.0.

Fourth, carrying cost. Build cost is a single payment; configuration surfaces, defaults and options levy rent for as long as they exist. The expert asks for the annual carrying cost before the build estimate, because the build estimate is the number everyone has already prepared.

Fifth, the refutation line. Before the data arrives, write the number that would change your mind. Malini had written on 5 September that she would accept the default if trial-to-paid conversion held above 17.0 per cent. It came in at 15.0. Pre-registration converts an instinct into evidence about the instinct.

Calls: 84,000 in control, 1,98,000 in treatment, because the default fires for every install that opens the camera, including the 32,400 who never finish an edit. Day-90 retention is projected from the four preceding cohorts — 60.0 per cent control, 50.0 per cent treatment. Scaled to 6,40,000 monthly installs, the final line is a loss of ₹7,98,752, about ₹7.99 lakh a month.

4. When the faculty applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions can be checked in advance. C1: the decision recurs often enough that deliberation costs more than error — true for Manzar's weekly surface changes, false for a default governing 6,40,000 installs a month, false for Mistri's roadmap of four such decisions a year. C2: the judge has had feedback on comparable judgements in this domain — true for Malini, four years into camera defaults; partly true for Nirav, fourteen months into enterprise software after a consumer career, which is why he bought a field test rather than trust the instinct that told him Mandovi was bluffing. C3: a cheap refutation exists — true at Manzar, where a fortnight and 1,20,000 installs cost only time; false at Mistri, where the cheapest honest test of the builder is to build a third of it. C4: the outcome that matters is observable inside the decision horizon — false in both, since day-90 retention is unknown on 1 October and Mandovi renews on 31 March 2027.

The faculty is actively misleading in four situations: when the population has changed, so the regularities the judge learned no longer hold while confidence survives; when the judge is a proxy for the buyer rather than the user, so taste optimises the demonstration; when the object is a distribution rather than an artefact, the condition of every AI-native product; and when the decision is irreversible and the instinct merely strong.

5. Hard edge cases, and what the seams do

In multi-product companies the unit of taste becomes the boundary between products: Manzar also ships a lightweight gallery application, and the Mukammal default in one but not the other would teach two stories about what the company believes photographs are for. In two-sided businesses the judgement concerns which side is scarce, and the error is to apply consumer taste to the abundant side while the scarce side starves. In regulated products taste works inside a boundary it did not draw — Mistri's warranty records are evidence in consumer disputes, so letting technicians edit a completed job is unavailable at any price. In hardware plus software, reversibility dominates: an elegant change to the dongle's indicator behaviour that confuses a technician costs a truck roll, which is why the hardware side holds a rarely questioned veto.

In AI-native products the problem changes character. Taste over a distribution means judging samples, not specimens, and the discipline that replaces the old eye is a rubric applied to a fixed set of hard cases. In Mitali's hand-scored sample of 400 enhanced portraits, 86 per cent of light-skinned and 61 per cent of dark-skinned subjects were judged faithful — a 25-point gap no screenshot reveals and no activation metric surfaces.

The organisational seam is where this fails. Design owns the artefact, growth the stage rate, support the consequence, finance the carrying cost, and the four never meet in one document. Mature companies say they solve it with written principles. What they do is narrower: name two or three people whose judgement binds on named surfaces, require a pre-registered refutation line before any default change, and keep post-mortems searchable.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Taste compresses the counterfactual; it does not skip it. The competent practitioner hears "I don't like it" as the end of an argument. The tell-tale sign of the expert is a fast verdict with a prediction attached: Malini's first sentence on 22 September was not "this is bad" but "activation will be up about ten points and paid conversion down about three." The obvious reading, that experts feel more acutely, is wrong; they feel specifically.

The first judgement is about mechanism, not magnitude. Experts estimate sizes poorly and name directions well. The tell is the shape of the opening claim: a mechanism — "a default removes the moment where the user decides the edit is theirs, and authorship is what people pay for" — rather than a number. Magnitudes come from the spreadsheet, direction from judgement, and confusing the two misassigns credit.

An early-stage metric can be purchased from a later one. Activation, first-session completion and demo-to-pilot are the most easily bought metrics in product management, because each rises when you remove a decision the user needed to make in order to care. The tell is a pair of movements: one rate up sharply, the rate below it down slightly. Competent practitioners celebrate the first and call the second noise; experts multiply the ratios and find a 31 per cent relative gain and two small losses netting to a 12 per cent fall.

A default is a statement of belief wearing the costume of a setting. Teams debate defaults as configuration and settle them by metric, which is a category error. The tell is the expert's question: what does this default teach a new user about what the product is for? At Manzar the honest answer was that it taught users the product improves photographs for them, when the subscription is sold on helping them improve their own.

The loud account is information about the account. Mandovi's request is a fact about Mandovi, not about appliance manufacturers. The tell is sequence: the expert asks for the silent base's number before engaging with the loud one's, because the silent base has no advocate in the room and its number is usually larger. Large customers are by construction atypical, which is why their roadmap is not the market's.

A figure must be located on a ledger before it is used. Manjula's ₹19,66,500 a month of avoided rework is real, and none of it is Mistri's: it sits in the accounts of thirty-eight manufacturers. Mistri's share is what it can defend at renewal, which Nirav put at a 2.0 per cent uplift on ₹2,850 lakh of recurring revenue, or ₹57 lakh a year — 24.2 per cent of the ₹235.98 lakh created. The tell is two columns, never added.

Taste in enterprise is restraint; in consumer it is specificity. The enterprise critique concerns what the product should refuse to absorb, since every absorbed request becomes a permanent configuration surface; the consumer critique concerns the first ninety seconds, where the promise is made or broken. The tell is vocabulary: "we are not going to be the place that stores that" against "show me the second screen a confused person reaches."

Configuration surfaces compound. Mistri's workflow builder costs 22 engineer-months to build, ₹57.2 lakh at ₹2.6 lakh an engineer-month. It then costs 1.5 engineer-months a quarter to maintain, ₹15.6 lakh a year, and generates support load across the other 37 accounts estimated at 2.4 tickets per account per month at ₹1,875 fully loaded, or ₹19.98 lakh a year. The tell is an expert asking for the third-year cost in the first meeting. Flexibility is not a gift; it is a tax collected in support tickets and paid by customers who never asked for it.

A judgement can be correct and unaffordable to act on. Mitali's 25-point faithfulness gap is the most serious finding in the Manzar file, and fixing it means retraining on a rebalanced corpus, a quarter of work. The expert separates "is this good" from "is this the decision available this quarter", and refuses to let the second corrupt the first. The tell is that verdict and recommendation are two sentences, not one.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The six questions are invariant; which answer carries the decision is not. Where there is no real difference it is worth saying so: the counterfactual split, ledger location and carrying cost apply everywhere, and practitioners who believe their category exempt are usually those who have never computed a third-year cost.

TypeWhere judgement concentratesCharacteristic errorHardest thing to see
ConsumerPromise, and the first ninety secondsBuying activation from conversionWhether the habit survives rewards
B2B and enterpriseWhat the product refuses to absorbServing the buyer, not the userCarrying cost of configuration
Platform, marketplaceWhich side is scarce this quarterSubsidising the abundant sideLiquidity composition
Hardware, physicalReversibility; cost of a field visitTreating firmware as softwareFailure modes seen only at scale
AI-nativeShape of the output distributionJudging a model from its best sampleTail behaviour, differential quality

Stage changes the owner rather than the method. In a company of twenty the founder's judgement is the product, and one person's blind spots become the product's. Between fifty and three hundred people the failure is inconsistency: ten teams making locally sensible calls that together feel like ten products, which is when a company first needs a named arbiter rather than a document. Past a thousand, experimentation absorbs the testable and judgement retreats to what to refuse and what to remove.

8. Three worked examples

A removal that worked. In March 2026 Manzar removed a collage tab used by 3.1 per cent of its 4,80,000 weekly active users — 14,880 people — to free one of five slots in the primary navigation. Of those collage users, 15.0 per cent, or 2,232 people, stopped using Manzar within sixty days. Against that, tap-through from the home screen into the editor rose 7.0 percentage points, which on 4,80,000 weekly actives is 33,600 additional editor sessions a week. A tab slot is the most expensive real estate in a consumer application, and 2,232 departures was a bounded price stated in advance, which is why it could be scored afterwards.

A test that bought a decision. Rather than trust his instinct, Nirav had Manjula run a fortnight of manual workaround with 160 technicians in Coimbatore, who recorded 4,800 jobs between them. Late records fell from 888 jobs, 18.5 per cent, to 336 jobs, 7.0 per cent — an 11.5-point improvement against the 12.5 points assumed. Applying 11.5 ÷ 12.5 to the ₹57 lakh annual capture gives ₹52.44 lakh a year, so the three-year benefit falls from ₹171.00 lakh to ₹157.32 lakh against a three-year cost of ₹39.00 lakh, a net of ₹118.32 lakh. He ran the test only because a result below about 4 points would have reversed him.

A taste call that failed, and the recovery. Navrasa Food Mills, a direct-to-consumer snacks brand, ran at ₹360 lakh of monthly revenue in 2025 when its founder, Nandish Thombre, withdrew the four-pack value bundle because discount formats cheapened a premium brand. The bundle accounted for ₹111.6 lakh, 31.0 per cent of monthly revenue, and he assumed most of that demand would migrate upward. Only 30 per cent did: ₹33.48 lakh moved to premium packs and ₹78.12 lakh disappeared, taking monthly revenue to ₹281.88 lakh, a fall of 21.7 per cent. His read on brand perception was defensible; the missing step was the counterfactual split. Recovery took five months: the format returned at a different price as a sharing pack, restoring ₹62.5 lakh, about 80 per cent of what was lost.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Metric purchased from downstreamOne rate jumps, the next sagsProduct of the stage ratios?A quarter of growth that reverses
Taste exported to a new domainVerdicts with no predictionWhen were you last wrong here?A build aimed at the wrong user
Loud-account captureRoadmap items named after customersHow many other accounts asked?A configuration surface held for years
Created read as capturedBenefit cases with no pricing pathWhose profit and loss is this?Renewal talks with no leverage
Distribution judged from a specimenDecks built on hand-picked outputsWhat does the worst fifth percentile do?Public quality failure after launch

The second row damages careers, because its warning sign is indistinguishable from competence at a distance. A practitioner right about consumer onboarding for six years sounds equally authoritative on technician dispatch, and nothing notices until a build has been spent.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a pre-registered refutation line should be binding. Malini holds that it must be, or the line is theatre. Nishad's steelman is serious: a line written on 5 September encodes only what was understood then, and new information arrived during the test — the activation gain was concentrated in first-time smartphone users, a segment Manzar has never served well and which monetises later. He rests on evidence that late-monetising cohorts exist and are valuable, and would be wrong if that segment's day-90 retention were no better than the arm average, measurable in January and not before.

Whether the loud account's churn risk recurs. Nirav treats the ₹1.05 crore of expected churn avoided — ₹4.2 crore of recurring revenue multiplied by the 25-point fall in churn probability, from 35 per cent to 10 per cent — as a one-renewal benefit, which makes the workflow builder a loss of ₹58.94 lakh over three years. Niyati's steelman is that an unserved request does not expire: Mandovi returns at every renewal with the same demand, so the benefit recurs and the three-year comparison becomes ₹315 lakh against ₹163.94 lakh of cost, a gain of ₹151.06 lakh that beats the offline mode's field-tested net of ₹118.32 lakh. She would be wrong if the builder, once shipped, failed to satisfy Mandovi's regions — a documented pattern, since configurable systems often expose the real disagreement rather than resolve it.

Whether taste transfers. The connoisseur school holds that judgement is domain-specific and cross-domain confidence the field's commonest error, resting on evidence that senior hires fail most often when they change category. Many general managers hold instead that what transfers is the method — the counterfactual split, the ledger question, the carrying-cost habit — and that the method is most of the value. Both cannot be right. The transfer position fails if method-carriers make worse first-year calls than domain insiders without it, and nobody has run that comparison.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces better-structured arguments. Someone who has internalised it differs in four observable ways. They state a verdict and a prediction in the same breath, so being wrong is cheap to discover. They ask for the third-year number before the build estimate. They separate, out loud, what they believe from what they can act on this quarter. And they keep a log of their own calls — Malini's records every default change since 2023 with the prediction and the outcome, which is why her ninety-second verdicts carry weight that Narendra's do not.

12. The decisions

On Thursday, 1 October 2026, Malini declined the default. She shipped Mukammal Portrait as a prominent one-tap option, preserving the authorship moment the subscription is sold on, and commissioned the rebalanced-corpus work to close Mitali's 25-point faithfulness gap, ahead of two revenue features. She conceded Nishad's point in falsifiable form: the first-time-smartphone cohort would be held in a separate treatment arm through January, and the decision revisited if its day-90 retention exceeded 60.0 per cent. Her written reason was the multiplication in Exhibit 3, and the observation that activation would have had to reach 52.5 per cent to break even.

On Monday, 5 October 2026, Nirav funded the offline mode for 9 engineer-months and declined the workflow builder, offering Mandovi three fixed job-stage templates configured by Mistri rather than by Mandovi, at no charge, with a joint review in January. He recorded his reasoning and Niyati's objection in one document, with the number that would settle it: two further accounts of comparable size raising the same demand before 31 January 2027 would reopen the builder.

Questions for discussion. First: Malini's refutation line was written on 5 September and the result fell two points below it. When is overriding your own pre-registered line good judgement rather than rationalisation, and who decides? Second: Mistri captures 24.2 per cent of the value the offline mode creates, while the builder defends a share of ₹4.2 crore it already has. Which number should govern the roadmap, and what does that imply about products whose best features are hardest to price? Third: Nandish Thombre's read on brand perception was probably correct, and the decision still cost 21.7 per cent of monthly revenue. What procedure catches that without blunting the judgement that made Navrasa distinctive?

13. Going deeper

Product deconstruction is the slow form of what taste does fast, and what you fall back on in an unfamiliar domain. Reasoning about trade-offs supplies the method for choices taste identifies but cannot settle, such as Malini's between activation and authorship. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill takes up what happens past a thousand people, when experimentation absorbs the testable. B2B versus B2C: the basic distinction explains why the faculty points towards restraint at Mistri and specificity at Manzar. First-principles reasoning rebuilds a judgement when pattern recognition has silently expired. Product critique makes taste transmissible rather than personal. Competitive teardown extends deconstruction to rivals, where the counterfactual is most often forgotten. Product vision and mission sets the standard for coherence. Product principles try to make one judgement reusable by many, and their failure modes explain why named arbiters outperform documents.
exp20v2-sense.taste:
Product sense and taste

Foundations: Product Thinking and Product Sense. Can I tell a good product decision from a bad one quickly, and say why?

1. A Tuesday review at Gharaunda

On Tuesday, 11 August 2026, Gayatri Venkataraman, Head of Product at Gharaunda Rent Network in Bengaluru, opened the weekly product review with a proposal she had not written and did not like. Gharaunda lets tenants pay monthly rent to their landlords by credit card or UPI, and issues the landlord a dated receipt. Founded in 2021, it had registered 2,40,000 tenants, of whom 48,000 paid rent through the app in a typical month, a monthly paying rate of 20 per cent. The chief executive, Govind Tendulkar, wanted a flat cashback of ₹200 on every rent payment for three months, starting on 1 September. Gayatri had until Friday, 14 August to say yes, no or something else.

The proposal had energy behind it. Established players such as CRED and NoBroker already offered rent payment by card, and Gagan Sethia, the growth lead in Jaipur, reported that two of every five July drop-outs named a rival's cashback. Ganga Pillai, the analyst in Chennai, had the economics in a spreadsheet. Fenil Ambekar, the designer in Pune, had sent a one-line message before the meeting: "It will work, and we will regret it."

Gayatri had formed a view in about ninety seconds, before opening the spreadsheet, and needed to know whether it was judgement or mood. If she was wrong, Gharaunda would hand tenants it had spent five years winning to rivals in the festival season. This page follows her through the decision and the skill she was exercising.

Exhibit 1. Gharaunda Rent Network, as of 11 August 2026
Registered tenants2,40,000
Tenants paying rent in a typical month48,000 (20 per cent of registered)
Average monthly rent paid₹25,000
Fee charged to the tenant1.2 per cent of rent = ₹300
Cost of the card and payment rails0.9 per cent of rent = ₹225
Proposal₹200 cashback on every payment, 1 September to 30 November 2026

Fee and rail cost are per payment. The difference, ₹75, is the contribution defined in Section 4.

2. The idea

Product sense is the ability to judge, quickly and with reasons, whether a product decision serves a real user and a viable business. Taste is the same ability applied to quality: a trained feel for which of two plausible options is better made, more coherent, or less likely to embarrass you in six months. They exist because decisions arrive faster than evidence: no team can run an experiment on every button, price and promotion, so someone decides on incomplete information.

The practice grew out of the design studios and consumer-software companies of the 1990s and 2000s, where product leaders argued that their main asset was a calibrated instinct. The modern teaching form is the teardown: a structured critique of a live product. The reader names the user, the job that user is hiring the product to do, the promise the product makes, the business model, the key metric, and the biggest assumption on which the whole arrangement rests.

Exhibit 2 shows why the exercise is useful. The first three boxes describe what the product does for a person; the last three, what it needs to stay alive. Weak decisions usually serve the first group while ignoring the second. The sentence Gayatri could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "Before we spend money, tell me what the customer is hiring us for, and what has to be true for them to keep hiring us after the money stops."

3. How it works in practice

Taste is fast, internalised deconstruction. A learner does the teardown slowly on paper; an experienced practitioner runs the same questions in seconds.

First, name the user and the job. Gayatri saw that the cashback spoke to a tenant wanting a reward, whereas Gharaunda's best tenants wanted a reliable receipt for house-rent allowance claims. Second, restate the promise in the user's words. Third, find the economic engine: what one transaction earns and costs. Fourth, and this is the step most often skipped, state the counterfactual: what would have happened without the change? A cashback is paid to everyone who qualifies, including those who would have paid anyway. Fifth, locate the biggest assumption; sixth, find the cheap evidence that tests it.

Applied to Gharaunda, the sequence gave her a view before the spreadsheet loaded. The economic engine was thin: a ₹300 fee against a ₹225 rail cost left ₹75 per payment. A ₹200 cashback was therefore more than two and a half times the contribution of the transaction it was meant to stimulate. That single comparison, ₹200 against ₹75, was what her ninety-second reaction had actually computed. Taste, in this sense, is pattern recognition over previous economics, launches and regrets.

4. A worked example, line by line

Ganga's spreadsheet formalised Gayatri's hunch. Contribution is the revenue a transaction earns minus the costs that rise with it: here, the fee minus the rail cost, or ₹300 minus ₹225, which is ₹75. The baseline is 48,000 payments a month at ₹75, which is ₹36,00,000, or ₹36 lakh. Gagan estimated that a blanket cashback would lift monthly payers from 48,000 to 60,000, an increase of 12,000. All figures below are in ₹ lakh per month.

LineWorking₹ lakh per month
A. Baseline contribution48,000 × ₹7536.0
B. Fee contribution during promotion60,000 × ₹7545.0
C. Cashback paid60,000 × ₹200120.0
D. Contribution during promotionB − C−75.0
E. Change against baselineD − A−111.0

The promotion would therefore cost ₹111 lakh against baseline in each of three months: ₹333 lakh in total, or ₹3.33 crore. Now the payback. Gagan assumed half of the 12,000 extra payers, 6,000 people, would remain after the cashback ended. Each earns ₹75 a month, so the gain is 6,000 × ₹75 = ₹4.5 lakh a month. Dividing ₹333 lakh by ₹4.5 lakh gives 74 months, more than six years, for a product that was five years old. The blanket proposal failed on arithmetic Gayatri could do aloud.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the cashback is paid once, only on the first payment of a tenant who has not paid through Gharaunda before, and the same 12,000 arrive. The cashback bill is 12,000 × ₹200 = ₹24 lakh. Those tenants also pay the fee in month one, 12,000 × ₹75 = ₹9 lakh, so the net in month one is −₹15 lakh. With 6,000 retained, each later month adds ₹4.5 lakh. The cumulative position runs as follows.

The position turns positive in the fifth month, four months after the first. Now change one more input: retention. If only a quarter of the 12,000 stay, that is 3,000 people earning 3,000 × ₹75 = ₹2.25 lakh a month. Recovering ₹15 lakh then takes 15 ÷ 2.25, about 6.7 further months, and the cumulative position first turns positive in the eighth month overall. That sensitivity, not the headline number, is what a reader should carry away.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Sense is not taste

Sense answers whether a decision is sound; taste answers whether it is well made. A cashback can be sound economics and still feel cheap to a premium user.

Taste is not preference

Taste in the working sense is liking that outcomes have corrected: the person has watched earlier judgements succeed or fail and adjusted.

Speed is earned, and it decays

Gayatri's ninety seconds rested on years of rent-payment economics. In a new domain, say lending, the same speed would be bluff. Outside familiar ground, run the teardown on paper.

It is routinely confused with a framework score

Prioritisation scores, such as ranking ideas by reach, impact and effort, are inputs to a conversation. A score cannot notice that the whole list is aimed at the wrong user.

The loudest voice is not evidence

The chief executive's conviction and a rival's visible cashback are both facts about the world, but neither is data about Gharaunda's tenants.

Taste cannot tell you what is unknown

No amount of skill reveals whether 6,000 of 12,000 will stay. It can tell you that retention is the lever and that the answer is cheap to test. A thoughtful newcomer should ask three questions before trusting a quick judgement: have I seen this kind of problem before, what would prove me wrong, and what does being wrong cost?

6. How it differs by product type and by stage

The six teardown questions stay constant, but the box that carries the weight moves. Gharaunda is a consumer product with a marketplace flavour, and Exhibit 6 sets the three families side by side.

Product typeWhere taste concentratesTypical trap
ConsumerThe promise and the first minute of experience; whether the habit forms without a rewardMistaking downloads or incentive-driven activity for love
B2BJob and buyer: the user, the approver and the payer are often three different peopleBuilding for the demo that wins the contract, not the Monday-morning user
MarketplaceThe business model and the side that is scarce; subsidising the wrong side fills the market with the wrong peoplePaying both sides and calling the volume liquidity

Exhibit 6. Where judgement concentrates, by product type.

Company size matters as much. In an early-stage company with a handful of customers, taste is exercised on a few decisions with little evidence, and the founder's instinct is the product. In a large company the volume of decisions is high, instinct is spread across many people, and the risk shifts to inconsistency: ten teams each making sensible choices that, together, produce a product that feels like ten products. At scale, taste becomes an editorial function: saying no and keeping the whole coherent, while experiments take over what can be tested.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom seen from outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Copying the competitorRoadmap mirrors a rival's launches with a lagAssuming the rival's economics and customers match yoursCompute the rival's feature at your own contribution per transaction
Confident vaguenessPraise or criticism with no reason attachedBelieving a strong feeling counts as judgementAsk for the user, the job and the assumption in one sentence each
Skipping the counterfactualCosts reported as gross, benefits as totalForgetting who would have acted anywaySplit the cohort into those who would have paid regardless and those who did not

Exhibit 7. Three mistakes and how to catch them.

The third is the most common and the hardest to see. In the blanket cashback, 48,000 of the 60,000 payers would have paid without any incentive, so 80 per cent of the cashback bill went to people it did not move: 48,000 × ₹200 = ₹96 lakh of the ₹120 lakh a month. The remaining ₹24 lakh bought the 12,000 people who actually changed behaviour.

8. What good looks like

A good version of Gayatri's Tuesday has four features. She states her reaction and labels it a hypothesis. She asks for the six boxes before the debate and lets Fenil, Gagan and Ganga each own one: Fenil the promise, Gagan the user, Ganga the economics. She separates what the data shows from what it cannot, and she proposes the cheapest test that would change the group's mind. The result is a one-page note naming the user, the job, the arithmetic and the single belief the decision depends on.

9. What Gayatri decided

On Friday, 14 August, she rejected the blanket cashback and proposed the targeted version: ₹200 once, on the first payment of tenants new to Gharaunda, from 1 September, with a pre-agreed rule. If after the first cohort retention proved below 25 per cent, which by the arithmetic of Section 4 pushes payback past six months, the offer would end. She also asked Fenil to make the receipt the headline of the product, since the best tenants valued it above any reward. Her reasoning in miniature: instinct was the start, arithmetic made it defensible, and the biggest assumption became the thing measured. Govind accepted, with visible reluctance, after seeing the ₹333 lakh figure.

The reader should go next to trade-off reasoning, because Gayatri's decision was in the end a choice between speed of growth and quality of customer, and a sound judgement needs a method for weighing such pairs. Then study editorial judgement: deciding what a product should refuse to do. Two questions to sit with: which decision did you make this month in under two minutes, and what evidence would have shown you wrong? And whose taste in your organisation has actually been corrected by outcomes, and how would you know?
case20v1-sense.taste:
Drishya Stores: The Grid and the Gallery

A decision case on product sense and taste

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Jaswant Namboodiri sat in Drishya Stores' office in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two screens open side by side. On the left was the home screen that eleven lakh monthly shoppers saw today. On the right were two redesigns that had just finished a fortnight of live testing. One had won on conversion. The other, he suspected, was the better product. He had until Monday, 19 October, to tell the engineers in Pune which of them to build for Diwali, which fell on Sunday, 8 November, and for the Dhanteras buying day two days before it.

Jaswant was Head of Product, and he trusted the numbers on his left screen less than he once had. They could say which redesign sold more in a fortnight. They could not say what kind of shop Drishya wanted to be.

2. Company background

Drishya Stores was founded in 2019 by Jishnu Nawathe, a former merchandiser at a large furniture chain, and sells home décor, lighting, kitchen and dining ware, small furniture and festive gifting through an app and a mobile site. It lists about 3,000 products from craft and small-brand suppliers in Jaipur, Moradabad, Channapatna and Kutch. Annual gross merchandise is about ₹160 crore.

The market around it is crowded. Pepperfry and Urban Ladder, now part of Reliance Retail, own the large-furniture end. IKEA has stores in Mumbai and Hyderabad. Amazon and Flipkart sell a vast, cheap range of décor, and Meesho sells cheaper still. Drishya's answer has always been that its shoppers, mostly in the metros and in cities such as Indore, Coimbatore and Lucknow, want fewer, better things and will pay for them. Payments run through UPI and Razorpay.

3. The situation

For two years Drishya's home screen had been a curated shelf of eight picks. In August, Jerin Nagpal, the Growth head, argued that competitors won with density and urgency. Design and Product therefore built two alternatives, and from 31 August to 13 September each ran against the existing screen for a fortnight, each on 1,20,000 sessions. Exhibit 1 sets out the results, and Exhibit 2 charts revenue per 1,000 sessions.

Read quickly, the tests pointed in two directions. Variant B lifted conversion from 3.0 to 3.4 per cent, a 13 per cent improvement on the existing screen, yet it cut the order value, unsettled buyers (returns rose from 8 to 13 per cent) and left only 9 per cent of buyers ordering again, against 14 per cent. Per thousand sessions it earned ₹1,000 less than A. Variant C converted worse, at 2.8 per cent, but its buyers spent ₹1,820 an order, returned less and came back more. It earned about 17 per cent more per session than A.

The overseas team saw it differently from their time zones. Janhvi Nagwekar, the design lead, wrote from Amsterdam, three and a half hours behind Bengaluru, that B's countdown timers and "only 3 left" labels were risky, since the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 dark-patterns guidelines list false urgency. Jerin, in Gurugram, replied that Diwali was no time for a museum.

4. The people

Jaswant Namboodiri, Head of Product, Bengaluru, owns the decision and answers to the founder. Jishnu Nawathe, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru, wants a Diwali that justifies the next fundraise, and cares about the brand as much as the quarter. Jerin Nagpal, Head of Growth, Gurugram, is measured on conversion and cost of acquisition, and points out that every paid install in October costs ₹180 or more. Janhvi Nagwekar, Design Lead, Amsterdam, wants a shop with a point of view, and admires how Nykaa and Lenskart look like themselves. Engineering in Pune needs a decision by Monday to meet the code freeze on 26 October.

5. What the exhibits do not say

Jaswant took the two redesigns apart before arguing about them. Exhibit 3 is the teardown he wrote on his phone on the way home: B serves a bargain-hunter and bets that urgency does not damage trust, while C serves someone furnishing a home and bets that she will browse long enough to be persuaded.

The catch was supply. Studio-grade photography existed for only 1,200 of the 3,000 products, so Variant C had been tested on Drishya's best-presented range, which probably also carried its best-selling lines. Exhibit 4 shows where the pictures were thin. Kitchen and dining was the least ready at 15 per cent. Jaswant could not tell how much of C's higher order value came from the design and how much from the products it was allowed to show.

6. The options

Option 1: ship Variant B across the app. Conversion rises 13 per cent, and the build is nearly done. The costs are an order value ₹200 lower, more returns, thinner repeat, and exposure to the dark-patterns guidelines, because the timers and scarcity labels would need to be true to survive scrutiny.

Option 2: commission full editorial photography and ship Variant C everywhere. The upside is a distinctive shop. The cost is ₹19.8 lakh, being the 1,800 products still unshot at ₹1,100 each, and time: two studios shoot 60 products a day, so the work takes 30 shoot days, and only 18 days remain between 19 October and Dhanteras.

Option 3: ship a hybrid. The editorial gallery would lead the home screen for the 1,200 ready products, followed by a plain grid for the rest with no invented urgency, and the shoot would continue category by category from kitchen and dining. It needs about a week of engineering and a ten per cent holdback on the old screen. Its cost is a compromise, and the lift is unproven, since the test did not run this mix.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 3, who is each variant's user and what is its biggest assumption? Which assumption would you most want to test before Diwali?

2. Variant B wins on conversion yet earns less per session than the existing screen. Which metric should Drishya use to judge a home screen, and why?

3. How far does Exhibit 4 weaken the evidence for Variant C, and what could Jaswant check quickly to separate design from product mix?

4. Which option would you take to the 19 October meeting, and what would make you change your mind before the 26 October freeze?

8. A note for the learner

Product sense is the ability to look at a decision and say, quickly and with reasons, whether it is good. Taste is the same skill after enough practice: deconstruction so internalised that it feels like instinct. A reader with sense does not stop at conversion. The better question is who the product is for and what promise it makes, then which numbers fit that promise. On those terms C earns more per session and keeps more customers, which fits the promise the brand has built.

A well-reasoned answer also respects what the evidence cannot show. C was tested on the best-photographed products, so its lead may be inflated, and no one tested a mix. That argues against Option 1, which sacrifices order value and trust for a conversion lift, and against Option 2, which cannot be completed in time and puts ₹19.8 lakh behind an untested claim.

One defensible path is Option 3. Lead with the gallery where the pictures are good, keep the rest of the screen honest and plain, retain a holdback, and let the shoot proceed from the least-ready category. If the holdback shows the hybrid earning less per session than the old screen by the Dhanteras weekend, fall back to Variant A. The decision stays reversible, protects the brand and gives the team a real measurement for January.
case40v1-sense.taste:
Nukta: The Silent Ledger

An ambiguous case on product sense and taste

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Tavleen Cariappa was still at her desk in Nukta's Bengaluru office, looking at two versions of one GST return for a Nagpur hardware shop. In the first, each of 214 classified line items carried a grey tick the shop's owner had tapped before signing. In the second, the same 214 lines carried no ticks. The software had decided, filed, and told nobody.

Tavleen was Vice-President of Product. At four the next afternoon a product council would convene across five time zones — Austin, Lisbon, Kraków, Melbourne and Bengaluru — to settle what Nukta would build. On Thursday 22 October the board would ask the same question in Pune, in blunter terms. The evidence was not thin; it pointed in two directions at once.

2. Nukta

Nukta Books Private Limited was founded in Pune in 2019 by Tathagata Chirmule, who had sold software to Maharashtra's pipe distributors and concluded that small businesses did not want accounting software. They wanted to not be fined. Nukta Books was a ledger and a GST filing tool with the accounting hidden behind it, and it grew through chartered accountants. Underneath sat Nakalbandi, a rules engine that coded each line by what that customer had called the item before: it covered only what it had seen, and never surprised anyone.

The decision that still constrains Nukta came in March 2021. In the January filing season a mapping update silently re-coded a class of freight charges, and ninety-one customers filed returns they had not meant to file. Tathagata's answer was a commitment printed in every contract since, Signed Is Sealed: once a customer signs a return, Nukta will never alter a posted line without showing the change and taking a fresh signature. It won the CA channel — 2,900 firms on 18 per cent of first-year fees, which introduced 20,020 of the 38,500 Books Pro customers, or 52 per cent. It also means a later correction is a conversation, not a script.

In January 2024 Nukta launched Nukta Hub for groups whose accounts-payable teams process invoices from hundreds of Indian suppliers. Exhibit 1 shows where the money comes from.

3. The industry

Nukta competes in one of India's most crowded markets. Tally Solutions is the installed habit of lakhs of accountants, Zoho Books sells a broader suite cheaper, ClearTax owns the compliance end, Vyapar and Khatabook own the phone-first micro-merchant, and Razorpay and PhonePe keep books as a side effect of payments. Above them sits the GST Network: every portal improvement removes a reason to pay for filing.

The ground moves too. E-invoicing thresholds have fallen year by year, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs issues clarifications that change how a line should be coded, and a GSTN schema revision lands on 1 January 2027. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 bears on Nukta's machine learning, whose training set is customers' own invoice lines: of 1,42,000 Books Starter customers, 44,020 — 31.0 per cent — accepted terms predating the July 2025 model-training clause.

Nukta's exposure beyond India runs through Hub. Its largest customer, Noorani Industries, is a Muscat trading and manufacturing group with four Indian subsidiaries and an accounts-payable hub of 38 clerks handling about 40,000 Indian supplier invoices a month. Its controller is measured on cost per invoice and audit findings, and did not buy software to employ people to check it.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

In February 2026 Tadeusz Ciesielski's team in Kraków finished Nishaan, a classifier trained on 9.4 crore lines of Nukta data. On a held-out set of 2,40,000 lines it classified 99.0 per cent correctly. That number went into the board pack, Tamal's deck and a press note.

From 1 June to 31 August 2026 Nukta ran a three-arm pilot across 1,800 businesses, 600 in each arm. Mode A was the status quo: Nakalbandi only, every unmatched line pushed to the user. Mode B had Nishaan propose a code for every line, reasoning shown, and the user confirm. Mode C had Nishaan classify and file, with a monthly digest. Exhibit 2 records the effort.

Through the pilot Mode C looked like a triumph. Then in September Tashi Chomal's support team in Coimbatore noticed something odd in the ticket pattern, and on 7 September Tavleen commissioned a re-audit of 4,000 of the 12,000 invoices in each arm. Exhibit 3 is its finding. Tashi's own view was that two chartered accountants would code a mixed consignment two ways anyway.

Exhibit 4 draws the two readings side by side; Exhibit 5 holds a second surprise. What had turned out to be wrong was the 99.0 per cent. Nishaan is excellent on the head of the distribution — the forty commonest HSN codes — and poor on the long tail. The held-out set was 96.5 per cent head lines; live traffic is 78.0 per cent. Neither was dishonest: they measured different populations, and the press note quoted the easier. Tadeusz's own note was precise and unhelpful — the model had not degraded, the evaluation had.

Read one way, Exhibit 6 vindicates Mode C: 89.1 per cent retention against Mode A's 85.4, and less than half the tickets. Read another way it is the most alarming page in the pack. The segment that retains best never opens the digest and has the worst error rate; the one that reads what the machine did is the one that leaves. The errors clustered: 211 of the 600 Mode C businesses carried one, and 24 of those — 11.4 per cent — raised a ticket. Nobody can say what the other 187 believe.

5. The people

Tavleen Cariappa, VP Product, Bengaluru, believes the pilot measured effort well and trust not at all. She is not saying she pushed Mode C into it over Teertha's objection, so her credibility rides on the worst-looking arm.

Tathagata Chirmule, co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune, wrote Signed Is Sealed and quotes it often. He wants a Series C in 2027 and knows investors ask about automation rate. He is not saying he has asked whether the digest could be made more prominent without being more honest.

Teertha Chinchalkar, Head of Tax Practice, Mumbai, a chartered accountant, holds that a return is a declaration signed by a person, and software that files unsigned has mistaken a convenience for a right. She is not saying her channel firms bill for the work Mode C removes.

Tabassum Chhatwal, Design Director, Lisbon, argues the question is wrong: she wants to know what a customer sees the moment the machine errs, and no option changes that. She is not saying she has a prototype nobody has seen, because it tests badly on every pilot metric.

Tadeusz Ciesielski, Principal Data Scientist, Kraków, built Nishaan and reported the mix problem himself. He wants long-tail lines labelled and estimates tail error could fall from 12.0 to about 5 per cent in two quarters. He is not saying that budget is unapproved.

Tanya Coutinho, Customer Success, Melbourne, produced Exhibit 6 and reads it as a warning: her renewals improve under Mode C, which is what worries her. She is not saying her bonus tracks net revenue retention.

Tamal Chundawat, Enterprise Sales, Austin, carries Noorani and eleven Hub prospects, all shown the 99.0 per cent figure. He argues the error is under one per cent of invoice value and Hub buyers can sample. He is not saying his largest prospect has asked for the pilot data.

6. Voices

"Three point one per cent of lines. Six point two of the tax. Nought point nine of the value. Pick whichever suits you and we can go home."

— Teertha Chinchalkar, product council, 8 October 2026

"Ninety-four per cent retention in micro is the best this company has produced, and it came from the arm you call a failure."

— Tadeusz Ciesielski, same meeting

"It came from the arm where nine per cent opened the digest. We did not retain them. We anaesthetised them."

— Tanya Coutinho, in reply

"Controller's words: 'I am not paying four crore so my clerks can read your suggestions.' Ship confirmation to Hub and we tell him the product got worse. He has a December termination right."

— Tamal Chundawat, email to Tavleen and Tathagata, 9 October 2026

"We argue about how much the machine should decide. Nobody has said what the screen reads when it is wrong. In Mode B it says 'check this' on every line, including the 77,376 it gets right — which is why people hate it and trust it. In Mode C it says nothing. Those are not two points on one dial."

— Tabassum Chhatwal, team chat, 11 October 2026, 13:40 Lisbon

7. The options as Tavleen sees them

Of the two options clearing Noorani's 92 per cent service level, Option 1 is the cheaper and the earlier. It also files 3.1 per cent of lines wrongly without telling anyone, in a company whose best-known sentence is about telling people. Option 4 defers and leaves the 99.0 per cent figure standing in eleven sales conversations.

Option 2 carries the strongest satisfaction and retention figures, 4.4 out of 5 and 91.6 per cent. At 71 per cent straight-through it breaches the Noorani service level at once, exposing ₹15.96 lakh of credits a quarter, ₹63.84 lakh a year, and hands the controller his December notice.

Option 3 is what everyone expects her to choose, and does not fit: 86 engineer-weeks against 81 available, shipping 23 February, eight weeks after the schema change it would be rebuilt around. It also makes Nukta say in public that Hub customers get what Books customers are spared.

Tribhuvan Chettiar, Director of Engineering in Pune, wrote Exhibit 7. What he is not saying is that his team has already built two-thirds of Mode C, and discarding it would be the third such reversal this year. He has also priced the compromise nobody asked for: automate the head, confirm the tail. Assuming lines fall independently and each invoice carries the average 6.5 lines, the share with no tail line is 0.78 to the power 6.5, about 20 per cent — worse than Mode A's 38 per cent. The elegant answer is arithmetically dead, and the independence assumption is untested.

Tabassum's objection, which Tavleen cannot dismiss, is that all four rows vary one quantity — how much the machine decides — and none varies what the customer is told. No option shows a customer, once a quarter, the three lines most likely to be wrong. That product is neither tested nor costed.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

Exhibit 8 sets out the Noorani contract clock and Exhibit 9 draws it to scale.

The council meets at four on Thursday 15 October, the board on 22 October. The GSTN revision of 1 January 2027 cannot be deferred. Nukta holds ₹61 crore and has burned ₹2.40 crore a month over the last six months, a runway of 25.4 months, so no option is forced by money — which Tavleen finds makes it harder. The DPDP consent gap covers 44,020 Starter customers. Signed Is Sealed sits in every Books Pro and Hub contract, so reclassifying the 2,418 pilot errors is not a migration script but 211 phone calls. The ₹37.83 lakh falls on the 211 affected businesses, ₹17,929 each, carrying about ₹2,958 of interest at 18 per cent over the eleven months to reconciliation; one business's single line carried ₹2.14 lakh of tax.

One figure Tamal has used twice in writing deserves a second look. Against Mode A, Mode C saves Noorani's hub 2,400 bookkeeper hours a month: at a fully loaded ₹760 an hour in Muscat, ₹18.24 lakh a month, ₹2.19 crore a year. Against Mode B — the only alternative on the table — it saves 1,133 hours, ₹8.61 lakh, ₹1.03 crore a year. Either way the fee is ₹4.26 crore.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibits 2 and 3, state each mode's user, job, promise, business model, key metric and biggest assumption. Which is least tested?
  2. Exhibit 3 states one error on three bases. Which should the board see, and which a Books Starter customer? Defend the possibility that they differ.
  3. Exhibit 5 shows a classifier whose per-population accuracy never changed. What should Nukta have measured in February 2026, and what follows for every future model?
  4. Micro firms are 53.0 per cent of the Mode C arm and 78.7 per cent of the paying base. Re-weight the error rate to the base. Does that change the option you prefer, or what you say to Noorani?
  5. Tanya and Tadeusz read the same three rows and conclude the opposite. Build the strongest version of each. What evidence, obtainable before 22 October, separates them?
  6. Tabassum argues Exhibit 7 varies the wrong quantity, so the real choice is what the product promises. What should Tavleen do on Monday 19 October, what should she say to the board, and what must she be willing to be wrong about in public to say it?

10. Still Wednesday night

Tavleen closed the Nagpur return and opened it again. In the Mode C version of Tamanna Chipalkatti's July filing the software had moved a consignment of brass fittings into a code three percentage points lower than the one she had used for four years, filed it, and been right — the re-audit confirmed it. Tamanna never knew. In the Mode B version she would have spent about ninety-five minutes confirming 214 lines, 167 of them in the forty commonest codes, learning only that the machine wanted checking.

Both versions were on the screen. One was the product Nukta had promised to be, and Tavleen could no longer say which — or whether the question was hers rather than Tamanna's.
case40v1-sense.vision:
Sookshma Labs: Three Sentences and One Report

An ambiguous Indian-context case on product vision and mission

1. The night before

At twenty minutes to midnight on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Chaula Hattangadi was still at the dining table of her flat in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with three slides open and the rest of the deck finished. The board of Sookshma Labs met at ten the next morning. Item four read: Approve the five-year product vision and the FY28–FY32 plan. Everything else on the agenda would take twenty minutes.

Chaula had been vice-president of product for nineteen months. In July, Shatadru Partners had issued a term sheet for a Series C of ₹340 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹2,480 crore, conditional on a board-approved vision and five-year plan. It expired on Friday, 30 October. The valuation was 38.8 times the ₹63.87 crore the company expected to earn in the year to 31 March 2027.

Each slide carried one sentence, and each described a different company: a different customer, rival, regulator and bill. What she could not settle was whether they were alternatives at all, or three ways of distributing one asset: a pathology report, 1.92 crore of them in the database, keyed to the wrong thing.

2. How Sookshma Labs came to be shaped this way

Cyrus Hathiramani and Chidanand Huddar founded Sookshma Labs in Hyderabad in June 2017; neither was a doctor. The first product, sold to eleven pathology labs in 2018, was a billing and accession module.

In February 2019 the founders made the decision that still governs what is possible. Building out the lab information system — named Shilalekh, the inscription — they chose to key every report to the lab's accession number and leave patient identity with the lab. The minutes record two reasons: the labs insisted the patient was theirs, and central identity would make Sookshma a data fiduciary, with consent machinery it could not then build. The consequence is that Shilalekh holds a history of accessions, not of people: 1.92 crore reports as at 31 March 2026 that cannot be assembled into an individual's record without re-keying, one at a time, against an identity the company does not hold.

Home collection, launched as Sookshma Collect in August 2020, became the business. In October 2021 the company licensed Shilalekh to Sidrah Medical Trust, a hospital group in Doha, for ₹52 lakh a month to 31 March 2028, with Gulf exclusivity as part of the price: no consumer-branded Sookshma product there until then. A Series B of ₹118 crore followed in March 2022, led by Shatadru Partners. Sookshma Pass, a consumer subscription at ₹750 a year including two tests, opened in April 2024.

3. The industry around it

Indian diagnostics is large and barely consolidated; trade estimates put it near ₹90,000 crore a year, with the organised chains holding under a fifth. Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis Healthcare, Thyrocare and Redcliffe Labs compete on brand and price per panel; Tata 1mg and PharmEasy sell tests to consumers online. None is Sookshma's customer; some are its competitors in two businesses at once.

Accreditation by NABL remains the signal that lets a small lab win corporate work. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, with ABHA identifiers and the National Health Authority's health-information-provider framework, has made a patient-held record the policy default; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 then fixed the price of holding health data: consent, purpose limitation, an auditable trail. Tax sharpens an asymmetry — diagnostic services are exempt from GST, while the software Sookshma sells the same labs is taxed at 18 per cent.

Abroad, the Doha licence is the company's only revenue. Its team is not: engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, design in Melbourne (five and a half hours ahead of Hyderabad in October), data science in Montreal (nine and a half behind), customer success in Kuala Lumpur (two and a half ahead), sales in Chicago (ten and a half behind). A data scientist in Montreal costs ₹1.42 crore a year fully loaded against ₹41 lakh for the equivalent grade in Bengaluru, a ratio of 3.5 to one.

4. The situation in detail

Four things the company believed have since proved wrong. In 2019 it believed labs would never permit patient-held identity; by September 2026, 450 of its 1,450 partner labs — 31 per cent — had asked for an ABHA-linked view. That constraint has loosened; the 1.92 crore legacy reports have not. In 2022 it believed Collect's economics would improve with density; Exhibit 3 shows Hyderabad at 25 per cent contribution on fee revenue and Patna at minus 13 per cent. In April 2024 it believed Pass would renew at two-thirds: the first cohort did, at 68 per cent, and Exhibit 4 shows every cohort since. In 2021 it believed Doha was a beachhead for international software; it is instead ₹624 lakh a year at a 66 per cent contribution margin and 11.9 per cent of revenue (Exhibits 1 and 2), and a veto over one of the three sentences.

On 14 July 2026 Shatadru Partners issued the term sheet, naming a board-approved vision as a condition. In August Chhaya Hukkeri circulated her memorandum. On Friday, 18 September, Corinne Hebert circulated a cohort analysis the chief executive described in writing as "unhelpful". On 26 September the strategy team produced Exhibit 5; on 2 October Chloe Hwang reported a corridor conversation in Doha.

5. The people

Cyrus Hathiramani, co-founder and chief executive, Hyderabad, wants the consumer record: 38.8 times forward revenue, he argues, prices a consumer franchise, not a lab vendor. Unsaid: he has already described the consumer path to Shatadru's investment committee, in a meeting with no minutes.

Chidanand Huddar, co-founder and head of the lab network, Pune, wants the lab-software sentence. The 1,450 partner labs are largely his relationships, and the day Sookshma brands a patient's record it competes with its customers. Unsaid: two buyers have approached him about acquiring Sookshma Panel as a standalone business.

Chhaya Hukkeri, chief financial officer, wrote the August memorandum and wants Collect shrunk to Hyderabad, Pune and Jaipur. Unsaid: her FY27 variable pay is set against a contribution target that exiting Patna, Indore and Kochi would deliver by subtraction.

Chellam Honnavar, engineering director, Bengaluru, owns Shilalekh and wrote the 2019 data model. He has estimated the re-keying of 1.92 crore reports at fourteen months and wants the work. Unsaid: the binding path in Exhibit 6 is not his but the eighteen months of legal re-contracting with 1,450 labs.

Corinne Hebert, principal data scientist, Montreal, built the dashboard that reported 68 per cent and now holds that it describes one cohort of 6,800 members and nothing else. Inside the Q1 FY26 cohort she finds direct joins renewing at 63 per cent against 37 per cent for the Sanjeevani Stores channel at ₹499. Unsaid: how thin that is — one quarter, and publishing it discredits her dashboard.

Charanjit Hayer, head of enterprise sales, Chicago, sells insurers and employer-health buyers who pay for verified records, and quotes 68 per cent renewal in every deck. Unsaid: his largest proposal describes a patient-level longitudinal record as an existing capability.

Chloe Hwang, customer success lead, Kuala Lumpur, owns the Sidrah account and wants the vision to say nothing that threatens it. On 2 October a Sidrah administrator told her, in a car park, that the Trust would not renew beyond 31 March 2028 if Sookshma launched a consumer brand. Notice falls due 30 September 2027; she has nothing in writing.

Clara Hewson, design lead, Melbourne, built the Pass app and has torn down all three sentences against the same six questions — user, job, promise, business model, key metric, biggest assumption — concluding that each names a channel, not a changed world. Unsaid: her team has already shipped, behind a flag, a screen showing a patient's previous three results for 240 members in Hyderabad.

7. Voices

"Thirty-eight times forward revenue is not a price for accession software sold to 1,450 labs. It prices the record. Write the smaller sentence and the round comes in at a number that makes it true."

— Cyrus Hathiramani, strategy review, 29 September

"I have asked four times which business earns more per rupee employed and had two answers from one finance team: one divides by what we earn, the other by what the patient pays the lab."

— Chokila Hangshing, independent director, to the audit committee, 6 October

"Sixty-eight per cent is one cohort of 6,800 people from 2024. The five that have completed a year blend to 52 per cent and fall in a straight line. I can tell you two stories about why, not which is true."

— Corinne Hebert, memorandum, 18 September

"Patna loses ₹42 lakh a year and has 14,700 Pass members. Chhaya reads a city to exit; I read the one place where people pay in advance because nobody else will hold their results."

— Clara Hewson, chat thread, 7 October, 03:40 IST

"Every buyer asks the same thing: show me this patient's last three years. If Monday's answer is that we will never hold a person's record, I will stop selling to insurers."

— Charanjit Hayer, sales forecast call, 8 October

8. The options as Chaula sees them tonight

A. Every pathology lab in India runs on one system. The customer is the lab owner, the promise that a small lab competes with a chain, the metric labs on Panel. Exhibit 2 gives it the best margin in the company, 75 per cent; Exhibit 5 the most FY32 contribution, ₹116.09 crore, on the least capital, ₹210 crore, which the round covers. Against it: at FY26 pricing the whole addressable base of about 30,000 labs is worth ₹90 crore a year, and Sookshma has 1,450 of them, or 4.8 per cent. Option A's FY32 revenue of ₹187.24 crore is 2.1 times that ceiling, reached by assuming the price per lab rises 5.4-fold. Nobody noticed the assumption on 26 September.

B. Any test, at any door, in any city. The customer is the household, the promise reach, the metric samples. It is what the company does best and what Exhibit 3 says it does worst outside Hyderabad, Pune and Jaipur. It needs ₹620 crore, 1.8 times the round, and about 16,400 phlebotomists on third-party rolls. Its FY32 contribution, ₹46.82 crore, is the lowest of the three on the second-highest revenue.

C. Every Indian carries their own results. The customer is the patient, the promise a history that travels, the metric records under consent. It is the only sentence that explains Patna, the only one Charanjit Hayer can sell to an insurer, and the only one requiring the 2019 decision to be unwound: ₹28.90 crore and an earliest ship of April 2028, which is FY29, while Exhibit 5 books ₹88.14 crore of Option C revenue in FY28. It needs ₹480 crore against the ₹340 crore round, is forbidden in the Gulf until 31 March 2028, and may cost the ₹624 lakh Doha licence the moment the intention is declared.

What Chaula wrote in her notebook and did not put on a slide was that A, B and C distribute one thing the company already owns, and that none says what should be different for the person whose blood was drawn.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday, 12 October. The Shatadru term sheet lapses on Friday, 30 October, and the firm's two nominees sit on the board that approves the vision it requires. At 30 September 2026 the company held ₹96 crore of cash against a net burn of ₹4.9 crore a month: 19.6 months, to about May 2028, one month after Option C could first ship. The Doha licence runs to 31 March 2028, with notice due 30 September 2027 and Gulf exclusivity until it ends. Nothing in Exhibit 5 funds Exhibit 6, and the DPDP Act's consent obligations attach the day Sookshma holds identity, not the day it launches. Whichever sentence is chosen, Cyrus Hathiramani has promised to read it aloud to all 1,240 employees on the morning of Diwali, 8 November.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, who is Sookshma's customer and what job is it paid for? Does the answer change on the network-value base rather than the revenue base?
  2. Exhibit 4 can be read as a product failing or a channel diluting. Which does the evidence support, and what one piece of data, obtainable before 30 October, would separate them?
  3. Patna is last on contribution and first on Pass density. Write the sentence that makes it strategic and the one that makes it an exit, naming the column each needs.
  4. For each option in Exhibit 5: who wins, what is different in the world, what must the company refuse? Which can reject a feature request on a Tuesday?
  5. Option A's FY32 revenue is 2.1 times the addressable market at today's prices, and Option C books FY28 revenue from a product that cannot ship before FY29. What should a board do with a plan holding both?
  6. You are Chaula Hattangadi at midnight. What do you do on Monday morning — which sentence, which exhibits, which omissions — and what do you say to the board about the one thing you are least sure of?

At a quarter past midnight she closed the laptop, the three slides still in the deck. The last thing she had done was open the screen Clara Hewson's team had built by hand for 240 members in Hyderabad, which showed a woman in Kukatpally her last three haemoglobin results in one place, and look for a number in the exhibits that said whether it mattered. There wasn't one.
exp20v2-sense.vision:
Product Vision and Mission

If this product succeeds completely, what is different in the world?

1. A Monday in March

On Monday 16 March 2026, Tanuja Bhalerao, head of product at Darpan Eye Care Network, was handed a deadline. Darpan, founded in Pune in 2021 by Ketan Wadkar, placed small screening kiosks in pharmacies and grain markets in towns of ten to forty thousand people. A technician photographed the eye, measured visual acuity (how small a line of letters the patient can read), and sent the results to a remote optometrist in Bengaluru, who cleared the patient or flagged a need for glasses or referral. The company had 212 kiosks in nine states. Its Series B pitch to investors was set for Monday 6 April, seeking ₹60 crore, and the board wanted a single paragraph at the top of the pitch saying what Darpan was for. Wadkar had given Bhalerao until Friday 27 March, eleven days, to produce it.

Praveen Cherian, the engineering lead in Bengaluru, had two quarters of roadmap that could go opposite ways: more kiosks, or a follow-up service that chased flagged patients until they had glasses. Elin Sorensen, an optometry researcher in Stockholm advising on the screening protocol, had warned that Darpan was good at finding people and poor at helping them. A vision rewarding the first would starve the second, and the pitch would lock the choice in for two years.

Exhibit 1. Darpan Eye Care Network, operating position, February 2026
ItemValue
Kiosks in operation212
Screenings per month38,000
Share of screenings flagged for glasses or referral21 per cent
Flagged patients who complete follow-up (glasses bought or treatment booked)30 per cent
Monthly operating cost of the whole network₹96 lakh
Capital cost of one new kiosk₹3.5 lakh

Wadkar's draft read: "To be India's largest eye-care network." Bhalerao suspected it said nothing about whom Darpan helped. This page follows her work to build one argument: a vision is a claim about a changed world, useful only if it forces a choice between two things you could build next.

2. The idea

A vision is a description of the world as it will be if the product succeeds completely. It names the people who are better off and says what has changed for them. A mission is the present-tense commitment: what the organisation does each day, for whom, to move toward that world. A strategy (the set of choices about where to compete and how to win) and a roadmap (the ordered list of things to build) come beneath both.

Peter Drucker's 1954 book The Practice of Management asked managers to answer "What is our business?" as the first duty of leadership. James Collins and Jerry Porras, in a 1996 Harvard Business Review article, "Building Your Company's Vision", separated a durable core ideology from an "envisioned future" with a vivid description of what achieving it would look like. Product teams borrowed the idea because, with many reasonable things to build and no shared destination, every argument becomes an argument about taste.

In Exhibit 2 each rung constrains the one below: a roadmap item is justified by a strategy, a strategy by a mission, a mission by a vision. When the top rung is vague, nothing below can be tested against it. Darpan's roadmap debate had stalled for exactly that reason.

The sentence Bhalerao could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "A vision tells us who is better off, how we would know, and what we would refuse to build."

3. How it actually works

Bhalerao worked through five steps, the first of which practitioners often skip. First, she chose a beneficiary: not "Indians" or "patients" but a specific person in a specific place. Her choice was an adult in a town of ten to forty thousand, who until now had to travel to a district hospital for an eye test and often did not go. Second, she wrote the before-and-after state in that person's terms. Before: the person endures blurred reading, delays for a year, and may lose work. After: the person is tested nearby and leaves with what the test showed was needed.

Third, she chose a unit of change: one countable event that proves the after-state has arrived for one person. Screenings were the easy unit, but a screening only shows that a person was looked at. The after-state required the person to have glasses or a treatment booked, so the unit became a completed follow-up.

Fourth came the refusal test: list three things the vision would let the company decline. A vision that cannot say no is decoration. Fifth, she derived the mission, the present-tense commitment that makes the vision reachable: screen people close to home, and stay with them until the problem is dealt with.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Bhalerao tested the unit of change against Exhibit 1. Each month, 38,000 screenings at a 21 per cent flag rate produced 38,000 × 0.21 = 7,980 flagged patients. At a 30 per cent follow-up rate, 7,980 × 0.30 = 2,394 patients reached the after-state. The monthly cost of ₹96 lakh (₹96,00,000) divided by 2,394 gives ₹4,010 per completed outcome, against ₹253 per screening (₹96,00,000 ÷ 38,000 = ₹252.63). A screening counts the people Darpan looked at; the completed outcome counts the people whose lives changed, and the second figure is about sixteen times the first in cost.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose Darpan raised follow-up completion from 30 to 45 per cent by calling flagged patients and partnering with local optical shops, at an added ₹12 lakh a month. Then 7,980 × 0.45 = 3,591 outcomes, at a monthly cost of ₹108 lakh, or ₹3,008 each. Suppose instead it doubled kiosks to 424, keeping 30 per cent completion: 76,000 screenings, 15,960 flagged, 4,788 outcomes, at ₹192 lakh a month, or ₹4,010 each, plus ₹742 lakh of capital (212 × ₹3.5 lakh).

Exhibit 4. Three ways to move the unit of change (all rupee figures in ₹ lakh except cost per outcome, in ₹)
TodayCompletion to 45%Kiosks doubled
Kiosks212212424
Screenings per month38,00038,00076,000
Flagged at 21%7,9807,98015,960
Follow-up completion30%45%30%
Completed outcomes per month2,3943,5914,788
Monthly operating cost (₹ lakh)96108192
