Cost per completed outcome (₹)4,0103,0084,010

Doubling kiosks doubles outcomes but leaves cost per outcome unchanged at ₹4,010. Lifting completion adds 1,197 outcomes a month for ₹12 lakh, or about ₹1,003 each, and cuts cost per outcome by about 25 per cent. The vision decides which line the roadmap follows.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Vision is not mission

A mission describes what you do now; a vision describes a condition of the world that may take a decade. "Screen eyes in small towns" is a mission. It says nothing about what happens afterwards.

Vision is not strategy

A vision names the destination, not the route. A statement containing "through partnerships" has started to describe how, and teams defend the how long after it stops working.

Vision is not a metric or a goal

A goal such as "500 kiosks by March 2027" can be met without the world changing. A metric is only the vision's measuring stick.

Aspiration is not forecast

"If this succeeds completely" invites a bold picture, yet it must stay coherent. A vision demanding that every Indian be tested within a day of need is merely unfalsifiable: no plausible evidence would count against it.

The winner and the payer may differ

Darpan's patients pay for glasses but not for screening; employers and pharmacies pay for part of the network. A vision should name who wins, even when someone else writes the cheque, or the product will drift toward whoever pays.

A vision must be able to lose

Ask what observation would show it had failed. Exhibit 6 applies four tests to three candidates.

Exhibit 6. Three candidate statements against four tests
CandidateNames who winsStates what changesCan be shown wrongRefuses something
A. "India's largest eye-care network"NoNoYes, by rankNo
B. "End avoidable blindness in India"VaguelyYesNoNo
C. "In every town we serve, no one who fails a screening leaves without glasses or a booked treatment"YesYesYesYes

What it cannot tell you

A vision does not say whether the market is large enough or which feature is next. It orders arguments; it does not settle them. Aravind Eye Care System, founded in Madurai in 1976, is often cited for combining volume with outcomes, which shows the combination is possible, not that Darpan will achieve it.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who is in the sentence? Which decision last month would it have changed?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

The shape of the sentence shifts with the business. In consumer products the vision centres on one person's changed day. In B2B, the buyer who signs and the user who lives with the product differ, and a vision naming only the buyer's saving produces software people resent. In a marketplace there are two sides, and the vision must state what each gains and which side the company will favour when the two conflict.

Exhibit 7. How the vision sentence shifts, using Darpan variants
SettingWho the sentence must nameDarpan illustration
ConsumerOne person and one changed dayA shopkeeper reads the price tags without squinting
B2BBuyer outcome and user changeAn employer saves lost days; the worker sees clearly
MarketplaceBoth sides and the tie-breakPatients get tested near home; optometrists fill idle hours

Stage matters as well. An early company with 212 kiosks can write a narrow, falsifiable vision, check it quarterly, and rewrite it. A company with several business units needs a vision that survives reorganisations, which makes it broader and harder to test.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 8. Mistakes, symptoms and the cheapest diagnostic
MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Vision as a ranking"Largest", "leading", "number one"Size is the changeAsk who is different on Monday
Vision as sloganAny roadmap fitsInspiration is the jobList three things it would refuse
Mission and vision swappedA present-tense activity called a futureDoing is the same as achievingCould it be finished by Friday?

The first is the draft Bhalerao inherited. The second shows up when two teams with opposite plans both claim the vision. The third appears when the "vision" is a verb in the present tense.

8. What good looks like

Bhalerao circulates three candidates, runs the four tests of Exhibit 6 in front of Wadkar and Sorensen, and lets the room see candidate A fail. She brings numbers, not adjectives: Exhibit 4 gives the board a choice it can argue about. The statement she carries to the pitch names a person, states a change, picks a unit, and sits beside a plain mission. It also admits a cost: some kiosk expansion will wait.

Exhibit 9. The final package
ElementWording
VisionIn every town Darpan serves, no one who fails a screening leaves without glasses or a booked treatment.
MissionTest eyes close to home, and stay with each flagged patient until the problem is dealt with.
Unit of changeCompleted follow-up per month
RefusesNew kiosks in a town before the existing ones reach the target completion rate

9. What Bhalerao decides

On Friday 27 March 2026, Bhalerao submits candidate C. She tells Wadkar the reasoning: the doubling plan yields 4,788 outcomes at an unchanged ₹4,010 each and ₹742 lakh of capital, whereas the follow-up programme yields 1,197 more outcomes a month for ₹12 lakh, about ₹1,003 each. Investors may prefer a size story, but it invites the question of why outcomes lag screenings. Wadkar agrees to lead with candidate C and keep "largest" as a supporting fact. Cherian shifts the first quarter to the follow-up service.

To go further, read next about product principles, which translate a vision into rules for trade-offs, then the North Star metric, which turns the unit of change into a single tracked number, and strategy versus roadmap versus plan, which sits beneath it.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Darpan's follow-up rate reached 45 per cent and screenings kept growing, would the vision be nearer, and how would you know the unit of change was not being gamed? Second, think of a product you use daily: whom does its stated vision leave out, and what would it refuse that it currently does?
exp40v2-sense.vision:
Product Vision and Mission

If this product succeeds completely, what is different in the world?

1. Two companies, one month, one unanswered question

On Tuesday 7 April 2026 Shubhra Phansalkar, vice-president of product at Nirmiti Factory Systems in Nashik, carried one page into her co-founder's room. Nirmiti sold shop-floor execution software to mid-size auto-component plants: downtime capture, dashboards, and for some an alert-to-work-order integration. On 31 March 2026 it held 61 accounts across 148 plants, ARR ₹24.51 crore. The page asked Anant Vaze a question four years had not settled: was Nirmiti in the business of making factories visible, or of stopping plants losing shifts?

Money made it urgent. An enterprise resource planning vendor offered to resell Nirmiti as its "plant visibility module" into roughly 900 plants at a wholesale ₹4.80 lakh per plant per year — 29 per cent of Nirmiti's ₹16.56 lakh average. Attractive if instrumentation breadth was the point; fatal if the point was the loop ending in a repaired machine, since the module carried no maintenance integration. Maret Vahtra, the reliability engineer in Tallinn who wrote the alerting logic, called the module "a smoke detector with no battery". Vaze had to answer the board on Friday 8 May, thirty-one days away.

Two days later Urmila Kakade met the same question in Indore. Mitti Farm Exchange, founded in 2022 by Sameer Bodhankar, matched farmer producer organisations in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra with processors, chains and exporters in soyabean, onion and chana. In January–March 2026 it moved 41,500 tonnes across 318 producer bodies and 74 buyers: GMV ₹180.71 crore, commission ₹289.1 lakh at a uniform 1.6 per cent take rate. A lender's term sheet required a published vision and one number reported quarterly. With Ritwik Sanyal, her engineering lead, and Harpal Takle on supply, Kakade had found that one of three crop lanes left farmers worse off than the local mandi while earning Mitti ₹24.7 lakh a quarter.

A vision is not a motivational artefact that happens to be written down. It is a constraint device, and its only test is whether it reorders two defensible plans. Both protagonists hold two, and in both the plan the vision chooses looks worse on the nearest measurement date.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

A vision describes a future state of the world, outside the company, that would obtain if the product succeeded completely; it names who is better off and what is different for them. A mission is the firm's present-tense commitment that makes that state reachable. Strategy is where to compete and how to win; a roadmap is the order of build. The first two differ in tense and in location: the world, or the firm.

Drucker's The Practice of Management (1954) made "what is our business?" the manager's first duty; Levitt's "Marketing Myopia" (1960) added the generative move, defining the business by the customer's purpose rather than the artefact. Collins and Porras, in "Building Your Company's Vision" (Harvard Business Review, 1996), split it into durable core ideology plus a vividly described envisioned future. Product teams adopted the apparatus because the problem is theirs: with no stated destination, prioritisation becomes an argument about taste, and the most senior taste wins.

Six positions are held by competent people, and they disagree about what a vision is for. The destination school (Collins and Porras; in practice Marty Cagan) signs a vivid world five to ten years out, judged only over that horizon, but not that a vision needs a metric. The sceptic school (Rumelt, 2011; Roger Martin) signs that only the implied refusal does work, not that inspiration is part of the job. The metric school signs that without a number rising as the vision is approached you have none, not that it should be timeless. The narrative school (Amazon's working-backwards memo) signs that the artefact is a document with a named customer, not a sentence. The emergence school (Mintzberg) signs that a vision is a hypothesis to rewrite when contradicted, not a stable core beneath flexing strategy. The identity school signs that its function is selection — staff, customers, investors — not that falsifiability matters. Both protagonists sit between the metric and destination schools.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic nobody writes down

Experts do five things, the middle three usually left implicit: name a beneficiary specific enough to be found; state the before-and-after in that beneficiary's terms; choose a unit of change, one countable event proving the after-state has arrived for one beneficiary; derive the value captured and compare it with the price; then write the sentence. The fourth step turns rhetoric into a quantitative claim.

Nirmiti's base splits three ways: plants that log downtime and act on nothing; plants where a supervisor reviews a dashboard most days; plants where alerts raise work orders someone closes. Two assumptions, from customers' cost sheets: a plant runs about 6,000 planned production hours a year, and an hour of line output carries about ₹46,000 of contribution.

Exhibit 3. Nirmiti's base by usage pattern, year to 31 March 2026 (value annual, per plant)

3. Closed loop123624.008647.4 → 4.915069.002.8897%

Hours saved = 6,000 × the fall in downtime share; value = hours × ₹46,000. In the total row ACV is an average and renewal is ARR-weighted, not summed: ₹2,116.32 lakh of ₹2,451 lakh.

Plants that merely log recover 30 hours a year, worth ₹13.80 lakh against a price of ₹12.00 lakh — a ratio of 1.15, which the customer knows. They renew at 71 per cent. Closed-loop plants recover 150 hours, worth ₹69.00 lakh against ₹24.00 lakh, a ratio of 2.88, and renew at 97 per cent. The relation is monotone, and that is all 61 accounts support: a line through groups 1 and 3 predicts 84 per cent for group 2 against an observed 88. Use the ordering, discard the slope. Breadth sells more instances of a 1.15 product; depth converts 1.15 customers into 2.88 ones.

Two second-order effects outrank the wording. The unit of change becomes the accounting unit within two quarters: whatever the vision counts, finance and sales count, or the vision loses. Naming the beneficiary also names who gains power inside — shifts-not-lost centres Vahtra's alerting logic and demotes the dashboard team.

4. When it applies, stated as claims you can test

Exhibit 4. Six conditions, tested on both protagonists
ConditionNirmitiMitti
C1. Two plans the vision would reorderYes: 96 plants or 60 conversions, both ₹960 lakhYes: GMV, or farmer surplus
C2. After-state observable outsideYes: the plant's own MISYes: published mandi prices
C3. End state beyond the plan horizonYes: a decadePartly: the lender wants it quarterly
C4. Enough of the causal chain heldYes for group 3, weak for group 1No for prices, yes for the spread
C5. Decision rights distributedYes: four squads, field, channelWeak: 31 people, founder in every call
C6. Problem will not evaporateYes: downtime is a century oldRisk: procurement and e-mandi policy

Where these fail, the idea misleads rather than merely wastes. A company whose survival horizon is shorter than its vision horizon needs a plan, not a destination; a product specified by a tender has no vision to write. Worse, a public end state works as an escalation shield: contrary evidence arrives as disloyalty. Mitti's C4 failure is instructive — it cannot move the price of soyabean, only the spread between what a buyer pays and what a producer body keeps. A vision to raise farmer incomes is unfalsifiable, the cycle swamping it; one to raise the share of the buyer's rupee reaching the farmer is testable quarterly.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

The two-sided case is sharpest: a marketplace vision naming both sides names neither. Kakade decomposed the buyer's rupee by lane — what reaches the producer body after logistics, grading and commission, against its mandi net after cartage.

Onion is interesting because it is not a scandal. Being perishable, its logistics and grading take 5.85 per cent of the buyer's price against 2.41 in soyabean, swallowing the ₹60 a quintal premium Mitti's buyers pay over the mandi benchmark. The lane suits buyers and pays Mitti; it is merely negative for the party Bodhankar's draft claimed to serve. A marketplace vision must say which side wins a conflict, and accept that the tie-break visibly costs revenue somewhere.

The other edge cases share a mechanism. In multi-product firms the vision migrates upward until it is true of everything and binding on nothing; mature companies let each line hold a vision that may contradict a sibling's, and name a forum to adjudicate. They say the divisions are aligned; in truth they arbitrate. In hardware-plus-software a vision must survive a bill of materials and a three-year tooling cycle, so one implying a hardware change is a capital commitment. In regulated products part of the end state is written elsewhere — a payments vision in India is bounded by what the Reserve Bank permits — so the honest form names the changed state while conceding the mechanism may change twice first. In AI-native products a vision stated as a mechanism ages at the speed of the model layer: "our assistant answers every maintenance query" dies once the capability is ambient; the shifts formulation survives. At the seams the usual failure is the platform team, which cannot link its work to a beneficiary's after-state and writes its own quasi-vision about reliability.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The output is a refusal list, not a sentence. The expert produces three things the company will decline, with a date. The tell: ask what was refused last quarter. No declined item, no vision — and alignment is cheap to simulate, since all agree with an end state that forbids nothing.

Visions fail at the seams, not at the top. The tell is the planning document of the team furthest from a customer, which never cites the vision. Experts hand it a translated clause — "alerts arrive within 90 seconds of the stoppage" — rather than exhorting it about shifts. Otherwise the effective vision is the union of private ones.

Beneficiary and payer differ, and drift follows the payer. The tell is who appears in the demo. Nirmiti's buyer is a plant head, its beneficiary a fitter. If every screen is a management dashboard the product improves for the signer, not the man whose shift is saved — which is how 58 plants sit at 1.15 and renew at 71 per cent.

Quantifying a vision changes it. A reported unit of change becomes a target, and Goodhart's law applies. The tell is gaming within two quarters: work orders closed without a repair; lots routed to lift surplus. Experts instrument the gaming too, keeping a second un-incentivised measure.

The vision's horizon must exceed the incentive horizon, or the pay plan is the real vision. The tell takes two minutes: read the vision, then the bonus formula. If the bonus pays on new logos while the vision is about depth, the vision loses silently. Vaze's plan paid on plants added — which is why breadth would have won unargued.

Breadth visions are self-funding in year one and self-defeating in year three. The tell is the renewal curve by cohort, not the revenue line. Section 8 is exact: breadth leads by ₹88.32 lakh after twelve months, trails by ₹236.28 lakh after twenty-four. Growth does sometimes buy the option to improve later; the expert says what would make that true here.

A vision is a selection device as much as a steering device. The tell is what the last three senior hires say, unprompted, about joining. If none mentions the end state, the vision is not doing the identity school's recruiting work.

Rewriting a vision costs re-litigated decisions. The tell is how many settled questions reopen in the eight weeks after. Experts distinguish a correction — the world changed, as for Mashaal Lighting Industries below — from a drift, the vision retuned to current practice. Drift is commoner; its sign is that no decision changes.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

Exhibit 6. What changes with product type, and what does not
TypeWhat its vision must nameWhat is no different
ConsumerOne person's changed day, observableThe refusal list does the work
B2B / enterpriseBuyer economics and user's work, separatelyValue-to-price predicts renewal
Platform / marketplaceWhich side wins the tie-breakThe unit of change rules accounting
Hardware plus softwareThe bill-of-materials consequenceThe beneficiary must be nameable
AI-nativeThe job, mechanism unstatedGoodhart applies to the metric

Stage matters less than is claimed. A seed-stage company of eleven needs a hypothesis, not a vision document. Mitti, at 31 people with Bodhankar in every decision, fails C5 and writes one because a lender asked. The inflection is where decisions are made by people the founder will not speak to that week — for most firms between 40 and 150. Beyond that the vision turns unfalsifiable and the usable artefact moves to the product line.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Nirmiti: the crossover the first measurement date hides

Both plans cost ₹960 lakh. Breadth lands 96 plants at ₹10 lakh each; they enter as group 1 at ₹12.00 lakh, adding ₹1,152 lakh of ARR. Depth converts 60 plants at ₹16 lakh each — 34 from group 1 at ₹12.00 lakh of uplift, 26 from group 2 at ₹7.50 lakh: ₹408 lakh plus ₹195 lakh, or ₹603 lakh. Each plan runs forward at each group's observed renewal rate, applied once a year, assuming — because it flatters breadth — the new ARR is in place from the start.

Exhibit 7. ARR in force (₹ lakh) from ₹2,451 lakh on 1 April 2026
PlanBooked at start31 Mar 202731 Mar 2028
Breadth: 96 new plants3,603.002,934.242,434.50
Depth: 60 conversions3,054.002,845.922,670.79
Breadth less depth+549.00+88.32−236.28

From full-precision group ARR and renewal rates. Breadth, 2027: 1,848.00 × 0.71 + 891 × 0.88 + 864 × 0.97 = 2,934.24. Depth: 288 × 0.71 + 462 × 0.88 + 2,304 × 0.97 = 2,845.92. The 2028 column applies the rates again, no further spend.

Nothing here settles which plan is right. It settles that whoever chooses breadth takes a plan ₹236.28 lakh poorer twenty-four months out, and must believe something specific: that the 154 group-1 plants convert later for under ₹16 lakh each. The vision's function is to force that belief into the open before the money goes.

Mitti: pricing the tie-break clause

Kakade built the same comparison for the quarter ending March 2027, holding per-quintal economics constant and varying only volume and lane design. Her metric, defined once and used throughout, is farmer surplus per rupee of Exchange revenue: what producer bodies net above their mandi alternative, over Mitti's commission — ₹627.8 lakh on ₹289.1 lakh, or 2.17.

Take rate is 1.6 per cent of the buyer's delivered price throughout, so a lane's GMV share equals its commission share. Commission and surplus are rounded to ₹0.1 lakh; each total is the exact sum of the full-precision rows (Plan 1 commission ₹537.088 lakh, Plan 2 GMV ₹291.7128 crore). The last column is a ratio, not a sum. Plan 2 prices committed onion at ₹1,712 a quintal, 4.4 per cent over ₹1,640, and cuts chana logistics to ₹110.

The farmer vision costs ₹70.3 lakh of quarterly commission and buys ₹195.5 lakh more surplus, ₹0.36 of forgone revenue per rupee of surplus, raising the ratio from 1.88 to 2.58. It also risks the balance sheet: the committed contract carries a floor of ₹1,560 a quintal. A vision naming the farmer is a decision to carry price risk.

Mashaal Lighting Industries: the vision whose world arrived without it

Mashaal Lighting Industries, founded in Jaipur in 2016, sold solar home lighting kits with an app and raised ₹86 crore between 2017 and 2021 against the vision "light in every off-grid home in India". Its 2017 model assumed 2.40 crore households without an electricity connection in its five states. By March 2022, after a decade of national electrification programmes, the figure was 31 lakh — a fall of 87.1 per cent. Units peaked at 1,86,000 in FY21, then collapsed to 64,000 in FY23 at ₹3,400 each, or ₹21.76 crore. About ₹41 crore of the ₹86 crore had built village channel infrastructure for a customer who now had grid power.

The failure was not optimism but naming a deficit rather than a job: the absence of a connection, which others were removing, instead of the need for light when supply failed. On 14 June 2023 the board accepted Gulnaaz Chitnavis's reframing — in Bhavesh Munde's words, "no household plans its evening around the power cut" — pointing at 4.6 crore households with connections and over four hours of daily outage. A grid-charging hybrid unit at ₹9,800 replaced the ₹3,400 kit and four of nine lines were cut. It shipped on 14 January 2025, nineteen months later. FY25 sales were 1,21,000 units, or ₹118.58 crore — 5.4 times FY23.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Exhibit 10. Failure modes, first sign, diagnostic, cost if caught late
ModeEarly signDiagnostic questionCost if late
Ranking vision ("largest")Nobody can say who is better offWho is different on Monday?A base of 1.15-ratio customers
Deficit, not jobAddressable base keeps movingWho else is removing it?Mashaal: ₹41 crore of channel wasted
No tie-break, two sidesBoth sides' advocates quote itWhich side loses?Lanes that earn and harm at once
Contradicted by payThe forecast ignores itWhat does the bonus pay on?Two years of mix drift
Escalation shieldContrary evidence reads as disloyaltyWhat would change our minds?The whole bet, compounded

Two are hard to see from inside. The pay contradiction is invisible because everyone agrees with the vision in the room and is paid for something else outside it; the detector is reading both documents together. The escalation shield destroys most capital, its symptom — unusual conviction — being what the destination school recommends cultivating.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Must a vision be falsifiable? The sceptics say a statement that cannot constrain is a cost without a benefit. The identity school replies that the return appears in recruiting and customer selection, where falsifiability is beside the point. For the sceptics to be wrong, vague visions would have to attract better people than precise ones; for the identity school to be wrong, vague-vision firms would hire no better than firms with none.

Stable or revisable? Collins and Porras rest on durable ideology, and rewrites cost re-litigation, so a vision revised annually is no vision. The emergence school rests on cases like Mashaal's, where holding the line would have been ruinous. The reconciliation offered — correct for the world, do not drift with the company — is weak: the two are separable only afterwards, and Mashaal's board took eleven months over a call obvious in hindsight.

Should the vision carry a number? The metric school's case is Exhibit 3: the value-to-price ratio made Nirmiti's choice arguable rather than aesthetic. The destination school's is Goodhart — work orders closed without a repair, in miniature. The usual compromise, a qualitative vision beside a separately owned unit of change, is unstable: the number gets quoted and the sentence does not.

Does the vision cause the performance? Studies of "visionary" companies are vulnerable to survivorship bias, and several firms praised in the 1990s literature later underperformed — consistent with winners narrating a vision afterwards. The defenders' reply is mechanistic: where hundreds make uncoordinated calls weekly, a written constraint demonstrably changes the calls. That claim is testable at the level of decisions, and almost never tested.

11. What mastery looks like

Four habits separate the practitioner who has internalised this from one who has studied it. They write the refusal list before the sentence, and date it. They compute captured value against price before claiming the end state is reachable: a product worth 1.15 times its price is a company renewing at 71 per cent. They state the tie-break and the horizon with the aspiration. And they can say unrehearsed what would make them abandon it.

12. What each protagonist decides

At the board meeting of Friday 8 May 2026 Vaze declines the bundling offer, accepting it only for a stripped logging tier priced separately, and commits the ₹960 lakh to 60 closed-loop conversions. The vision: no plant Nirmiti serves loses a shift to a problem it could have seen coming. The mission: put every stoppage before someone who can fix it, within the shift. The unit of change: a plant-year with unplanned downtime below 5 per cent of planned hours. The minuted refusal: no logging-only licence where no maintenance system can receive an alert. Phansalkar's condition was a bonus rebuilt on conversions.

Kakade takes Plan 2 to the lender with the tie-break stated: where buyers and producer bodies conflict, Mitti favours the producer body, and the published quarterly number is farmer surplus per rupee of Exchange revenue — 2.17 now, 2.58 targeted for the quarter to March 2027. Bodhankar's objection is on record: ₹70.3 lakh of forgone commission and up to ₹131.6 lakh of floor exposure is much to pay for a sentence, and he is not obviously wrong.

Three questions. First, breadth leads on the only date before Nirmiti's next fundraise: what evidence by May 2026 would justify choosing it? Second, Mitti's onion lane is profitable, good for buyers, marginally bad for farmers — is forcing its re-engineering a discipline or a conceit, and who decides? Third, what would have had to be true in 2019 to catch Mashaal's deficit framing, and would that instrument have condemned Nirmiti's closed-loop bet?

13. Going deeper

  • What a product manager does — what the role is for here.
  • Product principles — a vision turned into reusable trade-off rules.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — where vision stops and competitive choice starts.
  • North Star metric — the unit of change, formalised, Goodhart included.
  • What strategy is and isn't — Rumelt, read directly, inoculates against fluff.
  • Product deconstruction and Product critique — inferring user, job, promise, model, metric and chief assumption from a live product: the inverse of this.
  • B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction — why buyer-beneficiary divergence differs.
  • Product sense and taste — what is left to judgement after the arithmetic.
  • Reasoning about trade-offs and First-principles reasoning — what produced Exhibits 3 and 9.
case20v1-sense.vision:
Iravat Works: The Sentence on the Wall

An Indian-context decision case on product vision and mission

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Nirali Sarpal sat alone in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Iravat Works' office in Baner, Pune, looking at three sentences she had typed on a whiteboard and photographed. She was the company's chief product officer, and by Thursday, 29 October she had to put one of them in front of the board. The board would be approving the vision that Series B investors, in a round of up to ₹120 crore, would be asked to underwrite, and that Navroz Sheorey, the chief executive, had promised to read aloud to all staff on Sunday, 8 November, the morning of Diwali.

Each of the three sentences described a different company, with a different customer, a different rival and a different bill. Whichever she chose would decide what her product managers said no to until March 2031, more than four years away.

2. Company background

Iravat Works was founded in Pune in 2019 by Navroz Sheorey and two college friends. It builds software for India's FMCG distributors, the mid-sized businesses that buy from brands such as Hindustan Unilever, Parle and Amul and deliver to kirana stores. A typical distributor in Nashik or Indore serves about 400 retailers, and Iravat's app puts ordering, GST invoicing and collections on one screen, with retailers paying through UPI.

By March 2026 the company had 1,400 paying distributors, who between them served about 5,60,000 retailers. Its first product was a subscription. After a Series A in 2022, it launched, in 2024, a short-term credit product in which a partner non-banking finance company lends to the retailer, with Iravat acting as lending service provider under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending guidelines.

Udaan and Jumbotail sell to retailers directly and hold the inventory. Flipkart Wholesale and Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner network pull the same retailers toward larger platforms, ONDC could make any ordering app interchangeable, and Zoho sells accounting software many distributors already own. Iravat works for the distributor rather than against him.

3. The situation

The vision question arrived because the company's story had stopped being one story. Since the credit launch, the sales team described Iravat as a fintech, the engineers as an ordering platform, and the Series B investors as a retail operating system. In one week in September, three prospects in Lucknow, Coimbatore and Nagpur were each pitched a different product.

Nirali commissioned a survey of 60 distributors. Exhibit 1 shows what the company earned in the year to March 2026 and Exhibit 2 shows what the distributors said. Credit, which did not exist before 2024, already accounted for more than a quarter of revenue, and 620 of the 1,400 distributors, or 44.3 per cent, had used it at least once. Yet what distributors complained about was not ordering but waiting for money.

Exhibit 1. Iravat revenue by line, year to March 2026
Revenue lineBaseRevenue (₹ lakh)Share of revenue (%)
Subscriptions1,400 distributors at ₹36,000 a year50449.7
Order-flow fee₹1,200 crore of orders at 0.20%24023.7
Credit commission₹180 crore disbursed at 1.5%27026.6
TotalSum of the three lines1,014100.0

Source: company finance records. ₹1,014 lakh is ₹10.14 crore. Percentages are of the 1,014 lakh total.

Exhibit 2. What 60 distributors said in September 2026
StatementDistributorsShare of the 60 (%)
"I pay brands on time but wait weeks for my retailers to pay me"4270
"I would change my software for a better credit line"2745
"I would use it to sell categories beyond FMCG"915

Source: Iravat product research, 60 telephone and in-person interviews across eleven cities. Statements are not mutually exclusive.

The global team saw the same facts from different distances. In Lisbon, Nuala Sheridan, the lead designer, found that every screen she redesigned reflected whichever story the requesting manager believed. In Warsaw, Nikolai Sorokin, the data scientist who built the credit scoring model, noticed that the distributors who took credit left far less often than those who did not, but cautioned that distributors who take credit may simply be healthier businesses.

4. The people

Navroz Sheorey, chief executive, Pune. He wants a vision large enough to justify the round. He told Nirali that investors fund platforms, not distributor software, and that a small-sounding sentence would be priced as a small company.

Neena Shahane, head of lending partnerships, Mumbai. She wants a vision that treats credit as the heart of the company, but she is wary of any wording suggesting that Iravat itself lends, which would draw regulatory scrutiny it is not licensed to meet.

Nuala Sheridan, lead designer, Lisbon. She wants a sentence her team can test a screen against. A vision which cannot reject a feature, she says, is decoration.

Nikolai Sorokin, data scientist, Warsaw. He wants a vision whose success can be measured with data the company already holds.

5. The options

Nirali's whiteboard held three candidate sentences, and Exhibit 3 shows what each would commit the company to by March 2031, using her own planning assumptions of 400 retailers per distributor throughout.

Exhibit 3. What each vision commits Iravat to by March 2031
OptionDistributorsRetailers reached (lakh)Revenue per distributor (₹ lakh a year)Revenue (₹ crore)Capital needed (₹ crore)
A. Operating system for all retail9,000360.981220
B. Every distributor on one system4,000161.456140
C. No distributor waits for his money2,500102.46090

Source: Iravat strategy team planning assumptions. Retailers reached is distributors multiplied by 400, in lakh. Revenue is distributors multiplied by revenue per distributor. The 2026 base is about ₹0.72 lakh of revenue per distributor (₹1,014 lakh across 1,400).

Option A: India's operating system for every shop. It would extend Iravat to pharmacies, hardware stores and apparel retailers. The upside is the largest reach, 36 lakh retailers. The cost is a fight with Reliance Retail, Flipkart and Zoho at once, a requirement of ₹220 crore against a round of ₹120 crore, and revenue per distributor of only ₹0.9 lakh.

Option B: Every distributor in India on one system. It keeps the customer but broadens the job to ordering, billing, inventory and field-sales tools. The upside is a position Udaan and Jumbotail cannot easily copy. The cost is a feature list that never closes and a need for ₹140 crore, which is ₹20 crore more than the round.

Option C: No distributor waits for his money. It makes collections and working capital the product and treats ordering as the way in. The upside is a promise a distributor can feel, the best revenue per distributor at ₹2.4 lakh, and a ₹90 crore need that the round covers. The cost is the smallest reach, 10 lakh retailers, and a dependence on partner lenders and on RBI rules that could change.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, who is Iravat's customer today, what job do they hire it for, and what do they most want changed?
  2. For each option in Exhibit 3, who wins if the product succeeds completely, and what is different in the world? Which sentence says so most plainly?
  3. Which option can Nuala Sheridan use to reject a feature, and which can Nikolai Sorokin measure with data Iravat already holds?
  4. If you were Nirali, which sentence would you take to the board on 29 October, and how would you answer Navroz Sheorey's concern that it sounds too small?

7. A note for the learner

A product vision answers one question: if this product succeeds completely, what is different in the world? A well-formed answer names who wins and what changes for them. It is not a market-size claim or a fundraising line; it is judged by what it lets a team refuse, and principles, a North Star metric and a roadmap are derived from it.

Judged that way, Option A fails first. It names no winner more specific than "every shop" and it excludes nothing, so it cannot guide a designer. Option B names the distributor but describes the product, not the change. Option C names the winner and the change, and Exhibit 2 supports it, since 42 of 60 distributors, or 70 per cent, described exactly this pain while only 9, or 15 per cent, wanted a wider category scope.

One defensible path is to adopt Option C as the vision and keep Option B's ambition as the mission, the long-run work of putting every distributor on one system. The vision then supplies the outcome, and the mission supplies the means. Exhibit 3 gives this path the best revenue per distributor, at ₹2.4 lakh against ₹0.72 lakh today, and the only capital plan that fits inside the ₹120 crore round. Navroz Sheorey's worry about sounding small is answered by arithmetic: ₹60 crore is almost six times the ₹10.14 crore earned in the year to March 2026.

The sentence should be worded with Neena Shahane's constraint in mind: it should promise that distributors are paid, not that Iravat lends. Nikolai Sorokin's caution about selection should be tested first, by measuring whether credit lowers churn among comparable distributors; if it does not, the vision must be revisited.

This path makes the company depend on partner lenders and on RBI's stance, and concedes reach to larger rivals. A good answer says so plainly, names a signal that would force a rethink, and resists choosing the largest sentence merely because it sounds most fundable.
case40v1-sense.user.psych:
The Roster That Books Itself

Rahguzar Logistics Network and the evening peak — an ambiguous Indian-context case on applied behavioural psychology

1. The night before

At a quarter past ten on the night of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Bhargavi Ganesan had four bars on the wall screen of an empty eighth floor in Bengaluru. Rahguzar Logistics Network's operating committee would sit on Monday, 19 October, to choose which of four tested nudges went into the festive release. Freeze was Friday, 23 October; the surge window opened on 30 October and ran through Diwali on 8 November, volumes forty per cent above an ordinary week. Riwaaz Stores, worth roughly ₹98 crore of FY26 revenue — thirty-four per cent of the total — held a thirty-minute promise and a contractual on-time floor of 93 per cent a month.

The tallest bar belonged to the arm Bhargavi, vice-president of product for rider experience, trusted least: it pre-booked riders' evening blocks and worked as the literature says defaults work, enormously and without asking. The arm she found easiest to defend made the best money and added least capacity where capacity was shortest.

2. Company history, and the decision that still binds

Rahguzar was founded in 2019 by Bhalchandra Gogate to deliver for Pune pharmacies. Riders took three-hour blocks and clients bought guaranteed capacity, so Rahguzar carried the scheduling risk. The rider app, Rubaroo, shipped in 2020. By September 2026 it ran nine cities with 1.42 lakh registered riders, about 62,000 active in a week, and FY26 revenue of ₹289 crore on 7.6 crore deliveries, a blended ₹38 a delivery. In February 2025 Raagini Group led a ₹620 crore Series C at a ₹4,100 crore valuation, expecting contribution-positive trading by March 2027.

The constraint dates from 2021, when Rahguzar had four cities and no money. Rather than raise per-delivery pay it built Rozcard, a bonus engine with hard weekly cliffs: three evening blocks between Monday and Sunday earned ₹180, five earned ₹400, a week one block short paid nothing. Cliffs were cheap, since riders chase a threshold harder than a rupee-a-delivery rise, and the Monday reset was wired into the payout ledger and the contracts priced against it. Replacing it with a taper means rewriting the ledger: ₹2.6 crore over two quarters, no earlier than June 2027. Every option before Bhargavi takes the cliff as given.

3. The industry

Rahguzar's riders are not captive: the same two-wheeler can serve Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart or BigBasket in one evening, carry a passenger for Rapido, or run parcels for Delhivery. Quick-commerce dark stores have sharpened demand into the window between seven and ten at night, when riders would rather be home.

Rajasthan's gig worker welfare legislation of 2023 and Karnataka's later framework contemplate a levy on payouts, modelled at one to two per cent; on FY26 rider payouts of ₹197.6 crore — 7.6 crore deliveries at a ₹26 base — one per cent is about ₹1.98 crore a year. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has made Burhan Gheewala uneasy about the single "performance personalisation" consent, default on, taken at onboarding.

The exposure is not only Indian. Rintik Logistics of Jakarta, a 9,200-rider firm, has licensed the scheduling stack for ₹2.4 crore over two years, ₹60 lakh of it due when the rider-engagement module ships by 15 December 2026. A Dutch grocery chain in diligence asks whether the product pre-selects options.

4. How the situation developed

Evening coverage began slipping in January 2026. The diagnosis was price, and in March the five-block cliff rose from ₹340 to ₹400 at an annualised ₹1.9 crore. Coverage improved 1.4 percentage points for three weeks, then fell back. Baiju Gurnani cites that as proof money cannot fix the peak; Bulbul Grover, as proof the cliff had already taken all loss aversion had to give.

In April, Riwaaz renewed on tighter terms: a 93 per cent monthly on-time floor, ₹22 lakh for each full point below it, capped at ₹1.6 crore a quarter, next renewal 31 January 2027. In July a consent experiment in Indore offered 4,000 riders a specific permission screen; 3,112 of the 4,000 accepted (77.8 per cent). In August, Grover argued the peak was a choice-architecture problem: each Sunday night the app asked riders to plan with nothing to plan on.

The pilot ran four weeks, 31 August to 27 September 2026, in Pune, Jaipur and Kolkata: 30,000 riders in four arms of 7,500, entering in weekly waves of 1,875, accumulating 18,750 rider-weeks an arm and 75,000 in all (Exhibits 1 and 2).

Three things have since turned out otherwise. The publication rule changed on 9 September, mid-pilot, to publish fewer blocks where supply looked thin, making Exhibit 6's fill rates incomparable across that month. No-shows, first treated as a GPS artefact, were audited by hand: 5,382 of the 13,125 no-show blocks in the default arm (41.0 per cent) belonged to riders logged in for another platform, against 1,196 of the 4,125 in control (29.0 per cent). And Ganesh Chaturthi fell on 14 September, the pilot's third week, moving Pune demand and supply together.

5. The people

Bhargavi Ganesan, product, Bengaluru, owns the release and says the evidence should decide. Her bonus rides on coverage and on continuation, which point different ways. Unsaid: on her test account the auto-roster offended her.

Bhalchandra Gogate, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai, wants the Riwaaz renewal and a better contribution line before the January board: coverage first, elegance later. Unsaid: Raagini Group has asked twice whether supply growth is bought.

Baiju Gurnani, city operations, Pune, is measured on fill rate and surge spend and wants the default live by 30 October. Unsaid: his fill rate divides by blocks published, and his managers influence how many are published.

Bulbul Grover, rider behaviour science, Gurugram, designed the pilot and argues a default must meet a higher bar than a message, since it removes the deliberative step. Unsaid: she cannot say whether her objection is evidentiary or moral.

Bruno Galindo, data science, Mexico City, owns the randomisation, has recomputed every denominator and wants two more weeks. Unsaid: his August power calculation assumed a four-point effect, so small harms pass unseen.

Bram Groenewegen, design, Amsterdam, will not sign a flow where the release control is less prominent than the confirm. Unsaid: he has a stake in the Dutch diligence going well.

Burhan Gheewala, legal and policy, Mumbai, wants not the default dropped but a defensible consent basis, which on Indore evidence costs a fifth of the riders. Unsaid: he expects a welfare levy within eighteen months.

Bernadette Gatchalian, client partnerships, Manila, has the 15 December Rintik milestone in her commission plan, and the module she promised contains the default. Unsaid: her claim that Indonesia is less sensitive is untested.

7. Voices

"Fill is 94 per cent across the pilot zones. I do not understand what we are debating." — Baiju Gurnani, 7 October

8. The options as Bhargavi currently frames them

Option 1 — ship the auto-roster everywhere before 30 October. Pre-book each rider's usual blocks, one tap to release. It adds the most capacity, pays riders most, and alone might close the 17,800-block shortfall before Diwali. It costs about ₹2.02 crore of contribution a year, concentrates a 9.8-point continuation loss on the least active riders, and rests on a consent Gheewala cannot defend.

Option 2 — ship social proof only. Every booking stays explicit, and it is the best money in Exhibit 5, the best continuation in Exhibit 7A and the best sentiment in Exhibit 8. It adds least where the network is shortest, leaving the festive window to surge pricing.

Option 3 — segment. Default the top two thirds by activity, where continuation damage is 5.4 and 0.4 points, and give the lowest third social proof. The corollary: those protected from the default already earn most, and the capacity given up is what the shortfall is made of.

Option 4 — fix the cliff instead. Spend the ₹2.6 crore, rebuild Rozcard as a taper, run only messages this season. It treats the cliff as the cause of the pressure riders report rather than a lever, and cannot land before June 2027.

All four take the shortfall as a fact about rider behaviour. Exhibit 6 can equally be read as a statement about forecasting and publication, and the thirty-minute promise that creates the peak was a decision taken elsewhere.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee meets at 9 am on Monday, 19 October; freeze is 23 October; the surge window opens on 30 October. The quarter's rider-incentive budget is ₹14.6 crore, ₹9.2 crore of it committed, leaving ₹5.4 crore of headroom, and the Rozcard rewrite is not in it. Engineering is one squad of six, Groenewegen at sixty per cent. A fresh consent screen would, on the Indore result, leave about 31,900 of the 41,000 programme riders inside the nudge set, cutting social proof's annual contribution from ₹6.93 crore to about ₹5.39 crore. Kolkata's riders go home for Durga Puja, 17 to 21 October. Waves 3 and 4 mature on 20 and 27 October, the first a day after the committee sits.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Name the behavioural mechanism each arm in Exhibit 2 relies on, and explain the ordering of effects in Exhibit 3.
  2. The cliff reminder raised bookings and lost money. Using Exhibit 5, work out why, and what that implies about judging a nudge by the metric it was built to move.
  3. Exhibit 6 supports two opposite judgements about Kolkata South. Which denominator fits which decision, and who benefits from each?
  4. Exhibit 7B says the auto-roster works best on the riders it damages most. How would you price that, and what would you need to know?
  5. Is a pre-booked week with a one-tap release a legitimate default or a dark pattern? Does your answer change if riders earn ₹221 a week more, if 37.8 per cent felt pushed, or if the screen ships to Jakarta?
  6. What should Bhargavi Ganesan do on Monday morning, with the freeze on Friday and two waves of data still maturing — and what would she tell the board in January about how this supply was grown?

11. Still Wednesday night

Bhargavi put the four bars back up, then switched to Exhibit 7B. Somewhere in Kolkata South a rider she had never met would, if Option 1 shipped, open Rubaroo on Saturday and find her week already decided; she might be relieved, or spend Sunday tapping her way out of Tuesday. The cleanest number in the deck belonged to the option that did least where the network hurt most. She had not yet written the slide's title.
exp20v2-sense.user.psych:
Applied behavioural psychology: how people actually decide inside a product

1. A renewal screen and a ₹2.8 crore question

On Tuesday 14 July 2026, Saumya Rathod, head of product at Rehbar Policy Exchange, a Pune-based seller of motor and health insurance through an app, opened a spreadsheet that she had been avoiding. In October, 2,00,000 of Rehbar's policies would fall due for renewal. The average annual premium was ₹14,000, and roughly 60 per cent of policyholders renewed. Each percentage point of renewal across that cohort was 2,000 policies, or ₹2.8 crore of premium (2,000 × ₹14,000 = ₹2,80,00,000).

The renewal screen contained a small box reading "Renew automatically every year", unticked. Rohan Sabharwal, the head of analytics, had found that only 18 per cent of customers ticked it. Roos Hendriks, the designer working from Rotterdam, proposed changing a single thing: pre-tick the box and show, in the same line, what a lapse would cost (the loss of a no-claim bonus worth up to 50 per cent of premium). Sunita Rajadhyaksha, the chief financial officer, was sceptical: "If we tick it for them, are we selling or are we trapping?" The board would review the answer on Thursday 30 July 2026. A wrong call in either direction was expensive: leave the box unticked and forgo crores; tick it carelessly and invite complaints to the insurance regulator, IRDAI, and a wave of refund requests.

The real question was why customers who intended to renew often did not. That is the territory of applied behavioural psychology.

2. The idea

Applied behavioural psychology is the use of experimentally established regularities in human judgement to explain, and deliberately shape, the choices people make in a particular design. Its foundation is a finding that unsettled classical economics: people do not weigh options as a calculator would. They rely on shortcuts (heuristics), they evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point rather than in absolute terms, and they are strongly affected by how a choice is arranged.

Four regularities carry most of the weight in product work. Loss aversion is the tendency for a loss to feel larger than an equal gain; Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky formalised it as prospect theory in 1979, and later estimates put the loss weight at roughly two times the gain weight, with wide variation. A default is the option that takes effect if the person does nothing; Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein showed in 2003 that countries asking citizens to opt out of organ donation had near-universal consent, while opt-in countries sat far lower. Friction is any effort, delay or confusion between intention and action. Social proof is the habit of treating what others do as evidence of what is sensible, studied by Robert Cialdini from the 1980s. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the whole approach as "nudging" in 2008.

The sentence Saumya could repeat in the meeting: "Customers decide against a reference point, with limited attention, and the path of least effort, so the design of the choice is part of the product's price."

3. How it actually works

A decision inside a product passes through stages, and the psychology acts at specific ones. First the person must notice that a decision exists. Then they frame it: is this keeping something or buying something? Then they pay an effort cost to act. Finally they commit. Practitioners usually leave two steps implicit. The first is that doing nothing is also a decision, with its own outcome, and the default decides what that outcome is. The second is that every nudge works through one of the stages, so the useful question is never "which bias shall we use?" but "at which stage do we currently lose people?"

Figure 1 maps Rehbar's journey. A default does not persuade; it removes stage 3 for everyone who does not object. Loss framing acts at stage 2: "renew to keep your 50 per cent no-claim bonus" and "pay ₹14,000 for next year" describe the same event, but the first anchors on something the customer already owns. Social proof acts at stages 2 and 3 ("most customers in your city renew automatically"), and friction removal, such as one-tap payment, acts at stage 3. The diagram is diagnostic. If customers drop at stage 1, because the reminder never gets read, a default will not help, and the whole test is wasted.

4. A worked example, line by line

Rohan split the October cohort of 2,00,000 into two equal arms of 1,00,000 policyholders. Arm A kept the unticked box; arm B showed the pre-ticked box with the loss line. Customers who stayed enrolled were charged automatically at renewal; others renewed manually. The measured behaviour, and the arithmetic that follows from it, appears in Table 1.

Table 1. Renewal outcomes per arm of 1,00,000 policyholders; premium ₹14,000 per policy. Revenue in ₹ crore, exact to three decimals. Rates are shares of the arm.
LineArm A (unticked)Arm B (pre-ticked)
Policyholders in arm1,00,0001,00,000

Not enrolled82,00036,000
Enrolled who renew (A 95%, B 88%)17,10056,320

Read it down the columns. In arm A, 18,000 enrolled and 95 per cent of them renewed (18,000 × 0.95 = 17,100); of the remaining 82,000, 52 per cent renewed by hand (42,640); total 59,740. In arm B, 64,000 stayed enrolled, but only 88 per cent renewed (56,320), because customers who never actively chose auto-renew sometimes meet a failed mandate or a disputed charge. The 36,000 who unticked the box were a self-selected, engaged group, and 60 per cent renewed (21,600). The sum is 77,920. The lift is 77.92 − 59.74 = 18.18 percentage points, or 18,180 extra renewals worth 18,180 × ₹14,000 = ₹25.452 crore, which equals 109.088 − 83.636.

Now change one input. Suppose the enrolled renewal rate in arm B is not 88 but 80 per cent, because many accidental enrolees dispute the debit. Enrolled renewals fall to 51,200; with the same 21,600 manual renewals, total renewals are 72,800 (72.80 per cent), the lift over arm A is 13.06 points, and the extra premium is 13,060 × ₹14,000 = ₹18.284 crore. Eight points on one assumption removed about ₹7.168 crore (25.452 − 18.284). Figure 2 plots the three renewal rates.

The lesson is that the default's headline effect (enrolment up from 18 to 64 per cent, a 46-point jump) is not the business effect. The business effect depends on what happens to the people the default captured, who chose nothing and therefore carry no commitment.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A nudge is not a bias discovered; it is a hypothesis about a stage

Naming a bias explains nothing until it is tied to a stage in the journey, as in Figure 1. Teams that say "we will use loss aversion" are decorating; teams that say "customers drop at framing" are diagnosing.

Loss aversion needs a reference point the customer actually holds

Telling a first-time buyer that they will "lose" a bonus they never held does nothing. Rehbar's loss line works for renewers because the no-claim bonus is already theirs. The effect also varies; modern reviews find the size of loss aversion differs across settings and people, so the figure of two is a rough anchor, not a constant.

Defaults work through three channels, and they differ in ethics

A default can act as effort saving (customers cannot be bothered), implicit endorsement (the company must think this is sensible), or reference-setting (the default becomes the status quo, and leaving it feels like a loss). Only the first two are about inattention, and inattention is where trouble hides. Table 1 shows it: arm B's enrolees renewed less reliably.

Nudge versus sludge

Friction used to help a customer is a good nudge; friction used to stop them leaving, such as a cancellation flow buried six screens deep, is what Thaler later called sludge. A fair test: could a customer reverse this choice as easily as they made it?

Persuasion versus manipulation

Sunita's question is the right one. A useful test is whether the customer, shown exactly what the design does and why, would still endorse it. If the design works only while the customer is unaware, it is a dark pattern, and regulators in India have begun naming such patterns.

Statistical lift is not welfare

The test measures renewals. It cannot say whether the extra 18,180 customers wanted the policy, or whether they would have been better served by a lower-priced plan. Measure complaints, refunds and cancellations inside the free-look period alongside revenue.

Effects decay and transfer imperfectly

A result from Western pension plans or Austrian organ donation does not predict an Indian insurance renewal. Run your own test, and rerun it.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Which stage is leaking? What is the customer's reference point? What happens to the people the nudge captures? Can the choice be undone cheaply? If those cannot be answered, the idea is a slogan.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early-stage and large

In consumer products such as Rehbar's app, decisions are individual, fast and emotional, and defaults, framing and social proof act almost directly. In B2B, the buyer is not the user and decisions pass through committees: the reference point is the budget already approved, loss aversion appears as fear of blame for a failed rollout, and social proof takes the form of reference customers in the same industry. Defaults appear in configuration and contract terms: an annual auto-renewing clause is a default with a legal weight. In marketplaces there are two sides: social proof on one side (ratings, "booked 40 times this week") is a supply-quality signal for the other, and a default sort order silently allocates demand to sellers, which is a fairness matter as well as a conversion one.

An early-stage company with a few thousand customers cannot detect a three-point lift; it must rely on qualitative observation and large effects. A large firm such as Rehbar can test, but also carries regulatory exposure, brand risk and the possibility that a small percentage on millions of customers is a large harm.

7. Common mistakes

Counting enrolment instead of outcome

Symptom: a dashboard celebrating "64 per cent opt-in". Misunderstanding: the default measures its own uptake. Diagnostic: follow the captured group through to the business result, as Table 1 does.

Applying a lever to the wrong stage

Symptom: a new loss message with no change in conversion. Misunderstanding: the leak is at stage 1 or 3. Diagnostic: a stage-by-stage drop-off count before designing anything.

Stacking nudges

Symptom: screens with countdown timers, scarcity banners and pre-ticked boxes, and rising complaints. Misunderstanding: effects add up. Diagnostic: test one change at a time, and compare complaint rates.

Reading a short test as permanent

Symptom: a launch result that fades by the second year. Misunderstanding: novelty is durable. Diagnostic: hold out a small group and compare again after a full cycle.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Saumya's decision begins with the leak, not the lever. The team counts how many customers read the reminder, open the screen and pay, finds the leak at stage 3, and designs for it. It runs the two-arm test of Table 1 before launch and agrees beforehand which outcome counts: renewals retained after the free-look period, net of refunds and complaints, rather than raw enrolment. It writes down, on one line, the assumption that matters most (here, the enrolled renewal rate), and shows the board the sensitivity in Figure 2. It makes cancellation as easy as enrolment, sends a reminder before the first debit, and can explain the design to a regulator without embarrassment.

9. Closing

On 30 July, Saumya presented both columns of Table 1 together with the 80 per cent scenario. The board approved a version she shaped: the box would be pre-ticked, but only for customers renewing an existing policy; the loss line would stay; a reminder would arrive seven days before the first debit; and cancellation would take one tap. Rehbar would count success as the October renewal rate net of refunds and complaints, with a 5 per cent holdout left on the old screen. Her reasoning was that even the cautious scenario was worth about ₹18.284 crore, large enough to proceed, but only if the enrolled renewal rate held, so the design had to protect it.

To go deeper, read next about pricing psychology: anchoring, decoy options and how the framing of a number changes what it feels like to pay it. Before then, sit with two questions. First, think of a product you use: which of its defaults would you keep if the company told you exactly why it chose them? Second, if Rehbar's holdout showed a 20-point lift but a doubling of complaints, whose interests would you weigh, and what would you want to measure to decide?

Loss aversion, defaults, friction and social proof as one problem: managing the comparison a user is making.

The eleven weakest groups held ₹286 lakh. A twelve-week leaderboard pilot had lifted their DCR from 50.0 to 87.5 per cent, and Vandana wanted it on all 412 plants before the January renewals. Zeeshan had a second set of numbers from the same pilot, and a steering call on Thursday 8 October.

A product can create a reference point cheaply and cannot withdraw one cheaply. The question is not which bias to exploit but which reference point the business is willing to owe.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about what

Applied behavioural psychology, in product work, is the deliberate design of the comparison a user makes while choosing. Its load-bearing claim is reference dependence: people evaluate changes against a reference point, not states of the world, so one outcome is a gain or a loss depending on where that point sits. Loss aversion is the asymmetry that follows; a default is the outcome of inaction; friction is cost between intention and completion; social proof is a borrowed reference point.

It was invented against a failure of classical demand theory: choice was predicted from prices and stable preferences, so an arrangement leaving prices untouched should not change what people picked. Tversky and Kahneman's heuristics programme (1974) catalogued the departures; prospect theory (1979) replaced utility of wealth with a value function over gains and losses kinked at a reference point, and their 1992 version put the loss coefficient near 2.25. Thaler added the endowment effect (1980); Madrian and Shea (2001) showed automatic enrolment transforming American retirement saving; Kőszegi and Rabin (2006) made the reference point endogenous — it is what you have come to expect. Schultz's 2007 norms work showed the hazard: a descriptive norm pushes above-average households up as well as below-average ones down.

Table 3. Five positions and the proposition each would and would not sign. The disagreement is about the mechanism, and so about the remedy.
PositionWill signWill not sign
Reference dependence (Kahneman, Tversky, Thaler)Losses weigh about twice equivalent gainsThat a lab coefficient is a planning number
Expectations-based reference points (Kőszegi, Rabin)The reference point is what the user expectsThat it is simply the status quo

Boosting (Gigerenzer, Hertwig)Heuristics are adaptive; many biases are framing artefactsThat steering beats building competence
Scale sceptics (DellaVigna, Linos; List; Gal, Rucker)Published effects are inflated and shrink with experienceThat a pilot generalises to the installed base

Two of these matter for Vrinda. If rational inattention is the mechanism, the fix is to make the consequential option legible and no liability is created. If reference dependence is the mechanism, every benefit granted is a position the user holds, and the business has written an option against itself.

3. Mechanics: pricing the withdrawal before making the grant

Expert practice runs in five steps, of which the fourth is almost always skipped. State the comparison the user is making, in their words. Establish who holds the reference point and who pays the effort. Locate the leak. Price the withdrawal. Then test grant and withdrawal separately: they are not the same size.

Vihang had done both. The grant test ran the six weeks from 12 January to 22 February 2026 on 24,000 randomly assigned riders: 5,760 of 12,000 treated riders renewed the next pass (48.0 per cent) against 4,560 of 12,000 controls (38.0 per cent). Ten points, and on that basis it shipped. The withdrawal holdout ran from 1 July to 31 August 2026 on the 19,008 streak holders, one in eight of whom was moved silently to a no-streak price list.

4. The conditions, stated so they can fail

One: the user holds the reference point. Vihang passes emphatically; Zimmedari fails, because a supervisor holds no position in the DCR. Two: inaction has a visible consequence inside the decision window. A Vihang pass lapses on the first of the month; an unfiled checklist is invisible until a quarterly audit. Three: the user is choosing rather than complying. Filing a statutory checklist is a job duty, and where behaviour is mandated and measured a lever buys the measurement rather than the behaviour — the condition under which the idea is actively misleading. Four: the decision repeats often enough to learn from, but not so often that the effect decays. Twelve exposures a year is enough for novelty to fade and, as List suggests, for an endowment effect to attenuate.

5. Hard edges

The clean cases are rare; Table 6 sets out five that are not.

Then there is the organisational seam, where most damage happens. At Vihang, growth owned the renewal rate, finance the discount line, support the complaints; the reference-point liability appeared on nobody's statement until Zoya constructed it. What mature firms do is narrower than the literature: a sunset clause written into any earned benefit at launch, and a withdrawal-cost line beside the uplift.

6. Eight distinctions that separate command from competence

A bias is not a lever; the comparison is. The tell is a team naming the bias before the comparison. Vihang's riders were not weighing ₹1,850 against the value of a commute; they were weighing ₹1,650 against ₹1,850, and the whole twenty-five-point effect lives in that difference.

Granting and withdrawing are two experiments. The obvious reading is that an intervention worth ten points is worth ten in both directions; the tell is a business case quoting a launch uplift as the cost of reversal. At Vihang the numbers were ten and twenty-five.

The reference point is an expectation, not a possession. When Vihang withdrew the streak, renewal also fell six points among riders in the fourteen-to-seventeen boarding-day band, who had never qualified. They lost nothing they held, only something they expected to earn: an aspiration is also a liability.

Selection wears the costume of causation. Streak holders renewed at 75.0 per cent and non-holders at 30.8 per cent — 20,736 of 67,392 riders — a gap of 44.2 points where the holdout put the causal effect at 25.0, an overstatement of 1.77 times. The tell is a loyalty dashboard reporting the member gap with no holdout.

Effect sizes do not travel, and the published ones are the wrong size. DellaVigna and Linos's 2022 study of two nudge units found field effects averaging about 1.4 percentage points against roughly 8.7 in the literature behind them. Treat any borrowed coefficient, the 2.25 included, as a prior to overwrite.

Friction is a filter, not a tax. Carrying the stop and slot forward lifted completion 8.3 points and removed the moment riders checked their slot: mis-slotted boardings rose from 1.1 to 2.9 per cent of rides. One confirmation line added back cost 0.4 points and halved the error. Friction that prevents a reversal earns its keep.

A descriptive norm must be true, and flattering, on the particular screen. Vihang's line was accurate at route level on ninety-six routes of 240 and suppressed elsewhere, because the honest global statement — that fewer than half of riders renew — licenses leaving. That is Schultz's boomerang in product form.

Aim the loss frame at whoever's standing is at stake, and watch the unscored sibling of every metric you score. The supervisor filing a Zimmedari checklist bears the effort; Vikrant Lagoo, group safety head at Vajra Castings Industries, bears the exposure when the number is read out at a quarterly review. A frame aimed at the supervisor produces indifference; aimed at the plant head it produces action, part of it pressure to file rather than inspect. When the leaderboard raised DCR, near-miss reports fell from 3.10 to 1.20 per plant per four weeks.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products the levers act directly, because one person decides, pays and bears the effort: Vihang's twenty-five-point effect is a number only a consumer funnel produces. In business software the psychology is relocated rather than absent — the buyer holds the reference point, the user bears the effort, the loss that moves an enterprise is of standing rather than money, and the design question is which number reaches the customer's governance forum. In marketplaces, a default sort order is allocation policy. In hardware the architecture is tooled and shipped, so the experiment must precede manufacture. In AI products the default becomes a learned policy, so the reference point drifts without anyone deciding to move it.

Stage changes what is detectable, not what is true. A three-point lift on a 40.5 per cent base needs roughly 4,200 riders per arm at conventional power; a twenty-five-point lift needs about sixty. A seed-stage company cannot see most of the literature's interventions; a firm at Vihang's scale must resist shipping all it can see.

8. Three worked examples, one of which failed

The one that worked, net of its side effect. Vihang's carry-forward shipped on 19 September 2026, valued in Table 5 at ₹71.928 lakh a month gross and ₹70.828 lakh net. The confirmation line added back to control mis-slotting cost 0.4 points, leaving 38,678 of the 46,656 riders who reached payment completing it (82.9 per cent), an increase of 3,686 rather than 3,888 — ₹68.191 lakh gross, ₹67.091 lakh net, five per cent below the business case.

The one that failed. Zimmedari's leaderboard ran exactly twelve weeks, Monday 6 April to Sunday 28 June 2026, on 84 plants against 84 matched controls, each arm owing 84 × 3 × 84 = 21,168 filings.

A diagnostic instrument had become a compliance ritual, and under the Factories Act those filings are signed records.
