9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Reference-point debt without a sunset. Sign: an earned benefit with no expiry or withdrawal test. Diagnostic: what does reversal cost, and on whose statement? Late cost: ₹59.400 lakh a month.

Scoring the proxy and believing it. Sign: the metric improves faster than any mechanism could explain, as DCR did by 37.5 points in twelve weeks. Diagnostic: which unscored measure must move with this? Late cost: 7,409 implausible statutory records.

Reading selection as effect. Sign: value quoted as the member versus non-member gap. Diagnostic: where is the randomised arm? Late cost: a 1.77-fold overstatement in the next plan.

Aiming at the wrong person. Sign: a persuasion design aimed at a user with nothing at stake. Diagnostic: who holds the reference point, and who bears the effort? Late cost: compliance theatre nobody inspects.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Steer or equip. The nudge position holds that choice architecture is unavoidable and should therefore be designed deliberately, in the user's interest. Gigerenzer's boosting position holds that steering leaves people no more competent than it found them, and that teaching a rule — showing riders their own boarding record — is more durable and more respectful. Boosting fails if the competence does not transfer, or costs more than it is worth on a ₹1,850 decision taken twelve times a year.

Whether loss aversion is the mechanism. Gal and Rucker's 2018 review argues the evidence for a general loss asymmetry is weaker than the textbooks suggest and much of it inertia; the rational-inattention school reaches the same prediction from a different premise. The remedies diverge: if inattention is the mechanism, a clear reminder recovers most of the twenty-five points without keeping the discount. Vihang's withdrawal arm got no enhanced reminder, so its data cannot separate them.

Whether pilot effects survive. The scale sceptics have the stronger published evidence: List's finding that endowment effects attenuate with market experience suggests a monthly decision by a practised commuter is where the effect should fade. The practitioner's reply is that funnel effects of Vihang's size are not what the meta-analyses pool; that reply fails if the twenty-five points decay across later cohorts.

Where the ethical line falls. Sunstein's publicity test asks whether a design could be explained to those subject to it without embarrassment. Hausman and Welch object that bypassing deliberation is manipulation even when the outcome is good. A third position holds that reversibility is what matters: a choice undoable in one tap cannot extract much.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a list of biases and a screen to apply them to. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a question about the comparison, insists on knowing who holds the reference point before discussing design, and asks what withdrawal costs before approving the grant. They quote their own numbers, and read a metric moving faster than any mechanism allows as measurement capture.

12. The decisions

On 1 October, Vrinda neither defended the Seat Streak nor killed it. She proposed converting it: the ₹200 folded into a list price of ₹1,650 for riders above fifteen boarding days, and the streak itself paying a guaranteed window seat on the rider's registered service — a benefit that costs capacity rather than cash, and one retirable by route rather than withdrawn from a person. Her reasoning: the business could afford ₹28.512 lakh a month but not a second withdrawal, and the right move with a liability you cannot price is to change its currency while you hold the initiative.

On 8 October, Zeeshan shipped the redesign and took the harder meeting: he asked Vikrant Lagoo to change the number in Vajra Castings' quarterly review from DCR to near-miss reports surfaced per plant. He accepted ₹54.34 lakh of the ₹91.52 lakh, arguing that a vendor who sells a flattering number has sold the risk with it.

Three questions. First, the conversion changes the reference point rather than removing it: what would you measure in November to know whether riders coded the seat guarantee as a gain or the lost ₹200 as a loss? Second, had the redesign shown DCR at 60 per cent rather than 75, leaving the eleven accounts in the lowest band, what would you have shipped? Third, the holdout silently moved 2,376 riders onto a worse price: on which ethical test does it pass?

13. Going deeper

Product deconstruction is the prerequisite: you cannot name the comparison until you have named the user, the job and the promise. Pricing psychology is the continuation, because anchors and decoys are reference points chosen deliberately; and the asymmetry measured here is what makes a price rise more dangerous than a price that was always high. B2B versus B2C matters because the right-hand quadrants of Figure 3 are the whole of enterprise work. Product sense and taste supplies the judgement when data cannot; reasoning about trade-offs is how ₹91.52 lakh against ₹54.34 lakh gets decided; first-principles reasoning catches a borrowed coefficient. Product critique and competitive teardown are where the skill is practised: name the comparison a live renewal screen constructs, and price its withdrawal.
case20v1-sense.user.psych:
The Default Question at Hoysala Savings Labs

An Indian-context decision case on applied behavioural psychology

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Madan Rathore, chief product officer of Hoysala Savings Labs, sat in a glass meeting room in Bengaluru with a one-page summary of a pilot and a deadline. The product council would meet on Wednesday, 21 October, and whatever it approved had to be live in the app before Diwali on 8 November. The pilot had tested four ways of persuading customers to raise their monthly mutual fund contribution once a year. One had worked far better than the others, and Rathore was not sure he was allowed to like it.

2. Company background

Hoysala Savings Labs was founded in 2019 by two former bankers who noticed that Indians opened systematic investment plans (SIPs) with enthusiasm and then forgot them. Its app lets a salaried customer start a SIP from ₹500 a month through a UPI autopay mandate. By September 2026 it had 38 lakh registered users, of whom 12 lakh had an active SIP averaging ₹2,000 a month. It earns 0.5 per cent a year on the assets held through it, so revenue depends on how much each customer keeps adding.

The market is crowded. Zerodha's Coin and Groww dominate the first-time investor, PhonePe and Paytm Money reach customers through payments habits, and AMFI's "Mutual Funds Sahi Hai" campaign normalises SIPs. Hoysala retains customers well, but the median SIP had not moved in two years even though core-segment salaries rise roughly 8 to 10 per cent a year.

3. The situation

The company's behavioural researcher, Mekhala Rustagi, had argued since spring that the stagnation was not about affordability. Raising a SIP asked for effort, attention and a small act of self-denial, and the status quo asked for none of these. Rustagi proposed testing four conditions on randomly assigned customers, 20,000 in each arm, all of whom had an active SIP and a SIP anniversary falling between 1 and 15 June 2026.

The control arm received the existing screen: a plain, optional link to increase the SIP. The second arm saw a loss-framed message: "Skipping a 10 per cent step-up means giving up growth you could have had." The third saw social proof: "Customers like you in Pune raised their SIP by 10 per cent this year." The fourth received a default. The app pre-enrolled the customer in an annual 10 per cent step-up, effective at the next anniversary, that she could cancel with a single tap. Every arm was followed for 90 days, ending in mid-September (Exhibit 4 shows the timeline), and the team measured how many customers ended on a step-up and how many paused their SIP altogether.

The global team read the results differently. Marta Rosales, the lead designer in Lisbon, thought the default elegant but worried that colleagues in Europe would call it a dark pattern. The pause numbers troubled Rathore most, since a customer who stops a SIP is expensive to win back.

4. The people

Madan Rathore, chief product officer, Bengaluru, owns the decision and the quarterly target for assets raised. He wants growth that survives a market fall.

Mekhala Rustagi, behavioural researcher, Pune, designed the pilot. She wants the company to act on the evidence and is wary of over-reading a single quarter.

Mahir Rangnekar, head of compliance, Mumbai, watches SEBI's attention to misleading nudges and consent under the DPDP Act. He wants any change defensible to the regulator.

Marta Rosales, lead designer, Lisbon, wants customers to feel helped, not herded, and wants the cancel control as visible as enrolment.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out the pilot. Each arm held 20,000 customers, so rates are directly comparable. The control arm enrolled 8.0 per cent in a step-up, the loss-framed message 12.0 per cent, social proof 15.0 per cent and the default 70.0 per cent. With 20,000 customers per arm the standard error of an 8 per cent rate is about 0.19 percentage points (the square root of 0.08 × 0.92 ÷ 20,000), so a gap of 62 points is not noise. Exhibit 2 draws the same rates as bars.

The pause difference needs the same scrutiny as the enrolment difference. 6. The options

Option A: ship the default to all 12 lakh active SIP customers. A pre-enrolled 10 per cent annual step-up with a one-tap cancel. The upside is the largest by far, ₹888 net per customer. The cost is the 2.5-point rise in pauses, the regulatory optics of an opt-out, and lost trust among customers surprised on their anniversary.

Option B: ship only the messages. Run the social proof message, drop the loss-framed one, and keep enrolment voluntary. Every enrolment is an explicit choice, which satisfies Rangnekar and Rosales. The cost is the size of the prize: ₹168 per customer, about 19 per cent of the default's net.

Option C: delay and test further. Extend the pilot through Diwali with a 5 per cent default and a default-plus-social-proof arm. The upside is better information; the cost is losing the festive window.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Which behavioural forces explain the four enrolment rates in Exhibit 1? Why did the default dwarf the others?

2. Why did the loss-framed message, which raised enrolment, lose money in Exhibit 3? What does this say about measuring only the targeted metric?

3. Using Exhibit 3, how many extra pauses per 20,000 customers would eliminate the default's advantage? What does that margin tell you about the risk of Option A?

4. Is a pre-enrolled step-up with one-tap cancel a legitimate default or a dark pattern? What would make it defensible to SEBI and to customers?

8. A note for the learner

Applied behavioural psychology frames this decision by asking how customers actually decide, not what they say they want. People accept the path of least effort, which is why a default produced enrolment of 70 per cent where an invitation produced 8. The same lens warns that every nudge has a second-order effect: a default that feels like a surprise can trigger the abandonment that destroys the gain. A well-reasoned answer keeps both columns of Exhibit 1 in view and converts them into rupees as Exhibit 3 does.

One defensible path is Option A with guardrails. The default's gain of ₹1,488 per customer would be wiped out only if extra pauses reached 6.2 per cent of customers (1,488 ÷ 24,000), against 2.5 per cent observed, so the margin is wide. Send a notice seven days before each anniversary stating the new amount in rupees, place the cancel control beside the confirm button, and add the social proof message. Track the day-90 pause rate against a 5 per cent hold-out kept on the old screen, and pause the roll-out if the gap exceeds 4 points, well inside the break-even. Option B leaves value on the table; Option C trades a measured gain for a festive window that returns only next year.
exp40v2-sense.design.thinking:
Design thinking

Foundations › Product Thinking & Product Sense. Empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test — as a habit, not a workshop.

1. Two decisions, both live

On 9 June 2026 in Pune, Harita Mahabal watched her founder present a hardware roadmap aimed, she believed, at the wrong problem. Harita is VP product at Himsagar Cold Chain Industries, which sells refrigerated-transport telemetry to vaccine distributors and dairy unions. The base was 2,840 units at ₹14,400 a year of software renewal: 2,840 × ₹14,400 = ₹4,08,96,000, or ₹4.09 crore. Accounts covering 1,160 units, 40.8 per cent, had signalled non-renewal: ₹1,67,04,000, or ₹1.67 crore.

Hrishikesh Pansare, the founder, proposed Sentinel Pro: a hardware revision with a cabin siren and a cellular escalation chip, ₹1.90 crore over seven months. Harita's objection was not that the siren was wrong but that nobody could say, from evidence, why alerts went unanswered. Her counter cost ₹18.50 lakh, 9.7 per cent of the Pro build, over nine weeks.

On 2 October 2026 in Hyderabad, Ira Nagvekar faced the mirror image. Ira heads product at Ilaaka Neighbourhood Network, an AI-native app live in 46 localities across Hyderabad and Jaipur: a resident asks when the water tanker is due, and a language model answers from neighbours' posts and merchant listings. September 2026 brought 3,14,000 installs, of which 91,060 asked a question; the answer was marked useful in 42,798 cases — 47.0 per cent. Himmat Chavan, the founder, read that as a model problem and proposed a larger model with retrieval over licensed municipal data, ₹1.35 crore a year. Ira's alternative cost ₹9.42 lakh.

Both firms already did design thinking: Himsagar ran a sticky-note workshop in November 2025, Ilaaka runs fortnightly discovery. The question is whether it produces knowledge that changes commitments, or theatre.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Design thinking is a procedure for deciding about artefacts under uncertainty about what people need. Its content is sequencing: observe before you define, define before you generate, generate many before you choose, build the cheapest thing that can embarrass you, and let behaviour settle it. A prototype is anything cheap enough to discard that still lets a user act; a concierge one substitutes staff for software.

Herbert Simon's The Sciences of the Artificial (1969) treated design as devising courses of action, and introduced satisficing. Rittel and Webber's 1973 paper on wicked problems explained why a procedure was needed: where the formulation changes as you solve it, you cannot specify first and build second. Schön's The Reflective Practitioner (1983) called design a conversation with the materials; IDEO (1991), Stanford's d.school (2005) and Tim Brown's 2008 HBR article packaged it for managers.

Four schools claim the ground. The divergence school (IDEO, d.school) signs that the problem statement must be rewritten after observation, and not that a team may carry a solution hypothesis into the field. The hypothesis school (Blank, Ries) signs that the unit of work is a falsifiable claim with a pre-committed kill threshold, not immersion. The jobs school (Christensen, Ulwick) signs that the stable unit is the job to be done, rankable by survey on hundreds, and not that empathy with individuals is the primary input. The contextual school (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1998; Scandinavian participatory design) signs that the context of use is the data and the user a co-designer, and not five users and a five-day sprint.

A fifth voice dissents: Iskander argued in HBR in 2018 that the method is conservative, since empathising inside a system reproduces its assumptions.

3. Mechanics: the steps nobody writes down

From 15 June to 10 July 2026 — twenty-six days — Hemangi Talwalkar shadowed loading bays at nine Himsagar depots in Nagpur, Nashik and Hubballi, with a stopwatch and a seating chart: who was present when an alarm fired, and what they did next. The first unwritten step came before her: instrument the baseline, so findings can be sized.

Exhibit 1 reframed the roadmap before an interview was coded. A siren makes an alert louder, but 92.5 per cent of alerts were not excursions and 41.7 per cent repeated something already open; on that distribution a louder alarm only trains people to ignore it faster. Hemangi supplied the mechanism: the alert reached the contract signatory — a cold-chain officer such as Dr Ismat Baig at Indravati Biologics Services — not the supervisor at the vehicle. The define statement became: a loading supervisor must be told, by name, within minutes, that this vehicle needs attention.

Three further steps go unwritten: coding to rules fixed in advance, so the tally cannot drift toward what the team hoped; writing the kill threshold before the test; and naming an umpire with no stake. Inder Mirchandani, the hardware lead in Rajkot, who lost if software won, could alone declare failure.

The formal treatment is thinner than practitioners pretend, and lives in two habitually conflated places. For discovery — will we see a problem at all — Nielsen's detection model gives 1 − (1 − p)n: Harita assumed a depot practice visible at any one depot with probability 0.25, so across six, 1 − 0.756 = 1 − 0.1780 = 82.2 per cent — which justifies six depots, not sixty. For sizing, sampling error governs instead: Ira's 320 coded answers held 27 fabrications, 8.4 per cent, standard error √(0.0844 × 0.9156 / 320) = 0.0155, a 95 per cent interval of 5.4 to 11.5 per cent.

4. When the loop earns its cost, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable claims. One: the user's identity is uncertain. Strongly true at Himsagar — buyer, user and the person near the failure were three people; the product addressed only the first. Partly true at Ilaaka: the asker is obvious, the supplier of local facts was never designed for. Two: the mechanism is unknown. True at both; neither firm could explain its headline number. Three: a cheap artefact can produce the same behaviour as the real thing. True at both — a person in Pune can telephone a depot as software would, and a human can post what retrieval would have fetched. Four: being wrong costs more than finding out. ₹1.90 crore against ₹18.50 lakh; ₹1.35 crore a year against ₹9.42 lakh.

Where all four fail the loop is overhead: a payment flow under RBI's two-factor rules has a known user, a known mechanism and nothing to prototype away. Where claim three fails — the thing cannot be faked, as with a surgical device — the loop misleads, since the cheap artefact tests reaction to a description, which attracts uninformative enthusiasm.

A fifth condition is under-stated, and is where Iskander's critique bites: the system observed must not itself be the problem. Shadowing depot workers shows how to help them inside the current design; it cannot say whether cold chains should be monitored per vehicle rather than per consignment. That question needs a separate first-principles pass.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Himsagar is hardware plus software, which breaks the loop: the prototype cycle is four weeks for firmware and four months for a moulded enclosure, against two days for software. Teams fake a single cadence, then find the hardware decision was made irreversibly at month two on a software-speed insight. The honest handling is two loops at declared clock speeds and, per commitment, a date after which evidence cannot change it. Inder's tooling lock was 15 August 2026, which is why Harita's test closed on 16 August.

Ilaaka is AI-native and two-sided at once. The sides are not buyers and sellers but askers and tellers, and the model sits between them pretending the second does not exist. Testing answer quality with the corpus fixed measures the model; with it moving, the community. Ilaaka had run the first test for seven months. The model is also non-deterministic, so expert practice pins version, temperature and prompt for the test's duration.

At the seams: regulated access needs permissions that outlast the sprint, so mature teams keep a standing research agreement; and in a multi-product firm the finding that alerts reach the wrong phone belongs to no team, so it is rediscovered annually and acted on never. Firms that handle this keep one register of live assumptions with owners and last-tested dates. Most say they do; few can produce it.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The loop exists to change commitments, not to generate insight

A competent team measures discovery by output: interviews run, insights captured. An expert measures decisions reversed. The sign is a repository growing monthly beside a roadmap unchanged for two quarters; the obvious reading, that synthesis is weak, is wrong — what is missing is a decision waiting on it. Harita's test fixed its consequence first: routing shipped, or Sentinel Pro did.

Empathy is an evidence-collection technique, not a disposition

The word invites teams to treat sympathy as data; Hemangi's output was a seating chart and a stopwatch log. The tell is findings stated as feelings — "supervisors feel overwhelmed" — with no observable behind them. Users cannot report why they act: the 3,210 unacknowledged excursions were not an attitude but a geography.

The cheapest prototype is usually a person, and it feels like cheating

Concierge prototypes attract the objection that they do not scale, which is true and irrelevant: their job is to price the mechanism, not to be the product. Himsagar's human escalation cost ₹1,000 per excursion — ₹1.48 lakh over 148 escalations — against ₹62 automated. The tell of a team that has missed this is a prototype that is an unshipped build.

A test without a pre-committed threshold is a ceremony

The tell is that every test in the team's history succeeded. Ask what number would have stopped the project, and watch whether the answer comes from a document or the moment. Ira's was explicit: unless the operator arm beat control by four points, the supply hypothesis was dead.

Who you recruit decides what you learn, and the convenient sample is the enthusiast

Himsagar's 2025 workshop recruited fourteen users who had come to Pune for the annual conference — the most engaged customers in the base, selected by a filter nobody noticed applying. The remedy is not more people but a written screen, applied before anyone is contacted.

Small samples establish existence, never frequency

Two dozen conversations can prove a failure mode exists and suggest its mechanism, but not what share of the base it affects: the interval around a proportion from twenty-four observations is roughly ±20 points. Hence pairing each finding with a production-data query, as Exhibit 1 does.

Define is where the money is, and it is the step teams skip

Ideation is enjoyable and prototyping visible, so both get time; writing the problem statement is neither, so it gets fifteen minutes. Yet almost every expensive failure traces to a statement with the solution smuggled inside: "users need a louder siren" is a solution in a need's clothing. The diagnostic: do four different solutions satisfy it? Harita's admitted SMS, voice, a display board and a rota as well as a siren.

A successful prototype's second-order effects are where the cost hides

Himsagar's escalation worked at once in four of six treated depots. In the other two the phone roster was stale: of 29 treated excursions that went unacknowledged, 17 — 58.6 per cent — were at those two. The product therefore carries a dependency no specification would surface: someone at each depot must keep a list of humans current.

7. How the practice changes by product type and stage

Two supposed differences are overstated. Enterprise products are said to need less observation because requirements arrive in writing; but the requirement comes from the approver and describes the approver's problem — why enterprise software is bought and not used. AI products supposedly need a different method; they need this one with corpus and model pinned. Where a difference is small, say so: B2B and consumer teams write identical define statements and thresholds.

Stage matters more than type. In a firm of fifteen the founder talks to customers weekly and the risk is over-fitting to the three who answer the phone. At Himsagar's 170 people the risk is specialisation: research belongs to a function and those choosing the roadmap have not heard a customer in a year — why Hrishikesh sat through four of the nine shadowings. At large scale nobody owns a cross-product finding.

8. Three worked examples

One: Himsagar's escalation test (succeeded)

From 20 July to 16 August 2026, twenty-eight days, two staff in Pune watched six depots' dashboards and telephoned the nearest named handler on every genuine excursion. Six depots matched on units and prior excursion rate got nothing.

Applying the treated write-off rate of 9 in 148 to the quarter's 3,915 excursions gives 238 write-offs against the observed 874, so 636 are avoided, worth 636 × ₹1.20 lakh = ₹763.20 lakh, or ₹7.63 crore a quarter — to its customers, not to Himsagar, which captures value through renewal and a tier. The build was ₹46 lakh; running cost at ₹62 per escalation across 3,915 excursions is ₹2,42,730 a quarter, ₹9.71 lakh a year. Against ₹1.67 crore of at-risk renewal and a ₹3,600-per-unit tier taken by half the base — 1,420 units, ₹51.12 lakh — year one is ₹167.04 + ₹51.12 − ₹46.00 − ₹9.71 = ₹162.45 lakh, or ₹1.62 crore. Halving retention and cutting uptake to 20 per cent (568 units, ₹20.45 lakh) still gives ₹48.26 lakh. Break-even needs ₹55.71 lakh retained: 387 units at ₹14,400, or 33.4 per cent of the 1,160 at risk.

Two: Ilaaka's three-arm supply test (succeeded, and reversed the plan)

Exhibit 6 is the whole argument: the headline failure was a supply problem in a model problem's clothes. From 1 to 28 September 2026 twenty localities were split three ways: in eight, operators led by Ismail Zargar in Srinagar posted five local facts each morning; in four, residents were nudged to answer open questions; eight were controls.

The operator arm won on lift and lost on economics, which mattered more. Per point of acceptance the nudge cost ₹17.67 / 7.5 = ₹2.36 per first-question user against the operators' ₹172.97 / 13.1 = ₹13.20 — 5.6 times more efficient. Across 46 localities operators cost 46 × ₹1.12 lakh = ₹51.52 lakh a month, ₹6.18 crore a year; the nudge costs 46 × ₹11,500 = ₹5.29 lakh a month, ₹63.48 lakh a year. The ₹1.35 crore model upgrade addresses at best the 8.4 per cent of failures that are fabrications; since 53.0 per cent of answers were unaccepted, removing fabrication entirely buys 0.530 × 0.084 = 4.5 points, lifting acceptance to at most 51.5 per cent. Cost per point is therefore ₹30.00 lakh for the model (₹135 lakh / 4.5), ₹47.19 lakh for operators (₹618.24 lakh / 13.1) and ₹8.46 lakh for the nudge (₹63.48 lakh / 7.5).

Three: Himsagar's health card (failed, and what recovery cost)

In November 2025 Himsagar ran a two-day workshop in Pune with fourteen customers, all present because they had come for the annual conference. Sketches converged on a daily cold-chain health card, emailed to each account. It shipped on 12 January 2026 at a cost of ₹52 lakh and was withdrawn on 30 April 2026; across 2,840 units, 189 recipients opened it — 6.7 per cent. Three things went wrong and none was the idea. Recruitment was a convenience sample of the most engaged customers. The prototype was a rendered slide, so participants reacted to a description rather than acting on an artefact: claim three of section 4 had failed, untested. And "what would you find valuable?" elicits aspiration, where what mattered was "what did you do when an alarm last fired at 2 a.m.?" With no kill threshold, the card survived three quarterly reviews on praise. Recovery was the three boxes of Exhibit 2, plus salvage: ₹11 lakh of email infrastructure went to the escalation rota, a net write-off of ₹41 lakh.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The fifth nearly caught Ilaaka, and is subtlest because the test succeeded: a concierge prototype prices the mechanism at concierge cost, which is not the product's.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One: the value is the divergence, and hypothesis discipline kills it. Steelmanned: pre-committing narrows the search to options the team could already articulate — the set excluding the breakthrough. The evidence is the products whose insight came from an unplanned observation. For this to be wrong, teams generating options without a hypothesis would have to decide at a reasonable rate; the static roadmap says otherwise.

Two: without a falsifiable claim and a kill threshold, the method is not knowledge. Steelmanned by Blank and Ries: organisations do not lack ideas, they lack the ability to stop, and teams without written thresholds report universal success. For this to be wrong, pre-commitment would have to blind teams to findings outside the hypothesis, as it can.

Three (jobs school): empathy with individuals is the wrong unit of analysis. Steelmanned: individuals are idiosyncratic, but the job — keep this consignment at temperature; know what is happening on my street — is stable across decades and measurable on hundreds. For this to be wrong, the job would have to be unidentifiable without ethnography — plausible in new categories: nobody could have surveyed for Ilaaka's job before conversational interfaces existed.

Four (the critics): the method is conservative and its corporate form a credential. Steelmanned by Iskander and Vinsel: empathising inside a system cannot question the system, and a method teachable in five days without domain expertise will be used by people who have none. For this to be wrong there would need to be a record of programmes breaking frames; honestly, they optimise them.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied design thinking runs the loop when a project begins. Someone who has internalised it keeps a register of live assumptions with owners and last-tested dates, and can name unprepared the three beliefs the roadmap depends on and what each would cost to test. Their thresholds are written before data arrives; their umpire loses nothing by calling failure; their prototypes are embarrassing and their business cases priced at scale. They can say which decisions the method cannot make: the frame, the strategy, the regulated constraint. And when a test succeeds their first question is what obligation it creates — who, at every depot, keeps a list of humans current.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 1 September 2026 Harita recommended that Himsagar build the escalation routing — named-handler rota, SMS and voice, duplicate suppression — for ₹46 lakh over eleven weeks, deferring Sentinel Pro until it had been re-tested automated against the same threshold. Her reasoning: the cause was organisational, not acoustic; the 62.4-point gap survived heavy discounting; and break-even needed only 387 of the 1,160 at-risk units. Hrishikesh agreed, provided the automated version was tested against a control.

On 6 October 2026 Ira recommended building the resident supply loop for ₹38 lakh over ten weeks, keeping operators only in the four thinnest localities, and holding the ₹1.35 crore model upgrade against the 8.4 per cent fabrication slice until acceptance passed 60 per cent on supply alone. Himmat accepted the first two but argued that fabrication damages trust out of proportion to its frequency — which the test cannot settle.

Three questions. First, Harita's test produced a 62.4-point gap at roughly 13.5 standard errors: what result would have made her recommend Sentinel Pro, and did she write it down before 20 July? Second, Ilaaka's operator arm gave the larger lift and the worse decision — when should a manager ship the expensive arm anyway? Third, take a product you use daily: name the assumption which, if false, would cost its makers most, and the cheapest artefact that could falsify it.

13. Going deeper

Product deconstruction — naming a product's user, job, promise, business model, key metric and biggest assumption: the reflex behind Exhibit 6. B2B vs B2C — the buyer-user-approver split is why enterprise discovery yields products admired but unused. Product sense and taste — what to do when no test arrives in time. Reasoning about trade-offs — what turns a 13.1-point lift and a ₹6.18 crore cost into a decision. First-principles reasoning — the exercise that interrogates the frame. Product critique — arguing in public with evidence.
exp20v2-sense.design.thinking:
Design thinking

Foundations, Product Thinking and Product Sense. How to keep discovery, ideation and testing as habits rather than a workshop run once.

1. The board question

On 14 July 2026, Bhavna Iyengar, head of product at Bagicha Plant Services, sat in the Bengaluru office with a number she could not stop looking at. Bagicha sells indoor plants through an app and delivers them across eleven Indian cities. In the quarter that had just closed, 48,000 customers had placed a first order. Within thirty days, 9,600 of them, one in five, had filed a claim that the plant had died and asked for a refund.

The founder, Bipin Arora, had a remedy ready: a paid "Care Plan" subscription with scheduled advice, replacement guarantees and monthly soil top-ups. Engineering in Pune estimated twelve weeks and ₹36 lakh.

Bhavna thought Bipin had a hypothesis and was treating it as a finding. If the subscription addressed the wrong cause, Bagicha would spend ₹36 lakh and still lose roughly ₹40 lakh a quarter to refunds. She proposed an eight-week discovery programme, budgeted at ₹7 lakh. Charu Sinha, her designer in Kolkata, and Chetan Rawat, her engineer in Pune, were willing. Bipin asked: "Is this not just another workshop?" This page explains why the answer must be no.

2. The idea

Design thinking is a disciplined way of solving problems for other people. It starts with direct observation of them, states the problem in their terms, generates many answers, builds cheap versions of the best, and tests those with real users. The five stages are empathise (learn how the user experiences the situation by watching and listening), define, ideate, prototype (any inexpensive artefact, from a sketch to a hand-run service, that lets a user react before anything is built) and test.

The roots lie in Herbert Simon's 1969 book The Sciences of the Artificial, which described design as devising courses of action to turn an existing situation into a preferred one. The practice was packaged by the consultancy IDEO, founded in 1991 by David Kelley and colleagues, and by Stanford's d.school, which Kelley helped start in 2005. It was meant to solve a familiar problem: organisations built things people did not want, because builders mistook assumptions for knowledge.

The sentence Bhavna could repeat without sounding glib: "We will find out what is killing the plants before we decide what to build, in the cheapest way that could change our minds."

3. How it actually works

The diagram invites a misreading, that the stages run once in sequence. In practice the loop turns many times.

Empathise began on 20 July. Charu and Bhavna interviewed 24 customers whose plants had died, asking each to walk through the plant's life from the delivery box onwards: where it sat, who watered it, what they saw on which day. They avoided "why did it die?", because customers answer with a theory, usually blaming Bagicha. The interviews ran until 7 August.

The step practitioners usually leave implicit is coding: assigning each death to a cause using rules fixed beforehand, so the tally reflects the transcripts and not the team's preferences. Define then turned the tally into a problem statement of the form "[user] needs [need] because [insight]". Ideate generated roughly forty candidate responses without judging them. Prototype chose one that could be run by hand for a few thousand rupees. Test compared its results with an untreated group.

Two implicit steps deserve naming. Before testing, the team wrote down what result would make them abandon the idea. And they chose who could declare failure: Chetan, an engineer with no stake in any remedy.

4. A worked example

The coding of the 24 interviews gave the tally below; each percentage is the count divided by 24.

Overwatering led, and the subscription was not designed to fix it: the Care Plan assumed customers lacked supplies and replacement cover, not that they were drowning the plant with kindness. The problem statement became: "A first-time owner needs to know, in the first fortnight, when not to water, because the instinct to care is what kills the plant."

The prototype was a "concierge" service, one performed by people before any software exists. For 200 randomly chosen new customers, a staff member sent WhatsApp messages on days 3, 7 and 12 saying whether to water. Another 200, chosen the same way, received nothing extra. Staff time cost ₹150 per treated customer, so the prototype cost 200 × ₹150 = ₹30,000. Launched on 10 August, it was read 30 days later, on 9 September.

The treated group's rate was 8.5 per cent against 19.0 per cent, a gap of 10.5 percentage points, or 10.5 / 19.0 = 55.3 per cent fewer claims. To see what this is worth, scale to a quarter of 48,000 first-time customers. The avoided claims are 48,000 × 0.105 = 5,040, worth 5,040 × ₹420 = ₹21,16,800, or ₹21.17 lakh. Automated reminders would cost about ₹12 per customer, so 48,000 × ₹12 = ₹5,76,000, or ₹5.76 lakh. The net is ₹21,16,800 minus ₹5,76,000 = ₹15,40,800, about ₹15.41 lakh a quarter.

Now change one input. Suppose automation keeps only half the effect, a gap of 5.25 points. Avoided claims become 48,000 × 0.0525 = 2,520, worth 2,520 × ₹420 = ₹10,58,400; net of ₹5,76,000, the gain is ₹4,82,400, or about ₹4.82 lakh. Break-even is where savings equal cost: ₹5,76,000 / ₹420 = about 1,371 claims, or 1,371 / 48,000 = 2.9 percentage points. The idea survives unless automation loses more than about 72.8 per cent of the effect (1 − 2.857 / 10.5 = 0.728).

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Method is not mindset

A workshop with sticky notes is a method. The mindset is treating each belief about users as a hypothesis with a cheap test attached. A team can run the method every quarter and never be wrong in public. The measure is whether any plan changed.

Empathy is evidence, not sympathy

Empathising means collecting observations of behaviour. The Bagicha interviews recorded events, such as daily watering with no drainage hole, which customers had not connected to the death.

Stated and revealed need differ

Customers who say they want a subscription are predicting their behaviour, and people predict it poorly. What a user does in a prototype outranks what they say about a description.

The loop is for uncertainty, not for everything

Where need and solution are both known, such as a payment page that must follow RBI rules, design thinking adds delay. It earns its cost where it is unclear who the user is or what would work.

Confusions with neighbouring ideas

Design thinking is often confused with interface design, which concerns how a screen looks, and with agile delivery, which concerns building software in short cycles. It is the ancestor of continuous discovery, weekly customer contact. It is not market research, which measures a population and not the lived detail of a few people.

Small samples cannot size anything

Twenty-four interviews reveal which causes exist, not how common each is. Exhibit 3 guides what to test; it is not a forecast. Even the 400-customer test carries sampling error.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who exactly is the user? What would we do differently if the test said no? Who decides it failed?

6. Across product types and company stages

The loop is the same everywhere, but whom you observe and what you build differ.

In consumer products, tests resolve quickly because volume is large. In B2B, the user, the payer and the approver are usually different people; interviewing only the first yields a product that is loved and never bought, and a sample of ten accounts is a serious sample.

In a marketplace, there are two users and a relationship between them. A concierge prototype, with staff matching by hand, shows what each side values before an algorithm is built.

Stage matters too. In an early company the founder speaks to customers weekly. In a large one the danger is distance: research sits in a separate team and decision makers never hear a customer. The remedy is to put them in the room for a few interviews.

7. Common mistakes

Three mistakes recur, each visible from outside.

The first often follows a workshop: a wall of notes and nobody owning the link from insight to decision. Name a recent decision that changed because of what a customer did.

The second arises because friendly users are easy to find, and their reactions are warmer and less informative. If tested people differ from targeted people on attributes that drive behaviour, the result describes someone else.

The third is subtlest. If the team would have launched whatever the test showed, it was a ceremony. A written threshold held by a person without a stake turns ceremony into evidence.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the Bagicha decision looked like the plan below, presented to the board in July. It cost ₹7.00 lakh in total, 19.4 per cent of the ₹36 lakh subscription build.

Three features distinguish it. The question was written down first. The failure threshold was agreed in advance: a gap of at least 2.9 percentage points after automation, the break-even from Section 4. And Bipin sat in on three of the 24 interviews, so the evidence was not second-hand.

9. Closing: the decision

At the 11 September meeting, Bhavna presented Exhibits 3 and 4 and recommended that Bagicha automate the reminder sequence, at a running cost of ₹5.76 lakh a quarter, before committing to the Care Plan. Her reasoning: the dominant cause was behavioural, not a supply problem; the 10.5-point gap was large enough that even a halving would pay; and the subscription was not refuted, only deferred, to be tested later as a concierge offer with the same discipline.

Bipin accepted, on one condition: a repeat of the test on the automated version, with the same break-even rule. That condition is the point. Design thinking is a habit when the next question is how to test, not whether.

Next, study continuous discovery, where a team talks to customers weekly and keeps a map of assumptions, turning the loop from an episode into a rhythm. After that, learn experiment design and sample-size reasoning.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a product you use daily: which assumption about its users, if wrong, would cost its makers the most, and what is the cheapest way you could test it? Second, in your own team, who has the standing to say a test has failed, and would they be willing to say it?
case40v1-sense.design.thinking:
Sasya Field Networks: The Season After the Sprint

An ambiguous case. Sasya Field Networks is fictional; its market is real.

1. Sunday night, 15 November 2026

The flat in Kondapur was quiet by nine, a week after Diwali on Sunday 8 November. Charulekha Hublikar, senior vice-president for product at Sasya Field Networks, had laid six exhibits across the dining table in the order she meant to present them, changing it twice.

The board met at Gachibowli at nine the next morning, Monday 16 November, with one item, written by the chief executive: How will Sasya learn what its partners and farmers actually need, and what will that cost? The rabi spraying window opened on Thursday 10 December, twenty-four days later; whatever was decided had to be standing in a field by then, or wait for kharif.

Eight months earlier Sasya had spent ₹1.48 crore on an eleven-week human-centred design engagement: five personas, three journey maps, forty-one opportunity areas, twelve prioritised concepts. Three had shipped, and revenue per acre had fallen every quarter since. Charulekha did not think the money wasted; she also could not say what it had changed.

2. The company, and one decision that still binds

Sasya was registered in Hyderabad in June 2019 by Chirayu Hasabnis, an agri-input marketer, and Chandrabhan Haldankar, an agronomist from Nizamabad, selling soil testing and advisory through dealers. The Drone Rules of August 2021 changed it: by 2022 Sasya was flying spray sorties itself, and by March 2023 it had stopped flying and begun building a network of village entrepreneurs who bought a drone, took a DGCA remote-pilot certificate and worked bookings through the Sasya Partner app, while farmers and FPO staff raised demand on Sasya Khet.

Two decisions still bind. The first put the asset on the partner's balance sheet: in September 2024, to make kit loans available at all, Sasya guaranteed the first 8 per cent of losses on the pool lent by Sthaayi Finance Services, an NBFC. The pool is 318 loans averaging ₹6.4 lakh, or ₹20.35 crore, of which ₹14.6 crore is outstanding, so the cap is ₹1.63 crore. At 30 September 2026 loans ninety days overdue stood at ₹1.21 crore — 8.3 per cent of the ₹14.6 crore outstanding, 74.3 per cent of the cap.

The second: in 2023, 180 recruits were given a letter assuring them “not less than 600 acres of work in a full year”. Nobody can find who approved the wording, and legal opinion is divided on whether it binds. At the partner's 82 per cent share of the realised ₹478 an acre — ₹391.96 — a 170-acre shortfall is ₹66,633 a partner, ₹1.20 crore across the 180.

3. The industry

Drone spraying in India in 2026 has more supply than demand and more subsidy than either. State agriculture departments fund custom hiring centres, the Namo Drone Didi scheme places drones with women's self-help groups, and NABARD-refinanced loans with SMAM subsidy of up to 40 per cent in Sasya's states lower the cost of entry. IFFCO's Kisan Drones and Garuda Aerospace operate nationally; Dhanuka Agritech's and Coromandel International's drone-applied formulations and Mahindra's farm-mechanisation services push from the input side.

Regulation sits on both sides: DGCA governs the aircraft and the pilot certificate, the CIB&RC procedure what may be sprayed, at what dose, with what buffer. Spray services carry GST at 18 per cent, which farmer customers cannot set off, and farmer records, including the video design researchers love, fall under the DPDP Act. Jio's rural network makes the app possible and, where it does not reach, makes its data unreliable. The exposure is not only Indian: engineering sits in Bengaluru, design in Amsterdam, data science in Melbourne, sales in Chicago, and the largest prospective contract is with Samrudhi Greenhouse Industries in Abu Dhabi (Figure 2).

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Figure 1 is the sequence. Through 2025 the company believed that acres bound everything and adding partners added acres; that price was stable near ₹500 an acre; and that the app's data described the field.

Exhibit 1 is six quarters of operating record: acres rose, money did not follow. Across matched half-years, 1,81,000 acres in April–September 2026 against 1,66,000 a year earlier is a rise of 9.0 per cent on the 2025 base, while service revenue fell from ₹847.60 lakh to ₹830.54 lakh, down 2.0 per cent. Realised price per acre went from ₹510.60 to ₹458.86: a fall of ₹51.74, or 10.1 per cent of the earlier figure.

Exhibit 2 shows what the base does underneath: of 710 partners onboarded between April 2025 and March 2026, 391, or 55.1 per cent of those 710, were still flying past day 180.

Exhibit 3 is where the partner's own arithmetic appears and two company documents disagree. The left column is the sheet used to recruit partners since 2023; the right is the payout ledger for the 362 partners who flew in all twelve months to 30 September 2026, survivors who sprayed 1,55,660 acres, 50.2 per cent of the network's 3,10,000 acres.

Exhibit 4 is the only direct account of why partners stop, and it is incomplete: field operations reached 214 of the 319 not flying at day 180, 67.1 per cent of them. Of the 214, 173 — 80.8 per cent of them, and 54.2 per cent of all 319 — named something from the first months with the machine.

Exhibit 5 reads as proof, and has done the most damage. The redesigned app went live in six of the seventeen districts in June and July 2026. In Q2 FY27 those six averaged 169.27 acres per active partner against 125.80 in the other eleven, a gap of 34.6 per cent on the eleven-district figure. But the six were chosen because they were strongest: in Q4 FY26, before rollout, they averaged 142.95 against 89.29, a gap of 60.1 per cent on the same basis. The gap narrowed. The quarters are also different seasons — Q4 FY26 rabi, Q2 FY27 kharif — and are not comparable without an adjustment nobody has made.

Against all this sits the engagement. Svara Design Collective, a studio with offices in Amsterdam and Bengaluru, worked with Sasya for eleven weeks from Tuesday 6 January to Tuesday 24 March 2026: ₹93.50 lakh of retainer at ₹8.50 lakh a week, ₹14.60 lakh of field travel, ₹6.20 lakh of translation and video editing, ₹24.20 lakh of internal time (44 person-weeks at ₹55,000) and ₹9.80 lakh for the readout of 14 April 2026 — ₹148.30 lakh in all. Of the twelve concepts, three shipped, two are in build, four sit in the backlog, two were dropped and one cannot be traced to an owner. Chirayu divides ₹148.30 lakh by three and gets ₹49.43 lakh a shipped concept; Camiel Hoekstra says that is the wrong division. The research rested on 22 interviews, 19 in two districts.

5. The people

  • Charulekha Hublikar, SVP product, Hyderabad, owns the recommendation. She thinks discovery was run as an event rather than a habit, and knows that saying so sounds like a defence of the ₹1.48 crore she argued for. Unsaid: she has not sat through a spray day since February 2026.
  • Chirayu Hasabnis, co-founder and chief executive, wants one number and one owner on Monday. For February 2027's Series C he has shown Saamya Growth Partners a path to ₹60 crore of revenue in FY28, against FY26's ₹21.59 crore, of which ₹14.83 crore, or 68.7 per cent, was service revenue. Unsaid: he approved the Svara engagement over his finance head's objection.
  • Chandrabhan Haldankar, co-founder, field operations, Nizamabad, is measured on active partner count, which rose every quarter in Exhibit 1. Partners leave, he says, because the work is not there. Unsaid: the ₹18.70 lakh of top-ups came from floats he controls, in districts that now look like proof the redesign worked.
  • Chinmayi Herlekar, chief technology officer, Bengaluru, wants discovery frozen until the backlog clears, and has committed three engineers to Samrudhi from 1 December 2026. Unsaid: the three shipped concepts took two-fifths of squad capacity in Q1 FY27 and she cannot attach any to a metric.
  • Camiel Hoekstra, design lead, Amsterdam, four and a half hours behind Hyderabad in November, says the engagement was the start of a practice and was treated as a deliverable; he wants weekly teardowns and a standing partner panel. Unsaid: 19 of his 22 interviews were in two districts, and he has not visited a district since March.
  • Charlotte Haig, data scientist, Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead, built Exhibits 1, 2 and 5 and wrote the footnotes that contradict how they are read. She wants a holdout district before any further rollout. Unsaid: her two definitions of “active” are unreconciled, and the app under-counts sorties flown where the network does not reach.
  • Curtis Holbrook, enterprise sales, Chicago, eleven and a half hours behind, wants the money in plantations and greenhouses, and has Samrudhi's ₹3.80 crore letter of intent of 2 September 2026. Unsaid: 60 per cent of it is milestone-linked against unscoped milestones, and the contract assumes a nozzle Sasya does not make.
  • Charumathi Hombal, partner success, Hyderabad, says Exhibit 4's first row is the whole case: seven spares depots at ₹14 lakh each, ₹98 lakh in all, against a median eleven-day downtime. Unsaid: her team dropped the 105 unreached partners when calling hours ran out.

6. Voices

“You are reading a selection effect as an outcome. Those districts were ahead by 60.1 per cent before a screen changed and are ahead by 34.6 per cent now.”

Charlotte Haig, on the board pack draft, 11 November 2026

“I flew with Chandrakanth Hugar in Kalaburagi in February. His machine was down nineteen days that quarter and he never opened the app. Our analytics counted him inactive. He counted himself a man with a loan.”

Camiel Hoekstra, internal chat, 10 November 2026

“I am not against research. I am against research that arrives as a sprint item on a Thursday, when my engineers are owed to Samrudhi.”

Chinmayi Herlekar, engineering review, 5 November 2026

“Sir, the drone is good. The acres are not there. Last rabi I waited eleven days for one part, and in those days the dealer's machine took my village.”

Chandrakanth Hugar, Track A partner, Kalaburagi, 14 September 2026

7. The options as Charulekha sees them

Four options, costed in Exhibit 6 against FY26 revenue of ₹21.59 crore.

Option A buys depth and an owner, and repeats the shape of the thing now being audited. Option B can start before 10 December and puts empathising, ideating and testing inside the squads that ship, but it spends engineers already promised to Abu Dhabi, and has no answer to how a squad records a farmer's DPDP consent on a bund at six in the morning. Option C treats Exhibit 4's second row, empty days, as the cause and buys a quarter of calm, while turning a 2023 letter from a liability into a policy. Option D accepts that the village network may be the wrong business, on the evidence of a letter of intent rather than a customer. All four answer “how much research should we buy?” None answers what Exhibit 3 asks, whether a partner can earn at 430 acres at any price Sasya can charge.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

Sthaayi wrote on Sunday 11 October 2026 asking for ₹1.10 crore of additional cash collateral by Monday 30 November, citing the ₹1.21 crore of ninety-day arrears against the ₹1.63 crore cap. Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹38.40 crore against net burn of ₹2.90 crore a month: a runway of 13.2 months, to about the first week of November 2027. The board's July 2026 instruction is that revenue per acre stabilise at ₹480 or better by Q4 FY27, against ₹452 in Q2 FY27. Three engineers are committed to Samrudhi from 1 December, 60 per cent of that ₹3.80 crore being milestone-linked. Rabi opens on 10 December. CIB&RC and the August advisory restrict what may be sprayed; the DPDP Act, what may be recorded. The 180 letters, worth ₹1.20 crore if enforced, are untested.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Treat the Sasya Partner app as a live product: name its user, that user's job, its promise, business model, key metric and biggest unexamined assumption. Does the answer change if the product is the drone?
  2. Exhibit 1 shows acres up 9.0 per cent and service revenue down 2.0 per cent across matched half-years. Give the three most plausible explanations, and the exhibit that would separate them.
  3. Exhibit 5 has twice been read as evidence that the redesign worked. State what it does and does not support, and what the rollout should have looked like.
  4. Exhibits 3 and 4 disagree: one says the unit cannot earn, the other that the machine is down and the acres are missing. Can both be true? What would you measure in the first fortnight of rabi to tell?
  5. The readout produced 41 opportunity areas and 12 concepts; three shipped. Was that a failure of method, of ownership, or of what the company did on the Monday after? Which option in Exhibit 6 changes any of it?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November. What do you do before rabi opens on 10 December, what do you stop, who owns it, and what number by what date would tell you that you were wrong? What do you say to the board about the ₹1.48 crore already spent and Sthaayi's ₹1.10 crore due on 30 November?

10. Sunday night, continued

At eleven Charulekha put Exhibit 5 on top of the pack, moved it to the bottom, then put it back, because leaving it out would look like hiding it. Camiel's message was still unanswered: a photograph from February of Chandrakanth Hugar's drone with its arm off against a cot, and one line — we never went back.
case20v1-sense.design.thinking:
Iraada Systems: After the Workshop

A decision case in design thinking

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 13 October 2026, Navya Sheth stayed on in Iraada Systems' Pune office after the product floor emptied, a printout of the February workshop report on her desk and a calendar reminder on her screen: the board's budget meeting on Friday, 30 October. As head of product, she had to walk into that meeting with a single proposal for how Iraada would learn from its customers over the next twelve months. Three colleagues had already given her three different answers, each partly right.

The February workshop report was handsome, with journey maps and a ranked list of fourteen ideas. Eight months later it had changed very little: restaurant owners were still leaving in their first three months, at a rate that had worsened every quarter since.

2. Company background

Iraada Systems, founded in Pune in 2019, sells Iraada Counter, a tablet-based billing, table-ordering and kitchen-display system for independent restaurants, cafes and cloud kitchens. A typical customer is a single-outlet owner in Pune, Nagpur, Indore, Coimbatore, Lucknow or Surat who pays ₹2,000 a month. It prints GST-compliant bills, takes UPI payments through Razorpay and merges Zomato and Swiggy orders onto one kitchen screen.

The market is crowded. Established vendors such as Petpooja serve the same owners, and ONDC-linked apps are lowering the cost of listing a menu. Iraada's argument has always been speed of setup and simplicity during a Saturday-night rush. By October 2026 it had about 5,200 paying outlets, which at ₹2,000 a month is ₹12.48 crore of annual recurring revenue (5,200 × ₹2,000 × 12). Acquiring an outlet costs about ₹9,000 in sales time, hardware subsidy and onboarding.

3. The situation

Retention is the problem, and Exhibit 1 shows it. The company tracks the share of newly signed outlets still active ninety days later. For the cohort that signed between July and September 2025 the figure was 77.0 per cent; for the cohort that signed between April and June 2026, the most recent to have matured, it was 69.1 per cent. Across all four cohorts, 2,700 outlets signed and 1,964 were still active at ninety days, a blended 72.7 per cent. The simple average of the four quarterly rates is 73.0 per cent, which flatters the picture because the weaker cohorts were also the larger ones.

The workshop was held on Thursday and Friday, 12 and 13 February 2026, in a hotel in Pune. Twenty-two people attended, a facilitator was hired for ₹6.5 lakh, and venue and travel cost another ₹3.5 lakh, ₹10 lakh in all. Participants produced fourteen ideas. By 31 March, three had shipped, six sat in the backlog, three had been dropped as too costly, and two could not be traced to anyone. The Jan–Mar cohort, which signed during and just after the workshop, retained at 71.0 per cent; the next cohort, at 69.1 per cent. No one had visited a restaurant in person since February.

Nurul Samsudin's customer-success team in Kuala Lumpur had called the 235 outlets that signed between April and June but were gone by day ninety (760 signed less 525 active). Exhibit 2 shows what they said.

Only 18 outlets cited price. Of the 235, 207 (94 + 71 + 42, or 88.1 per cent) point to something in the first days of use. Each lost outlet wasted roughly ₹9,000 of acquisition spend, so the 235 cost about ₹21.15 lakh in that one quarter alone.

4. The people

Neeraj Saxena, co-founder and chief executive in Pune, wants a number to take to the board and is wary of anything that sounds like another workshop.

Nishith Sawhney, chief technology officer in Bengaluru, leads the engineers who built the order-sync layer. He fears that every field finding becomes an unplanned sprint item.

Nael Soares, the lead designer, works from Lisbon, five and a half hours behind Pune in winter. He facilitated the internal side of the February workshop and has been arguing since March that a workshop was never the point: "We ran the ritual and skipped the habit." He wants a standing research function.

Nurul Samsudin, head of customer success in Kuala Lumpur, hears the exit calls and the Saturday-night complaints first. She wants her team's findings to reach the people who change the product within the same week.

Nyambura Sang, the data scientist in Nairobi, has built the retention dashboard behind Exhibit 1. She can show where in the funnel outlets stall, though not why, and she is uneasy that the company might treat her charts as a substitute for talking to owners.

5. The options

Navya has narrowed the choice to three, costed in Exhibit 3. The base for the percentages is annual recurring revenue of ₹12.48 crore.

Option A builds a permanent team, led by Nael, that runs a research sprint every quarter. Its upside is depth and independence from the delivery calendar. Its cost is ₹1.8 crore, a first sprint no earlier than January 2027 given hiring time, and a risk that squads wait on research rather than do it.

Option B makes the practice belong to the six product squads. Each squad runs one customer session a week, in a restaurant or by phone from Kuala Lumpur, testing a small prototype or a changed screen with a real owner and cook. A coordinator keeps the calendar and log. It starts within a week and costs ₹38.4 lakh, but it takes squad time and depends on engineers attending.

Option C doubles down on the dashboard and A/B tests. It is the cheapest and fits Neeraj's wish for numbers. The cost is that it can only test what the company has already thought to build and cannot explain why a cook gave up during a rush.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, who is the user Iraada is failing, what job were they hiring the product to do, and what is the promise they feel was broken?

2. What did the February workshop produce, and what did it leave out? Which of the five stages (empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test) did Iraada practise once and which never?

3. In Exhibit 3, which option best matches the evidence in Exhibit 2, and what does each assume about where learning should live?

4. What would you recommend to the board on 30 October, and what result by what date would tell you the choice was wrong?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Design thinking is useful here not as an event but as a loop that has to run again and again: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test. Iraada ran the first two stages in a hotel for two days and then stopped. The exit calls show that the biggest losses, 207 of 235 outlets, come from moments only visible by watching an owner and a cook use the product: slow menu import, a screen that fails at rush hour, an order feed that drifts.

One defensible path: Option B, with Nyambura's data in support. It matches the evidence, costs 3.1 per cent of ARR against Option A's 14.4 per cent, and starts before Diwali on 8 November, when restaurants are busiest and the learning is sharpest. An extra retained outlet is worth ₹24,000 a year (₹2,000 × 12), so ₹38.4 lakh is recovered by about 160 additional retained outlets. At the Apr–Jun pace of 760 sign-ups a quarter, or roughly 3,040 a year, that is about 5.3 percentage points of retention. Returning from 69.1 to the 77.0 per cent the company achieved a year earlier is 7.9 points, so the plan only has to deliver two-thirds of the recovery to break even, before counting the avoided acquisition spend.

Making it a habit rather than a ritual. The board paper should specify the loop, not the budget alone: a fixed weekly slot, a shared log, a rule that every squad ships or kills one change from the log each fortnight, and Nishith's engineers attending at least one session each month so findings do not pass through a translator. Nurul's team feeds the pipeline; Nyambura's dashboard is the test that a change worked. Nael coaches the squads, and a review after two quarters decides whether Option A is then justified. The ninety-day retention of each cohort, measured exactly as in Exhibit 1, is the metric. The risk: if engineers treat sessions as optional, Option B degrades into another workshop with a lower price tag.
case20v1-sense.idea.criteria:
Three Ideas, One Squad

Jivanta Pharmacy Systems and the choice of what to build next

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 12 October 2026, Onkar Tidke stood at the whiteboard in the Baner office of Jivanta Pharmacy Systems in Pune, looking at three sticky notes he had stuck up in a row. Each carried one line: "stock credit", "prescription scan", "expiry returns". The company could afford to put exactly one engineering squad on a new product for the next three quarters, and the board would meet on Friday, 23 October, eleven days away, to approve the plan. The Diwali roadmap freeze, which fell on Sunday, 8 November that year, left no room to dither afterwards.

Each idea had a champion on his leadership team and a deck. What Tidke, the co-founder and chief executive, lacked was a common yardstick. He put the question simply: which of these ideas is worth a team's time, and on which criterion is each one weakest?

2. Company background

Jivanta, founded in 2018, sells billing, inventory and GST-compliance software to independent pharmacies, the neighbourhood chemists that still dispense most of the medicines bought in Indian towns. At the end of September 2026 it had 24,000 pharmacies on annual subscriptions averaging ₹6,000 each, an annual subscription revenue of ₹14.4 crore (24,000 × ₹6,000). Customers were concentrated in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.

Marg ERP and Zoho Books were the incumbents in pharmacy accounting. Tata 1mg, PharmEasy, Netmeds and Apollo Pharmacy pulled prescription demand towards chains and apps, while ONDC and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission opened standards for open-network commerce and health data. CDSCO and state drug controllers regulate medicine sales, and the DPDP Act governs customer health data. Jivanta's advantage was that its software sat open on the pharmacist's counter all day.

3. The situation

Between 31 August and 2 October 2026, five weeks of fieldwork, Jivanta's product team interviewed 60 pharmacy owners in Pune, Nagpur, Indore, Jaipur and Lucknow. Each owner named their three biggest operating problems unprompted, then said what they already spent money or time on to cope. Three ideas emerged from that work, and Exhibit 1 sets out what the owners said. Every percentage in it is taken against the same base of 60 owners.

Stock credit. Distributors expect payment quickly, while insurers and corporate accounts pay pharmacies late. Jivanta would let an owner draw short-term stock credit from a partner non-banking lender, with the order flowing through its software. Forty-two of the 60 owners (70 per cent) put cash flow among their top three problems, and 30 (50 per cent) already used informal credit from distributors or moneylenders.

Prescription scan. A phone camera would read a doctor's handwritten prescription and fill the bill. Only 15 of 60 owners (25 per cent) listed prescription entry in their top three problems; just 6 (10 per cent) did anything about it today.

Expiry returns. Pharmacies lose money on stock that goes near expiry. Distributors will often take it back, but the paperwork, the timing windows and the credit notes are handled on WhatsApp and paper. Jivanta would flag near-expiry batches from the inventory it already holds and raise return requests to distributors. Thirty-six of 60 owners (60 per cent) put expiry losses in their top three, and 24 (40 per cent) already spent staff time chasing returns.

4. The people

  • Onkar Tidke, Pune. Chief executive and owner of the decision; wants a bet that matters without threatening the core business.
  • Omesh Telkar, Jaipur. Head of sales. He champions stock credit: owners talk about credit "as though it were oxygen", and he fears losing accounts to Marg ERP.
  • Ojasvi Tambolkar, Pune. Head of engineering. She favours the scan as the most buildable and distrusts anything that depends on a partner's systems.
  • Oorja Thengdi, Nairobi. Data scientist. She is candid that handwriting from small-town clinics is far noisier than her demonstration samples, and wants the idea with the clearest metric.
  • Oviya Tapkire, Lisbon. Lead designer. Watching the recordings from a different time zone, she saw owners light up on expiry and go flat on prescriptions.

5. The numbers behind the ideas

Tidke asked the finance lead for a sizing of each idea against the existing 24,000-pharmacy base only, ignoring new customers. Exhibit 2 shows the result. The adoption rates are planning assumptions agreed with the team, not measurements. Revenue per adopting pharmacy is a fee of ₹1,200 a year for the scan and ₹3,000 a year for expiry returns. Stock credit earns a 1.5 per cent fee on credit disbursed, and the plan assumes each adopting pharmacy draws ₹12 lakh a year, which gives ₹18,000 a year per pharmacy.

Read quickly, Exhibit 2 favours stock credit: it would add 60 per cent to current revenue against 15 per cent for expiry returns. But it depends on a lender taking the risk on ₹576 crore of annual disbursals, under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions, and Jivanta has no credit team. The scan's ₹0.432 crore would cover only 36 per cent of its ₹1.2 crore squad cost in a year (0.432 ÷ 1.2).

Tidke then asked each of the five leaders to score the ideas on five criteria drawn from the failure literature he had read: unmet need, viable solution, market, timing and team. Each criterion was scored from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong). Exhibit 3 gives the averaged judgments.

The totals are close, so the information is in the weakest cell of each column. Stock credit scores 5 on market but 2 on solution and team. The scan scores 1 on market, which no engineering will repair. Expiry returns has nothing below 3, but depends on distributors accepting returns through Jivanta; of three regional distributors approached, two said they would try it.

6. The options

  1. Option 1: Build stock credit. Upside: ₹8.64 crore a year at assumption and strong need. Cost: ₹1.60 crore, a lender dependency, regulatory exposure and no credit experience.
  2. Option 2: Build prescription scan. Upside: quickest to build. Cost: ₹1.2 crore for ₹0.432 crore a year, and only a quarter of owners see the problem.
  3. Option 3: Build expiry returns, in stages. Upside: clear need and data Jivanta already holds; ₹2.16 crore a year. Cost: ₹1.2 crore, and distributors may not play along.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. For each idea, what do Exhibit 1's two columns tell you about who has the problem and whether they would pay to solve it?
  2. Exhibit 2 puts stock credit far ahead on revenue. What would have to be true for that figure to be reliable, and which of the five criteria does it fail to capture?
  3. Why might the lowest score in each column matter more than the total in Exhibit 3? How would you describe each idea's biggest assumption?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 23 October, what would you test first, and what result would make you stop?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as the reasons products fail, turned around: a real unmet need, a buildable solution, a large enough market, a reason to work now, and a capable team. The discipline is to name each idea's weakest criterion rather than let one strong score (market, for stock credit) cover a weak one. A good answer treats Exhibit 1 as behavioural evidence, with money or time already spent counting more than stated pain, and Exhibit 2 as assumptions rather than facts.

One defensible path is Option 3. Expiry returns has the best total (18 of 25), no score below 3, and 60 per cent of owners name the problem. Stock credit has the largest prize, but its weakest criteria, solution and team, cannot be fixed within nine months; park it until a lending partner and credit lead exist. The scan fails on market, the criterion least open to improvement.

Option 3's weakness is the distributor link, so test it first: a six-week pilot from Monday, 16 November to Friday, 25 December 2026 with the two willing distributors and a few hundred pharmacies. Set the stop rule in advance: if distributors accept fewer than half the return requests raised, the idea has failed its weakest criterion, and the board should reopen the choice.
exp40v2-sense.idea.criteria:
What Makes a Good Product Idea

The five criteria as a conditional structure, not a scorecard.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On Tuesday 15 September 2026, Kanishka Jadhav, vice-president of product at Kasauti Diagnostics Industries in Pune, had twenty-three days before her board's investment committee met on Thursday 8 October. Kasauti builds point-of-care haematology analysers and their reporting software, sold to small pathology labs and nursing homes. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it earned ₹86.40 crore, of which ₹46.97 crore — 54.4 per cent — came from reagents rather than machines. The base stood at 4,200 analysers across 2,900 sites.

The committee had ₹14.50 crore for six quarters and two programmes competing for it. Programme S was a connected-reporting subscription at ₹2,500 a month per analyser, sold into the base Kasauti already owns; Komal Jaitley, the data lead in Indore, had a working prototype. Programme H was a stripped-down analyser at ₹1,15,000 against the current ₹2,65,000, aimed at clinics too small to buy today; Keshav Jogalekar, who runs hardware engineering, wanted eighteen months, a new reagent chemistry and a device licence.

Two days later, on Thursday 17 September, Jayanti Kurup faced it in miniature at Karuna Elder Care Services in Bengaluru. Karuna sends attendants to elderly parents' homes in six cities, keeping 22 per cent of each booking. FY2026 brought ₹24.80 crore of gross bookings and ₹5.46 crore of net revenue. In August 2026 its 11,400 active households made 18,600 shift requests, an average of 1.63 each, of which 14,508 were filled — exactly 78.0 per cent — leaving 4,092 unfilled. Nine engineers came free on Monday 5 October, eighteen days away. The founder, Jairaj Kantharia, wanted them on a remote-monitoring subscription: sensors in the flat, a nurse desk round the clock, ₹1,200 a month. Jayanti wanted rostering software.

Both knew the standard screen — unmet need, viable solution, market, timing, team, and the rule that an idea is only as strong as its weakest criterion. Both found that it said where to look and not what to do.

2. The idea: a conditional structure, and who disagrees

Define the terms; looseness is where arguments start. An unmet need is a problem an identified group already spends money, time or risk on, served badly by today's alternatives. A viable solution is an artefact buildable with the technology at hand, good enough for that group to switch. A market is a count of payers, a price and a reachable path to them — not a count of people with the problem. Timing is a change in cost, regulation or behaviour that makes the thing possible now. Team is whoever will build and sell it, plus the distribution they command.

The framework was assembled from failure. Levitt's Marketing Myopia (1960) showed that firms define their business by their product and are then surprised by demand; Drucker's Innovation and Entrepreneurship (1985) located opportunity in external change; Blank's customer-development work from 2005 reframed a start-up as a search for a fact. The modern five-part list is the 2010s post-mortem literature read backwards — and a checklist derived from failure rejects well and ranks poorly.

This page argues the last position, bounded by the fourth. The criteria are not five scores to average but five conditions that must jointly hold — multiplicatively. Give each the probability that it holds on present evidence and the idea's probability is their product, which changes the arithmetic by a factor of four.

Exhibit 2. 0.730 ÷ 0.17136 = 4.26.

3. Mechanics: leverage, and the price of finding out

Kanishka's team put probabilities on both programmes, each tied to named evidence. S scored 0.40 on need — Komal's twenty-eight lab interviews found labs already forwarding results by hand on WhatsApp and treating it as free — 0.90 on solution, the prototype existing, then 0.70, 0.80 and 0.85 on market, timing and team. H scored 0.80 on need, 0.55 on solution with the cheaper chemistry unproven, 0.75 on market, 0.45 on timing because the device licence sits on a regulatory calendar nobody controls, and 0.70 on team.

Because the structure is multiplicative, the sensitivity of the joint to any one criterion is the joint divided by that criterion's own probability: if J = Π pi, then ∂J/∂pi = J ÷ pi. The lowest criterion therefore always has the highest leverage, being the smallest divisor. The weakest-link heuristic is not folklore; it is a derivative. It is also silent on how far a criterion can be moved, what moving it costs, and how large the prize behind it is.
