Exhibit 6. Two of five preconditions fail somewhere — the normal case.

Three situations make the screen misleading. The defensive move — a payments-rail migration, a localisation rule, a platform shift — scores badly on need and market by construction and must be done anyway; applied uniformly, the screen defers it until it is an emergency. In a lottery-shaped prize, multiplying a probability by one point estimate is the wrong statistic. And applied to a feature it says no about something that may still be right to build, since a feature has no market of its own.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Karuna's monitoring idea illustrates this cleanest. Of the 11,400 active households, Karthik Jambunathan in Coimbatore identified 3,100 — 27.2 per cent — with a resident over seventy-five alone by day. A survey found 41 per cent of those 3,100, or 1,271 households, intending to subscribe; Karuna's record across three earlier launches puts the intent-to-payment ratio at 0.34, giving 432 paying households. At ₹1,200 a month that is ₹62.21 lakh a year. The nurse desk alone — nine nurses at ₹58,000 a month — costs ₹62.64 lakh. Break-even is 435 subscribers.

Exhibit 7. ₹62,64,000 ÷ ₹14,400 = 435 households exactly; the estimate of 432 falls three short, before hardware or engineering.

The first-year picture is worse. Sensor kits at ₹7,400 for 432 households cost ₹31.97 lakh; nine engineers for two quarters at ₹20.00 lakh a year fully loaded cost ₹90.00 lakh; with the desk, ₹184.61 lakh against ₹62.21 lakh of revenue, a ratio of 0.34. Jayanti's alternative attacks the fill rate. Raising it from 78.0 to 86.0 per cent would fill 15,996 of the same 18,600 requests, adding 1,488 shifts a month, ₹29.02 lakh of gross bookings and ₹6.38 lakh of net revenue a month, or ₹76.60 lakh a year. It also touches churn: the 4,092 unfilled requests came from 2,760 distinct households, which churn at 9.5 per cent a month against a base of 3.9. Cutting unfilled requests by 36.4 per cent returns 1,005 of them to the base rate, retaining 56 a month. At ₹6,552 of net revenue per household a year (August's ₹62.24 lakh across 11,400 households, annualised), a first-year cohort of 675 carries ₹44.23 lakh. Against the same ₹90.00 lakh, rostering returns ₹120.83 lakh, a ratio of 1.34.

Four other edge cases deserve naming. In multi-product firms the criteria must be scored at the margin: H's real need score is the probability that clinics refusing a ₹2,65,000 analyser buy a ₹1,15,000 one and that existing buyers do not trade down. In regulated products timing becomes a queue — Kasauti's licence sits with the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, and conviction does not shorten it. In hardware-plus-software the solution criterion hinges at tooling, after which a wrong cost assumption cannot be patched as a software one can. In AI-native products solution becomes a distribution over output quality, so the question is whether it reaches a reliability the payer tolerates; defensibility, omitted from the list, is the hard criterion.

What mature companies do differs from what they describe. The stated process is a stage gate with a rubric. In practice market is owned by whoever holds the CRM, need by whoever ran the last study, and timing by nobody, so it defaults to the loudest view. Gates are almost never failed; the decision is made in the pre-read by whoever drafted the slide. Experts therefore spend their effort there.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

Weak because unknown, or weak because arithmetic

A criterion can be low because evidence is thin or because an identity forbids it. Karuna's market score is the second kind: 435 subscribers cover the desk, the estimate is 432, and only a different cost structure changes that. The tell is that the proposed test and the suspected answer are the same thing.

Leverage is not value

Since ∂J/∂pi = J ÷ pi, the weakest criterion always has the most leverage, which tempts practitioners to read leverage as importance. Exhibit 5 refutes that: S has the greater leverage and the cheaper test, yet H carries the higher expected value because its prize is ₹9.3858 crore against ₹5.0400 crore. The tell is hard work on a weak criterion attached to a small prize.

Every criterion has a ceiling, and the ceilings differ

What matters is the achievable probability, not the current one. Team usually lifts above 0.90 with one hire, solution often with a prototype. Timing frequently cannot be lifted at all — H's 0.45 is a regulatory calendar, and a test reveals the number without raising it. The tell is a mitigation reading "we will work harder on it".

The criteria are not independent, and multiplying pretends they are

H's solution and timing both rest on the same unproven chemistry, so 0.55 × 0.45 = 0.2475 understates the pair: if the chemistry works, both rise together. The tell is two scores moving in lockstep under one assumption. A joint probability that silently assumes independence biases every idea downwards by an unknown amount.

Need must be indexed to a payer, not a sufferer

In India the payer is so often not the user that this becomes load-bearing. Families pay for elder care; the parent is the user and frequently the one resisting a sensor in the bedroom. Mills pay in agricultural marketplaces; farmers do not. The tell is an interview transcript in which nobody is asked who signs. Need scored on the sufferer and market on the payer's budget yields a consistent, confident, wrong answer.

Too early and too late look identical in the data

Both show low conversion, polite interest and long cycles. What separates them is competitor count and price trajectory, not enthusiasm. Jharna Water Works read its ₹1,85,000 dispensing units falling from 412 in FY2024 to 143 in FY2025 as weak demand; it was commoditisation, with imports at ₹96,000. The tell is a team debating psychology instead of reading a price list.

Re-scoping beats re-scoring

When an idea fails the screen, the competent argue about the numbers and the expert changes the idea until a number changes. Programme S at ₹2,500 a month to a lab is a 0.40 need; the same capability at ₹40 a test to the lab's own patients is a different idea with a different payer. Scores that move while the description does not are advocacy.

The invisible sixth criterion is opportunity cost

The five criteria compare an idea with nothing; the decision compares it with the best alternative use of the same people. Jayanti's monitoring idea is not bad against a blank sheet, only against rostering, which returns ₹120.83 lakh for the same ₹90.00 lakh. The tell is a case with no named alternative.

7. How the practice changes by product type and stage

Exhibit 8. Unchanged by context: the definition of need, and naming the payer.

These are tendencies, weakest where asserted most confidently. "Consumer is distribution, B2B is need" fails on Karuna, which is consumer-facing, acquires through doctors, and was constrained by the fixed cost of a desk.

8. Three worked examples

Where it worked. In March 2024 Kasauti considered moving reagents from per-order sale to an annual commitment plan. Need and solution were high and uninteresting; the binding criterion was market — whether small labs would pre-commit cash. The test cost under ₹3 lakh: offer the plan to sixty labs in one district for eight weeks. Twenty-two signed, 36.7 per cent.

Exhibit 9. The plan covers 41.9 per cent of the base and lifts revenue per analyser by 33.7 per cent; reagents are 54.4 per cent of ₹86.40 crore.

Where the approach itself failed. Kosh Payroll Systems in Noida ran the screen in early 2025 on a payroll product for firms of twenty to two hundred employees, scoring every criterion four out of five on an industry estimate of 62,000 such firms in the National Capital Region. Between April 2025 and February 2026 it took 2,480 trials and converted 186 — 7.5 per cent — at ₹38,400 a year: ₹71.42 lakh of revenue against ₹2.31 crore of marketing spend. Acquisition cost was ₹1,24,194; at a 72 per cent gross margin the contribution was ₹27,648 a year, so payback ran to 4.49 years. No criterion had been scored wrongly; the screen had been applied to the category rather than the wedge, since the need was real for firms with an in-house accountant and those were not reachable by advertising. The recovery changed the channel, not the product: 340 accounting firms signed, each bringing 6.4 clients — 2,176 paying firms — at a blended acquisition cost of ₹14,600 against an 18 per cent commission of ₹6,912, leaving ₹20,736 of contribution and an 8.4-month payback.

Where recovery meant a new business model. Jharna Water Works, after unit sales fell from 412 to 143, sold water instead of dispensers: ₹0.55 a litre on 1,200 litres a day, or ₹2,40,900 a year a site, against ₹1,10,000 of capital — an imported unit at ₹96,000 plus ₹14,000 of installation — and ₹1,02,000 of annual operating cost. Contribution of ₹1,38,900 repays the capital in 9.5 months. By FY2026 it had 520 units on service, ₹12.53 crore of revenue and ₹7.22 crore of contribution. What moved was the definition of the product — the lever the five criteria never name.

Exhibit 10. Each row is a mode practitioners have shipped.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether to score at all. The option-and-portfolio position holds that probabilities force disclosure: writing 0.40 beside need obliges you to say what evidence produced it, and the product makes fragility visible — teams that average reach 0.73 where teams that multiply reach 0.17 from identical beliefs. Operators answer that numbers on unknowable quantities launder opinion into authority, and that a written claim plus a named killer assumption does the same work without false precision. The calibration evidence that would settle it does not exist.

The second concerns which term dominates. The market-and-timing school rests on real evidence: outcomes cluster by cohort and category far more than by team quality, and Gross's ranking of timing above idea and team fits the pattern of one idea failing in one decade and succeeding in the next. The need-first school answers that timing is observable only in hindsight — a good explanation and a poor instrument — whereas need intensity is measurable before you build. To break the market school you would need tightly held needs served profitably before any enabling shift; to break the need school, products whose users lacked the problem beforehand.

The third is practical and, at Kasauti, decisive. One camp holds that a weak criterion attached to a large prize should be funded and fixed, because prizes are rarer than fixes; the other that a weak criterion is information about the firm's fit with the opportunity. Keshav held the first view about H's timing, Komal the second. Nothing in the framework adjudicates. What does is the firm's capacity to survive an eighteen-month commitment that fails — a balance-sheet question in product costume.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the criteria produces a scored grid and a recommendation. Someone who has internalised them produces three things: a sentence naming the one fact that would change the decision; a price for that fact in rupees and days, set against the cost of the build; and the alternative use of the same people. They also refuse to score a criterion they consider unknowable. And they revise the idea rather than the scores.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Thursday 8 October 2026 Kanishka recommended no programme. She asked for ₹29.00 lakh — 2.0 per cent of the ₹14.50 crore at stake — to run both tests in parallel, and for a decision on Thursday 19 November, forty-two days later. Her reasoning: H carried the higher expected value at ₹0.9757 crore against ₹0.8637 crore; its binding criterion was timing at 0.45; timing has a ceiling no test can raise; and eighteen months of tooling against an unmeasured 0.45 was the only irreversible move. She recorded that H's 0.55 and 0.45 were not independent, so 0.10395 was too low by an unquantifiable amount.

Jayanti decided faster and alone. She put the nine engineers on rostering from Monday 5 October, on the arithmetic that it returns ₹120.83 lakh against ₹90.00 lakh while monitoring returns ₹62.21 lakh against ₹184.61 lakh. She did not kill monitoring: Dr Jyoti Kelshikar, the clinical adviser in Nagpur, would run sixty households on sensors with no desk and no charge, since the defect was a cost structure rather than a need.

Three questions. First, if the committee could fund one programme and no tests, which should it choose, and does the answer depend on Kasauti's capacity to survive a failed eighteen-month commitment rather than on the ideas? Second, monitoring breaks even at 435 subscribers and is estimated at 432 — rounding error or verdict? Third, if H's solution and timing scores are driven by one chemistry, how should that be written down for a board expecting five numbers?

13. Going deeper

Why products fail — the criteria are these causes inverted. Why now: technology and market timing — the highest-leverage, lowest-ceiling term at Kasauti. Product deconstruction — the teardown behind each score. B2B vs B2C — sharpens the payer-versus-user split that Exhibit 6 shows failing at Karuna. Product sense and taste — what generates the slate the criteria rank. Reasoning about trade-offs — machinery for the leverage-versus-prize tension of Exhibit 5. First-principles reasoning — telling an identity from an unknown, the distinction that decided Karuna. Product critique — this module's signature exercise.
case40v1-sense.idea.criteria:
Seventy Days of Waiting

One squad, nine months, three product ideas — and three bodies of evidence gathered by different people, in different windows, against different bases.

1. Opening: Sunday night, Ahmedabad

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 1 November 2026, Dipali Irani sat at the dining table of her Thaltej flat in Ahmedabad, three printed decks squared off before her. In the morning she would tell her leadership team which of three products Tvisha Works would build; on Thursday, 5 November, the board. On Sunday, 8 November, Diwali would freeze the roster until the new year.

Tvisha could staff one squad of seven for the nine months from Tuesday, 1 December 2026 to Tuesday, 31 August 2027, inside a board cap of ₹3.00 crore. Three ideas had champions, decks and numbers; two cost more than the cap. All three were sized by different people in different windows, and laid side by side the decks looked less like three answers to one question than three answers to three different questions.

What she kept returning to was one figure from her data team: of the 105 days a job took from survey to subsidy, 70 belonged to stages none of the three ideas touched.

2. The company, and the clause of August 2023

Tvisha Works was founded in Ahmedabad in March 2019 to sell software to the firms that install rooftop solar in India: the two-to-forty-person outfits that survey a roof, quote a system, file the net-metering paperwork, buy the modules and inverters, raise the plant, then answer the homeowner's calls for five years. It did quotation and shade design, DISCOM and subsidy filing, procurement and warranty records, for ₹60,000 per firm a year plus ₹260 per kilowatt commissioned.

In the year to 31 March 2026 the platform carried 2,10,000 kW of commissioned capacity: 1,34,400 kW residential, over roughly 42,000 rooftops at an average 3.2 kW, and 75,600 kW commercial. Licences on 2,240 contracted firms produced ₹13.44 crore and the per-kW fee ₹5.46 crore: platform revenue of ₹18.90 crore.

A third line of ₹2.40 crore came from one contract, and that contract is why Irani's choice is narrower than it looks. On Monday, 14 August 2023 Tvisha signed a white-label agreement with Taponidhi Energy Depot, a module and inverter distributor in western India. Taponidhi embedded Tvisha's tool in its dealer portal, bringing some 900 firms onto the platform. In exchange, clause 9.2 bars Tvisha from operating "any marketplace, exchange or aggregated purchasing arrangement for photovoltaic modules or inverters" until the agreement expires on Friday, 31 March 2028. Reported revenue was therefore ₹21.30 crore: licences ₹13.44 crore (63.1 per cent), per-kW fees ₹5.46 crore (25.6 per cent), Taponidhi ₹2.40 crore (11.3 per cent), each as a share of ₹21.30 crore. Debjani Ingawale's planning model uses the ₹18.90 crore platform figure; the board deck quotes ₹21.30 crore. Both are correct, and the two travel separately.

3. The industry

Rooftop solar in India in 2026 is subsidised, regulated and state-by-state. Under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, launched in February 2024, central assistance runs at ₹30,000 per kW for the first two kilowatts and ₹18,000 for the third, capped at ₹78,000 for a 3 kW system, and reaches the homeowner only after the discom inspects the plant and the national portal clears the claim. Modules must come from the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers, and the discoms — Torrent Power in Gujarat, JVVNL in Jaipur, MSEDCL in Maharashtra — own the queue.

Tvisha's customers compete with vertically integrated installers such as SolarSquare and Freyr Energy, which write their own software, and with Tata Power's dealers; Tvisha's own rivals are a procurement-first marketplace giving away a free quotation tool, and spreadsheets. Its overseas customer, Tarweej Energy Services of Muscat, signed in January 2026 on a three-year frame worth ₹4.80 crore — ₹1.60 crore a year, 7.5 per cent of reported revenue — buys commercial, not residential, workflows, and renews annually, next on Sunday, 31 January 2027.

Two forces remain: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act makes streaming household generation data a consent-and-fiduciary matter, not merely an engineering one, and revised scheme targets leave 2027's residential volume anyone's guess.

4. The situation in detail

Tvisha Assure (Idea A) began in Dakshesh Isapure's support queue: homeowners call their installer when the bill does not fall as promised, and installers call Tvisha. Assure would stream inverter telemetry, flag underperforming plants and run the warranty claim with the manufacturer, at ₹1,800 per rooftop per year. A pilot ran in Jaipur and Nashik over the nine working weeks from Monday, 2 February to Friday, 3 April 2026 — sixty-one calendar days inclusive — and Exhibit 4 gives its funnel. In April it read as a success. By September telemetry was known to be readable from only two of the seven inverter brands on Tvisha's jobs, and the attach rate had two defensible values, 42.0 and 27.3 per cent.

Tvisha Karya (Idea B) came from Durgesh Injeti's instinct that Tvisha's data was its asset. Karya is a crew app — scheduling, routing, material-at-site confirmation, photo-verified steps, offline-first — at ₹18,000 per firm per year. Its case rests on Exhibit 2, built in September 2026 from platform telemetry and commissioned to support Karya. It does not.

Tvisha Mandi (Idea C) came from Damodar Ittira's sales calls and from Exhibit 1, a questionnaire sent between Tuesday, 18 August and Friday, 11 September 2026 to all 2,240 contracted firms, of which 486 replied. Material prices and terms were named in the top three problems by 341 of them, 70.2 per cent — the most-named of six. Mandi would aggregate demand and take 1.8 per cent of order value, earning ₹3.86 crore a year on Exhibit 3's sizing. Clause 9.2, signed three years before Mandi was thought of, excludes modules and inverters from that value, and they are 78 per cent of the material basket.

What has shifted is not any one idea but the ground under all three. Of the 105 days of median elapsed time in Exhibit 2, the four stages a Tvisha product can touch today — quotation, advance, material at site, installation — account for 31 days, 29.5 per cent of 105. The discom and portal stages account for 70 days, 66.7 per cent; the remaining 4 days, 3.8 per cent, is filing. Exhibit 1's second column agrees: 302 of the 486 respondents, 62.1 per cent, already pay someone — usually a liaison agent — for approvals, against 188 of 486, 38.7 per cent, for procurement. The problem installers name most often is not the one they spend money on, and neither is the one that eats their calendar.

5. The people

Dipali Irani, co-founder and chief executive, Ahmedabad, owns the decision and has promised the board one idea, not three. Her incentive is a mid-2027 Series C that wants a second revenue line. Unsaid: she has already decided Karya is the dullest of the three.

Durgesh Injeti, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru, champions Karya because his team can ship it without depending on anyone else's systems. Unsaid: he commissioned Exhibit 2 expecting support for Karya, knows it gives none, and has not said so.

Damodar Ittira, chief revenue officer, Jaipur, champions Mandi and quotes the pilot's attach rate as 42 per cent — the share of homeowners offered Assure who signed. His variable pay rides on new licence revenue to 31 March 2027. Unsaid: two of his largest accounts, ₹47 lakh a year together, are testing a free rival tool.

Debjani Ingawale, vice-president finance, Ahmedabad, built Exhibits 3 and 5 and alone has priced all three ideas on one page; the ₹3.00 crore cap is hers as much as the board's. Unsaid: she left the working-capital exclusion in a footnote rather than raise it, believing that losing Taponidhi would end the Series C.

Dakshesh Isapure, head of installer success, Kuala Lumpur, owns the Assure idea. Generation complaints are 61 per cent of his queue, so the problem looks enormous from where he sits; in Exhibit 1 only 112 of 486, 23.0 per cent, name it. Unsaid: his team of nine is justified by ticket volume.

Dayita Idnani, principal designer, Kraków, ran the pilot's homeowner interviews at six in the morning her time and concluded that homeowners want someone accountable for an outcome, not a monitoring app. She alone has said the framing — three products, one squad — may be the problem.

Dilnawaz Ilkal, staff data scientist, Melbourne, produced Exhibits 2, 4 and 6 and insists the attach rate is 27.3 per cent of commissioned sites, not 42 per cent of offered sites. Her memo of 28 September put it plainly: forty-two per cent is a number about a conversation at handover, twenty-seven a number about a roof. Her Exhibit 6 caveat sat in a footnote Ittira's deck dropped. Unsaid: she is interviewing elsewhere.

Darayus Iswaran, partner at Tapovan Growth Partners, Chennai, on the board since 2022, wants the biggest market and calls Mandi "the only one that could be a company". He has not read clause 9.2, and his fund is marked at a 2024 valuation.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Seventy per cent of them put material cost in their top three. Seventy. We have 2,240 firms buying ₹714 crore of material a year through jobs that already sit in our system, and we are debating a crew app."

Damodar Ittira, leadership call, 20 October 2026

"Seventy per cent of the four hundred and eighty-six who answered. Three in five of those sit in two states. And the thing they pay for is the approvals man, not the cheaper panel."

Dilnawaz Ilkal, same thread, 21 October, 06:40 Ahmedabad time

"Clause 9.2 — please read it before Thursday. We can run an exchange for cables, structures and meters, twenty-two per cent of the basket, or we can ask Taponidhi for a carve-out and put ₹2.40 crore a year on the table."

Debjani Ingawale, email to Irani and Iswaran, 23 October 2026

"Then somebody explain why we are spending nine months on the thirty per cent of the calendar we already control."

Durgesh Injeti, privately to Irani, 31 October 2026

8. The options as Irani sees them

Option 1: Build Assure. Worth ₹2.06 crore a year on the headline basis, or ₹1.51 crore if only live sites are billable — 63.9 or 46.8 per cent of its ₹3.225 crore cost. It needs certification with five more inverter brands, DPDP consent from tens of thousands of households, and a promise about generation Tvisha cannot keep without the manufacturers. Only 23.0 per cent of installers name the problem.

Option 2: Build Karya. The only option inside the cap, at ₹2.77 crore, with no external dependency. It earns ₹1.41 crore on the contracted base or ₹1.08 crore on the active base, and attacks 31 of 105 days. Installers rank crew scheduling fifth of six.

Option 3: Build Mandi. The largest prize, ₹3.86 crore, and the one the board wants. It is barred from 78 per cent of its own order value until 31 March 2028; the permitted remainder earns ₹0.85 crore, 26.0 per cent of its ₹3.27 crore cost, before the ₹6.00 crore of working capital Exhibit 5 excludes.

Irani has written the three options on one page three times, and each time been uneasy. The shape of the choice was fixed in September, when the decks were commissioned, and the evidence that arrived afterwards does not fit it. Nothing in Exhibits 1, 2 or 6 is about any of the three ideas; all three describe the same thing from different angles — the 70 days, the 62.1 per cent of respondents already paying a liaison agent, the 33- and 41-day tails no crew scheduling will shorten. A fourth idea, an approvals product built around the discoms' own queues, which Injeti sketched in August and dropped for want of evidence that a discom would cooperate, sits in no deck, with no owner and no champion. It is the only option whose feasibility nobody has tested.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money: ₹3.00 crore for new product to 31 March 2027, on reported revenue of ₹21.30 crore and cash of ₹22 crore at roughly break-even; Options 1 and 3 exceed the cap by ₹22.5 lakh and ₹26.5 lakh before working capital. People: seven heads, the Melbourne data scientist a flight risk and the Kraków designer unwilling to relocate. Contract: clause 9.2 runs to 31 March 2028, and Taponidhi's ₹2.40 crore is 11.3 per cent of reported revenue. Customers: Tarweej's ₹1.60 crore a year renews on 31 January 2027 and wants commercial features none of the three provides. Regulation: DPDP consent for Assure, ALMM and net-metering rules throughout. Calendar: leadership Monday, 2 November; board Thursday, 5 November; the roster freezes after Diwali on Sunday, 8 November, a week after tonight.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of Exhibits 1 and 2 measure, against which base, and why does treating them as rival estimates of one quantity go wrong?
  2. For each idea, name the criterion on which it is weakest — unmet need, viable solution, market, timing or team — and the evidence that establishes it.
  3. Ittira's 42.0 per cent and Ilkal's 27.3 per cent are both correct. Which should Exhibit 3 use, and what changes on the stricter reading of every rate in Exhibit 4?
  4. Exhibit 6 gives a 41-day median for Uttar Pradesh on 22 jobs, which Ittira's deck quotes without the caveat. What would you require of an exhibit before a board sees it?
  5. Clause 9.2 was signed for good reasons and now rules out the largest idea on the page. How should a company price the optionality it gives away in a distribution deal?
  6. It is Monday morning, 2 November 2026. What does Irani do — and on Thursday, what does she tell a board whose lead investor has called Mandi "the only one that could be a company", if she has concluded that the right product is not among the three?

Near midnight Irani turned to the last page of Ilkal's memo, where a sentence sat under the funnel without comment: of the 105 days the median job takes, 70 are spent waiting for somebody who does not work here. She read it twice. Outside, the first Diwali lights had gone up along the lane, and a neighbour's inverter clicked over to battery as the evening load came on.
exp20v2-sense.idea.criteria:
What Makes a Good Product Idea

1. Eleven days to choose

On Monday 6 July 2026, Deepti Karandikar, head of product at Dhaan Mandi Exchange in Gurugram, opened a shared spreadsheet containing three ideas and a deadline. Dhaan Mandi Exchange runs a procurement platform on which paddy farmers in Haryana and Punjab sell to rice mills, and the company earns a commission on each transaction. Its board would meet on Friday 17 July, eleven days away, and would release ₹1.2 crore to fund exactly one new product line: six people for two quarters, starting Monday 3 August 2026 and running into the first week of February 2027.

The chief executive, Ekansh Rastogi, had been blunt. The company could afford one bet, not three, and he wanted the choice defended on the page rather than by whoever argued longest. Idea A was a WhatsApp service that sends farmers daily mandi price alerts. Idea B was a grading kit for the mill gate, using moisture meters and photographs so that disputes about paddy quality are settled in minutes instead of hours. Idea C was a short-term cash advance to farmers against a confirmed delivery.

What is at stake is concrete. If the team builds the wrong thing, the company spends ₹1.2 crore and half a year, and the next chance to fund a new line arrives only after the following budget cycle. This page follows the method Deepti used: a short list of criteria for judging an idea before anyone writes code.

2. The idea: five criteria and a weakest link

A product idea, in this context, is a specific claim: that a defined group of people has a problem worth solving, and that a particular thing, built by a particular team, can solve it well enough to sustain a business. A good idea is one whose claim survives scrutiny on every part of that sentence. Product managers condense the parts into five criteria: unmet need (a real problem that current alternatives serve badly), viable solution (something that can actually be built and that works for the user), market (enough paying customers to justify the effort), timing (a reason this is possible or necessary now), and team (the people at hand can build and sell it).

The framework grew out of the study of start-up failure and venture investing, where analysts in the 2010s repeatedly sorted post-mortems into the same handful of causes: building something nobody needed, running out of money, being outcompeted, launching too early or too late, and having the wrong team. The criteria are those failure causes read in reverse.

The sentence Deepti could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: an idea is only as good as its weakest criterion, so find that one first. The point is that the five criteria are links in a chain and not items in a sum.

Exhibit 1. The five criteria as a chain. Fill colour marks the weakest link for Idea A.

3. How it works in practice

The mechanics have five steps. First, the idea is written as a one-paragraph claim naming the user, the problem, the proposed product and the reason it will win. Second, each criterion is scored on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 means the evidence says no and 5 means the evidence says strongly yes. Third, and this is the step practitioners usually leave implicit, every score must be attached to a piece of evidence, such as an interview count, a number from a dataset, or a prototype test. Fourth, the scores are compared, and the lowest is identified. Fifth, the team asks what cheap test could raise or lower that lowest score within a fortnight.

Deepti asked the three sponsors to fill in the grid with evidence. Dhruvil Parmar, the design lead in Ahmedabad, had interviewed twenty farmers in June about price information, and most already got prices from a neighbour or an existing app. Ela Varghese, an analyst in Kochi, had pulled mill-gate dispute data. The resulting scores appear below.

Exhibit 2. Scores out of 5 for the three ideas on the five criteria. Each bar is labelled with its score.

Idea A has a perfect solution score because a WhatsApp alert is easy to build, but its need score is only 3 and its market score is 2, because farmers do not pay for prices. Idea C has the strongest need and market, at 5 each, but its solution score of 2 and team score of 2 reflect that the company has no lending licence, no underwriting staff and no collection process. Idea B has no score above 4 and none below 3.

4. A worked example, line by line

The scores above can mislead if read as a total. Add each idea's five scores and the totals are 3 + 5 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 18 for A, 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 18 for B, and 5 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 18 for C. Every idea scores 18 out of 25. An average-minded committee would call the contest a draw and fund the loudest sponsor. The weakest-link rule breaks the tie: the lowest score is 2 for A (market), 3 for B (timing and market) and 2 for C (solution and team). Idea B is the only one with a floor of 3.

Scores alone are still opinion, so the market criterion needs arithmetic. The company knows of 2,000 rice mills in its two states. Of these, 1,200 operate lines large enough to justify a grading kit, which is 60 per cent of the total. Dhaan Mandi Exchange estimates it can win 20 per cent of the reachable mills within three years, which is 1,200 × 0.20 = 240 mills. At a subscription of ₹1,50,000 per mill per year, 240 × 1,50,000 = ₹3,60,00,000, or ₹3.6 crore a year. Against an investment of ₹1.2 crore, the ratio is 3.6 ÷ 1.2 = 3.0. The company's own rule of thumb is that an idea should show a plausible path to three times its initial investment in annual revenue by year three, and Idea B meets it exactly, with no margin.

Exhibit 3. Market funnel for Idea B, base case.

Now change one input. Dhruvil's field visits suggest that only mills with lines of at least four tonnes an hour can use the kit, and that this cuts the reachable set from 1,200 to 900, or 45 per cent of 2,000. Holding the win rate at 20 per cent gives 900 × 0.20 = 180 mills, and 180 × 1,50,000 = ₹2,70,00,000, or ₹2.7 crore. The ratio falls to 2.7 ÷ 1.2 = 2.25, below the threshold. One assumption moved and the verdict flipped from pass to fail. That sensitivity tells the team which fact to test first: how many mills genuinely qualify.

Exhibit 4. Market funnel for Idea B, second pass with 900 reachable mills.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A score is a claim about evidence, not about the idea

Two people can give the same idea different scores because they know different things. The remedy is to write the evidence beside each number. When evidence is thin, say so, and treat the score as provisional.

The weakest-link rule is a heuristic, not a law

Some weak criteria can be repaired cheaply and others cannot. A team score of 2 can be lifted by hiring in a quarter; a need score of 1 cannot be lifted by anything. The rule tells you where to look first, not what to conclude. Ask of the lowest score: is this fixable, and at what price?

Need is not the same as demand

A need is a problem that exists. Demand is willingness to give up something, such as money or habit, to solve it. Farmers need better prices, yet few will pay for price information. Interviews should therefore end with a request for action, such as a deposit or a trial, and not with praise.

Market means paying customers, not people

The market criterion counts those who will pay, how much, and how many you can plausibly reach. The funnel above counts mills, who pay, not farmers, who mostly do not.

The criteria cannot tell you the answer to a bad question

The framework ranks ideas you have already thought of. It cannot generate the best idea, and it cannot tell you that all three options are poor. If every idea has a floor of 1 or 2, the right decision may be to look for a fourth idea.

6. How it differs across product types and company sizes

In consumer products the market criterion is usually a question of reach and habit: a large number of people each paying little or nothing, so timing and distribution carry the weight. In business-to-business products, the market is a count of buyers, as Idea B shows, and the weakest link is often the sales cycle, which belongs under team. In marketplaces, which Dhaan Mandi Exchange itself is, a good idea must work on both sides at once, so each criterion is scored twice, once for farmers and once for mills, and the lower side governs.

Company size changes which criteria bite. An early-stage company is short of money and people, so the team and viable-solution criteria dominate, and a promising idea it cannot build is worthless. A large company has capacity but suffers from the opposite failure: it can build almost anything, so it must be strict about market and need. A ₹3.6 crore product can be a rounding error to a conglomerate.

7. Common mistakes

Averaging the scores. The symptom is a three-way tie and a decision made by the most senior voice. The misunderstanding is that strengths offset weaknesses; they do not, since a chain breaks at its weakest link. The cheapest diagnostic is to circle the lowest score for each idea before reading any totals.

Scoring the solution first. The symptom is a roadmap full of impressive demos and no paying customer. The diagnostic is to ask for one named person who has the problem and has already tried to fix it.

Treating interest as evidence. The symptom is a list of twenty friendly interviews and no commitments. Polite people say yes to hypothetical products. The diagnostic is to ask for something small and costly, such as a signed letter of intent.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the exercise ends with a recommendation that names its own weak points. Deepti's one-page note to the board would state that Idea B has the highest floor, with a minimum score of 3, but that its market criterion rests on one unproven number, the 1,200 qualifying mills. It would show both funnels, one giving ₹3.6 crore and one giving ₹2.7 crore, and would explain that the base case meets the three-times threshold only at the boundary.

The note would also propose a two-week test before the team starts: Ela and two colleagues visit or call a sample of mills to learn how many qualify, and Dhruvil asks ten mill owners to sign a letter of intent. The recommendation is explicit about what would change the answer. A reader who disagrees can see which input to challenge.

9. The decision, and what comes next

Deepti recommended Idea B, conditional on the test. If at least 1,200 of the 2,000 mills qualified, the ratio would stay at 3.0 or better at the same win rate; if fewer did, she would return to the board with Idea C and a plan to partner with a licensed lender, which would repair its solution and team scores. Her reasoning was that B's weakest criteria were both 3, whereas the weakest criteria of A and C were 2 and could not be repaired inside two quarters at the budget on offer. The board approved the conditional plan on Friday 17 July.

To go further, read the next topic in this module, which treats timing: why a sound idea can fail merely because it arrived too early or too late.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Idea B's market had been borderline at 2 and its team a strong 5, would you still call it the best option, and what does your answer reveal about when the weakest-link rule should yield? Second, think of a product you use daily: which of the five criteria was weakest on the day it launched, and how did its makers raise that score?
case40v1-sense.tradeoffs:
Patang Automation Works: Ten Weeks of Engineers

An ambiguous case on reasoning about trade-offs

1. The night before

At twenty to ten on the night of Sunday, 18 October 2026, the assembly floor at Chakan, north of Pune, was dark but for the test loop, where a P9 robot carried an empty rack in slow circles. In the office above, Apoorva Enjeti, Chief Product Officer of Patang Automation Works, had two printouts on her desk. One said the robots were breaking; the other said the software was stalling. They described the same thirty-one warehouses over the same thirteen weeks.

At nine the next morning Enjeti would tell Ahalya Erumalla, her vice-president of engineering in Bengaluru, how the platform squad would spend the ten weeks from Monday, 19 October to Friday, 25 December. Four pieces of work had been asked for; the squad could do about two. One was legally committed. Two were defended by people she trusted, from the same exhibits, to opposite conclusions. The fourth had been promised, informally, to a client in São Paulo that supplied thirty-one per cent of revenue and whose renewal fell due on 31 March 2027.

Enjeti had written one line on a notepad and had not been able to finish it: whatever we pick, the people who pay for it are —

2. How Patang got here

Patang was founded in 2017 by Atharv Edulji and two classmates from the College of Engineering, Pune, to build autonomous mobile robots for warehouses: squat shuttles that lift a rack and carry it to a picker. By the year to March 2026 it ran 3,120 robots across 48 sites on revenue of ₹186.0 crore, split as Exhibit 1 shows between hardware, a subscription to its fleet operating system, Parwaaz, and service.

The decision that constrains tonight was taken in August 2023, when Pirapora Armazéns, a warehousing group with six distribution centres around São Paulo, agreed to standardise on Patang. The largest contract Patang had signed carried two clauses the founders treated as paperwork: clause 7.2, requiring Pirapora's sites to run a dedicated on-premise build with no off-site control plane, asked for under Brazil's LGPD statute; and clause 11.4, requiring 180 days' notice and Pirapora's approval before any change to the operator console.

Erumalla's team believed the on-premise build would be a configuration flag. By January 2024 it was four files. It is now Parwaaz On-Site 3.6, a fork two releases behind mainline Parwaaz 4.2, maintained by six of the twenty-two platform engineers. Eleven older Indian sites still run Pehra, the control stack of 2019, which emits no event stream and so appears in none of the telemetry on Enjeti's desk.

3. The industry

Indian warehouse automation in 2026 has real incumbents: GreyOrange and Addverb Technologies at national scale, Unbox Robotics in sortation, Geek+ and Hai Robotics with imported fleets. Demand comes from quick-commerce dark stores, Flipkart and Reliance Retail distribution centres, Delhivery and Blue Dart hubs, and from manufacturers wanting twelve robots, not three hundred. The festival peak, running into Diwali on 8 November, is when operators decide whether automation held up.

Three forces press on Patang's choices. Cost: the encoder module in the P9's lift comes from Pingtung Opto Works in Taipei, attracts 7.5 per cent customs duty and is priced in dollars. Regulation: the cameras the P9 uses for navigation capture the faces of warehouse associates, and counsel has ruled that under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act the frames must be masked on the device by 31 January 2027. Concentration: the exposure set out in Exhibit 2 is the first question every investor asks, and Amália Esteves, Pirapora's operations director, knows it.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Pirapora's uptime first fell below the contracted 99.0 per cent in June 2025 and penalty accrual began; by the close of the year to March 2026 the account had absorbed ₹0.92 crore of penalties, which is why, as Exhibit 3 shows, its service line lost money. Anders Ekvall, who sells from Chicago, called it a service problem a release would fix. In April 2026 Parwaaz 4.0 shipped with a rewritten scheduler and a multi-tenant control plane, and the India fleet took it. The fork could not: clause 7.2 forbade the control plane and clause 11.4 covered the console the release redrew. The May engineering review recorded the divergence as "temporary".

Over the thirteen weeks from 1 July to 29 September 2026 the company instrumented what it could. On 2 October, Akhila Etikala's field organisation circulated column A of Exhibit 5: on the thirty-one sites running Parwaaz 4.2 or later, mechanical faults were 43.9 per cent of lost robot-hours, nearly three times the software share. Hyderabad concluded that the P9's lift arm, whose actuator comes from Pitamber Drive Systems in Coimbatore, needed a retrofit.

On 6 October, Alonso Espinosa sent column B from Montréal. From Parwaaz event logs on the same sites over the same weeks, he found more lost hours than the tickets did, and the largest cause to be the fleet controller stalling: 35.4 per cent against 14.9 per cent. Three beliefs have not survived the fortnight: that the on-premise variant was a flag; that mechanical faults dominate downtime; and that the fork would be merged back by the third quarter, as the plan to March 2027 assumes. On 13 October Espinosa noticed that Erumalla's merge estimate says nothing about the eleven Pehra sites.

5. The people

Atharv Edulji, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, wants the renewal secured above all: the growth story he has shown Panna Capital Partners rests on it. Unsaid: the August plan counts both the renewal and the ₹31.8 crore mid-market pipeline.

Ahalya Erumalla, vice-president, engineering, Bengaluru, wants the merge: one codebase, 150 engineer-weeks, an end to the tax she pays on every release. She is judged on release cadence. Unsaid: two of her six fork engineers will leave after another year on 3.6, and her 150 excludes the Pehra migration.

Akhila Etikala, head of field service, Hyderabad, has 34 engineers for 42 Indian sites and wants the arm retrofit; penalties and overtime land on her budget. Unsaid: the cause code on a closed ticket comes from a drop-down whose first entry is "mechanical", and at eleven at night the default closes fastest.

Astrid Ebeling, principal designer, Hamburg, three and a half hours behind Pune, wrote the note of 9 October: the throughput gap in Exhibit 6 is an artefact of Pirapora's purpose-built aisles, not of the fork's scheduler. Her private worry: the team optimises robots per site because that number is easy to collect.

Alonso Espinosa, data scientist, Montréal, owns the telemetry. He is candid that it counts stalls under five minutes that never became tickets, and cannot say what they cost. He would rather buy information than capability.

Aisyah Erlangga, customer-success lead, Jakarta, takes Pirapora's weekly call because São Paulo is awake when Pune is not. Esteves, she reports, has stopped asking about the three features and asks about uptime — a warning, to Erlangga; a relief, to Ekvall.

Anders Ekvall, head of enterprise sales, Americas, Chicago, earns a material part of his year on the renewal. He has told Enjeti the three features are "what the renewal is about". Unsaid: in August he told Esteves that two would land before Christmas.

"Thirty-one per cent of revenue. I don't understand what else there is to discuss."

"I can tell you how many hours the controller cost us, not how many picks, because a four-minute stall in a slow shift costs nothing. Anyone quoting my 35.4 per cent as a rupee number is quoting me wrongly."

Alonso Espinosa, memo of 6 October

8. The options as Enjeti sees them tonight

Three lines are on her whiteboard, from the requests Exhibit 7 costs and Figure 1 measures. A fills the ten weeks alone, since nothing fits beside it; the other three cannot all be done together, so they pair.

Merge, and tell Pirapora later. Request A at 150 engineer-weeks fits inside 175. It also means the features Ekvall has effectively promised do not exist at Christmas, and clause 11.4 puts the earliest console change at Pirapora's sites on 17 April 2027. If Espinosa is right about the Pehra migration, A is 190 to 220, and does not fit at all.

Honour the contract, then sell India. B at 96 plus D at 72 is 168 engineer-weeks, inside capacity by seven. Pirapora gets what it was promised and the mid-market product is quotable in January; nothing is done about the arm or the fork, which will then sit three releases behind. The arithmetic that worries Enjeti most: if D slips instead, the ₹241.0 crore plan to March 2027 becomes ₹209.2 crore and Pirapora's share rises from 25.3 per cent to 29.2 per cent — the wrong direction for the Panna covenant.

Fix the robot, then sell India. C at 54 plus D at 72 is 126 engineer-weeks and leaves 49 spare, but costs ₹6.81 crore before the Series B closes. It is the only path that touches what Erlangga's clients complain about — if column A is true. If column B is, the retrofit buys back 4,895 hours a quarter rather than 6,985, and neither column covers São Paulo, where the penalties are.

What she has not written is the suspicion that the three lines are the wrong frame. Serving the clause 11.4 notice costs no engineer-weeks and could be done on Monday, making an April console change possible under any path. Etikala's bench of 34 engineers for 42 sites, and its 26 per cent attrition, appears nowhere in Exhibit 4, and no request adds a field engineer. Espinosa's offer — three weeks of instrumentation to learn what a stalled hour is worth in picks — is not on the whiteboard either, because it ships nothing.

10. Questions for discussion
