  2. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3 describe the same account; Ekvall reads one, Erumalla the other. What would you need to know to decide whether revenue or gross profit is the right base?
  3. The two columns of Exhibit 5 cannot both be the whole truth. Design the cheapest test that separates them, and say what you would stop doing to pay for it.
  4. Exhibit 6 shows the fork with lower uptime and higher throughput. If both readings are trusted, what does merging cost, and who notices first?
  5. Patang's plan treats the renewal and the mid-market as additive; Exhibit 7 and the Panna covenant suggest they are not. Which is the company choosing between, and over what horizon?
  6. It is nine on Monday and Erumalla is waiting. What do you tell her, what do you tell Ekvall before he speaks to São Paulo, and what do you say to the board on 26 October about the costs you have chosen to accept?

At eleven she put the printouts side by side once more and found she could build from the same pages a defensible case for each of the three lines, and a fourth for buying information instead. The test loop downstairs had stopped. She read the unfinished line on the notepad and put it down again.
exp20v2-sense.tradeoffs:
Reasoning about trade-offs

Foundations › Product Thinking & Product Sense. The question this page answers: what does this choice cost, and who pays?

1. A promise with a price

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Lakshita Menon, head of product at Lazzat Tiffin Services in Hyderabad, opened a one-page request from the chief executive. Lazzat sells home-style lunch subscriptions, cooked in 38 partner home kitchens and carried to offices and apartments by about 1,400 riders. It handles roughly 12,500 lunch orders on a working day. The request read, in full: “Swiggy and Zomato both promise speed. We promise nothing. Give me a delivery guarantee by the board meeting on Friday 16 October.”

The idea was easy to like. The wide window was the most common complaint in customer surveys, and a promise of “at your desk by 1:00 p.m. or Rs 60 back as credit” would answer it. Omprakash Reddy, the chief operating officer, was enthusiastic. Lalima Shetty, the engineering manager, estimated six weeks of work. Olivia Fernandes, who manages the kitchen partners, said only: “Ask them what time they start cooking.”

Lakshita did, and learned the catch. A 1:00 p.m. guarantee would need the order cutoff to move from 11:30 to 10:30 a.m., because kitchens need ninety minutes of lead time. Every customer who orders in that last hour would be turned away, and every kitchen would start earlier. A feature that looked like an addition was a swap. The page that follows uses this decision to build one skill: making the cost of a choice explicit before the choice is made, so that the people who will pay it are named in the room rather than discovered in the quarterly review.

FactValue today
Lunch orders per working day12,500
Order cutoff / delivery window11:30 a.m. / 12:30–2:00 p.m.
Contribution per order, after food, rider and payment costsRs 38
Share of orders placed between 10:30 and 11:30 a.m.14 per cent
Proposed promiseBy 1:00 p.m., else Rs 60 credit

Exhibit 1. Lazzat’s starting position, from the product team’s own order data. Contribution is revenue minus the costs that move with each order; it excludes fixed salaries.

2. The idea

A trade-off exists whenever getting more of one thing you want means getting less of another. The economist’s name for the lost alternative is opportunity cost: the value of the best option you did not take. Friedrich von Wieser, an Austrian economist, gave the idea its name in the early 1910s, and Vilfredo Pareto, the Italian economist, supplied a useful test around 1906. A change is a free improvement only if it leaves nobody worse off. Almost nothing in a real product passes that test, and that is the point. The discipline was invented to stop decision-makers from counting benefits loudly and costs quietly.

For product work, the module’s learning objective states the practice precisely: make the costs of every choice explicit by asking four questions. Who loses? What gets slower? What can we no longer do? And, as a fourth that experienced people add, what can we not undo? The first three come from the learning objective; the fourth is where trade-offs become expensive.

Exhibit 2 shows that the costs land on different people in different currencies. Lost orders hurt the company; an earlier start hurts kitchens, who are partners and so invisible on Lazzat’s own accounts; the six-week delay hurts customers waiting for the displaced feature.

The sentence Lakshita could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib: “Every yes is paid for by someone, so before we vote, let us name who.”

3. How it works, step by step

The mechanics are simple to state and easy to skip; practitioners usually do the first two steps in their heads and the last two not at all.

StepLazzat’s version
1. Baseline12,500 orders at Rs 38; complaints persist
2. Exact optionCutoff 10:30; Rs 60 credit if late
3. Trace to partiesLate orderers, 38 kitchens, 1,400 riders, engineers
4. Unit per costOrders, rupees of credit, weeks of delay
5. Break-evenOrders needed to match today
6. Mark reversibilityPilot in one zone first

Exhibit 3. Six steps for making a choice’s costs explicit.

Step 1, the baseline, is where most reasoning fails: people compare the option against an imagined perfect present rather than the real one, which is a known level of complaint and churn. Step 2 forces precision: “a guarantee” is a slogan, while “a 10:30 cutoff plus a Rs 60 credit” can be costed. Step 5 turns an argument about feelings into one about numbers.

Lucas Almeida, an analytics lead working from Lisbon, built the model in one afternoon, expressing every cost as a daily rupee figure.

4. A worked example, line by line

Lucas’s model rests on five inputs. Three come straight from Exhibit 1. The other two are estimates, and the page flags them as such: that 40 per cent of customers who would have ordered between 10:30 and 11:30 would simply order earlier, and that 4 per cent of delivered orders would still miss the 1:00 p.m. promise and trigger the credit.

The baseline. Twelve thousand five hundred orders at Rs 38 give Rs 4,75,000 a day, which is Rs 4.75 lakh (1 lakh is 100,000 rupees).

Orders lost. The share of orders placed in the closed hour is 14 per cent of 12,500, which is 1,750 orders. Of those, 40 per cent, or 700, move earlier. The remaining 1,050 are lost. Retained orders are therefore 12,500 − 1,050 = 11,450.

Credits paid. Four per cent of 11,450 is 458 late orders. At Rs 60 each, that is Rs 27,480 in credits.

Margin lost. The 1,050 lost orders each carried Rs 38, which is Rs 39,900.

Daily cost of the guarantee, before any benefitLate rate 4% (Rs)Late rate 8% (Rs)
Contribution on lost orders (1,050 × Rs 38)39,90039,900
Late credits (458 or 916 orders × Rs 60)27,48054,960
Total daily gap against today67,38094,860

Exhibit 4. Rs 67,380 a day over 26 working days is Rs 17,51,880 a month, about Rs 17.5 lakh. At the 8 per cent late rate, 26 days give Rs 24,66,360, about Rs 24.7 lakh. Both columns are exact sums of their rows; nothing is rounded.

Now the break-even step. Each retained order now earns Rs 38 less the expected credit. At a 4 per cent late rate the expected credit is 0.04 × Rs 60 = Rs 2.40, so each order earns Rs 35.60. To recover Rs 4,75,000 requires 4,75,000 ÷ 35.60 = 13,342.7 orders, which rounds up to 13,343 a day. That is 1,893 more than the 11,450 retained, a 16.5 per cent increase, and 843 more than the 12,500 Lazzat handles today. In plain terms: the guarantee must attract or retain enough new demand to exceed today’s volume by about 6.7 per cent before it merely breaks even.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose kitchens, forced to start earlier, miss the promise twice as often, so the late rate is 8 per cent rather than 4. Nothing else moves. The expected credit becomes Rs 4.80, and each order earns Rs 33.20. The total daily gap, per the second column of Exhibit 4, grows from Rs 67,380 to Rs 94,860. The break-even volume rises to 4,75,000 ÷ 33.20 = 14,307.2, which rounds up to 14,308 orders, or 2,858 more than the retained 11,450. One quality assumption, doubled, lifts the required growth from 1,893 extra orders to 2,858, a 51 per cent increase in the hurdle.

The guarantee may well be a good idea. But the argument for it is now a testable claim: it must lift volume by at least 1,893 orders a day, and more if kitchens struggle.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Opportunity cost is not the same as cost

The six engineering weeks cost Lazzat the salaries of the engineers, but the opportunity cost is the dinner pre-order feature they would otherwise have built. Salaries are paid either way; the foregone feature is the real price.

A trade-off is not a compromise

Choosing an 11:00 cutoff to “meet in the middle” does not avoid the trade-off. It mixes the costs of both options and the benefits of neither, because a guarantee that kitchens cannot honour at 11:00 costs credits without delivering trust.

Some trade-offs are false

If rider routing could fix what looks like a kitchen constraint, speed and coverage might both improve. Ask whether a constraint is real or merely the current implementation.

Reversibility changes the right amount of analysis

A four-week pilot warrants a quick estimate; a national campaign warrants the full ledger. Spending a week analysing a choice you can undo in a day is itself a poor trade-off.

The method cannot tell you what to value

Exhibit 4 cannot say whether a faster lunch is worth Rs 17.5 lakh a month. That is a judgement; the ledger disciplines it but does not replace it.

Estimates carry the conclusion

The 40 per cent and the 4 per cent are guesses. Ask which input, if wrong, would flip the answer, and measure that one first.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The method is constant; who pays changes. Lazzat is a marketplace in disguise, so its costs landed on a third party.

SettingWho usually paysTypical hidden cost
Consumer appUsers of the displaced feature; users with older phonesAttention and clutter; lost simplicity
B2B productThe customer with a custom need; the support team; the implementation teamRoadmap bent toward the largest account
MarketplaceThe side that is not the one being courtedSupply-side goodwill spent to buy demand-side delight

Exhibit 6. Where costs tend to fall, by product type.

Company size matters too. In a ten-person start-up the ledger can be a whiteboard. In a large firm the payers sit three reporting lines from the deciders, so each cost needs a named owner who agrees it is accurate. Lazzat sits between, and Lakshita chose the written version.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom seen from outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Listing only benefitsA launch memo with no “risks” section, or a section of generic risksCosts are seen as obstacles to be managed, not as part of the choiceAsk: who is worse off on day one, by name?
Comparing against a perfect presentOption scored against an ideal, so everything beats itThe baseline is not a real, measured stateWrite the do-nothing numbers first
Leaving out third partiesPartners or support staff learn of the change from the announcementCost is thought to matter only if it shows on the company’s own accountsShow the draft to one affected outsider before approval
False precisionA ledger to the last rupee built on a guessed inputArithmetic is mistaken for evidenceVary the weakest input and see whether the verdict flips

Exhibit 7. Four ways trade-off reasoning goes wrong.

The fourth is a risk of this very page: Exhibit 4 is exact arithmetic on assumed inputs, and its precision says nothing about whether 40 or 4 per cent is right. The second pass is the antidote.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled week looks like this. By Thursday 8 October Lakshita has a one-page ledger with the four questions answered and the Exhibit 4 numbers. She has spoken to Olivia and three kitchen owners, and learned that two could start earlier only if Lazzat guaranteed a minimum daily order count: a cost the first draft missed, now a line in the ledger with a question mark. She has stated the break-even in one sentence, named the late rate as the input to measure first, and proposed a pilot with a written stop rule instead of a launch. The chief executive receives three costed options, with the payers of each named.

9. The decision, and what comes next

On Friday 16 October, Lakshita told the board that Lazzat would not launch a city-wide guarantee. It would pilot a 1:00 p.m. promise in one zone from 26 October, with the cutoff at 10:30 a.m. only for orders that opted into the guarantee, leaving the 11:30 cutoff available for everyone else. The reasoning rested on Exhibit 4: a pilot capped the daily downside well below Rs 67,380, because only a fraction of orders would carry the new rules, and it would measure the late rate, the one input that could take the gap from Rs 67,380 to Rs 94,860 a day. It also kept the choice reversible, and reversibility was the cost she could least afford to lose.

To go further, study first-principles reasoning, which asks what is truly fixed in a trade-off, and systems thinking, which follows costs through feedback loops, such as kitchens leaving because of the early start.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a product you use daily: whose cost paid for its latest feature, and how would you know? Second, in Lakshita’s ledger, which cost was the hardest to put a number on, and what would you do with a cost you could name but not measure?
exp40v2-sense.tradeoffs:
Reasoning about trade-offs

Foundations › Product Thinking & Product Sense. The question this page answers: what does this choice cost, and who pays?

1. Two decisions, two currencies

On Monday 28 September 2026, Yashodhara Walimbe, vice-president of product at Yantrashala Medical Systems in Pune, got one line from the chief executive, Yashpal Dandavate: “A Chennai distributor is showing a twenty-four-an-hour analyser at trade fairs. Ship Rapid Mode. Product council, 15 October.” Seventeen days.

Yantrashala sells the Y-220 bench immunoassay analyser to pathology labs: 1,240 units in service on 30 September, each consuming cartridges at ₹118 a test, ₹74 of it cartridge cost and ₹44 contribution. Rapid Mode shortened the wash step, cutting the cycle from 200 seconds to 150 and lifting throughput from 18 tests an hour to 24. It also raised the rate at which a run is flagged by quality control and repeated, from 1.8 per cent to a measured mean of 4.6. The lab pays for the repeat cartridge.

That makes this a trade-off, not an improvement, and points the cost at a party with no seat at the council. Wahida Sheikh, who runs the 41-engineer service network, added a second: the shorter wash fouls the optical block faster, so the cleaning interval falls from 5,000 runs to 3,200. Yogesh Katdare, of clinical and regulatory affairs, added a third: Rapid Mode changes a declared performance characteristic, so a fresh validation package is needed, occupying his only two scientists for eleven weeks — the same two who must validate the HbA1c assay, which therefore slips a quarter.

Thirty-nine days earlier, Waman Kelkar faced another version of the problem. Kelkar is head of product at Wapsi Materials Exchange in Ahmedabad, a marketplace on which factories and municipal contractors sell industrial scrap to recyclers registered under extended-producer-responsibility rules. Wapsi runs a sealed-bid auction and takes 4.5 per cent of the winning bid. In September it listed 9,400 lots, of which 6,580 cleared — 70.0 per cent — at an average cleared value of ₹1,42,000: ₹93.44 crore of merchandise value, ₹4.2046 crore of commission, a median 9.5 days to payment.

On 14 September the chief financial officer, Yuvraj Kanade, proposed Instant Quote: Wapsi would name a firm price within twenty minutes of a photo set and weighbridge slip, buy the lot onto its own book, pay in 24 hours and resell at a posted price. Kelkar’s board paper was due Friday 23 October. His problem was not whether sellers would like it; they would. It was that the parties who would pay — 1,302 small aggregators whose margin came from under-bid lots, and Wapsi’s balance sheet — appeared nowhere in it.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

A trade-off exists when the feasible set is bounded, so that more of one thing you value means less of another. The discipline is the practice of naming the sacrificed quantity, its unit, the bearer and the period over which it is paid, before the choice is made. The operational form is three questions — who loses, what gets slower, what we cannot do now — plus a fourth: what we cannot undo.

The lineage is clean. Frédéric Bastiat, in 1850, framed it as ce qu’on ne voit pas: the visible benefit is counted, the invisible alternative is not. Vilfredo Pareto, in 1906, supplied the geometry of a bounded feasible set; Friedrich von Wieser, around 1914, named the sacrificed alternative Opportunitätskosten. In 1939 Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks sharpened it into the test that does most of the work here: a change is an improvement if the winners could compensate the losers. That word carries the problem, because they almost never do.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Frontier (Pareto; Porter, 1996)A position is what it refuses; a rival who matches you costlessly leaves none.Most trade-offs dissolve under better engineering.
Constraint-dissolving (lean; TRIZ)Most stated trade-offs are artefacts of the instrument.The frontier is fixed over the horizon that matters.
Decision-analytic (Raiffa; Howard; Keeney)State your throughput-versus-error exchange rate before seeing the data.The decisive costs are the unquantifiable ones.
Lexicographic (rights-based ethics; safety practice)Some axes admit no exchange rate: a wrong clinical result is not purchasable.Everything has a price if you are honest enough to name it.

Exhibit 1. Yantrashala’s council held adherents of all four and did not know it; the heat on 15 October was argument across these lines.

A fifth, the real-options view (Dixit and Pindyck, 1994), holds that the right question is the value of waiting, not the exchange rate.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice runs through eight steps. Most practitioners do one, two and four; six and eight hold the expertise.

  1. Fix the counterfactual at a measured level, with a date — “September: 34,667 reportable results a day at 1.8 per cent repeats”.
  2. Specify the option as a mechanism. “Rapid Mode” is unpriceable; “firmware 4.3, default on” is priceable.
  3. Enumerate bearers, including non-customers; give each cost a unit before converting.
  4. Build the ledger in the unit of the decision — monthly contribution.
  5. Find the pivotal input, and report its range, not its mean.
  6. Separate transfers from creation. A rupee moved from a customer is not created; a rupee burned in reagent is neither.
  7. Price the option: what does a month of waiting cost, and buy?
  8. Write the stop rule where the next team will find it.

Yukta Sabharwal, the data lead, classified all 1,240 analysers by arrivals in the 9 to 10 a.m. collection-run hour, when a lab has capacity or none.

Peak-hour segmentAnalysersAvg peak-hour arrivalsReportable results a working day
Constrained — above the 18-test ceiling21421.49,844
Occasionally tight — 12 to 1733114.610,923
Comfortable — below 126958.213,900
Total1,24012.234,667

Exhibit 3. Arrivals is a fleet average, not a sum. Reportable results exclude repeats: 34,667 at 1.8 per cent means 35,302 runs a working day, 635 of them repeats.

Exhibit 3 settles what the council could not. The ceiling binds for 214 analysers, 17.3 per cent of the fleet; the 695 comfortable units, at 8.2 arrivals an hour, queue at neither ceiling and get the repeat rate without the throughput.

A lab buys reportable results, not runs, so its unit cost is price divided by one minus the repeat rate: ₹118 ÷ 0.982 = ₹120.16 today, ₹118 ÷ 0.954 = ₹123.69 under Rapid Mode. The comfortable segment pays ₹3.5268 more per result — displayed as ₹3.53 — on 13,900 results a working day: over 25 days, ₹12.2556 lakh a month, rounding to ₹12.26 lakh. The displayed ₹3.53 would give ₹12.27 lakh; the page uses full precision.

Against that, the gain. Constrained labs lose 1.6 tests per analyser per working day entirely — referred out, or abandoned when a four-hour stability limit expires in the queue — so 214 analysers recapture 342 reportable results. Demand rises to 35,009; at 4.6 per cent repeats that needs 36,697 runs, 1,688 of them repeats, against 35,302 today. The extra 1,395 runs a working day earn ₹44 each. Service cost rises: 9,17,425 runs a month need 287 cleanings at the 3,200-run interval against 177 at 5,000, and 57 per cent of the 110 extra need a ₹1,850 trip.

Rapid Mode, default on, all 1,240 analysersMonthly effect, ₹ lakh
Extra cartridge contribution, 1,395 runs a day × ₹44 × 2515.35
Extra field service, 63 trips × ₹1,850−1.17
Total, net effect on Yantrashala14.18

Exhibit 4. Baseline consumables contribution is ₹388.32 lakh a month, so this is a 3.7 per cent lift. The ₹67.70 lakh HbA1c slip is a one-off.

Step six earns the fee. Of the ₹12.26 lakh the comfortable labs pay, Yantrashala keeps only contribution: 415 extra cartridges a working day at ₹44, or ₹4.57 lakh a month. The other ₹7.69 lakh is reagent, plastic and freight consumed for no result — destruction, not transfer. Fleet-wide, excess repeats run to 1,046 a working day, burning ₹19.35 lakh a month against recaptured volume worth ₹10.09 lakh even at the full ₹118. Default-on is privately profitable by ₹14.18 lakh a month and socially negative by roughly ₹9 lakh.

Step five asks which number decides. Setting reagent burned equal to recaptured value puts the break-even repeat rate at 3.3 per cent. Wimal Rajapaksa, who ran the trials from Colombo, had measured three validation sites at 3.1, 4.4 and 6.4 per cent — a mean of 4.6, and a range straddling the break-even.

The output is not a verdict but a measurement instruction: Rapid Mode is defensible only if the field repeat rate settles below roughly 3.3 per cent — and nobody knew.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four testable conditions. The feasible set is truly bounded. True at Yantrashala: carryover is chemistry. Partly false at Wapsi, where the seller’s complaint was the 9.5-day wait — a financing problem, not a market-design one. The costs land on an identifiable party. True in both: 695 labs, 1,302 aggregators. The costs are large relative to measurement error. True at Wapsi; borderline at Yantrashala, where the pivotal rate’s range exceeds its own effect. The choice is not cheaply reversible. A firmware flag is reversible in a service visit; a posted-price market is not, because small buyers who leave do not return.

The idea misleads in three situations. Where the trade-off is an artefact of the instrument, costing a false dichotomy yields a confident wrong answer that looks better the more rigorous it is. Where the option is cheap and reversible, analysis costs more than the mistake. And where an axis is lexicographic, quantification invites the firm to pay the price it just named.

5. Hard edge cases

In two-sided markets the costs land on the side not being courted, and arrive late. Wapsi’s small aggregators bought a median 2.1 lots a month at an average 6.8 per cent below reference; posted pricing removes exactly that margin. If a fifth go inactive, bidders per lot falls from 3.4 to 2.7, and Wapsi’s history shows clearance falling about 4.1 points per bidder lost. On the 6,392 lots remaining in the auction, a 2.9-point fall is 185 fewer cleared lots and ₹11.82 lakh of commission a month — arriving in the third quarter, once the pilot has been called a success.

In hardware plus software the trade-off is made once and paid for a decade: the base includes 2019 units whose optical blocks were specified for the 5,000-run interval, so Rapid Mode silently reprices old service contracts. In regulated settings part of the cost is procedural and — the point most teams miss — does not scale with scope: eleven weeks is the same for 1,240 analysers or 214. In AI-native products the sacrificed quantity is usually evaluation coverage, because a model change that lifts aggregate accuracy degrades some slice with no benchmark. At the organisational seams, mature firms do not reason better; they route. Service cost sits in a budget Sheikh defends and Walimbe does not, so it resolves by whoever has the chief executive’s ear.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Transfers are not gains

The competent practitioner computes ₹14.18 lakh a month and stops. The expert finds ₹4.57 lakh moved from customers who gained nothing and ₹7.69 lakh of reagent destroyed. The tell-tale sign is a benefit matching an outsider’s cost.

The default is the decision

Whether firmware 4.3 ships default-on or opt-in is treated as a rollout detail and is the whole trade-off, because opt-in moves the choice to whoever knows if the ceiling binds. The tell-tale sign is a specification naming a capability but not its default.

Revenue from your own defect

Under default-on, Yantrashala earns ₹44 on every repeat its firmware causes. Nobody designed that, and it will shape later decisions on tuning the wash. The tell-tale sign is a quality metric that, if it worsened, would raise revenue.

Adverse selection makes the average case a lie

Instant Quote looks fine on a representative lot and collapses on a selected one, because sellers route each lot to the channel that suits them. An expert never models a marketplace on the average case. The tell-tale sign is a pilot whose entrants the counterparty picks.

Capital and risk are different costs

Kelkar’s alternative carries an average balance of ₹14.19 crore against Instant Quote’s ₹12.19 crore: more capital, far less exposure, because it never takes a price position. Conflating the two is how committees approve the riskier option on the smaller sheet.

Metric asymmetry decides most arguments

Gains are instrumented weekly, costs quarterly or never. Exhibit 2’s third column is the habitual question: in which review would this cost first show? The tell-tale sign is an agreed cost that no dashboard shows for two quarters.

The pivotal input is the deliverable

A ledger producing one number invites a vote; one producing a break-even of 3.3 per cent against a measured range of 3.1 to 6.4 invites an experiment. The tell-tale sign is a sensitivity table varying every input by ten per cent instead of one across its range.

Opportunity cost often does not scale with scope

Narrowing Rapid Mode to 214 analysers cuts the transfer and the service cost but not one week of the eleven. The tell-tale sign is a phased plan whose first phase carries the whole toll.

Some axes should be refused out loud

Walimbe declined to price the clinical consequence of a wrong result, and said so. Naming an axis lexicographic is more honest than giving it a large number, which merely moves the argument to that number. The tell-tale sign is a risk register pricing a catastrophe.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the bearer is a silent minority — users of the displaced feature, users on cheaper devices — and the cost is attention, not money, so it is hard to ledger. In business-to-business and enterprise products the bearer is identifiable and will say so, which is why enterprise trade-offs are better reasoned and worse resolved: the loudest account wins, not the largest cost. In platforms and marketplaces the costs are structural and lagged, as Wapsi’s loop shows. In hardware they are fixed at tooling and paid across a service life, so reversibility dominates. In AI products the cost is distributional and undiscovered until a user finds it, so the ledger needs an evaluation-coverage line.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. A fifteen-person company holds the bearer map in one conversation and needs no ledger for a reversible choice. A firm of Yantrashala’s size cannot: its bearers sit in different budgets, so the written map is what makes an invisible cost arguable.

8. Three worked examples

Warq Packaging Mills, Vapi, 2025. A corrugation line ran four changeovers a shift at 38 minutes each, leaving 328 of 480 minutes productive. An E-flute grade would raise changeovers to seven, leaving 214 minutes — a fall of 34.8 per cent. At ₹1,420 of contribution per productive minute, two shifts, 300 days, the sacrifice was ₹9.71 crore a year against a grade forecast to add ₹2.9 crore of revenue and, at a 26 per cent margin, ₹75.4 lakh: almost thirteen rupees given up for each one gained. Warq ran E-flute on its slowest line only.

Waqt Scheduling Systems, Noida, 2026 — a trade-off that was not one. No-shows ran at 23 per cent of 2,86,000 monthly appointments. A ₹200 deposit cut no-shows to 9 per cent but bookings by 17, so completions fell from 2,20,220 to 2,16,016: the remedy destroyed 4,204 appointments a month. A two-hour reminder with one-tap reschedule cut no-shows to 12 per cent with no friction, giving 2,51,680 completions, 31,460 above baseline. The frontier between friction and reliability was an artefact of the instrument.

Waada Warranty Services, Gurugram, 2026 — where the approach failed. On Monday 9 February Waada raised the threshold for automatic claim approval from ₹2,500 to ₹6,000, and median settlement fell from 6.4 days to 1.9. The ledger priced leakage at the historic 2.1 per cent: 18,400 claims a month averaging ₹3,900 is ₹7.176 crore, so ₹15.07 lakh. Actual leakage settled at 5.8 per cent, or ₹41.62 lakh — up ₹26.5512 lakh — against a renewal benefit of seven points on the 35,000 policies renewing each month, 4,20,000 a year, at ₹690 of contribution: ₹16.905 lakh. Net effect, minus ₹9.6462 lakh a month.

The ledger was not wrong; the instrumentation was. Settlement time sat on the weekly dashboard and leakage was reported quarterly, so the cost stayed invisible for fourteen weeks and surfaced on 18 May — 98 days at that rate, or ₹31.51 lakh, the price of a reporting cadence. The threshold then moved to ₹4,200 with a device-serial check: leakage settled at 3.3 per cent, or ₹23.68 lakh, which is ₹8.6112 lakh above baseline, against a retained five-point renewal gain of ₹12.075 lakh — plus ₹3.4638 lakh a month.

9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Benefit counted, cost narratedNumeric upside, prose risk sectionWhich line is the cost, in what unit?The bearer discovers it after launch
Transfer booked as creationA gain matching an outsider’s lossDid we create this rupee or move it?Churn in the paying segment
Average-case modelling of a selected setThe counterparty picks the entrantsWho chooses what enters the pilot?Wapsi’s ₹7,956 a switched lot, at scale
Metric asymmetryGain weekly, cost quarterlyOn what date would this cost appear?Waada’s ₹31.51 lakh over 98 days
False dichotomy, rigorously costedThe constraint is named after a mechanismWhat would improve both axes?Waqt’s 4,204 lost appointments a month

Exhibit 6. Two errors of accounting, two of modelling, one of framing — the last is the expensive one.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether most trade-offs are real. The constraint-dissolving school points at Waqt: the deposit frontier was an artefact and a better instrument dominated both options. Its evidence is how many costed trade-offs dissolve within two years of someone attacking the mechanism. The frontier school points at Yantrashala: carryover is chemistry, and twenty years of wash-protocol work has not removed it. It would be wrong if a cheap engineering move reliably recovered the lost axis — and nobody knows the base rate: dissolved cases are celebrated, failures are not.

Whether to quantify costs that resist measurement. The decision-analytic school holds that refusing to price partner goodwill or clinical risk does not remove the exchange rate, only hides it, and hidden rates are set by whoever speaks last; Exhibit 2’s third column is its argument. The lexicographic school replies that pricing changes the decision: once a wrong result has a rupee value, someone finds a volume at which paying it is worthwhile. It would be wrong if firms that priced catastrophic costs avoided them more often; the evidence is mixed.

Whether speed makes the analysis obsolete. One camp argues that when building is cheap the answer to a contested trade-off is to run both arms rather than argue, and that elaborate ledgers tax learning. The other replies that cheap building made choices cheaper to implement, not to unwind: Wapsi could have launched Instant Quote in five weeks, and the attrition would still take three quarters to show. Neither has the data.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a thorough ledger. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They ask who pays before asking whether it works, which changes the first week of analysis, not the last. They arrive with a pivotal input and a measurement plan, not a recommendation. They separate transfers from creation unprompted. And they write it down, bearers named, for the next team — because its cost is mostly paid by people who were not in the room.

12. The decisions

At the product council on Thursday 15 October 2026, Walimbe neither recommended shipping Rapid Mode nor shelving it. She proposed firmware 4.3 with Rapid Mode default off, settable per analyser, the repeat rate on the enabling screen. Expected adoption: all 214 constrained analysers, 198 occasionally tight, 35 comfortable — 447 units, worth ₹9.56 lakh a month of extra contribution less ₹0.59 lakh of service, a net ₹8.97 lakh. She then gave most of it away: Yantrashala would credit the cartridge on any quality-control repeat on a Rapid-Mode analyser, costing ₹5.73 lakh and leaving ₹3.24 lakh. The gap between ₹14.18 lakh and ₹3.24 lakh, she argued, was not profit earned but a charge on labs that gained nothing, plus revenue from her own firmware’s defects.

Kelkar’s board paper of Friday 23 October recommended against Instant Quote. His ledger, built with Yara Fonseca in Porto on 34 months of lot-level data, assumed 1,180 induced listings, 1,560 previously unclearing lots and 1,448 switched out of the auction — 22 per cent of the 6,580 that cleared.

The total is the exact sum of the displayed rows; at full precision −₹92.7885 lakh, which alone would round to −₹92.79.

Instant Quote would also require Wapsi to buy ₹45.74 crore of material a month and hold it just under 8.0 days on average: ₹12.19 crore of permanent inventory costing ₹14.22 lakh a month at a 14 per cent cost of capital. Discussion questions. First, Walimbe gave away ₹10.94 lakh a month that was lawfully hers; which school in Exhibit 1 is she reasoning from? Second, Kelkar rejected Instant Quote partly on an ₹11.82 lakh second-order cost he cannot measure in advance; on what evidence should a board accept such a number? Third, both chose the smaller measured upside. When is that judgement, and when is it an organisation talking itself out of growth?

13. Going deeper

  • Product sense and taste — the prior on which costs to hunt for.
  • First-principles reasoning — is the constraint chemistry, or just the current mechanism?
  • Systems thinking for products — costs around loops: attrition becomes clearance.
  • Auditing irreversible product decisions and decision speed versus decision quality — reversibility as a priced item; how much analysis is warranted.
  • When building gets cheap and deciding does not, and taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill — the third disagreement, and what remains when the exchange rate is still a choice.
  • Product deconstruction and product critique — name user, job, promise, model, metric and assumption, then ask who pays for each.
  • Competitive teardown and B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction — a rival’s refusals show its trade-offs; the split decides whether the bearer can speak.
  • Product vision and mission, product principles — pre-committed exchange rates.
case20v1-sense.tradeoffs:
Godaam Works: The Cost of a Faster Sign-up

A decision case on reasoning about trade-offs

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Lopamudra Pangarkar sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of the Godaam Works office in Baner, Pune, with a single printed page in front of her. It showed the September sign-up funnel, with one line circled twice in red: of every 100 shopkeepers who began registering, only 52 finished verification.

Pangarkar, the Chief Product Officer, had until Monday, 19 October, to tell her engineering squad what to build in the three weeks before Diwali, which falls on 8 November this year. Her chief executive wanted more shopkeepers on the app for the festival season. Her head of credit wanted no change at all. The squad could build only one of the options on her desk.

2. Company background

Godaam Works, founded in Pune in 2019, runs a business-to-business ordering app for kirana stores. A shopkeeper in Nashik, Indore or Coimbatore orders biscuits, edible oil, detergent and tea from regional distributors and receives the goods the next morning. Godaam earns a margin on each order and, for retailers who qualify, a fee on short-term credit that lets the shopkeeper pay the distributor in thirty days rather than on delivery. The credit is funded by a partner non-banking finance company, so the lending is bound by the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules and know-your-customer requirements.

In the year to March 2026 the company handled goods worth ₹1,860 crore across roughly 3.4 lakh active retailers in 140 cities. It competes with Udaan, Flipkart Wholesale and JioMart Partner, and it watches the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) as a possible future channel. The kirana owner distrusts forms, and a distributor's salesman with a handwritten ledger already offers him credit on a handshake.

3. The situation

Since 2022 Godaam has required full verification before a retailer's first order: PAN, a GST or Udyam certificate, Aadhaar-based eKYC, a bank account and a geotagged shop photograph. Every retailer is offered credit on day one, and the lending partner will not release it otherwise.

Exhibit 1 shows what the rule costs. In September, 40,000 shopkeepers began registering. Only 20,800 completed verification, and 14,560 of those placed an order within thirty days. Lindiwe Pretorius, the data scientist in Cape Town, found that most people quit at the document step, usually because the Udyam certificate was with an accountant. A lighter flow, she estimated, would lift completion to about 78 per cent.

The lighter flow would also admit weaker borrowers. Godaam's current credit loss is 1.8 per cent of the amount drawn, and Pretorius's model, trained on a small pilot in Surat and Jaipur, suggested that retailers admitted on light checks and given credit immediately would default at about 5.5 per cent. She was candid that the pilot covered only 900 retailers.

Three options had emerged. Exhibit 2 shows what each would have produced for the September cohort, and Exhibit 3 shows what each would cost to build and when it would go live.

4. The people

Laxman Paranjpe, Head of Credit and Risk, works from Mumbai, close to the finance partner. He has watched small-ticket lending lose money when onboarding was loosened, and he wants full verification kept for anyone who borrows.

Leelavathi Pawar, Head of Field Sales, is based in Hyderabad and manages 160 representatives who visit shops. She hears the complaint directly: the Udaan agent signs a shopkeeper up in four minutes. She wants the flow shortened before the festival, when orders peak.

Leonor Paiva, the lead designer, works from Lisbon and several hours behind Pune. She has prototyped a staged flow in which the shopkeeper orders first and is asked for documents only when he asks for credit. She worries that the team will measure sign-up completion simply because it is easy to measure.

Lindiwe Pretorius, the data scientist in Cape Town, owns the estimates. She wants the decision to be reversible, with a cap on early exposure until the pilot grows.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: keep full verification. Nothing is built, and Exhibit 2 shows a net of ₹361.09 lakh for the cohort. Losses stay at 1.8 per cent. The cost falls on the 19,200 shopkeepers who began registering and did not finish. Leelavathi Pawar's representatives will keep losing sign-ups to competitors whose forms are shorter.

Option B: light checks, credit from day one. This is the fastest to build, two weeks and ₹9.0 lakh, and goes live five days before Diwali. It raises ordering retailers from 14,560 to 19,344, the chief executive's headline. Yet credit loss rises to ₹425.57 lakh and the net falls to ₹193.44 lakh. The upside is visible in the first week; the cost arrives in the third month, when the credit falls due, and lands on Godaam and its lender.

Option C: light checks, credit after the third order. A shopkeeper registers with a mobile number, PAN and shop photograph, orders against cash or UPI, and is asked for full verification only when he reaches three orders and wants credit. Net rises to ₹385.07 lakh, the highest of the three. The cost is time and focus: ten weeks, ₹45.0 lakh and a go-live on 29 December, which misses Diwali and pushes back the ONDC pilot. C also depends on an untested assumption: that half of ordering retailers will upgrade.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. For each option, who gains, who pays and what becomes slower or impossible?
  2. Exhibit 1 shows B lifting completed verifications from 20,800 to 31,200 and Exhibit 2 shows it producing the lowest net. What does that tell you about the metric the team is currently watching?
  3. Option C's result rests on the assumption that half of ordering retailers upgrade. What share of upgrades would make C no better than A, and how likely does that seem?
  4. Given that C misses Diwali, what would you tell the chief executive on Monday?

8. A note for the learner

This topic asks one thing of the decision-maker: before choosing, state what each choice costs and who pays. Each option here has a visible winner and a hidden loser. Option A's loser is the shopkeeper who quit and never appears in a report. Option B's loser appears three months later in a different department. Option C's losers are those who wait: festival-season sign-ups and the ONDC pilot.

A well-reasoned answer does not choose the best headline: Option B wins on sign-ups and loses on net. A careful reader also checks the assumption behind the best-looking number. Setting the upgrade share in Design C at zero, the 20,592 ordering retailers contribute 20,592 times ₹1,500, or ₹308.88 lakh, below Design A's ₹361.09 lakh. Solving for the break-even gives an upgrade share of about 34 per cent. The assumed 50 per cent leaves a modest cushion, and the pilot was small.

One defensible path is Option C, with two safeguards. First, pay for the ten weeks: C's advantage over A is ₹385.07 lakh less ₹361.09 lakh, or ₹23.98 lakh per monthly cohort, so the ₹45.0 lakh build is recovered in under two months of cohorts if volumes hold, and the festival months will probably be larger. Second, cap early exposure for the first cohorts, as Pretorius suggested, so that a wrong upgrade assumption is cheap to discover. Meanwhile Pawar's representatives can help shopkeepers finish the existing flow in person. The decision costs Godaam a Diwali without the new flow. That is a real price, and the discipline of the topic is to name it plainly to the chief executive and accept it.

Reasonable people could pick Option A while the pilot grows. They could not defensibly pick Option B unless they could show that the 5.5 per cent loss rate was wrong.
case40v1-sense.b2b.b2c:
Oorja Network: Who Is the Customer at Two in the Morning?

An ambiguous case on buyers, users, sales motions and assets

1. Sunday night, 15 November 2026

The drizzle had come back over Domlur, and Vasanti Desai had the Bengaluru office to herself. On the whiteboard were two curves crossing near midnight: the hourly shape of the electricity Oorja Network sold to scooter riders, and of what it sold to one logistics company's cargo three-wheelers. They were drawn to settle an argument about hardware.

Next morning her board wanted an answer on Omaya Services' term sheet. Omaya's committee met on Thursday 19 November and wanted signature by Friday 20 November — 53 days after the proposal of Monday 28 September, 284 days after Omaya first raised it on Monday 9 February. Oorja held ₹480.00 lakh of cash at 31 October 2026, and three ways to spend it.

2. How Oorja got here

Oorja Network was incorporated in Bengaluru on Thursday 11 March 2021 by Desai and Viraj Dholakia, an engineer, on the thesis that India would electrify two wheels first. It raised ₹3.20 crore of seed money in 2021 and ₹14.50 crore from Ojus Partners on Tuesday 17 October 2023; of the ₹17.70 crore, ₹4.05 crore became a gross block of chargers and grid connections, the rest losses.

Everything is now shaped by Tuesday 2 August 2022, when Dholakia signed the first Site Host Agreement, with a fuel-pump dealer in Hosur. The host gave space and a connection; Oorja owned the chargers and paid ₹2.10 a unit dispensed. Clause 7.3 obliged Oorja to keep every bay open to any vehicle of the right connector type; clause 9.2 barred it from managing a third party's points within two kilometres. Sixty-four of 96 live sites run on that template, and 41 sit within two kilometres of a site Oorja now wants to manage for someone else.

3. The industry

By 2026 Indian charging had split into three businesses sharing nothing but a plug: highway networks such as Tata Power's EZ Charge and Jio-bp pulse; captive estates such as Ather Grid and Ola Electric's Hypercharger; and independents like Statiq and ChargeZone, which also sell software. Oorja, at 318 points, was small in all three. The Ministry of Power's guidelines let any entity run a public station without a licence and resell electricity at a service tariff, with the Bureau of Energy Efficiency as nodal agency; neither that nor PM E-DRIVE changed the two numbers that governed Oorja — the discom tariff, ₹7.90 a unit at public sites and ₹6.40 inside depots, and the share of the day a charger ran. Every figure here is before 18 per cent GST.

Demand came from elsewhere. Zomato, Swiggy, Flipkart and Amazon had committed to electric last-mile delivery, and the fleets serving them bought three-wheelers from Mahindra and Bajaj in thousands. They wanted no charging experience: a cost per kilometre, a depot cleared by six, an invoice. Oorja's payroll suited neither customer — operations in Bengaluru, design in Amsterdam, data science in Montreal, success in Jakarta, partnerships in Austin.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

On Monday 20 January 2025 Vaidika Damle circulated a forecast from Montreal projecting 14 per cent public utilisation by mid-2026, and the board approved 120 more points on it. In the six months to 30 September 2026 those points ran at 6.0 per cent — 4,68,000 units against the 78,00,192 of rated capacity that 240 chargers at 7.4 kW deliver in 183 days (Exhibit 1). The forecast missed one thing: a scooter's 3 to 4 kWh pack fills overnight from a household socket at domestic rates: public charging is insurance bought in a hurry, not a routine. Only 62,000 vehicles charged at all.

The fleet business began as a favour. In September 2025 Vaishali Daftary, chief operating officer of Omaya Services, a Chennai last-mile operator of cargo three-wheelers, asked for six chargers inside two depots. The pilot ran 91 days to Sunday 14 December 2025; a master services agreement followed on Monday 9 February 2026, and Oorja built to 78 DC points across 11 depots — 70 live by 1 April 2026, four at Jigani from 1 July, four at Nelamangala from 1 August (Exhibit 2). Energy flowed at ₹14.20 a unit against a per-point monthly minimum, plus ₹260 a vehicle a month for software. Those points dispensed 11,30,000 units at 22.0 per cent of rated capacity. Three things complicate that, none in the board's deck.

The average is an artefact. Three of the 11 depots produced 6,67,000 of the 11,30,000 units, or 59.0 per cent of fleet volume, from 31 of the 78 fleet points, which is 39.7 per cent of them. The median depot ran at 18.6 per cent, and six sat below their contractual minimum — which has never been enforced. The agreement sets 2,600 units a point a month; pro-rated for months live, the half-year minimum was 11,44,000 units against 11,30,000 delivered, 14,000 short, worth ₹1.26 lakh at the ₹9.00 shortfall charge. Vasudev Dalmia, the controller, nets strong depots against weak. Read as written, depot by depot, the six deficient depots fell 2,24,400 units below their combined minimum of 6,08,400, or 36.9 per cent of it, worth ₹20.20 lakh. No invoice has gone out.

Oorja does not see the whole fleet. The 1,41,250 fleet sessions over 183 days average 772 a night against 1,480 Omaya vehicles, about 52 per cent of the fleet on any night; the rest use 140 points Omaya bought from another vendor in 2024. Oorja is asked for exclusivity it is not offered. And Omaya pays late: against 30-day terms the average is 74 days, which on half-year fleet revenue of ₹183.55 lakh leaves ₹74.22 lakh outstanding, 15.5 per cent of the ₹480.00 lakh of cash — and the term sheet proposes 90-day terms as a term, not an apology.

5. The people

Vasanti Desai, co-founder and chief executive. Needs a round Ojus Partners says requires either contracted revenue or a credible consumer cohort, not both. Not saying: she no longer believes her own January 2025 forecast.

Viraj Dholakia, co-founder, network operations. Not saying: clause 9.2, which he wrote, blocks the option he privately prefers, and the board does not know how many sites it touches.

Vedika Dwivedi, consumer product. Argues the 62,000 riders are the only customers who chose Oorja. Not saying: monthly actives have been flat since February and she has stopped reporting them.

Varun Duggal, global partnerships, Austin. Paid commission on contracted value at signature. Not saying: Ovi Freight Collective approached him in August about 40 points, and Omaya's exclusivity schedule names Ovi.

Vaidika Damle, data scientist, Montreal. Wants the model rebuilt before capital is spent. Not saying: it used mall parking surveys as a proxy for charging demand, undocumented.

Vrushali Dhingra, customer success, Jakarta. Runs the rider helpline and the Omaya account from one team of nine. Not saying: two resign on 31 December.

Vaishali Daftary, chief operating officer, Omaya Services, Chennai. Wants cost per kilometre down and one accountable vendor. Not saying: her board wants the option of owning charging assets — hence its right to terminate on 90 days' notice from 9 February 2027 and buy the points at book value.

Option 1: sign Omaya. Build 180 DC points at 19 depots, take fleet points to 258, accept ₹13.40 a unit on all fleet volume, 90-day terms, exclusivity against three named rivals, and the funding in Exhibit 5. It cuts the price on volume Oorja already has: 22,54,000 units at ₹0.80 less is ₹18.03 lakh a year given away before a new point is energised. The enlarged estate runs at 12.4 per cent of rated capacity on the management case and 10.6 per cent at the minimum, against the 22.0 per cent the first 78 points achieved, because depots are sized for the four hours when every vehicle plugs in at once. Per vehicle the minimum implies 1,059 kWh a year against 1,523 kWh for the existing 1,480 vehicles annualised: a floor at 70 per cent of what Omaya's fleet already does.

Option 2: build for riders. Decline, add 300 public points, spend ₹92.00 lakh on marketing; Exhibit 4 assumes utilisation rising from 6.0 to 7.2 per cent. Desai has worked out the number she has not put in the model: at a margin of ₹10.78 a unit after power, host share and payment costs, the public estate's ₹66.78 lakh of maintenance, field operations and marketing is covered at about 6,19,000 units — on the same 240 points, 7.9 per cent utilisation, 32 per cent more volume. The consumer line is nearer break-even than a contribution of minus ₹16.32 lakh suggests, and still short of it on the plan she would fund.

Option 3: sell the software. Stop buying chargers; license the platform, app and roaming at ₹1,100 a point a month. Exhibit 4 makes it the least bad net result, with ₹34.00 lakh of capital and 98.5 per cent of today's cash intact at year end, against 55.9 per cent under Option 1 and 50.6 per cent under Option 2. It has no signed customer, needs 41 landlords to waive clause 9.2, and the most-favoured-customer clause would reprice Omaya's energy to match any licensee discount.

Desai has written the three up as a choice between a buyer and a user. Clause 9.2, Daftary's 140 private points and the curves in Exhibit 3 suggest the axis may run instead between owning assets and owning demand — and that Oorja, at 318 points and 62,000 riders, is too small to own either.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Omaya wants signature by Friday 20 November 2026, and Daftary has hinted that a refusal triggers a tender in January. Omaya may terminate on 90 days' notice from 9 February 2027 and buy the 78 installed points at written-down value, so the ₹376.23 lakh of fleet revenue in Options 2 and 3 is contractual only to 10 May 2027 and discretionary after that. Omisha Partners requires 1.25 times debt-service cover and the ring-fenced project delivers 1.14. Cash is ₹480.00 lakh against central overhead of ₹96.40 lakh a half-year, and Dhingra loses two of nine on 31 December. Omaya's draft annexure assumes per-driver session data flows to it; under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act Oorja is the fiduciary for people who installed its app, and the consent notices served do not contemplate that.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. For each of Oorja's two lines, name the buyer, user, blocker and signatory. Where are they one person?
  2. Exhibit 1 puts fleet utilisation at 22.0 per cent and Exhibit 2 puts it at 23.4 for the same units, while the network figure is 12.4 against a simple mean of 14.0. Which belongs in a board pack, and what would a careless reader conclude?
  3. The fleet line contributes ₹5.70 a unit and the public line loses ₹3.49. Why might that not tell Desai which to grow? Use Option 2's break-even volume and Option 1's dilution.
  4. Omaya has delivered 98.8 per cent of its aggregate minimum, 63.1 per cent at six of eleven depots, and pays at 74 days against 30. What has Oorja sold it — energy, availability, or an option?
  5. Clause 9.2 was written in 2022 to defend one forecourt and now constrains every option. Which clause in Omaya's draft is 2029's 9.2?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November. What does Desai do before the call, what does she say to the board, and which single number does she commit to by 31 March 2027? If the board asks which business to stop, what is her answer?

Past eleven, Desai rubbed out the curves to see what was written beneath. There was something: ₹20.20 lakh, a fortnight old, in Dalmia's hand, with a question mark. Monday wanted a direction, and she had three, each resting on a figure that was correct and a denominator she was no longer sure she had chosen.
case20v1-sense.b2b.b2c:
Ekavali Systems: One Borrower Base, Two Kinds of Customer

A decision case in product sense: who is the customer, and who is the user?

1. Opening

On Monday 12 October 2026, Kalpana Oswal sat in a glass-walled meeting room at her company's office in Baner, Pune, with a one-page term sheet and a calendar open to Friday 30 October. By then Vanshree Housing Finance, a mid-sized non-banking finance company in Chennai, expected a yes or no on a three-year contract to embed Ekavali's bill-and-EMI reminder product inside Vanshree's own borrower app.

Oswal, the founder and chief executive of Ekavali Systems, had built the product for ordinary households. Now a single buyer wanted it. Accepting would change whom she designed for, how she sold and what she measured. Ekavali had cash for roughly thirteen months, and she had eighteen days to decide.

2. Company background

Ekavali Systems was founded in 2019 by Oswal, a former product manager, and two engineers. Its consumer app, Ekavali Bills, reads due dates for utilities, credit cards and loans from SMS and email, reminds users, and lets them pay through BBPS, the Bharat BillPay system run by NPCI. The basic app is free; a ₹149-a-year tier adds family sharing.

PhonePe, Paytm, Google Pay and CRED all remind users of bills inside wider payments or credit relationships, and none charges for the reminder. By March 2026 Ekavali had 18,00,000 cumulative downloads, 4,20,000 monthly active users and 31 employees. The next round would depend on a visible revenue model.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows the consumer business for the year to March 2026. Revenue of ₹69.29 lakh was ₹31.29 lakh from 21,000 premium subscribers at ₹149 plus ₹38.00 lakh in BBPS commission. Costs were ₹284 lakh, so the company lost ₹214.71 lakh. Revenue per monthly active user, total over total, was ₹16.50 a year. Ekavali spent ₹96 lakh to bring in 3,20,000 installs, of which 9,600 became paying subscribers, a conversion of 3.0 per cent and a cost of ₹1,000 for each subscriber who then paid ₹149 a year.

Against that arithmetic, an enquiry arrived on Monday 9 March 2026 from Kajal Odhekar, head of collections at Vanshree Housing Finance. Vanshree had 6,50,000 active borrowers on small home-improvement loans, and late instalments were its main cost. Odhekar wanted reminders inside Vanshree's own app, under Vanshree's name.

Vanshree's security team sent a questionnaire, cleared on 22 April once Ekavali documented how it would handle borrower data as a processor under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, with Vanshree as data fiduciary, and how this fitted RBI expectations on outsourcing by NBFCs. A pilot then ran for 13 weeks, 91 days, from Monday 15 June to Monday 14 September. Vanshree invited 5,000 borrowers to the reminders and left a comparable 5,000 untouched. In the invited group 1,850 activated, 37.0 per cent of those invited. On-time instalment payment was 91.2 per cent among the 5,000 invited (4,560 borrowers) and 88.0 per cent among the 5,000 not invited (4,400), a gap of 3.2 percentage points, or 160 more on-time payers per 5,000 borrowers.

Vanshree's proposal followed on Monday 28 September: a one-time integration fee of ₹45 lakh and ₹38 per active borrower per year. If 30 per cent of the 6,50,000 borrowers, 1,95,000, became active, the recurring fee would be ₹74.10 lakh a year, or ₹11.40 for every borrower on the book. Vanshree's board would meet on Friday 30 October, 235 days after the first message. Diwali is Sunday 8 November.

The global team saw it differently. Keyur Odak in Bengaluru feared enterprise features would crowd out the consumer roadmap. Kavish Oza in Chicago, ten and a half hours behind Pune, called the pilot the first real evidence of anything. Kamya Ombale in Kuala Lumpur, two and a half hours ahead, worried about supporting a lender with a thin team. Kunjan Okhade in Lisbon, four and a half hours behind, feared a lender's brand rules would strip out the product's calm.

4. The people

Kalpana Oswal, chief executive in Pune, wants a company that survives eighteen months without losing its purpose. Keyur Odak, head of engineering, wants weekly releases to millions of phones. Kavish Oza, sales head, hired in January, wants a commitment to enterprise. Kamya Ombale, customer success, wants a choice her team can support. Kunjan Okhade, designer, wants design kept with people who care. Kajal Odhekar at Vanshree wants fewer late payments and a vendor her security team will not reject.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out the consumer business. Exhibit 2 projects each option below for the twelve months from November 2026, starting from ₹240 lakh of cash. Exhibit 3 compares the two ways of selling.

6. The options

Option A: stay consumer. Decline Vanshree and raise paid acquisition to ₹150 lakh. The upside is focus: one buyer who is also the user, and weekly releases. The cost is in Exhibit 2: spend rises while revenue per user stays at ₹16.50, and runway shortens to 12.0 months, before any fundraising can rescue it.

Option B: full pivot. Stop paid acquisition, put the consumer app in maintenance and hire four people to sell to and support lenders. The upside is recurring, contracted revenue from buyers with budgets, and 16.5 months of runway. The cost is a bet on one pilot: revenue depends on a second client not yet identified, in a market where a sale took 235 days here, and on a team that has never supported a regulated customer.

Option C: anchor client, bounded. Sign Vanshree, keep the consumer app on organic growth and a ₹24 lakh paid budget, and add two enterprise hires, a solutions engineer and a compliance lead, costing ₹66 lakh. The upside is the longest runway, 26.6 months. The cost is attention: 31 people serve two kinds of customer, one sold in minutes and one over months.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Who are the buyer, the user and the possible blocker for Ekavali Bills and for the Vanshree product, and what does each want?
  2. Using Exhibit 3, why does revenue per head look similar while the cost of earning it differs so much?
  3. What does the 91.2 versus 88.0 per cent result prove, and what does it not?
  4. Which option would you choose by 30 October, and what evidence would change your mind by March 2027?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. In consumer products the person who pays, chooses and uses is usually one, and the sale takes minutes. In business products the buyer, the user, the security reviewer and the signatory are often different people, and the cycle is months. Success is measured on the buyer's outcome, here on-time repayment, not on the user's delight.

A defensible path: Option C, with gates. Option A scales the weakest economics, ₹1,000 to win a user worth ₹149 a year. Option B is rational only if the market is proven, and one pilot is evidence of one customer. Option C converts the strongest signal, a 3.2 point gap a lender can measure, into ₹169.87 lakh of first-year revenue while holding cash for 26.6 months. Oswal should ring-fence a small enterprise squad so that Odak's roadmap is not hostage to Vanshree's requests, keep Ekavali a processor to Vanshree's borrowers, and set one review on 31 March 2027: if no second lender has signed or entered a paid pilot, the enterprise bet is unproven and she should revisit the choice.
exp20v2-sense.b2b.b2c:
B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction

1. A free app and a six-thousand-rupee promise

On the morning of 12 March 2026, Ananya Chaturvedi, head of product at Banjara Billing Systems, opened a spreadsheet with two columns and one uncomfortable line beneath them. Banjara sold billing and stock software to kirana stores, the neighbourhood grocers of Indian towns. It had 18,400 paying stores, each on a plan of ₹6,000 a year. The arithmetic of that base was simple: 18,400 × ₹6,000 = ₹11,04,00,000, or ₹11.04 crore of annual subscription revenue.

The line beneath the columns was a proposal from the chief executive, due before the board in fourteen days, on 26 March. Banjara would build a free consumer app through which shoppers in a lane could order from their own kirana, and spend ₹60 lakh in a pilot to acquire 1,00,000 installs. "Our stores already have the customers," the chief executive had written. "Why are we selling to one shopkeeper at a time when we could sell to a whole lane?"

Charan Bedi, head of sales, replied within the hour that a consumer app was not a bigger version of the product they had; it was a different business. Carlos Baptista, the designer who worked from Lisbon, added a quieter point: he could never say who the "customer" was in the product he drew. Was it the shopkeeper who paid, the nephew who typed bills at the counter, or the shopper who would press "Order"? All three disagreements were one disagreement. If she answered it wrongly, Banjara would spend ₹60 lakh learning something a spreadsheet could have told it for nothing, and might neglect the 18,400 stores that paid the salaries.

2. The idea

B2B (business-to-business) means a product sold to an organisation that uses it to earn money or run its operations. B2C (business-to-consumer) means a product sold to an individual for personal use. The labels sound like a description of the buyer. The more useful reading is that they describe a whole set of linked differences: who decides, who uses, how much a customer is worth, how the product is sold, and how long a sale takes.

The distinction was invented to solve a practical problem. Early marketing theory treated every buyer as an individual weighing price and taste, which predicted little for industrial sellers of machinery and chemicals. Researchers in the 1950s and 1960s studied "industrial buying", and in 1972 Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind gave the idea its most durable form, the buying centre: the group of people inside a customer organisation who share in a purchase decision, each with different motives.

The sentence Ananya could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "In B2C one person buys, uses and pays; in B2B those are usually three different people, and our product has to satisfy all of them before it earns a rupee."

3. How it actually works

Take the buying process step by step, using Banjara's own store product. First, a trigger occurs: a store owner is fined for a mismatched GST invoice, or sees a competitor print a neat bill. Second, someone learns of the product, typically through a field representative or wholesaler. Third comes evaluation, which for a business means a demonstration and a trial on real stock. Fourth, approval: the owner pays, but only after consulting the person who will live with the software and, often, the chartered accountant who files the returns. Fifth, adoption: the counter staff must actually enter the bills. Sixth, renewal, twelve months later, when the owner asks whether the product earned its fee.

A consumer purchase compresses these steps. A shopper sees an app, installs it in a minute, and decides within a few sessions whether to stay. The buyer, user and payer are one person, and nobody must be convinced on her behalf. The steps practitioners leave implicit are the ones that vanish in B2C and dominate in B2B: approval by someone who will not use the product, adoption by someone who did not choose it, and renewal judged on business results rather than enjoyment.

Figure 1 shows why Carlos could not name "the customer". In the existing product he was designing for a payer and a user simultaneously, and their interests diverge: the owner wants fewer errors and lower cost; the nephew at the counter wants to finish a bill in eight seconds with a queue waiting. A feature that lengthens each bill will be quietly abandoned by the person whose behaviour decides whether the owner sees any value.

4. A worked example

Ananya compared the two businesses with one yardstick. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is total spend to win customers divided by the customers won. LTV (lifetime value) is the gross profit one customer yields over their lifetime, here annual gross profit divided by annual churn, where churn is the share of customers lost each year. The ratio LTV ÷ CAC says how many rupees come back for each rupee spent.

For stores, she took one month's sales effort: 1,000 leads, of which 30 per cent (300) accepted a demonstration; 40 per cent of those (120) started a trial; and 50 per cent of trials (60) converted to paid. Field staff and marketing cost ₹4,50,000 that month. So CAC = ₹4,50,000 ÷ 60 = ₹7,500. A store pays ₹6,000 a year at a 70 per cent gross margin, so gross profit is ₹4,200 a year (₹350 a month). With 20 per cent annual churn, expected lifetime is 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5 years, so LTV = ₹4,200 × 5 = ₹21,000.

For shoppers, the pilot spend was ₹60 lakh (₹60,00,000) for 1,00,000 installs, and she assumed 20 per cent became active buyers: 20,000. CAC = ₹60,00,000 ÷ 20,000 = ₹300. Commission on orders would yield ₹240 gross profit per active shopper per year (₹20 a month). With 70 per cent annual churn, lifetime is 1 ÷ 0.70 = 1.4286 years, so LTV = ₹240 × 1.4286 = ₹342.86, shown as ₹343.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Buyer, user and payer are roles, not people

In a small store the owner can occupy all three; in a chain of fifty outlets they are distinct. The question to ask is not "is this B2B?" but "how many separate people must say yes, and who can say no?"

B2B is not the same as "expensive" or "enterprise"

Banjara's ₹6,000 plan is cheap, yet its buyer is a business. Price sets the sales motion, meaning the way a product reaches customers: self-serve sign-up for small tickets, field or inside sales for larger ones.

The sales cycle is a cost, not a delay

The sales cycle is the time from first contact to signed deal. Longer cycles tie up representatives and slow experiments: Banjara learns one result per month from its funnel, while a consumer team may run a test per day.

Consumer products sometimes bill businesses, and vice versa

A product used by individuals but bought by employers (a work chat tool, say) is B2B in how it is paid for and B2C in how it is adopted. Classify by who pays and who decides, then separately by who uses.

The Banjara app would be a marketplace-like hybrid

Shoppers order from stores, so the app needs both sides. An assumption sound for one side (stores pay for reliability) may fail for the other (shoppers pay for nothing).

The framework cannot tell you demand

Classifying a product as B2B or B2C predicts how it must be sold, not whether anyone wants it. The rates above are assumptions until measured.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who signs? Who uses on a Tuesday? Who is blamed if it fails? What would make the payer cancel even if the user loves it?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace compared

In consumer products the central work is attention and habit: the key metrics are activation, retention and frequency, and teams iterate through experiments on large audiences. In B2B the central work is trust and integration: metrics include pipeline, win rate, net revenue retention and renewals, and the product must meet audit and workflow requirements consumers never see. In marketplaces, which connect two groups of customers, the central work is balance: too few sellers drive buyers away.

Scale changes things too. An early-stage B2B company usually sells through its founders, who personally hear why deals fail and tailor the product accordingly. A large one separates product, sales and customer success, and information degrades between them. Banjara has a mature field team and no consumer muscle at all.

7. Common mistakes

Designing for the user and forgetting the payer

Symptom: delighted trials that never convert. Misunderstanding: assuming the person who enjoys the product holds the budget. Diagnostic: ask three lost deals who finally refused, and why.

Applying consumer growth metrics to business products

Symptom: celebrating installs while revenue stalls. Misunderstanding: counting users, not accounts that renew. Diagnostic: compute CAC and recovery months per paying account, as above.

Treating a long cycle as a sign of failure

Symptom: panic when a deal takes three weeks. Misunderstanding: expecting consumer speed. Diagnostic: compare the cycle with deals already won.

Assuming a free consumer layer will sell the paid business product

Symptom: large usage, no willingness to pay. Misunderstanding: believing reach converts to revenue. Diagnostic: before building, ask twenty shoppers and twenty owners what they would give up to have it.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Ananya's decision begins by naming each role aloud: owner (payer), counter staff (user), accountant (influencer), shopper (a new consumer). It then puts a number on each path before any code is written, as the tables did, and finds the cheapest test that could change it. It does not ask "should we be B2B or B2C?" but "which customer's behaviour must change, who can stop it, and what will it cost us to reach them?" It also writes down in advance what result would make the experiment stop.

9. Closing

Ananya took a narrower proposal to the board on 26 March. She recommended no ₹60 lakh pilot. Instead she asked for a small experiment inside the existing product: let 500 existing stores share an order link with their regular shoppers, and measure how many orders arrive and whether those stores renew. Her reasoning was that the store was already the paying customer and the route to the shopper; the pilot would test whether shoppers add value to the B2B product before Banjara committed to a second, lower-value business. The base case showed ₹343 of value for ₹300 of cost, a margin too thin to build on without evidence, while the store business returned ₹2.80 per rupee spent.

To go further, study next the roles of buyer, user, influencer and blocker, which refines the three-person picture used here; then B2B versus B2C strategy, which turns the distinction into choices about pricing and channels; and the segment landscapes of small business, mid-market and enterprise.

Two questions to sit with. Think of one product you use at work and one at home: who chose each, and who pays? And if Banjara's trial conversion fell to 35 per cent, which assumption in the consumer table would you check first, and why?

B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction

1. Two companies, two crossings

On Tuesday, 8 September 2026, Meenakshi Lalwani, head of product at Niyam Fitness Network in Pune, printed the August acquisition report. Niyam sold a consumer subscription — guided exercise and physiotherapy on a phone, ₹2,400 a year — to 1,45,000 subscribers, an annual recurring revenue of ₹34.8 crore. The August funnel was the cleanest she had seen and the least encouraging.

Exhibit 1. Niyam Fitness Network: consumer acquisition funnel, August 2026.

Niyam had spent ₹1.68 crore in August, so each subscriber cost ₹2,500. A subscriber paid ₹2,400 a year against ₹600 of variable cost, leaving ₹1,800 of gross profit, and 58 per cent lapsed within the year. At that churn the base lost 84,100 a year while adding 80,640 — twelve months of 6,720. Niyam was shrinking by 3,460 a year while spending ₹20.16 crore to do it. The board met on Friday, 13 November 2026, sixty-six days later.

The proposal was corporate wellness: seats sold to employers at ₹900 per employee per year, minimum 500. Lokendra Nalawade, who ran growth, called it the only honest answer. Manjiri Pawaskar, the physiotherapy lead, asked who she would be treating — the employee, or the human-resources head reading a utilisation dashboard. Nuno Pacheco, the design lead in Porto, said every screen he had drawn assumed its viewer had chosen to be there.

In Coimbatore, Marichi Solar Industries was arguing the same line from the other side. Marichi made rooftop-solar monitoring controllers and the portal that read them, selling to 2,140 factory and commercial sites through 184 engineering and construction partners. Revenue for the year to 31 March 2026 was ₹138 crore.

Exhibit 2. Marichi Solar Industries: revenue mix, year to 31 March 2026.

Installation and commissioning24.617.8%
Monitoring subscriptions13.810.0%
