On Tuesday, 22 September 2026, Pallav Mohile, vice-president of product, circulated a proposal for Marichi Nilay: a ₹14,000 home kit with a ₹1,200 annual subscription, for households installing rooftop solar under the national residential subsidy scheme. A ₹3.2 crore pilot would acquire 8,000 households. Maitreyi Lobo, the chief financial officer, said the management committee would take it on Friday, 16 October 2026 — twenty-four days later — if somebody showed her the per-household contribution. Lavina Pinto, who ran service operations, said she knew it already.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

B2B describes a product whose purchase is authorised by an organisation and justified by its effect on that organisation's money or risk. B2C describes a product whose purchase is authorised by the individual who will use it and justified by her own preference. The definition turns on authorisation rather than the buyer's legal form, because that is where the consequences live.

The distinction was not born in product management. Mid-century marketing theory modelled a single utility-maximising shopper, which explained little about why a steel mill took nine months to buy a pump. Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind, in 1972, proposed the buying centre — the people inside a customer organisation who share a purchase decision, each with a distinct motive and veto. Jagdish Sheth's 1973 model added that the group's disagreements, not its preferences, drive a purchase's timing; a separate line, through Anderson and Narus, held that a business buyer can be shown the rupees the product adds.

Four schools now disagree about what the distinction is worth. The buying-centre school signs that the unit of analysis is the decision-making group, and that a product failing any role in it stalls regardless of quality; it will not sign that the group is stable — the same ₹10 lakh deal passes a different cast at a 400-person firm and a 40,000-person one. The motion school, behind product-led growth, signs that one classifies by how the product reaches the customer and who can block it, since a ₹900 seat and a ₹9 crore platform have nothing in common; it will not sign that "B2B" and "B2C" name coherent categories.

The jobs school signs that the job the product is hired to do is the unit of design and buyer identity a downstream fact; it will not sign that the payer's constraints should shape the product, the road to building something nobody wants. The platform-economics school, from Rochet and Tirole, signs that with two distinct user groups the question is which side you subsidise; it will not sign that there is a single customer, and so calls the question badly posed.

On Niyam's proposal the buying-centre and jobs schools instruct oppositely: build the utilisation dashboard first, because the human-resources head renews; or the knee-pain programme, because nothing renews if nobody exercises.

3. Mechanics: one yardstick, worked

Experts do not settle this with labels. They reduce both options to one comparable number, then attack its assumptions. The yardstick here is retention-weighted five-year contribution per rupee of acquisition cost. Contribution is revenue less the costs of serving a customer; retention-weighting multiplies each future year by the probability the customer is still there, so with annual churn c, year t counts (1−c)t.

For Niyam's consumer subscriber, annual contribution is ₹1,800 and churn 58 per cent, so the five-year multiplier is 1 + 0.42 + 0.42² + 0.42³ + 0.42⁴ = 1.7016. Five-year contribution is ₹3,062.89 against ₹2,500 of acquisition: a ratio of 1.23, before salary, rent or engineering.

The corporate seat is where the second-order effects appear. An average account is 1,200 seats at ₹900, so ₹10,80,000 a year — but an employer buys seats, not users. Niyam's pilot showed 22 per cent of seats activating: 264 employees in a 1,200-seat account, so serving cost scales with 264, not 1,200. At ₹600 per active per year that is ₹132 per seat, plus ₹60 of account management, giving ₹192 of cost and ₹708 of contribution per seat — a 78.7 per cent margin, better than the consumer product. The employer pays ₹4,090.91 for every employee who actually uses the service, against ₹2,400 from a consumer who chose it. Low engagement raises the margin and lowers the renewal probability at once, an opposition no consumer business faces.

Account contribution is ₹8,49,600 a year. A quarter of selling cost ₹48 lakh and closed ten accounts, so acquisition is ₹4,80,000 each. At 18 per cent account churn the five-year multiplier is 3.4959, giving ₹29,70,108 and a ratio of 6.19.

The step practitioners leave implicit is the next one: which input in the better number is a measurement, and which a hope. Niyam has measured ₹2,500, ₹1,800 and 58 per cent across 1,45,000 subscribers; it has measured nothing about 18 per cent account churn, having never renewed an account.

Exhibit 3. Niyam corporate account: the one assumption nobody has measured. Annual contribution held at ₹8,49,600, acquisition at ₹4,80,000.

Lifetime contribution is the perpetuity ₹8,49,600 ÷ churn, so it exceeds the five-year ₹29,70,108.

4. When the distinction applies, and when it misleads

The distinction earns its keep when three testable claims hold.

One: at least one person who must approve the purchase will never use the product. True at Niyam's employers, where the human-resources head signs and never opens a workout; trivially false for its consumer. True at Marichi's factories; only partly false for its households, since the installer recommends the kit and the spouse who paid for the panels has views.

Two: the purchase is justified by a number the buyer can defend to someone else. True for Marichi's commercial sites: a controller catching a string fault within a day pays for itself in recovered generation. For a household the same fault recovers perhaps ₹900 a year of electricity, which does not defend ₹14,000. This is the claim that kills Marichi Nilay.

Three: customers are few enough to be known individually. True for Marichi's 2,140 sites and Niyam's ten prospective accounts a quarter; false for 2,80,000 monthly installs. This claim governs method rather than design, and is the one most often overlooked.

The distinction misleads in two situations. First, when used to predict demand: calling Marichi Nilay a consumer product says much about how it must be sold and nothing about whether anyone wants it. Second, when used to justify a motion by analogy. Niyam's instinct was to hire enterprise representatives because corporate wellness "is B2B". But at ten closed deals from 250 approaches, a win rate of 25 per cent of pilots carries a 95 per cent confidence interval of roughly 11.6 to 38.4 per cent: Niyam cannot tell a good quarter from a bad one. Its consumer team, testing 20,000 installs per arm against a 16 per cent activation rate, resolves 0.72 percentage points. The company would go from learning four things a week to one a year, and nobody costed that.

5. Hard edge cases

Hardware plus software. Software costs almost nothing to serve a bad-fit customer; a controller costs ₹8,600 whether or not the household keeps it. Lavina Pinto's data showed 7 per cent of consumer-channel kits returned within ninety days, each costing ₹11,500 in written-down stock and reverse logistics — unremarkable in consumer electronics, catastrophic in a business built on ₹1,195 of contribution per unit.

Regulated. Marichi's commercial customer wants a monitoring report that survives a performance dispute with its own developer. The household needs its system approved by a state distribution utility for net metering, and that approval is the installer's job — so the consumer product inherits a dependency it cannot control. Niyam's corporate product touches employee health data and so the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: a security review the consumer app, collecting the same data with consent, never faced.

Two-sided. Marichi Nilay would be sold through the same installers who buy nothing and recommend everything, making the installer a third party with a veto and no contract — the platform school's point, and why a household is not a small factory.

AI-native. Niyam's movement-analysis model costs ₹2.80 per analysed session. A consumer training 3.2 times a week does 166.4 sessions a year, costing ₹465.92 — lifting variable cost from ₹600 to ₹1,065.92, cutting contribution from ₹1,800 to ₹1,334.08, and dropping the five-year ratio from 1.23 to 0.91. In a corporate account the same feature costs ₹44.84 per seat, because only 264 of 1,200 seats are active and actives train 1.4 times a week: contribution per seat falls from ₹708 to ₹663.16 and the ratio only from 6.19 to 5.80. One feature, unaffordable in one motion and free in the other, because of a usage distribution rather than a buyer type.

At the organisational seams. Mature companies claim to run one product with two motions; when a quarter is tight they staff the shorter feedback loop and starve the other. The tell is the roadmap: a company that cannot name what it last shipped for the smaller motion has chosen.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert

Authorisation, not payment, is the line. The competent ask who pays; the expert asks who authorises, since the payer often merely executes. The tell is a deal "waiting on procurement" for eleven weeks: money was never the obstacle.

Seats are a unit of revenue and of risk. Niyam's 22 per cent activation makes the margin magnificent and the renewal fragile. The expert reads a high per-seat margin as a warning and asks for utilisation first.

Cheap does not mean consumer. A ₹900 seat is a business purchase; a ₹14,000 home kit is not. The tell is whether the buyer must justify the spend to a third party, which bears no relation to price.

The sales cycle is a learning-rate tax. Practitioners treat Marichi's 148-day median cycle as a revenue-timing problem. The expert treats it as epistemic: two observations a year per account team, so information must be bought through instrumented pilots and loss interviews.

Enthusiastic users are not evidence of a business. The most dangerous signal in a crossing is a delighted pilot; the tell is a champion who cannot say which budget line the renewal comes from.

A free consumer base is not a channel into firms. The obvious reading — reach converts to revenue — fails because the person using the free product usually cannot authorise a paid one, and competes with it in the same building.

Classify the product twice. Once by who authorises, once by who uses. A corporate wellness app is a business purchase and a consumer experience, and the two generate different, both-valid roadmaps. Experts hold both and name the conflict.

Variable cost, not buyer type, decides whether a feature ships. In a high-frequency consumer product per-use costs multiply by engaged users; in a seat-priced one, by the disengaged average. The obvious reading — business customers afford more — is right about price and wrong about why.

7. How the practice actually differs

Three differences across product types are real and one is largely imagined. In consumer products the binding constraint is attention, the method experimentation at scale, the metric retained cohorts. In business products it is trust, instrumented pilots and net revenue retention. In platform products it is balance between sides. In hardware it is the irreversibility of a unit shipped, and the distinction bites hardest there, because channel structure and warranty exposure differ by an order of magnitude. In AI products the advertised difference is imagined: serving cost is a frequency problem, and a high-frequency business product has the consumer problem.

Stage changes the answer more than product type does. At Niyam's scale the consumer motion is a machine with 1,45,000 customers and known constants; the corporate motion is a start-up inside a scale-up with ten data points. Early-stage companies cross this line well because the same three people sell and build and cannot dodge the evidence. Firms of Niyam's size cross it badly because the crossing is delegated to a team with a target, and the information that would stop it arrives through two layers of summary.

8. Three worked examples

Lipi Document Labs: the failure, and what recovery looked like

Lipi Document Labs of Noida had a consumer document-scanning app with 1.9 crore lifetime installs. In the year to March 2025 its chief executive, Nandan Lotlikar, launched a ₹24,000-a-year plan for chartered-accountancy firms, reasoning that the firms were already in the base. Nayantara Pilgaonkar spent ₹6.4 crore on engineering and a fourteen-person sales team.

Exhibit 6. Lipi Document Labs: the consumer base converting to the firm plan, year to March 2025.

The 188 firms produced ₹45.12 lakh of recurring revenue for ₹6.4 crore of spend — ₹3,40,426 per firm, 14.2 times the annual price. The diagnosis was not pricing. The user was a junior article clerk; the authoriser a partner who had never opened the app. Firms needed audit-trail retention and a ledger integration the consumer architecture could not provide, and the free app, already on every clerk's phone, was the paid plan's best competitor.

Recovery meant selling to the people who already sold to firms. Lipi licensed its scanning engine as an embedded component to three accounting-software vendors, taking minimum guarantees of ₹1.10 crore, ₹0.90 crore and ₹0.60 crore — ₹2.6 crore committed. The contracts cost ₹38 lakh of business development, ₹12,66,667 each, a return of 6.84 times. Lipi had not learned to sell to businesses; it had found the one business motion its asset suited.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Designing for the user and forgetting the authoriser. Early sign: pilots that extend rather than convert. Diagnostic: which budget line funds the renewal? Caught late, a full sales year.

Importing consumer metrics into a business motion. Early sign: a dashboard headlining seats sold, not seats used. Diagnostic: contribution per active user — at Niyam ₹4,090.91 against ₹2,400. Caught late, a renewal cliff in month thirteen.

Assuming a consumer base converts. Early sign: a plan whose first line is the install base. Diagnostic: can the person using it authorise paying for it? Caught late, ₹6.4 crore.

Ignoring the physical tail in a consumer hardware move. Early sign: a business case with no returns line. Diagnostic: ask service operations for the channel-wise return rate before marketing is briefed. Caught late, write-downs two quarters after launch.

Starving the slower motion. Early sign: a roadmap with no items for it. Diagnostic: name the last three things shipped for it. Caught late, two mediocre products.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the distinction be retired? The motion school's strongest form: the categories group a ₹900 seat with a ₹9 crore platform and separate that seat from a ₹14,000 kit, which is backwards operationally; a taxonomy of motions — self-serve, inside sales, field sales, channel, embedded — predicts cost and cycle better. Its evidence is the dispersion of acquisition cost inside each category. It fails if the buyer–authoriser split predicts architecture independently of motion, as Lipi suggests: audit retention was architectural, not a sales matter.

Has bottom-up adoption dissolved the payer's veto? Steelmanned: in much business software the product is adopted by users and the purchase ratifies a fait accompli, so designing for the user is designing for the buyer. Its evidence is a decade of products that grew inside companies before anyone signed. It fails wherever a security gate sits upstream of adoption — Niyam exactly, since employee health data cannot be adopted quietly.

Can business products be learned about experimentally? The pessimists hold ten deals a quarter a hopeless sample, so judgement must replace measurement. The optimists hold the unit of analysis wrong: instrument the deal, not the quarter, and one loss interview outweighs a thousand consumer sessions. Each has the other's weakness — the pessimists cannot explain why some firms improve win rates reliably, the optimists cannot show loss interviews are not merely narrative.

Is seat pricing legitimate? One camp reads Niyam's 78.7 per cent per-seat margin as fair payment for capacity made available; the other as a tax on inattention that invites non-renewal the moment a finance head audits usage. The disagreement is empirical and unsettled.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this recites the buying centre and tells you B2B has longer cycles. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. She reduces a crossing to one comparable number before she has an opinion, and says aloud which inputs are measured and which assumed — the difference between Niyam's ₹2,500 and its 18 per cent. She asks who can say no, separately from who says yes, and hunts the gate nobody named. She treats cycle length as a cost of learning. And she refuses the question as asked: "should we go B2B?" is unanswerable, while "whose behaviour must change, who can block it, and what is the cheapest evidence that would stop us?" is not.

12. The decisions

At the board meeting on 13 November 2026, Meenakshi Lalwani recommended the corporate motion with two conditions not in the original proposal. First, pricing would move from ₹900 a seat to a floor plus a charge on activated employees, because the ₹4,090.91 figure had convinced her that selling unused seats was selling her own renewal risk. Second, no enterprise sales team until four accounts had completed a renewal cycle, since the 18 per cent churn assumption carried the case and the company had no right to it. The consumer business kept its ₹20.16 crore, the shrinkage accepted and the AI analysis restricted to subscribers past month three.

At the Marichi management committee on 16 October 2026, Maitreyi Lobo declined the ₹3.2 crore pilot and Pallav Mohile did not contest it. The committee approved instead a ₹40 lakh experiment of a different shape: Marichi would sell a residential controller to its 184 installation partners as a line item in their own quotations, at ₹9,400, with no support obligation and no Marichi-branded app. Prateek Nigudkar's firmware team would build the telemetry; Lavina Pinto's service operation would not take a household call.

Three questions for discussion. First: Meenakshi's conditions slow the corporate motion by three quarters while the base shrinks by 3,460 subscribers a year. Prudent sequencing of evidence, or an expensive way to avoid deciding? Second: Marichi's partner channel preserves the business economics but surrenders the customer relationship and the ₹1,200 subscription. If residential rooftop installations in India triple over five years, which error proves larger? Third: Lipi recovered by finding a third motion rather than fixing the second. When is that insight, and when is it giving up on a market?

13. Going deeper

Product deconstruction is the prerequisite: naming a product's user, job, promise, business model and biggest assumption is how the distinction stops being a label. Buyer, user, influencer, blocker refines the roles used here into the split that explains why Niyam's security gate behaves unlike its finance gate. B2B vs B2C strategy turns the distinction into choices about pricing, packaging and channel — the Marichi partner decision in general form. The consumer product landscape supplies the base rates that make 58 per cent churn interpretable, and the B2B landscape: SMB, mid-market, enterprise explains why a 1,200-seat average hides two businesses. Product sense and taste is what remains once two defensible numbers point opposite ways; reasoning about trade-offs names Meenakshi's exchange of learning speed for revenue; first-principles reasoning produced the per-active-user figure nobody asked for. Product critique and competitive teardown train the reading of a company's motion off its surfaces. Product vision and mission matters last and most: leaving the homeowner as the installer's customer is coherent only inside a view of what Marichi is for.
case40v1-sense.timing:
Olakh Health Works: One Hour, and Six Months

An ambiguous case on technology and market timing

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Vennela Dorairaj was at the kitchen table of her flat in Bengaluru's Jayanagar with a cold coffee and a sheet of paper on which she had written two numbers: 171, the days left until 31 March 2027, and 90, the accuracy threshold her Chief Medical Officer had refused to move for seven weeks.

Dorairaj was Chief Product Officer of Olakh Health Works, which sold claims software to Indian health insurers. By nine on Monday she had to send Vallabh Dhamija, the co-founder and chief executive, a recommendation on whether to build Olakh Autopass, a system that would decide cashless claims without a human reading them. The board met in Mumbai on Friday, 23 October, and she would have to defend it.

Everyone who briefed her that month used the same phrase and meant something different by it. The window is now. Vithika Dasgupta meant that the cost of machine-reading a discharge summary had collapsed; Vishal Dhavale, that a rival would sign the insurers first; Vipasha Dubash, that a clause expired on 31 March. Velmurugan Devarajan thought the window had not opened at all. She had spent the weekend working out which of them described the shift that made the product possible, and which their calendars.

2. The company, and the contract that still binds it

Olakh was founded in 2017 by Dhamija, after eleven years running operations at a third-party administrator. Its first product, Olakh Verify, digitised the paper that accompanies an Indian cashless claim — pre-authorisation forms, discharge summaries, itemised bills — and ran rule checks before a medical officer saw the file. It decided nothing. It made deciding faster.

In September 2021 Olakh signed the agreement that defined the next five years. Ovara General Insurance would deploy Verify across its whole health book on three conditions: it would sit on Ovara's own servers with no outbound calls to any hosted model; Ovara would pay ₹22 lakh a month; and no capability built on Ovara's claim data could be offered to another IRDAI-registered general insurer before 31 March 2027, after which the fee stepped down to ₹6 lakh a month.

The term ran from 1 October 2021 to 31 March 2027, sixty-six months. In 2021 it was a good trade: Olakh had eighteen months of cash, Ovara eleven million lives. But Verify had never been rewritten to call anything outside a customer's data centre, which was what Autopass required, and the clause that had been a price of entry now read, to Dubash, like a starting gun.

In the year to 31 March 2026 revenue was ₹38.6 crore: ₹16.4 crore of Verify licences in India, ₹11.3 crore of per-claim fees, ₹8.1 crore from Ombak Health Assurance in Jakarta and ₹2.8 crore of implementation work. Ostara Capital had put in ₹210 crore in July 2024 at a ₹1,480 crore valuation. At end-September 2026 Olakh held ₹71 crore in cash, burned ₹2.1 crore a month and employed 316 people, 219 in Bengaluru and Pune.

3. The industry

Indian health insurance had spent three years being rebuilt around two interventions, neither Olakh's. The first was the National Health Claims Exchange, opened in late 2023 by the National Health Authority with the IRDAI under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission: it gave hospitals and insurers a common channel and format, so a claim arrived as structured fields, not a scanned PDF. The second was the IRDAI's master circular of May 2024, requiring an insurer to authorise a cashless request within one hour and clear a discharge within three.

The one-hour rule changed what insurers bought. Before it a claims team optimised for leakage; after it, for leakage subject to a clock it could be penalised on. Administrators such as Medi Assist and Vidal Health added medical officers, insurers including Niva Bupa, Star Health and HDFC Ergo invested in in-house automation, and hospital groups, bearing the working-capital cost of a slow approval, began to care too.

Olakh's exposure ran outwards too. Ombak Health Assurance in Jakarta had taken Verify in 2023 and twice asked for automated adjudication, on a regime with no one-hour rule. The DPDP Act of 2023 pulled the other way: a discharge summary is health data, purpose limitation is explicit, and consent for an automated decision was a question Olakh's counsel in Mumbai, Vijaya Durve, had twice declined to answer in writing.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 Dasgupta, in Nairobi, scored a prototype against 18,400 historical Ovara claims from the 2024–25 book. The model agreed with the officer's recorded decision on 87.5 per cent. Three beliefs followed, and two have since weakened.

The first was that cost was the binding constraint and had just been released. Exhibit 2 is the quarterly benchmark her team had run since 2023 on a fixed set of 4,000 claim document sets: the cost of machine-reading one set fell from ₹41.00 to ₹6.40, a reduction of 84.4 per cent. By September 2026 she had changed her mind about what the series said. The steepest proportional fall, 29.0 per cent, came between the second half of 2024 and the first half of 2025; the latest quarter fell 12.3 per cent, the shallowest. If cost was the shift, it had enabled the product eighteen months earlier.

The second was that NHCX adoption had reached the point where structured claims arrived by default. Exhibit 1 shows 11,400 hospitals live as at 30 September 2026, and Dhavale's deck, built in early October from that figure, told prospects that 45 per cent of the empanelled network was live. Varsha Doiphode, in Pune, asked a different question: what share of the claims Olakh's insurers received came from a live hospital? Exhibit 3 is her answer, and it is not 45 per cent.

The third belief has held: insurers are short of medical officers and long of clock. A fully loaded officer costs Olakh ₹1,32,060 a month and clears 930 decisions, or ₹142.00 a decision. Autopass was priced at ₹95 a claim, so an insurer saves ₹47.00, or 33.1 per cent of the human cost. Olakh's direct cost is ₹22.60 — ₹6.40 of machine reading, ₹14.20 for an officer audit of a ten per cent sample, ₹2.00 of hosting — leaving ₹72.40 of contribution.

What has gone wrong is narrower. In July 2026 Devarajan's team audited 1,200 claims on which model and officer had disagreed; in 61 per cent the model would have approved and the officer queried, at an average excess billed of ₹27,400. Take 1,00,000 claims at the mix in Exhibit 4: 19,000 of them, 19 per cent, are emergency medical admissions. The model disagrees with the officer on 29 per cent of emergency claims, which is 5,510 claims; 61 per cent of those, or 3,361 claims, are approvals the officer would have queried; at ₹27,400 each that is ₹9.21 crore. The saving on the same 1,00,000 claims, at ₹47.00 each, is ₹0.47 crore — about a twentieth of the exposure, if emergency claims are automated at all.

5. The people

Vennela Dorairaj, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Owns the recommendation, and wrote the 2021 memo accepting Ovara's on-premises condition. She has not said she suspects the real shift is the one-hour rule rather than the models, because she cannot show it.

Vallabh Dhamija, co-founder and Chief Executive, Hyderabad. Wants a decision he can present as decisive, and has told two directors Autopass will be live "in the first quarter after the clause goes". He has not told Dorairaj that Ostara wants revenue tripled by 2029.

Vipasha Dubash, Chief Financial Officer, Bengaluru. For her 31 March is the only date: the clause lapses and ₹16 lakh a month of licence revenue with it, ₹1.92 crore a year. She has not circulated the Exhibit 5 recomputation of what that does to the margin she quotes the board.

Velmurugan Devarajan, Chief Medical Officer, Chennai. A physician for fourteen years before joining. He will not sign off below 90 per cent agreement on any automated category, and his ₹9.21 crore calculation is why. He has not mentioned that two of his own officers, double-scoring 600 claims, disagreed on 9 per cent.

Vithika Dasgupta, Lead Data Scientist, Nairobi. Two and a half hours behind Bengaluru, and the only person to have read the whole cost series. She argues the window opened in 2025 and is closing, and that the asset is the 4.1 lakh officer-labelled decisions in the archive, not the model. Most of those labels are Ovara's, encumbered until 31 March.

Varsha Doiphode, Vice-President, Engineering, Pune. She must rebuild Verify to call a hosted model, and estimates fourteen months for the five non-Ovara deployments. She believes NHCX's structured fields, not cost, are the shift that matters. The estimate assumes nine engineers she does not have.

Vishal Dhavale, Head of Sales, Austin. Ten and a half hours behind Bengaluru, paid on signed contract value. He wants the threshold at 85 per cent so maternity comes in scope, lifting automated volume from 55 to 63 per cent. He has not corrected the 45 per cent figure in his deck.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Friday, 23 October 2026 and expects a recommendation, not options. The clause and the fee step-down both fall on 31 March 2027. Doiphode's fourteen-month estimate assumes nine engineers not yet recruited, and Bengaluru bands for the senior two have moved 18 per cent in a year. Devarajan's sign-off is a condition of Ovara's renewal. Durve holds that a standalone health insurer is arguably outside the clause, but will not say when Ovara would agree.

Cash is ₹71 crore against a burn of ₹2.1 crore a month, 33.8 months at that rate. Option A adds ₹26 crore over eighteen months, ₹1.44 crore a month, taking burn to ₹3.54 crore and runway to 20.1 months; Option B adds ₹0.49 crore for ₹2.59 crore and 27.4 months; Option C ₹0.13 crore for ₹2.23 crore and 31.8 months; Option D ₹0.77 crore for ₹2.87 crore and 24.7 months.   1. List every shift in Exhibit 1 offered as a reason this product is possible now. For each, say whether it is necessary, merely helpful, or available to every competitor.
  2. Dasgupta and Doiphode read the same cost series and NHCX data and disagree about when the window opened. State the strongest version of each from Exhibits 2 and 3, and what would settle it.
  3. Exhibit 3 reports 45.4 per cent on one base and 41.2 per cent on another. Which does Dhavale's pipeline claim require, and what does the August-only column do to both?

  6. Dorairaj's note says all four options assume a decision engine. If the shift is really the one-hour clock, or the labelled archive, what fifth option appears? What do you send Dhamija at nine on Monday, and what do you tell the board on 23 October?

It was past midnight. Dorairaj turned the sheet over and wrote, under the 171 and the 90, a third line: which of these dates is mine, and which somebody else's? Then she put the pen down, because she did not know.
exp40v2-sense.timing:
Foundations › Product Thinking & Product Sense

Why now: technology and market timing

How practitioners establish that an idea has become possible, where the method is rigorous, and where it is theatre.

1. Two desks, a fortnight apart

On Tuesday 10 November 2026, ten days before her board met on Friday 20 November, Prajakta Vaidya had a memo to finish and a sentence she could not write. Vaidya runs product at Prabhaat Storage Industries in Coimbatore, which builds behind-the-meter battery systems for factories. The board paper asked for ₹22.00 crore to install 240 systems at knitwear units around Tiruppur: 100 kWh of usable lithium-iron-phosphate storage each, nothing paid up front, Prabhaat keeping 70 per cent of the measured electricity saving for seven years.

Nobody disputed the physics. The same proposal had gone to the same board in March 2023 and been rejected, and Pushpal Dhond, the chief financial officer, asked what had changed since, as a number rather than a mood. Dhond also applied a five-year payback hurdle to anything on Prabhaat's balance sheet, which proved to be the hinge.

A fortnight after that board, Qamar Pathak faced the mirror image. Pathak is chief product officer of Qalam Underwriting Labs in Hyderabad, whose software reads a small firm's bank statements, tax returns and invoices and returns an underwriting pack to a lender. A 91-day pilot ran from 1 September to 30 November 2026 with a mid-sized non-banking financial company, putting 1,80,000 loan applications through the product. On Friday 4 December Pathak had to decide whether to spend nine months and ₹4.80 crore rebuilding for straight-through underwriting with no analyst in the loop. His investors said the moment had come because running a large language model over a loan file had become fifteen times cheaper in three years. The pilot said that fall had never been the obstacle.

The argument of this page: a why now claim is worth only as much as the gate that actually binds, and that gate is almost never the one on the slide.

2. The idea, its history, and the three camps

An enabling shift is a change in some quantity outside the firm's control — a price, a coverage rate, a permission, a behaviour — that was previously the reason an idea did not work. A gate is one such quantity plus a threshold: the level at which the idea becomes workable. The quantity is exogenous; the threshold is endogenous. The cell price is the world's; the price at which Prabhaat's seven-year contract repays is Prabhaat's. Two firms can read the same number and correctly reach opposite conclusions. A window is the interval in which every gate is open at once and no incumbent has occupied the space.

Four lineages matter. From diffusion research — Everett Rogers in 1962, later Geoffrey Moore's chasm — comes the insistence that a product launched before its prerequisite behaviours exist fails not gradually but invisibly. From Theodore Wright's 1936 study of airframe costs, and the learning curves the Boston Consulting Group turned into strategy, comes the claim that unit cost falls by a constant percentage for every doubling of cumulative output, making some declines forecastable rather than lucky. From Clayton Christensen comes the vocabulary of enabling technologies, from Carlota Perez the rhythm in which a technology is installed before it is deployed. And from David Teece's 1986 paper comes the warning the others omit: an innovation can be ready and still impossible, because the complementary assets it needs are absent.

Three camps then disagree. The threshold camp holds that timing is analysable: it will sign that a few external variables determine feasibility, each with a threshold derivable from the firm's own economics; it will not sign that crossing them tells you anyone wants the product. The option camp, from real-options finance and the lean-startup literature, holds that windows cannot be usefully dated in advance and that the answer to timing uncertainty is a cheaper experiment; it will not sign that you can know, before committing capital, which year a window opened. The pre-emption camp holds that windows are captured by whoever already stands in the doorway, and will not sign that early losses are evidence of a mistake.

3. Mechanics: how the work is actually done

Step one: state the barrier as a quantity with units. “Batteries were expensive” is not a barrier; “a landed lithium-iron-phosphate cell cost ₹8,200 per kWh, so a 100 kWh system cost ₹11.00 lakh installed” is. Vaidya's two files differ in four line items.

Installed cost of one 100 kWh systemMarch 2023 (₹ lakh)November 2026 (₹ lakh)
Cells, 100 kWh usable8.204.90
Inverter, battery management, enclosure2.101.80
Installation and civil work0.450.45
Controller hardware and firmware0.250.25
Total installed cost11.007.40

Exhibit 1. Both columns are exact sums of their rows: 8.20 + 2.10 + 0.45 + 0.25 = 11.00 and 4.90 + 1.80 + 0.45 + 0.25 = 7.40.

Step two: derive the threshold from your own economics before looking up the reading, because a threshold computed afterwards gets adjusted until it is cleared. The tariff order effective 1 April 2026 charges Vaidya's customers ₹11.20 per kWh in two peak windows and ₹7.10 off peak, a spread of ₹4.10. A system with a 90 per cent round trip imports 100 ÷ 0.90 = 111.11 kWh off peak to deliver 100 kWh at peak, so one cycle avoids 100 × 11.20 = ₹1,120 and incurs 111.11 × 7.10 = ₹788.89, a net saving of ₹331.11. Two peak windows allow two cycles on each of 300 working days: 600 × 331.11 = ₹1,98,666.67 a year. Prabhaat's 70 per cent share is ₹1,39,066.67; less ₹9,000 of monitoring and ₹6,500 of warranty reserve, net cash is ₹1,23,566.67 — on ₹7.40 lakh, a payback of 5.99 years.

Now invert it. Writing s for the spread, annual cash is 0.70 × 600 × (100s − 78.89) − 15,500, or 42,000s − 48,633.33. Payback at the seven-year contract needs ₹3.67 per kWh; at Dhond's five-year hurdle, ₹4.68; below ₹1.16 the system never repays. Today's ₹4.10 clears the contract with about 12 per cent of headroom and fails the hurdle.

Exhibit 2. Payback against the spread, with the 2026 bill of materials, two cycles a day and 300 working days fixed: 7,40,000 ÷ (42,000s − 48,633.33) gives 9.6 years at ₹3.00, 20.9 at ₹2.00 and no payback at ₹1.16.

Step three: read the current value and date the crossing, which tells you how late you are. Prabhaat's four gates crossed at four separate moments.

Exhibit 3. Each bar begins where that gate crossed Prabhaat's own threshold; the window is the intersection. It opened on 1 April 2026, seven months before the memo.

Step four: compute a margin of safety, not a verdict. Prabhaat's margins are unequal: cycle life clears the 4,200 cycles required with a 6,000-cycle rating, the cell price has a fifth of slack against ₹6,150 per kWh, the spread about 12 per cent. The binding gate is the one a regulator controls on a review cycle.

Step five: check the interactions, because opening one gate can raise another's threshold. By creating a second peak window the tariff order made two cycles a day profitable, doubling annual cycles from 300 to 600 and so doubling the cycle life a seven-year contract needs, from 2,100 to 4,200. A cell rated for 3,000 cycles was adequate for the 2023 product and inadequate for the 2026 one, though nothing about the cell changed. Step six asks what the shift does for everyone else.

Where a gate is a cost, learning curves give a forecast rather than a hope. Prabhaat's cell price went from ₹11,500 per kWh in 2021 to ₹4,900 in 2026, a ratio of 0.426; if cumulative global output roughly quadrupled, that is two doublings and about 35 per cent of decline per doubling, against a published rate for lithium-ion nearer 20 per cent. The gap is a warning: a decline faster than the structural rate usually contains a cyclical component, and cyclical declines reverse. At 20 per cent, reaching the ₹3,678 per kWh Dhond's hurdle needs takes about 1.3 further doublings: years, not quarters.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as testable claims. First, the barrier must be external and measurable; if last time's failure was your own execution there is no gate, only a retrospective. Second, the threshold must be derivable from your own economics. Vaidya derives ₹3.67 per kWh; Pathak derives, from a contractual minimum of 60,000 decisions a quarter, that consent completion must exceed 44.4 per cent of applications. Third, the shift must leave you something to accumulate, or the window closes on you rather than for you. Fourth, demand must pre-exist the shift: Tiruppur units were already paying peak tariffs and complaining.

The method misleads in three situations. Where the gate is a discretionary permission rather than a trend — a tariff order, a sandbox, a credit committee — the language of curves implies an inevitability that does not exist. Where the real constraint is distribution or trust, the analysis reports open gates while the product fails for reasons it cannot see. And where the “shift” is your own learning, calling it enabling makes a proprietary advantage public in the telling.

5. Hard edge cases

Hardware plus software. Prabhaat's window must stay open for seven years, not merely be open on decision day, because the capital is sunk into an asset whose return is a stream. The question becomes the probability the gate survives the payback period — a question about review cycles.

Two-sided markets. A marketplace has a gate no cost curve shows: liquidity. Pankti Charge Network, in Section 8, had every technical gate open and failed anyway, because the dense local fleet it needed was itself waiting on lender behaviour.

Regulated products. Qalam's gates include the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions and the account aggregator consent framework, where a gate can open by fiat on a date. Dating is then easy and durability hard, which is why mature firms keep a standing regulatory watch.

Multi-product firms and the organisational seams. The window for a feature is not the window for a company. The seam that mattered at Prabhaat was internal: product computed payback against a seven-year contract while finance applied a five-year hurdle inherited from outright equipment sales. Neither number was wrong, nobody owned the inconsistency, and such a window gets argued about as though it were a question of fact. What mature firms do is settle it in the capital allocation committee, where the loudest sponsor wins; the better ones set hurdle and contract length together.

AI-native products. When the shift is the falling cost of a model you do not own, it continues after you launch: your advantage decays at the rate your input improves, and what you built around the old limitation becomes dead weight. Pathak's team had an elaborate document-chunking layer for a model that no longer needed it.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert from the competent

The threshold belongs to you, not to the industry. The tell is a memo quoting a benchmark — “storage is viable below ₹6,000 per kWh” — without deriving it. Viability is a property of a contract, not of a technology: Prabhaat's threshold is ₹6,150 per kWh on seven years and ₹3,678 on five. Same cell, same week, two answers.

Gates are conjunctive, and the binding one moves. Only the gate with the least slack is worth managing. Halving Qalam's inference cost again would save ₹5.22 lakh in a quarter, while one percentage point of consent completion was worth ₹3.09 lakh. The tell is a team watching the gate in the news rather than the one with the smallest margin.

Open and binding are different questions. A gate is open if the reading clears the threshold and binding if moving it changes the outcome most. Qalam's consent gate was open at 69.0 per cent against a 44.4 per cent threshold and was still the binding constraint on value. Teams scoring gates as red and green lights lose the distinction.

Opening one gate can raise another's threshold. The tariff order doubled Prabhaat's duty cycle and so doubled its cycle-life requirement. The tell is a specification carried forward unchanged after an assumption beneath it moved; the diagnostic is to recompute every derived quantity whenever a gate changes, which takes an afternoon and is almost never done.

Distinguish structural decline from cyclical. A cost falling faster than its learning rate is usually falling partly for reasons that reverse: overcapacity, subsidy, a vendor buying share. The tell is a straight line on a log scale with no account of where the capacity came from. The consequence is a contract clause — Vaidya's memo included fixed-price cell supply for the first cohort.

A public shift is a public window. Timing is never itself a moat: Pratap Switchgear Works, a panel maker in Coimbatore with 400 factory relationships, read the same order in the same week. The question is what remains at the end that a fast follower cannot buy — for Prabhaat, three years of 15-minute load data from 240 sites.

Demand-side gates are behaviours, not devices. Penetration and coverage are poor proxies. The sharper test is whether users already perform the behaviour in some clumsier form without you: Tiruppur units were already shifting work manually to dodge peak tariffs, and that, not metering penetration, was the evidence.

Date the crossing by when a competitor could have known. Teams date a window from when they noticed; the disciplined version uses the earliest moment the information was public, which measures how late you are. Prabhaat's window opened on 1 April 2026 and the memo is dated 10 November — seven months of lead spent on internal debate.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the demand-side gates dominate and windows are short, because a common behaviour is visible to everybody and the product is cheap to copy. In B2B and enterprise the gates are organisational or regulatory — a compliance deadline, an interface that finally exists, a budget line that did not — and they open on schedules, easy to date and hard to exploit early. Platforms and marketplaces add liquidity, which is endogenous and therefore not a gate at all. In hardware the binding question is the window's durability rather than its existence; in AI products the shift is continuous, so the useful object is a rate rather than a window.

By stage the question changes shape rather than substance. An early-stage firm measures timing against runway; a scaled firm measures what being late costs. The analysis is the same and only the hurdle differs, which is why large firms need a different threshold rather than a different method.

8. Three worked examples

Qalam: the celebrated shift was never the barrier

Of 1,80,000 applications, consent was completed on 1,24,200; tax data was retrievable for 93,150 of those, giving a full file; the model decided 55,890 full files above its confidence threshold and 37,260 went to analysts. The lender sanctioned 22,356 and disbursed 16,767.

Exhibit 4. Bars are drawn at one unit per 360 applications, so 1,80,000 is 500 units and 1,24,200 is 345, exactly 69 per cent of it; the 93,150 bar is 258.75 units, 51.75 per cent of the top bar, as 0.69 × 0.75 requires.

Two readings follow. First, ₹89.42 lakh of the ₹127.17 lakh cost base, 70.3 per cent, is human review of files the model would not decide, so the economics are governed by the straight-through rate and not by inference pricing, 8.2 per cent of cost. Pathak therefore compared two uses of nine months. The rebuild would lift straight-through eligibility from 60 to 80 per cent, cutting review files to 18,630 and raising quarterly contribution to ₹239.84 lakh, a gain of ₹44.71 lakh for ₹4.80 crore: about 10.7 quarters to repay. A ₹35 lakh consent-flow redesign, aimed at 80 per cent consent completion, would raise full files to 1,08,000 and contribution to ₹229.10 lakh, a gain of ₹33.98 lakh repaying in one quarter.

Prabhaat: right about the window, wrong about the instrument

Vaidya's second surprise was that the standard remedy for timing uncertainty — stage the commitment — made her numbers worse. At 240 systems the programme costs ₹17.76 crore of hardware, ₹2.80 crore of platform build and ₹1.44 crore of working capital, ₹22.00 crore in all, returning 240 × ₹1,23,566.67 = ₹296.56 lakh a year: a payback of 7.42 years, longer than the contract. Halving the cohort does not help, because the platform spend does not halve: ₹12.40 crore against ₹148.28 lakh is 8.36 years. A second cohort of 240, hardware only, repays in 1,776 ÷ 296.56 = 5.99 years. Where a large fixed cost sits in front of a per-unit annuity, timing and scale are one question.

Pankti Charge Network: a correct technical reading and a dead company

Pankti Charge Network launched battery swapping for electric three-wheelers around Nagpur in March 2023 on a reading accurate as far as it went: pack costs had fallen, station hardware was off the shelf, the vehicles existed. It built 60 stations at ₹14.50 lakh each, ₹8.70 crore of capital, needing 48 swaps per station per day to break even. In its sixth month, August 2023, it averaged 17. The gate nobody had written down was financing: a swappable pack meant the vehicle was sold without a battery, and lenders would not finance an asset whose residual value they could not assess, so the swap-compatible fleet in its three districts stood at about 4,200 vehicles against the 11,800 needed. Twenty-two months after launch, in January 2025, Pankti decommissioned 38 stations, retained 22 on consolidated leases that lowered break-even to 36 swaps a day, wrote down ₹3.40 crore, and signed a battery-leasing arrangement so drivers financed the vehicle and rented the pack. By June 2025 the surviving 22 averaged 41 swaps a day: at ₹48 a swap, 41 × 22 × 30 = 27,060 swaps and ₹12.99 lakh of monthly revenue. The recovery was not a better forecast but the creation of the missing complement by contract.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
The trend slideA rising curve, no threshold markedWhat value here would make the idea fail?A build cycle spent on an untested gate
Single-gate thinkingExcitement about one supplier's priceHow many conditions must hold at once?Pankti: ₹3.40 crore written off
Threshold driftThe viability number moves after the dataWas the threshold written first?A hurdle fitted to the sponsor's answer
Borrowed benchmarkAn industry figure, no derivationWhich contract term produced it?A right market view, an uneconomic contract
Carried-forward assumptionsSpecifications unchanged after a gate movedWhat derived quantity changed?Reserves set for half the duty cycle
Window without an exitNo closing mechanism, no tripwireWhat reading stops us installing?Capital committed into a closing window

Exhibit 6. The first three are errors of analysis, the last three errors of governance and the more expensive. These diagnostics belong at the memo stage.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is what to do when a gate has only just cleared. The threshold camp argues the margin of safety is the whole decision: Prabhaat clears a seven-year contract by about 12 per cent on a gate a regulator controls, thin enough that the answer is to change the contract until the margin is adequate. For it to be wrong, margins of safety would have to be unforecastable.

The option camp argues that every threshold is a point estimate in disguise and that the rational response is small reversible positions; its evidence is the poor accuracy of threshold forecasts. For it to be wrong, there would have to be businesses in which options are not cheap — and Prabhaat is one, its small version being strictly worse than its large one.

The pre-emption camp argues that returns accrue to whoever holds the complementary assets when the window opens, and those take years to build; its evidence is Pankti's eventual lender arrangement, which an incumbent lender could have had on day one. For it to be wrong, such assets would have to be rentable at short notice — which Pankti proved, at ₹3.40 crore and twenty-two months. The same case serves two camps.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They write the threshold before looking up the reading and keep the derivation attached, so a change of contract changes the threshold with it. They can say without preparation which gate has the least slack and what reading would stop the programme. They treat timing as a question about contracts and governance rather than forecasting, and are unembarrassed about the limits: the method says nothing about whether the customer will sign.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 20 November 2026 Vaidya recommended approving the full 240-system cohort on amended terms: the savings share raised from 70 to 78 per cent and the contract extended from seven to nine years. At 78 per cent the annual saving of ₹1,98,666.67 yields ₹1,54,960 gross and ₹1,39,460 net, a per-system payback of 5.31 years; at 240 systems that is ₹334.70 lakh a year, so the programme repays in 2,200 ÷ 334.70 = 6.57 years. She was explicit about the prices: nine years at 600 cycles consumes 5,400 of the cells' 6,000 rated cycles, leaving 11 per cent of margin on the most comfortable gate, and the customer's annual saving falls from ₹59,600 to ₹43,706.67. One tripwire: if the next tariff review resets the spread below ₹3.67 per kWh, installations stop.

On 4 December Pathak deferred the rebuild and funded the ₹35 lakh consent programme, reasoning that the gate with the largest effect on contribution was also the one partly within his control, while inference pricing had nineteen times the slack it needed. The rebuild decision returns in April 2027 against one reading: consent completion at or above 78 per cent.

Three questions. First, Vaidya changed the contract rather than the cohort size; when would staging have been the better instrument? Second, take a product you know well, name its open-but-binding gate and its celebrated-but-never-shut gate, and state the numbers that tell them apart. Third, when is building a missing complement better than waiting for a gate to open?

13. Going deeper

  1. What makes a good product idea — where timing sits among the other tests an idea must pass.
  2. Technology trend analysis — finding and dating shifts, with the learning-curve arithmetic of Section 3.
  3. Problem decay and re-validation — the same gates run backwards as windows close.
  4. Product deconstruction — teardowns reveal which shift a live product stands on.
  5. B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction — why gates are behavioural on one side, organisational on the other.
  6. Product sense and taste — what remains to be judged once timing is settled.
  7. Reasoning about trade-offs — the share, hurdle and contract-length trade-offs in Prabhaat's case.
  8. First-principles reasoning — how a derived threshold replaces a borrowed benchmark.
  9. Product critique — defending a timing claim against someone hunting the gate you skipped.
exp20v2-sense.timing:
Why now: technology and market timing

Foundations › Product Thinking & Product Sense

1. The Monday before the board

On Monday 7 September 2026, Aarushi Bakshi, head of product at Aakaar Voice Ledger Labs in Pune, opened a spreadsheet that her chief executive, Arvind Bhosale, had asked her to settle before the board met on Friday 18 September. The company sold a bookkeeping app to small shopkeepers. Its text-based ledger had 61,000 monthly active merchants and almost no paying ones, because typing an entry between customers is a chore few merchants will pay for. The proposal on the table was a voice-first rebuild, in which a merchant speaks in Hindi, Marathi or Telugu (“Sharma ji, four hundred and twenty, udhaar”) and the app writes the entry. The rebuild would cost ₹6 crore over fourteen months, about a third of the company's remaining cash.

Bhosale's instinct was to go. Bakshi's was to ask a question that the pitch deck did not answer: why had nobody made this work in 2023? Two competitors had tried versions and quietly retreated. If something had changed, the idea was timely; if not, Aakaar was about to repeat their mistake. A wrong yes burned ₹6 crore on economics that did not close. A wrong no handed a better-funded rival the window.

2. The idea: timing is a property of the world, not the team

Why now is the discipline of explaining what has changed in technology, behaviour, regulation or cost that makes an idea workable today when it was not workable earlier. The change is called an enabling shift: an external development, outside the company's control, that removes a specific barrier. The span during which the barrier is gone and the incumbents have not yet adapted is the window.

The idea has two lineages. Venture investors have long asked it as the “Why now?” slide in a pitch, because early-stage firms keep rediscovering that good products launched at the wrong moment die. The entrepreneur Bill Gross, founder of the incubator Idealab, compared the companies he had been involved with and reported in a 2015 talk that timing explained more of the gap between success and failure than the idea, the team or the funding; he put it at 42 per cent, a figure best read as one practitioner's judgement rather than a measured law. A second lineage is the biologist Stuart Kauffman's adjacent possible, popularised by the writer Steven Johnson: at any moment only inventions one step from existing components can be built.

The sentence Bakshi could repeat in the board meeting without sounding glib was this: an idea is ready when the thing that made it uneconomic has become cheap enough, and the people who need it already behave in the way it requires. Note the two halves. One is about supply (can we build it at a cost that works?) and the other about demand (will users do what we assume?).

3. How it actually works

The method has five steps, and practitioners usually leave the first two implicit. Step one: name the barrier. State precisely what stopped the idea earlier. “The market was not ready” is not a barrier. “Speech recognition for Indian languages cost ₹1.20 per minute of audio and made every merchant a loss-making customer” is one. Step two: decompose the barrier into gates. A product usually needs several things to be true at once. Bakshi's list had four: speech recognition cheap enough, merchants owning a handset and data plan good enough to use it, a daily payment habit that generates things worth recording, and open digital rails (UPI, the interoperable payments network run by the National Payments Corporation of India, and machine-readable invoicing) that let an entry connect to something useful.

Exhibit 1. The four gates behind the voice-ledger idea. The window exists only when all are open together; any one closed makes the idea early.

Step three: put a number on each gate and find where it crosses its threshold. A gate is only informative if you know the level at which it opens. Demand-side gates 2 and 3 had opened gradually: by 2026 roughly seven in ten of the 40 lakh shops in Aakaar's target segment accepted UPI QR payments daily, against about three and a half in ten in 2023. The supply-side threshold is derived in the next section. Step four: check the incumbents. A window is valuable only if unoccupied; the existing ledger apps were built for typing. Step five: date the window. Estimate when the gates opened, when rivals will arrive, and how long the lead will last.

4. A worked example, line by line

Bakshi built the supply-side calculation from four facts. A paying merchant would be charged ₹149 per month. A typical merchant speaks 40 entries per working day, 26 working days a month, which is 1,040 entries; each is about 15 seconds of audio, or 0.25 minute, so the monthly audio is 1,040 × 0.25 = 260 minutes. Hosting costs ₹12 per merchant per month and support another ₹18, a fixed ₹30. The variable is the vendor's speech price per minute. Contribution here means price minus all costs that scale with a merchant, the figure that tells you whether each additional customer helps or hurts.

YearSpeech price (₹/min)Speech cost (₹/merchant/month)Total cost incl. ₹30 fixed (₹)Contribution at ₹149 (₹)Margin on price
20231.20312342−193−129.5%

20250.30781084127.5%
20260.1539698053.7%

Exhibit 2. Unit economics of the voice ledger. Speech cost = 260 × price; total cost = speech cost + 30; contribution = 149 − total cost; margin = contribution ÷ 149, rounded to one decimal. The figures are exact; only the margin is rounded.

Read the 2023 row first: ₹1.20 × 260 = ₹312 of speech cost to collect ₹149, a loss of ₹193 on every merchant who actually used the product. By 2026, 0.15 × 260 = ₹39 and the same merchant yields ₹80. The break-even speech price is the point at which contribution is zero: (149 − 30) ÷ 260 = 119 ÷ 260, or about ₹0.46 per minute. The 2024 price of ₹0.60 was above it; the 2025 price of ₹0.30 was below it. The supply gate therefore opened sometime between those two years, consistent with the two competitors retreating in 2024.

Exhibit 3. The same four contributions as bars. The sign flips between 2024 and 2025, exactly where the price crosses ₹0.46 per minute.

Now the demand side, as a rate chain. Of 40 lakh target shops, 70 per cent use UPI QR daily: 40,00,000 × 0.70 = 28,00,000 shops. If 3 per cent of those pay, that is 28,00,000 × 0.03 = 84,000 paying merchants. At ₹149 a month their revenue is 84,000 × 149 = ₹1,25,16,000, or ₹125.16 lakh a month, and contribution at ₹80 is 84,000 × 80 = ₹67.2 lakh a month. Annual revenue is ₹1,501.92 lakh, about ₹15.02 crore.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the dominant speech vendor raises its price from ₹0.15 to ₹0.30 per minute. Speech cost becomes 260 × 0.30 = ₹78, total cost ₹108, contribution ₹41, margin 27.5 per cent. Contribution roughly halves and the ₹67.2 lakh a month becomes 84,000 × 41 = ₹34.44 lakh. Now change usage instead: if merchants speak 60 entries a day, audio is 60 × 26 × 0.25 = 390 minutes, speech cost at ₹0.15 is ₹58.50, and contribution is 149 − 58.50 − 30 = ₹60.50. The lesson is that the window is not a date but a margin of safety. Aakaar's cost sits at about a third of break-even (0.15 against 0.46), which is comfortable; a team whose cost sat at 0.44 would be calling a coin-flip a window.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

Enabling shift versus trend. A trend is something everyone is talking about; an enabling shift is a change in a specific input that crosses a specific threshold. Only the second can be tested.

Necessary versus sufficient. Open gates make an idea possible; they do not make it good. The shift tells you the lock has changed, not that anyone wants what is behind the door.

Too early and too late are different failures. Too early looks like users who try the product and cannot sustain it, or unit economics that never close. Too late looks like acquisition costs that rise month on month because several firms bid for the same attention.

Supply-side and demand-side shifts. Cheaper technology is the more visible kind; changed behaviour is the more durable. A cost advantage can be matched within a year; a habit favours everyone equally.

The shift is shared. If the enabling change is public, so is the window. Timing alone is never a moat. What converts a window into an advantage is something you can accumulate while it is open: data, distribution, trust, integrations.

What it cannot tell you. A why-now analysis cannot say how large the prize is, whether your team can execute, or what the sensible price is. It narrows the question from “is this a good idea?” to “is this the moment?” and no further. Before relying on one, ask: which gate am I least sure of, who benefits equally from the same shift, and what would I see in six months if I were wrong?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early stage and large

In consumer products the demand-side gates dominate (devices, data prices, habits) and windows are short because copying is quick. In B2B products the gates are often organisational, such as a compliance deadline or an integration that finally exists; windows last longer but open on a fixed schedule. In marketplaces there is an added gate, liquidity: payments and logistics may be ready and the marketplace still early, because buyers and sellers must arrive together. Aakaar sits between consumer and B2B.

Company size changes the question. An early-stage company asks can we survive until the window pays? and measures timing against runway. A large company asks can we afford to be late? and measures timing against the cost of a rival capturing the habit first. Large firms err toward waiting; small ones toward launching before a gate has fully opened. Aakaar sat in the uncomfortable middle.

7. Common mistakes

The trend slide. Symptom: a deck showing a rising curve (AI adoption, smartphone users) with no threshold marked. Misunderstanding: believing a growing market is a timing argument. Cheapest diagnostic: ask “what number on that curve would have to be different for the idea to fail?” If nobody can answer, there is no gate.

Single-gate thinking. Symptom: the team is excited by one technical breakthrough and ignores user behaviour. Misunderstanding: treating the supply side as the whole story. Diagnostic: list every condition the user must satisfy to get value and score each one open or closed.

Declaring victory too early. Symptom: a prototype demo works and the window is declared open. Misunderstanding: confusing “it can be done” with “it can be done at a price users pay.” Diagnostic: compute contribution per customer at realistic heavy usage, as Exhibit 2 does.

8. What good looks like

The handled-well version of Bakshi's decision begins with a one-page memo. It names the barrier (speech cost above ₹0.46 per minute), lists the four gates with their thresholds and current readings, and states that three were open with comfortable margin while the fourth was open with a margin she could quantify. It states two tripwires that would end the bet: the vendor price rising past ₹0.30 or paying conversion below 1.5 per cent after six months. And it is honest about what it cannot say, which is whether merchants will actually pay ₹149, a question that no timing analysis answers.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On 18 September Bakshi recommended a staged bet in place of the full ₹6 crore. Fund the first six months of the voice rebuild, tie the second tranche to the two tripwires, and sign a price-protection clause with the speech vendor. Her reasoning was that the numbers showed the window had opened, with a speech cost at about a third of break-even, yet only the economics were proven. Willingness to pay and the durable edge remained open, and a staged commitment let Aakaar act inside the window without betting the whole balance sheet on a forecast. The board approved the first tranche.

To go further, study technology trend analysis, which teaches you to find and date shifts systematically rather than by intuition, and problem decay and re-validation, the mirror image: a window that opened can close, and a problem that was real can fade.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a product you use daily and identify the enabling shift behind it: what was the specific threshold, and what year was it crossed? Second, pick an idea you believe is ahead of its time and write down which gate is still closed, and what reading would convince you it had opened.
case20v1-sense.timing:
Ekhata Labs: The Voice Ledger Decision

A decision case on technology and market timing

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Kavin Ostwal sat in Ekhata Labs' Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with a printed page that said, in his own handwriting, "Why is this possible now?" He was the company's Head of Product, and he had until the board meeting on Friday, 30 October to recommend how, and whether, Ekhata should build a voice-first ledger for India's small shopkeepers. Diwali fell on 8 November, and Chopda pujan, when traders open fresh account books, was the one moment each year when a shopkeeper might change how she keeps accounts.

Kavin had been here before. In 2023 his team built a voice prototype that merchants loved in the demo and that cost more to run than the merchant would ever pay. He had shelved it. Now his colleagues told him the moment had come, and his job was to decide whether they were right for the right reasons.

2. Company background

Ekhata Labs was founded in 2019 by two former bankers and an engineer, and sells a bookkeeping app to kirana stores, tailors, pharmacies and small wholesalers. A merchant records credit given to customers, sends polite payment reminders by WhatsApp, and sees a daily cash summary. The app costs ₹149 a month. By September 2026 it had 3,20,000 paying merchants, mostly in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, which meant monthly revenue of about ₹4.77 crore, or roughly ₹57.2 crore a year. The company employed 140 people and held ₹38 crore in the bank.

The competition was crowded and well known. Khatabook and OkCredit had popularised the digital khata. Paytm's soundbox had taught millions of shopkeepers to trust a small speaker that announced each UPI payment. Almost every product in this crowd was typed. Ekhata's churn survey showed why that mattered: the commonest reason for leaving, at 41 per cent of lapsed merchants, was "no time to type during the rush."

3. The situation

Merchants plainly wanted to speak their entries. Kiara Obhan, Ekhata's designer, had spent two weeks in September watching shopkeepers in Lucknow and Nashik. A grocer would say, "Sharma-ji, do kilo cheeni, udhaar" and keep weighing rice.

The question was why the idea worked now when it had not in 2023. Kavin drew up the comparison shown in Exhibit 1, using Ekhata's own survey of 1,200 merchants and its engineering logs. Four things had moved. Smartphone ownership among surveyed shopkeepers had risen from 52 per cent to 78 per cent. The share of their daily sales arriving by UPI, the NPCI payments rail, had roughly doubled from 31 per cent to 64 per cent, so a digital record of each sale already existed. Government-backed language datasets under the Bhashini mission and cheaper speech models had cut word errors on shop-counter Hindi from 24 per cent to 9 per cent. And the cost of processing one spoken entry had fallen from ₹0.30 to ₹0.06.

That last number mattered most to the economics. Exhibit 2 shows that a merchant making 25 voice entries a day generates 750 a month. At the 2023 price of ₹0.30, speech processing alone cost ₹225 against a ₹149 subscription, a loss on every merchant. At ₹0.06 the cost is ₹45, leaving ₹104 of margin before hosting and support.

The team saw the window differently from different places. Kiara, working from Lisbon, four and a half hours behind Bengaluru, worried that Marathi and Tamil speakers mixed English words into their sentences and that the 9 per cent error figure was measured only on Hindi. Kanwar Ojha, the engineering lead in Pune, argued that the cost curve was public and that any rival could ride it. Kavin knew the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 also mattered: a recording of a shopkeeper naming her customers was personal data, and consent screens would add friction.

4. The people

Kavin Ostwal, Head of Product, Bengaluru. He owns the recommendation and wants a decision he can defend if it goes wrong.

Kanwar Ojha, Engineering Lead, Pune. He believes the cost curve will not wait and wants to build all four languages at once, since the architecture is cheaper to design once.

Kiara Obhan, Designer, Lisbon. She wants a proper accuracy test in Marathi and Tamil before any promise is made to merchants,, since a product that mishears a debt damages trust.

Kishan Odeyar, Head of Sales, Lucknow. He manages 120 field agents and wants a Diwali launch. He fears Khatabook or OkCredit will announce voice features first.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out what changed between 2023 and 2026, and Exhibit 2 translates one change into a unit margin. Exhibit 3, further below, prices the three options.

6. The options

Option A: launch everywhere before Diwali. Build Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and Kannada voice entry and offer it to all 3,20,000 merchants for a ₹9 crore investment over twelve months. The upside is speed against Khatabook and OkCredit. The cost is that three languages are untested and a poor launch would reach the whole base.

Option B: wait twelve months. Spend ₹1.2 crore on collecting Marathi and Tamil speech data and revisit in October 2027. This is cheapest and respects the lesson of 2023, but a rival could own the Diwali habit and the voice data.

Option C: a staged Hindi launch. Release Hindi voice entry to 60,000 merchants in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh at Diwali for ₹2.4 crore, run a Marathi and Tamil accuracy test in parallel, and expand only if the pilot meets set thresholds. The upside is learning with limited downside; the cost is slower reach.
