In Exhibit 3, Option C needs the highest share of its audience, 32.1 per cent, to repay itself, because its audience is the smallest. But it needs 19,231 merchants, far fewer than the 72,116 Option A requires.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, explain in two sentences why the 2023 prototype failed and what has changed. Which of the four shifts is necessary, and which merely helpful?

2. Kanwar says the cost curve is public. If every rival can use it, what, if anything, remains as Ekhata's advantage in the window?

3. Kiara's 9 per cent error rate covers Hindi alone. What would you want to know about Marathi and Tamil before spending ₹9 crore, and how could you learn it cheaply?

4. Compare the three options in Exhibit 3. Which would you recommend to the board on 30 October, and what evidence would make you change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. "Why now" asks which shifts made an idea possible, and which of them every competitor shares. Kavin's four shifts are enabling conditions, available to anyone. The window they open is real but it is not proprietary. A good answer separates a shift that makes the idea possible from the advantage that makes Ekhata the one to win it, and it checks that each shift holds in the specific market being entered. Here the Hindi evidence is strong and the Marathi and Tamil evidence is absent.

One defensible path. Option C. The speech cost drop turns the 2023 loss of ₹76 per merchant into a ₹104 monthly margin, so the timing argument is sound. But the argument rests on Hindi measurements, and the cost of being wrong in four languages at once is ₹9 crore, nearly a quarter of Ekhata's ₹38 crore in the bank. Option C spends ₹2.4 crore, about 6.3 per cent of that cash, holds the Diwali date that Kishan needs, and buys the one thing the team lacks, which is evidence from real counters. Its weakness is exposure to a faster rival, and the mitigation is to set clear gates: expand to Marathi and Tamil only if the Hindi pilot shows that voice users stay longer than typed users, and if the accuracy tests reach an error rate close to Hindi's 9 per cent.

Why not the others. Option A bets the base on untested assumptions. Option B treats a closing window as permanent, although a rival's launch would also teach merchants to expect voice. A student who picks A or B can still score well by naming what must be true for it to win.
exp20v2-sense.deconstruct:
Product deconstruction

Taking a live product apart from the outside: user, job, promise, model, metric, moat.

1. Opening: a Monday in August

On Monday, 3 August 2026, Indrani Hosangadi opened a shared document titled simply "Jodidaar". Indrani was a senior product manager at Hamraah Commute Network, a Bengaluru company that sells seats on intercity buses through an app and a network of roughly 2,400 operator partners. Hamraah was healthy, profitable on its core business, and nervous. A rival named Jodidaar Pool Services, which let private-car owners offer spare seats on trips they were making anyway, had been growing on the Bengaluru–Mysuru corridor, one of Hamraah's busiest routes.

Jignesh Parikh, Hamraah's head of product, had given Indrani a precise assignment. A board review was set for Friday, 21 August, eighteen days away. Management would either approve a twelve-month pilot of a Hamraah carpooling product, budgeted at ₹18 lakh a month, or ₹2.16 crore in all, or shelve the idea. Jignesh wanted to know, in his words, "why Jodidaar is built the way it is, and whether any of that survives being built by us."

The risk ran two ways: copy Jodidaar's surface and spend ₹2.16 crore reproducing features whose purpose was not understood, or dismiss it and lose the commuter who books every Friday evening. Isabel Teixeira, a design researcher in Lisbon, joined the document with one comment: "Before we compare features, can we say what job this product is hired to do?" Indrani had the app, a debit card, two weekends and a method.

2. The idea

Product deconstruction is the discipline of explaining, from the outside, why a live product has the shape it has. You treat the product as the visible end of a chain of decisions and work backwards: from what the screen shows, to the person it is aimed at, to the problem they hire it for, to how the company earns money, to the number it must move, to the thing that would make it hard to copy. The practice was invented for a practical reason. Managers needed to learn from products they could not see inside, whether a competitor's, an admired company's, or a product inherited in an acquisition, and "this feels good" teaches nothing transferable. Teardown habits spread through engineering and strategy writing from the 1990s, and the six-layer product form was popularised in the 2010s by product-sense interviews at large technology firms.

The six layers used here are these. The user is the specific person for whom the product is built, not "everyone". The job is the progress that person is trying to make, a term from the jobs-to-be-done tradition associated with the late Harvard scholar Clayton Christensen. The promise is what the product says it will do, in the user's language. The model is how the company converts usage into money. The key metric is the single number whose movement most closely tracks whether the promise is being kept. The moat is whatever makes the whole arrangement hard for a competitor to reproduce. A seventh item, the biggest assumption, is what must be true for the other six to hold together.

"Every visible feature is the answer to a question; deconstruction is recovering the question."

That sentence is the one Indrani could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib, because it states a method rather than a slogan.

3. How it actually works

Indrani began with the step practitioners most often skip: separating what she saw from what she concluded. Her document had two columns for every claim, "observed" and "inferred". The map and the seat count were observed. The belief that drivers cared more about petrol savings than about profit was inferred, and she marked it so.

The second step was to walk the funnel as a real user would. She booked seven rides between Bengaluru and Mysuru over two weekends, as rider and, with a colleague's car, as driver. Jodidaar asked riders for a phone number and a government-verified identity before showing a price, but let drivers publish a trip with a number alone. That asymmetry is evidence: trust is demanded of the side that takes the risk of a stranger in the car, and friction is spared the side that supplies the scarce seats.

The third step was to read the commercial surface: the fare breakdown on the receipt, the driver earnings screen, the cancellation policy, the app-store listing, the job postings, and customer reviews. The fourth was to write each layer as a falsifiable sentence. "The user is a salaried Bengaluru professional aged 25 to 40, travelling home to Mysuru most weekends" can be wrong, and that is its virtue. The fifth, usually left implicit, was to ask what would have to be true for the opposite design to be better. If Jodidaar had built a fixed-route shuttle, what would that imply about its user? Imagining the road not taken sharpened what the chosen road assumed.

4. A worked example

Indrani's central inference concerned the model. From the receipt she could see a rider's fare of ₹350 per seat. From the driver app, which showed earnings after each trip, she could see what the driver received on an average sampled trip: ₹714. Across fifty sampled public trips she and a colleague counted 150 seats offered (three per car) and 120 seats booked. Her definitions were explicit, as they must be.

Paying seats per trip3 × 80%2.4

The take rate of 15 per cent is not hidden; it is simply not stated, so it counts as derived from two observed numbers. The next step required assumptions, which she labelled as such. Payment processing, she assumed, cost 2 per cent of booking value, which is ₹16.80 on ₹840. Support, insurance cover and verification she assumed at ₹20 a trip. Contribution per trip, the money left after the costs that vary with each trip, was therefore ₹126.00 − ₹16.80 − ₹20.00 = ₹89.20.

The decisive question was what volume Jodidaar needs to cover its own fixed costs. Isabel's reading of job postings, together with a rough view of team size, suggested a monthly fixed cost near ₹18 lakh, which is ₹18,00,000. Dividing by contribution per trip gives ₹18,00,000 ÷ ₹89.20 = 20,179.4, so Jodidaar needs about 20,180 trips a month to break even.

The 15 per cent fee is ₹94.50, processing 2 per cent of ₹630 is ₹12.60, support stays ₹20, so contribution is ₹94.50 − ₹12.60 − ₹20.00 = ₹61.90, and break-even is ₹18,00,000 ÷ ₹61.90 = 29,079.2, or about 29,080 trips.

A fall of twenty percentage points in fill raises required volume from 20,180 to 29,080, an increase of 8,900 trips, or 44.1 per cent (8,900 ÷ 20,180). Fill rate, in other words, behaves as the lever that matters. This is the quantitative reason that a team deconstructing Jodidaar should care less about its feature list than about how it keeps seats full.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Observed versus inferred

Everything in the table above is arithmetic on observations plus labelled assumptions. The most common failure is to let an inferred sentence migrate into the observed column because it was repeated often enough. Keep the two columns physically separate.

The user is not the customer, and not always the payer

In Jodidaar the rider pays, but the driver is the supplier whose behaviour determines whether the product exists at all. Deconstruct both, and write down which of them the interface treats as the user.

The job is not the category

"Carpooling" is a category. The job might be "get home on Friday without spending four hours in a bus queue" or "stop the petrol bill eating my weekend". Those jobs imply different products. Always phrase the job as progress in a situation, with a trigger and a constraint.

A metric is a choice, not a fact

Jodidaar publishes no metrics. Whether it optimises booked seats, repeat riders in the second month, or fill rate on the busiest hour is inferred from what it nags users about. Different inferences give different teardowns, so state the evidence.

What deconstruction cannot tell you

It cannot tell you retention curves, margins by city, or whether the founders will persist. The ₹18 lakh fixed-cost figure above is a reasoned guess, and the break-even is only as good as that guess. It also cannot tell you whether you could succeed with the same design, since your assets differ.

Questions a newcomer should ask before relying on it

How many sessions did I observe, and on which days? Was my sample of fifty trips biased to the busy weekend? Who benefits from my believing this product is clever? Would a person inside the company find my inference plausible or laughable?

6. How it differs across product types and company stages

In consumer products the teardown leans on user and job, and the moat is often habit or brand. In B2B products the buyer, user and signatory are often three people, so the model layer maps who pays and who suffers, and the moat is often integration cost.

In marketplaces, which includes Jodidaar, the first question is always which side is scarce. Here it is the driver with a spare seat on a given route and hour. The moat is local liquidity: the probability that a rider searching at 6 p.m. on Friday finds a match, and this does not transfer from Bengaluru to a new city. A teardown of a marketplace must therefore be done per route, not per country.

7. Common mistakes

The feature inventory

Symptom: a long list of screens with no claim about why. Misunderstanding: description is mistaken for explanation. Cheapest diagnostic: for each item, write "this exists so that ___ ". If you cannot finish the sentence, you have not done the work.

The flattering model

Symptom: the teardown concludes the product is brilliant, or foolish, in every layer. Misunderstanding: inference is being driven by a prior opinion. Diagnostic: ask a colleague to argue the opposite using the same observations.

Numbers with no stated definition

Symptom: "the fill rate is about 80" with no denominator. Misunderstanding: a ratio is treated as a fact rather than a definition applied to counts. Diagnostic: state the numerator and denominator beside every ratio, as the table in section 4 does.

8. What good looks like

A strong version of Indrani's document fits on four pages. It opens with the one-line claim: "Jodidaar is a Friday-evening product for Bengaluru professionals who go home weekly, funded by a 15 per cent fee, and viable only if seats fill." Each layer follows with its observed and inferred columns, its confidence level, and the cheapest test that would change her mind. The break-even table is present, with both fill-rate scenarios. The document says plainly what it cannot know, names two people at Hamraah who could supply missing facts (finance on payment costs, legal on state permit rules), and ends with a recommendation that is proportionate to the evidence rather than to the enthusiasm in the room.

9. Closing

On Friday, 21 August, Indrani did not ask the board to approve ₹2.16 crore. She proposed a smaller, staged commitment: a six-month test on the Bengaluru–Mysuru route, limited to Hamraah's existing weekly bus customers, with a gate on fill rate. Her reasoning was the arithmetic of section 4. If fill rate in a Hamraah product stays near the 80 per cent she observed at Jodidaar, the unit economics work at about 20,180 trips a month; if it falls to 60 per cent, the requirement rises past 29,000, and no bus-customer base on a single corridor was likely to supply that. The test would reveal whether Hamraah's repeat weekly travellers behave like Jodidaar's riders.

What to learn next: competitive teardown, which places several rivals on the same six layers so that gaps become visible, and product sense and taste, because deconstruction yields understanding while taste decides what to do with it. Applied behavioural psychology will also help with the job layer, where users rarely say what they mean.

Two questions to sit with. First, choose a product you use daily and write its biggest assumption in one sentence; what single observation would prove that sentence wrong? Second, which of your own conclusions about it did you place in the "observed" column, and how many of them truly belong there?
case40v1-sense.deconstruct:
Raahat Pet Network: What Is the Product?

Raahat, Ruhani, Riyasat, Rawnaq and every person named here are fictional; the brands, regulators and institutions are real.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Thursday 19 November 2026, eleven days after Diwali, Bhavini Galgali was still at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, three decks in front of her. The board of Raahat Pet Network met at nine the next morning, Friday 20 November, with one item on the agenda: Product direction, FY27 H2 — single recommendation from VP Product.

For twelve weeks, from Monday 24 August 2026, she had done to Raahat what she would have done to a competitor: pulled it apart layer by layer, asking who the user was, what job it was hired for, how the money moved, which number told the truth, and what a rival could not copy. The teardown produced a sentence she believed and could not prove: Raahat is a medical relationship with a grocery habit stapled to it. Each deck described a different company, and the one that followed from it risked Raahat's largest contract.

2. How Raahat came to be shaped this way

Raahat was founded in Pune on Tuesday 14 July 2020 by Bhushan Gharpure, a former retail category head, and Dr Bhavika Gurav, who had run a small-animal clinic in Mahim, Mumbai, for nine years. Lockdown had filled Indian homes with first-time dogs and cats and emptied the clinics. Raahat began as a teleconsult page and a WhatsApp number; commerce came later, because owners told to switch foods asked where to buy.

By 2022 there were three businesses in one app: food and supplies, a prescription pharmacy through licensed partners, and paid teleconsults. Then came the decision that still governs Raahat's options. To escape the thin margins of reselling Drools, Royal Canin and Pedigree against Amazon and Flipkart, it launched its own label and signed, on Tuesday 14 March 2023, a five-year exclusive manufacturing agreement with Ruhani Feeds Industries of Hosur, running to Monday 13 March 2028. It gave Raahat a recipe of its own and a minimum quarterly offtake of 1,100 tonnes, any shortfall payable at ₹22 per kilogram.

In May 2024 came Rakhwali, a membership at ₹400 a month bundling unlimited teleconsults, ten per cent off food and free delivery, built on card standing instructions because that was what the stack supported. Both looked like moats; both now behave like a floor.

3. The industry around it

Indian pet care is no longer a niche. Supertails and Heads Up For Tails court the same urban owner with commerce, clinics and content; Zigly has pushed into stores and grooming; Amazon, Flipkart and Nykaa carry every brand Raahat resells and discount it at will. Since 2025 the sharper threat has been convenience: Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto stock dog food in ten-minute slots in the cities where Raahat earns most of its money.

Regulation touches every layer. Veterinary prescription medicines sit under the Drugs rules administered by CDSCO and the state drug controllers, which is why the pharmacy is fulfilled through licensed partner premises. Teleconsultation follows Veterinary Council of India guidance, dog feed is specified by the Bureau of Indian Standards, and pet food attracts GST at eighteen per cent. Recurring payments fall under the Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework, with additional-factor authentication and per-debit caps, while NPCI's UPI Autopay offers a rail Raahat's architecture does not use. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the owner records inside every pet profile.

The exposure is not only Indian: Benny Gracias, who runs international business from Austin, holds an unsigned twelve-month order from Rawnaq Pet Trading Partners in Riyadh worth ₹18.60 crore of own-label food.

4. What happened, and what has since looked wrong

Exhibit 2 sets out the sequence. Four beliefs held firmly at the time have become doubtful, and the doubt arrived in a different order from the decisions.

The first belief was that owning a recipe would buy a cost advantage. It did, briefly. Ruhani's input costs then rose while the marketplaces discounted the imported brands Raahat was undercutting, flattening the price it can hold. Own label is still the largest single contributor to gross margin, as Exhibit 4 shows, and also the line Raahat is obliged to keep feeding.

The second belief was that membership churn was a pricing problem. Exhibit 5, from Barun Ghorpade's team in Bengaluru, says otherwise: of the 32,500 mandates presented for debit in September 2026, 26,000 collected, and 2,990 of the 6,500 failures, or 46.0 per cent, failed on mandate mechanics rather than on any owner's decision.

The third belief, from a memo of October 2026, was that teleconsults cause retention, with Exhibit 6 as the evidence. Exhibit 7, built by Bela Gundecha in Nairobi in early November and not yet read by Bhushan, makes that much harder to hold.

The fourth belief was that quick commerce would be incremental. A note from Bijoy Gollapudi's team argues that Raahat's listings on the ten-minute apps cannibalised app reorders in Pune and Bengaluru — but it sets channel volumes for July to September 2026 against reorder rates for the April to June 2026 cohort. The windows do not overlap; the case says so because the note does not.

5. The people

Bhavini Galgali, 38, VP Product, Pune, since January 2025. Position: the product is the medical relationship, and the record inside it is what a rival cannot buy. Incentive: her first large bet here. Not saying: her teardown rests on an axis she invented, and Exhibit 4 puts the two medical lines at 18.38 per cent of GMV, 17.30 per cent of gross margin.

Bhushan Gharpure, 44, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: Rakhwali is the product; the rest is inventory. Incentive: he has told Riyasat Growth Partners members will double. Not saying: his October investor update quoted "about forty-one and a half per cent" — the mean of Exhibit 4's line rates, not the blended 25.83.

Dr Bhavika Gurav, 41, co-founder and chief veterinary officer, Mumbai. Position: the panel is understaffed and the pharmacy carries clinical risk it was not built for; unlimited consults at ₹400 cannot hold past March. Incentive: her licence. Not saying: she has told two clinics they may use Raahat's record format free.

Binita Godbole, 47, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Position: Exhibit 8 is the only exhibit that matters, and it says non-members pay the bills. Incentive: the Riyasat covenant. Not saying: View B was built to rebut the October memo, and she has not seen Exhibit 7.

Barun Ghorpade, 36, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: migrate to UPI Autopay first; no plan survives a rail that drops a fifth of its debits. Incentive: a finishable project. Not saying: the migration needs every member to re-authenticate, and he cannot say how many would.

Bela Gundecha, 31, staff data scientist, Nairobi, two and a half hours behind Pune. Position: neither Exhibit 6 nor 7 identifies a cause; a holdout test would cost ₹18 lakh and eight weeks. Incentive: to be right rather than useful. Not saying: she thinks the October memo was her own error.

Bijoy Gollapudi, 43, head of clinic network, Coimbatore. Position: the clinics are the real customers — 310 of the 1,240 partner clinics, or 25.0 per cent, account for ₹610.60 lakh of the ₹860.00 lakh pharmacy GMV, 71.0 per cent. Incentive: a field budget. Not saying: it credits a clinic wherever the owner bought.

6. Voices

Bhushan Gharpure, board pre-read, 16 November 2026. "We are a membership business with a logistics problem. A member is worth nearly three times a non-member. The answer is more members, and I would like the board to stop asking what the product is."

Binita Godbole, reply to all, same thread. "Three times each, yes. There are 26,000 of them and 1,70,000 of the others. Multiply before concluding."

Barun Ghorpade, engineering channel, 12 November. "We argue about strategy on a rail that loses one debit in five. Those 2,990 owners did not leave us. We dropped them."

Bijoy Gollapudi, field call, 14 November. "In Coimbatore the owner does what the vet says. We build screens for a decision made in a consulting room."

Beena Ganjoo, principal designer, Lisbon, 17 November. "Owners type the animal's weight before buying anything. Nobody does that for a grocery app. Twelve usability sessions is all I have, nine of them in Mumbai."

7. The options as Bhavini currently frames them

Option 1: deepen the membership. ₹9.60 crore over two quarters. Rebuild Rakhwali on UPI Autopay, add a shared pet health record, and raise the price from ₹400 to ₹549. Bhushan's option. The arithmetic is thin: halving the 2,990 monthly mechanical failures recovers about 1,495 members, worth ₹5.98 lakh of fees and, at the member contribution of ₹1,160.40 in Exhibit 8, about ₹17.35 lakh — 10.4 per cent of the gap to be closed. The price rise adds ₹149 for each surviving member and forfeits the whole ₹1,160.40 for each one who leaves, so it breaks even at a churn of 2,959 members, 11.4 per cent of the 26,000.

Option 2: unbundle into a clinic rail. ₹7.20 crore. White-label the prescription and record layer into the 1,240 partner clinics, charge per prescription and record, and let food become whatever the owner buys next. Bijoy's option, and in another form Bhavika's. It is what Bhavini's teardown implies and what frightens Binita: own-label volume would fall, and under the DPDP Act a record made for an owner cannot pass to a clinic without consent for that purpose.

Option 3: become a supplier. ₹4.80 crore. Push own label into Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart, Zepto, Amazon and Flipkart, sign Rawnaq's order, and let the app become a thin shell. At an own-label cost of ₹182.90 a kilogram, a wholesale price of ₹205.00 earns ₹22.10, or 10.78 per cent of that price, against ₹112.10 in the app — 19.71 per cent as much. The export order at ₹260.00 a kilogram, after ₹31.00 of freight and compliance, earns ₹46.10, or 17.73 per cent of the export price. Every kilogram, however thin, counts toward Ruhani.

Beneath the three, in pencil, is a fourth line she has not costed: what if the user is the clinic and the owner is the channel? Exhibit 1 assumes the owner decides. Bijoy's concentration figure, Bhavika's gift of the record format and the 1,08,000 profiles completed before any purchase in Exhibit 3 all sit badly with that. No option here is written for a world in which the clinic is the customer, and none names the record as the asset.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹31.00 crore. September's contribution of ₹1,003.28 lakh against fixed costs of ₹1,420.00 lakh gives a monthly loss of ₹416.72 lakh, or ₹4.17 crore, exhausting the cash in the second week of May 2027. Riyasat Growth Partners has offered ₹210 crore conditional on that loss falling below ₹2.50 crore by the quarter ending 31 March 2027: ₹166.72 lakh a month of extra contribution, a 16.62 per cent improvement on September's ₹1,003.28 lakh, in four months.

Binita will release ₹14.00 crore and no more: Option 1 alone, or Options 2 and 3 together with ₹2.00 crore spare. Own label at ₹1,420.00 lakh a month and a realisation of ₹295.00 a kilogram is 481.36 tonnes a month, 1,444.07 tonnes a quarter against Ruhani's 1,100-tonne minimum — headroom of 344.07 tonnes, 23.83 per cent of current quarterly volume. A forty per cent fall would leave 866.44 tonnes and cost ₹51.38 lakh a quarter; a full stop would cost ₹2.42 crore a quarter, and five quarters remain from 1 January 2027 to 13 March 2028 — ₹12.10 crore. Rawnaq's order is 715.38 tonnes a year, 178.85 a quarter, 16.3 per cent of the minimum.

Three constraints are not financial: Bhavika's panel cannot absorb unlimited consults past March without hiring; the UPI Autopay migration needs every member to re-authenticate; and the DPDP Act's purpose limitation means Option 2 needs fresh consent from owners whose records were made for another reason.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Take Raahat apart as an outsider would: name the user, the job, the promise, the model, the metric and the biggest assumption. Where in the exhibits is each answer visible, and where absent?
  2. Exhibit 4 puts teleconsults at 1.85 per cent of GMV and 3.22 per cent of gross margin, yet Bhavini calls the medical relationship the product. Can both be true, and what would settle it?
  3. Exhibit 6 was used to prove consults drive retention, then reorders; Exhibit 7 reconciles to both. What does Exhibit 7 license you to conclude, and what must Bela's test look like to be worth eight weeks?
  4. Bhushan reads Exhibit 8 as "a member is worth three times a non-member"; Binita as "non-members pay the bills". Both are correct. Which should govern the FY27 H2 bet, and what metric does your choice put on the wall?
  5. The Ruhani agreement was a margin decision in 2023 and a volume obligation in 2026. How much of the option set follows from it, and how would you price the freedom to walk away before 13 March 2028?
  6. Bhavini's pencil line asks whether the clinic is the user. If it is, all three options answer the wrong question. What should she do on Monday morning, 23 November, and what should she say to the board on 20 November — including about the 41.5 per cent in Bhushan's update?

10. Half past one

At half past one Bhavini turned the decks face down and wrote on the back of the top one: I can defend any of these for forty minutes and none for four quarters. Option 1 bought her Bhushan and the covenant but asked Bhavika to promise what she had said she could not; Option 2 followed the teardown but broke the Ruhani arithmetic; Option 3 kept the tonnage and the cash and ended the argument about what Raahat was by making it nothing.

She thought about the 1,08,000 owners who had typed in their animal's weight before buying anything, and the 2,990 whose mandates Raahat had dropped without asking whether they wanted to stay. Somewhere between those two numbers, she thought, was the product. Then she put the pencil down.
exp40v2-sense.deconstruct:
Product deconstruction in depth

Recovering a product's hidden design decisions from the outside — and where the method quietly stops working.

1. Two decisions, thirty-eight days each

On Monday, 7 September 2026, Vasanti Mhaskar was handed a question she could not answer from inside her own company. Vasanti was vice-president of product at Vinimay Trade Systems, a Pune firm selling spend-management and approvals software to mid-market Indian manufacturers. Vinimay had closed FY2026 at ₹46 crore of revenue with 310 employees, and had lost three renewals in six weeks to a Gurugram competitor, Vyavastha Procure Exchange. Vikramjeet Sodhi, the sales head, had a diagnosis and a remedy: Vyavastha had a supplier network, Vinimay did not, and Vinimay should build one. Yashwant Potdar, the founder, set a board review for Thursday, 15 October, thirty-eight days away. "Tell me why their product is shaped like that," he said, "and what it would cost us to be shaped the same way."

In Coimbatore, Udayraj Salgaonkar faced a structurally identical problem in a different product category. Udayraj was chief product officer at Ujjwal Appliance Industries, which manufactured domestic air purifiers and sold them outright through about 1,900 dealers. On Tuesday, 22 September 2026 he had three competitor units delivered to his test bench. They belonged to Zarurat Home Systems, which did not sell purifiers at all: it installed them free and charged ₹699 a month on a thirty-six-month contract, filters and service included. Zarurat had taken visible share in Chennai and Bengaluru apartment complexes. Ujjwal's board wanted a decision by Friday, 30 October, also thirty-eight days out, on whether to commit ₹23.8 crore of working capital to a subscription line of its own.

Both had the same instrument and the same temptation to misuse it: Vasanti could list Vyavastha's screens, Udayraj could put a purifier in a vice. Neither act alone answers what the board asked.

2. The idea, and the four schools that fight over it

Product deconstruction is the practice of reconstructing, from externally observable evidence, the chain of decisions that produced a product's present shape — and then stating each link as a claim that could be shown false. The observable surface is the output; user, job, promise, revenue model, governing metric and defensibility are inputs the analyst must infer. The method answers a specific constraint: managers must learn from products whose internal reasoning is closed to them, and aesthetic reaction teaches nothing that transfers. Hardware teardown culture supplied the metaphor, competitive intelligence the evidence discipline, and the jobs-to-be-done tradition associated with Clayton Christensen the demand-side vocabulary.

Competent practitioners disagree about what determines a product's shape, and the disagreement is not cosmetic. Four positions each generate a different teardown.

The structural school holds that revenue mechanics dominate. It would sign the proposition that you can predict next year's roadmap from this year's unit economics. It would not sign the proposition that founders' taste is a material cause. The demand school holds that the job the user hires the product for dominates, and that products with near-identical economics diverge because their users' situations differ; it would not sign that the model layer is the primary cause of anything. The craft school, descended from design critique, holds that much of what you observe is the residue of individual judgement, path dependence and accident; it will not sign that every feature answers a question, which it regards as the method's central superstition. The organisational school holds that a product is a photograph of its builders' incentives and reporting lines; it would sign that a visible seam in a user flow is usually a seam between two teams, and would not sign that the design was in any meaningful sense chosen.

"The amateur asks what the product does. The professional asks what it would have had to believe to do that."

An expert picks no single school, but notices which one is doing the explanatory work in a given teardown and says so, because that is where the analysis is most likely wrong.

3. Mechanics: inferring a model from a price list

Vasanti's analyst Zubeida Khatri, in Hyderabad, assembled Vyavastha's commercial surface in nine days from four public sources: the buyer price list, a supplier onboarding pack circulated as a PDF, the customer logo wall, and 140 job postings archived over eighteen months. Every line of the resulting revenue statement carried a tag — observed, derived or assumed — and the tags mattered more than the figures.

List price for the standard buyer tier was ₹18 lakh a year. Vinimay's own discounting experience in the same segment suggested a realised price near 65 per cent of list, or 0.65 × ₹18 lakh = ₹11.70 lakh. The logo wall showed 68 buyers, so buyer-side revenue was 68 × ₹11.70 lakh = ₹795.6 lakh, or ₹7.956 crore. The supplier pack disclosed a network fee of 0.30 per cent of invoice value, and Vyavastha's marketing claimed ₹4,250 crore of spend processed in FY2026, giving 0.0030 × ₹4,250 crore = ₹12.75 crore.

Inferred FY2026 revenue, Vyavastha Procure Exchange

That asymmetry is the first real finding, and a feature comparison cannot produce it. Vyavastha's product is designed for buyers and monetised through suppliers. The buyer-facing interface can afford generosity, being an acquisition surface, not a revenue surface. The supplier-facing interface can afford tedium, because suppliers do not choose Vyavastha; their customers choose it for them.

The second-order step, which most teardowns omit, asks what cost structure that revenue structure implies. The job postings did the work. Of 240 employees, 54 held supplier-onboarding titles — 22.5 per cent of the company doing manual data work — and one posting stated an expectation of 18 suppliers onboarded per specialist per month. Vyavastha claimed 1,40,000 connected suppliers. The arithmetic is unforgiving: 54 specialists × 18 × 12 = 11,664 suppliers a year, and 1,40,000 ÷ 11,664 = 12.0 years of work at that establishment. Vyavastha was nine years old, so either the claimed count included dormant records or the team had once been larger — a question Vasanti flagged rather than resolved.

Either way, the replacement cost was computable. To assemble the same asset in three years, Vinimay would need 1,40,000 ÷ (3 × 18 × 12) = 1,40,000 ÷ 648 = 216.0 specialists. At a fully loaded ₹9 lakh each, that is 216 × ₹9 lakh = ₹1,944 lakh, or ₹19.44 crore a year, and ₹58.32 crore over the three years. Vinimay's entire product and engineering budget was 30 per cent of its ₹46 crore revenue, which is ₹13.80 crore. The catch-up cost was 19.44 ÷ 13.80 = 1.41 times the whole product budget, every year, for three years, and 42.3 per cent of annual revenue.

Revenue per head completes the picture. Vyavastha earned ₹20.706 crore across 240 people, or ₹8.63 lakh per employee; Vinimay ₹46 crore across 310 people, or ₹14.84 lakh. Vyavastha was not a better software business but a worse one with a better position — a labour-intensive operation that had converted payroll into an asset competitors could not rent.

4. When the method applies, stated as tests

Deconstruction is not universally informative, and the conditions under which it works can be written as checkable claims. First: the commercial surface must be visible in enough detail to constrain inference. Vasanti passed — published prices, a disclosed fee percentage, a logo wall. Udayraj passed differently: Zarurat's price was public, and because Ujjwal built the same class of device, its cost engineers could price a rival's bill of materials to within a few per cent by taking one apart.

Second: the product's shape must still be a consequence of deliberate choice rather than accumulated obligation. A twenty-year-old enterprise suite is a museum of commitments to old customers, and reading intention into it is a category error. Third: the analyst needs at least one demand-side informant who is not a customer of their own company, or the job layer merely reproduces in-house folklore.

The method actively misleads in three situations. Mid-pivot, a product's surface encodes a strategy management has abandoned, and a confident teardown describes a corpse. Where a competitor spends venture capital to buy behaviour, engagement reflects subsidy rather than fit, and inferring a job from it reads the price tag as a preference. And where shape is set by regulation — a lending flow built to a Reserve Bank of India digital-lending requirement, say — the analyst who credits the team with a clever decision is crediting a statute.

5. Hard edges: two sides, hardware, seams and AI

Udayraj's case holds most of the hard edges at once. Zarurat is a hardware-plus-software-plus-consumables business, so its product has no single unit of analysis: device, contract, filter visit and app are four artefacts with four economics. Udayraj's team therefore deconstructed the contract, not the product. The dismantled unit's bill of materials came to ₹4,850; installation with the first filter fitted cost an estimated ₹1,100, giving ₹5,950 committed per subscriber before the first rupee arrives. Filter life was four months, and a replacement visit cost ₹480 for the cartridge plus ₹150 for the technician, or ₹630. Processing on the mandate ran at 1.8 per cent of collections. Wasim Tambe, Ujjwal's service operations head, put the residual value of a recovered and refurbished unit at ₹1,400.

The convention, stated in the exhibit, was that a replacement visit falls due after each completed four-month block and the visit due in the month a contract ends is not made; replacements over a term of n months are the integer part of (n−1)÷4.

At 36 months the contract runs to term and the unit is not recovered, so no residual value is credited. Without the residual credit, the 14-month column would contribute ₹1,769.85, a margin of 18.1 per cent.

Two-sidedness belongs to Vasanti's case, and it changes the question from "who is the user" to "which side is scarce, where, and when". Vyavastha's scarce side was not suppliers in aggregate but verified suppliers already in a given buyer's vendor master — which is why the moat was per-account rather than national, and why three lost renewals in one segment said almost nothing about a fourth.

At the organisational seams, mature companies behave differently from how they describe themselves. Both Vinimay and Ujjwal ran competitive-intelligence functions reporting to marketing, and in both the output was a feature-comparison slide. The teardowns that changed anything were done by product people with a finance partner and a deadline, circulated as four-page memos. For AI-native products the difficulty is sharper: the observable surface is a prompt box, and nearly every design decision — retrieval scope, evaluation thresholds, which failures are tolerated — is invisible. Deconstructing one means deconstructing its refusals and its latency, not its interface.

6. Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

The payer is often not the user, and the user often not the beneficiary. The tell-tale sign is an interface lavish on one side and punitive on the other. The obvious reading — that the punitive side is neglected — is wrong; it is priced. Improving Vyavastha's supplier portal would have changed nothing about who bought.

A moat built from payroll reads as a weakness and behaves as a strength. The signal is a high headcount ratio in an operational function alongside low revenue per employee: 22.5 per cent in onboarding, ₹8.63 lakh per head. The naive reading calls this inefficiency and expects software to erase it. The catch-up arithmetic — ₹58.32 crore over three years — says otherwise.

A subscription is frequently a consumables-compliance mechanism wearing financing clothes. Over the same thirty-six months a Zarurat subscriber consumes 1 fitted filter plus 8 replacements, or 9 cartridges, while an Ujjwal dealer customer consumes the factory filter plus an observed 1.6 purchases, or 2.6 cartridges — a ratio of 3.46 to 1. The obvious reading of ₹699 a month is that Zarurat spreads the cost of a device. The correct reading is that it removes the customer's opportunity to skip a filter.

The governing metric can be inferred from what the product nags about, not from what it reports. Zarurat's app sent no usage summaries and no air-quality reports; it sent mandate-failure recovery messages. The expert concludes the number being managed is contract survival. The competent practitioner, reading the marketing site, concludes it is air quality.

Break-even and crossover are different thresholds, and teams routinely conflate them. On the figures above, a Zarurat subscriber who keeps the unit covers the ₹5,950 of committed capital in month 11, when cumulative contribution turns positive at ₹340.60. The threshold that matters to Ujjwal, though, is the month at which subscribing beats selling: month 12, where ₹2,427.02 first exceeds the ₹2,329.32 an outright sale plus three years of filter attachment delivers.

Confidence belongs per layer, not per document. The expert tags every sentence, because the user layer is usually well supported and the metric layer almost never is. A teardown with one overall confidence level has laundered its weakest claim through its strongest.

The counterfactual design is more informative than the actual one. Asking what Zarurat would have had to believe to sell outright instead — that filter attachment could be fixed through dealers — located the belief Ujjwal had already tested and failed, its own attachment rate standing at 1.6.

A claimed stock is not an active stock. The 1,40,000 supplier figure, divided by the demonstrated onboarding rate, implied twelve years of effort at a nine-year-old company. The expert treats the inconsistency as the finding, not as an error to smooth away.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the job and the habit loop carry the explanatory load, and the model is simple enough to read off an app-store listing. In B2B and enterprise, buyer, user and signatory are three people, and the hardest work is mapping who feels the pain against who signs — exactly what Zubeida's revenue split did. In platforms and marketplaces the only honest unit of analysis is the local match, which is why Vyavastha's defensibility had to be assessed account by account.

In hardware and physical goods deconstruction becomes partly literal and the balance sheet enters the analysis: Ujjwal's ₹23.8 crore of working capital for 40,000 subscribers has no software analogue. In AI products the genuinely new element is that behaviour is statistical, so one observation is weak evidence and the teardown must be sampled rather than inspected.

By stage the differences are smaller than commonly claimed. At seed the product is mostly the founders' hypothesis. At growth it is a record of what worked, and most informative. At maturity it is a settlement between obligations, revealing the company's past rather than its intentions. What does not change is the discipline of separating observation from inference; "too messy to deconstruct" is an excuse, not an analysis.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Vinimay: the decision not to copy

Vasanti's conclusion rested on the ₹19.44 crore annual figure set against a ₹13.80 crore product budget. Rather than build a supplier network, she proposed targeting manufacturers whose vendor masters held fewer than 400 suppliers, where the match rate Vyavastha offered was no better than a direct integration. Vinimay's base contained 61 such accounts and Vikramjeet's pipeline another 94, a total of 155 named companies.

Ujjwal: the subscription that works only just

Taking Zarurat's observed median retention of 14 months as the planning assumption, 40,000 subscribers generate 40,000 × ₹3,169.85 = ₹12.68 crore of contribution against 40,000 × ₹2,329.32 = ₹9.32 crore from selling the same 40,000 units outright. The gain of ₹3.36 crore sits on ₹23.8 crore of working capital: a return of 14.1 per cent against Ujjwal's 11.2 per cent cost of borrowing, a spread of 2.9 points. If median retention came in at 9 months, contribution per subscriber would collapse to ₹367.76, or ₹1.47 crore in total, destroying ₹7.85 crore relative to simply selling the units.

Wazan Logistics Network: the teardown that found the wrong moat

The instructive failure belongs to a third company. In September 2024 Yogiraj Dharap, then head of product at Wazan Logistics Network in Nagpur, deconstructed a rival truck-matching platform and concluded its advantage lay in a reverse-auction bidding interface truckers evidently liked. Wazan spent ₹6.2 crore over the following eleven months building an equivalent, and by August 2025 had 310 loads a month against the rival's 2,900.

What Yogiraj had missed sat on the rival's balance sheet, not its screen. The rival paid truckers one day after delivery while collecting from shippers on day 38, carrying 37 days of float. At 2,900 loads a month and an average load value of ₹42,000, monthly load value was ₹12.18 crore, or ₹40.6 lakh a day, so the float stood at 37 × ₹40.6 lakh = ₹1,502.2 lakh, or ₹15.022 crore. Funded at 14.5 per cent that cost ₹2.18 crore a year, or ₹2,17,81,900 ÷ 34,800 annual loads = ₹626 per load — 18.6 per cent of the ₹3,360 the rival took at 8 per cent of load value. It was not a marketplace with a nice interface. It was a receivables business with a marketplace attached, spending nearly a fifth of its take rate on being the party that waited.

The recovery is the useful part. On 15 September 2025 Wazan negotiated a ₹16 crore invoice-discounting line — deliberately above the ₹15.022 crore the float arithmetic implied — and relaunched with a 48-hour payment promise rather than a better auction. By 15 April 2026, seven months later, monthly loads had risen from 310 to 1,850, a factor of 5.97. The bidding interface was kept and, by Yogiraj's account, made no measurable difference.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Feature inventory in place of explanation. The early warning is a document whose longest section is a comparison grid. Pick any row and finish the sentence "this exists so that …". Caught late, the cost is a roadmap of copied features: Wazan's ₹6.2 crore.

Screen-only evidence. The warning sign is a teardown containing no money, no headcount and no balance sheet. Ask what the product costs to run; if nobody knows, the work is incomplete by construction.

Inference laundering. An assumption repeated in three meetings arrives at the fourth as a fact; the warning sign is hedging language disappearing between drafts. Demand a source for any sentence lacking one. Vasanti kept the observed, derived and assumed tags in the board version precisely to make this impossible.

Confirmation of the plan already made. The warning sign is a recommendation matching what the loudest executive wanted beforehand. The diagnostic is a second analyst arguing the opposite conclusion from identical evidence.

Rates compared across mismatched windows. Setting Zarurat's filter consumption over 36 months against Ujjwal's over 12 would have produced a ratio three times too favourable. Write the window beside every rate before comparing any two.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether deconstruction is predictive or merely explanatory. The structural position, steelmanned, is that unit economics bind behaviour: Vyavastha cannot abandon supplier fees because 61.6 per cent of its revenue is there, so its roadmap is forecastable within limits. The evidence is a long record of firms doing what their revenue mix required. For this to be wrong, firms would have to routinely accept large revenue disruption for strategic reasons — which they occasionally do, which is why the position is a tendency rather than a law.

The second is whether the "biggest assumption" is a property of a product or an artefact of the analyst. The craft school's strongest form is that products accumulate rather than cohere, that no single belief holds them together, and that naming one flatters the analyst's taste for narrative. Its evidence is how often insiders, shown a teardown of their own product, fail to recognise the assumption attributed to them. The reply is that insiders are poor witnesses to their own constraints. Settling it would need systematic comparison of external teardowns against internal strategy documents, which almost nobody is permitted to do.

The third concerns scope: deconstruct the product, or the company? The organisational school argues the product is downstream of the operating model, so studying the artefact is studying a shadow; its evidence is how reliably interface seams track team boundaries. The product-first camp replies that the operating model is unobservable from outside while the product sits on your bench — a bench Udayraj had and Vasanti did not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three visible ways. They reach for money early: the first question is who pays and how much, not what the product does. They quantify what they have decided not to do, as Vasanti did in pricing a supplier network at ₹58.32 crore rather than calling it expensive. And they state in writing the one observation that would overturn their conclusion — for Udayraj, an Ujjwal cohort whose median retention fell below 12 months. Someone who has merely studied the method produces a longer document with more screenshots and no number that could be wrong.

12. The decisions, and three questions

At the board review on 15 October, Vasanti recommended against building a supplier network and won. Her argument was the ₹19.44 crore annual cost against a ₹13.80 crore product budget; her alternative, the 155 small-vendor-master accounts where Vyavastha's asset did not bind. Yashwant's one amendment was a quarterly re-test of the 18-suppliers-per-specialist figure, since one automation change at Vyavastha would invalidate the analysis.

On 30 October, Udayraj proposed a conditional commitment: a 6,000-subscriber pilot in Coimbatore and Kochi needing 6,000 × ₹5,950 = ₹3.57 crore of working capital rather than ₹23.8 crore, with one gate — median retention at month 12, where ₹2,427.02 first exceeds ₹2,329.32 — and a pre-agreed decision to stop below it. He also began selling replacement filters on a four-monthly standing mandate to existing dealer customers: the Zarurat mechanism stripped of the device.

Three questions. First: Vasanti's case rests on one number from one job posting — what sensitivity analysis around 18 suppliers per specialist per month is defensible, and at what value does her recommendation reverse? Second: if the subscription really is a consumables-compliance mechanism, why did Zarurat install the hardware free, and what should its pricing look like in three years? Third: Yogiraj examined the correct product and reached the wrong conclusion — what procedural change, rather than analytical insight, would have caught it before ₹6.2 crore was spent?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does and the end-to-end product lifecycle supply the question set and the stage map a teardown's layers correspond to. B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction matters next, because the payer-user split that drove Vasanti's finding is its central consequence. Product critique and competitive teardown extend the method — the first inward on quality, the second across several rivals on one frame. Product sense and taste decides what to do with understanding, and product sense rounds is where the skill is examined. Applied behavioural psychology strengthens the job layer, where users misreport. First-principles reasoning and reasoning about trade-offs are the habits behind the arithmetic here; systems thinking for products and design thinking supply the feedback and empathy lenses. Product vision and mission and product principles explain the commitments that constrain a mature product, and building a personal pattern library compounds twenty teardowns into judgement.
case20v1-sense.deconstruct:
Hariyali Works: The Teardown Before the Board

A decision case on product deconstruction

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday 19 October 2026, Manasi Raut closed her laptop in the Hariyali Works office in Madhapur, Hyderabad, and walked to the whiteboard she had filled over three weeks. Across the top she had written: user, job, promise, model, metric. As head of product, she had been asked by the chief executive, Mohan Rajgopal, to put a single recommendation in front of the board on Friday 30 October, nine days before Diwali on Sunday 8 November, when restaurant and sweet-shop orders traditionally surge.

Hariyali had money for one major product bet in the next two quarters, and three were on the table. Manasi believed the team was arguing about what to build without agreeing what the product was, so she had spent three weeks, starting on Monday 28 September, taking Hariyali apart as an outsider would a rival's app, and she now had to turn that into a decision.

2. Company background

Hariyali Works supplies fresh vegetables, fruit and dairy to small restaurants, tiffin kitchens, sweet shops and neighbourhood kirana stores. Buyers order in the evening and receive delivery before the morning rush. Hariyali buys from farmer groups and mandi traders and earns a margin on each order. Founded in 2021 by Mohan and two classmates, it served 3,000 active buyers in Hyderabad, Pune and Bengaluru by September 2026.

The market around it is crowded. Zomato's Hyperpure supplies restaurants from its own sourcing network. Ninjacart moves produce from farms to retailers and food businesses. Udaan and Jumbotail run broader business-to-business marketplaces, and Udaan is known for offering credit to buyers. Reliance Retail's JioMart court the same kitchens at larger scale, and the ONDC network is slowly letting small sellers be found on any compliant buyer app. Hariyali's founders call it "the weekly shop for people who cook for a living", a line Manasi noticed was about a habit, not a catalogue.

3. The situation

By the third quarter of 2026 the numbers looked healthy but uneven. Exhibit 1 shows the three cities in September. The company had 3,000 active buyers who together placed orders worth ₹47.10 crore that month. Hyderabad, the oldest market, had the highest take rate; Bengaluru, the newest, the lowest reorder rate and thinnest margin.

The teardown began with the first question a stranger would ask: who is this for? Manasi pulled six months of order logs and sat in on buyer calls. The user, she concluded, was the person who buys for the kitchen, usually the owner or head cook, judged each morning by whether the kitchen ran out of anything. The job was not "buy vegetables cheaply". It was "never be caught short at six in the morning, without being cheated on price".

That reading changed how she saw the app. The saved "Usual list", which pre-fills last week's order and which the product team treated as a convenience, turned out to be the heart of the promise. Exhibit 2 splits the 3,000 buyers by how they actually behave.

Forty per cent of buyers, those who order regularly and use the Usual list, produced 57.3 per cent of GMV. A list user spent ₹2.25 lakh a month on average, against ₹0.99 lakh for an occasional buyer. So Hariyali was a subscription-like habit disguised as a marketplace, earning a margin on repeat volume. The key metric was therefore weekly reorder rate. The biggest assumption, which Manasi underlined twice, was that kitchens prize reliability above the last rupee of price. The moat, a buyer's own list that no rival could copy, rested on it.

The team was not in one place, and each member saw the problem from a different seat. Her designer in Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead, saw only screens; the operations head in Doha, two and a half hours behind, saw only trucks and temperatures.

4. The people

Mohan Rajgopal, chief executive, Hyderabad. Mohan wants a story the board and the next investors can repeat in one sentence. He is drawn to anything that makes Hariyali look like a larger platform.

Mahendra Ranganathan, engineering lead, Pune. Mahendra wants a bounded project his team can finish before the Diwali freeze and is wary of anything touching payments.

Mustafa Rizvi, head of operations, Doha. Mustafa believes a guaranteed early slot wins kitchens, because buyers who leave, he says, leave after one late morning.

Mia Rowland, lead designer, Melbourne. Mia wants to redesign the home screen. Her usability sessions show new buyers struggling, and she believes the product is built for people who already know it.

5. The options

Manasi framed three courses of action, each costed from figures in Exhibits 1 and 2.

Option A: guarantee a 6 a.m. delivery slot. This is Mustafa's proposal. It would need a larger hub in each city, costing ₹1.10 crore to set up per city, or ₹3.30 crore across the three, and ₹14 lakh a month per city to run, or ₹42 lakh a month in total. That running cost equals about 16 per cent of the current monthly net revenue of ₹263.25 lakh. The upside is a sharper promise; the cost is a heavy fixed commitment before anyone has shown that lateness drives occasional buyers away.

Option B: offer 15-day credit, as Udaan does. Credit appeals to small kitchens that pay late. If Hariyali extended it to 1,000 buyers at the average ₹1.57 lakh a month, those buyers would order ₹1,570 lakh a month, and half a month of that, ₹785 lakh or ₹7.85 crore, would be outstanding at any time. Funding it at 12 per cent a year would cost ₹7.85 lakh a month before any defaults. The upside is a new hook; the cost is a lending business that sits awkwardly with the RBI's digital lending rules.

Option C: deepen the Usual list. This is the option the teardown points to. Manasi proposes ₹60 lakh of engineering and design over two quarters to make the list smarter, with festival-week suggestions and shared owner and head-cook access, and to move buyers toward it. Her target is the 450 search-first steady buyers. If each moved to the list-user average of ₹2.25 lakh from ₹1.50 lakh, that adds ₹0.75 lakh each, or ₹337.5 lakh a month, a 7.2 per cent rise on the current ₹4,710 lakh GMV. At the blended take rate that is about ₹18.9 lakh a month of net revenue, so the ₹60 lakh would be recovered in a little over three months of run-rate.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, state Hariyali's user, job, business model, key metric and biggest assumption. Which option does each fit?
  2. Why is the blended take rate of 5.59 per cent a better guide to the business than the simple mean of the city rates, and what does Bengaluru's 41 per cent steady-buyer share tell you about where the model is weakest?
  3. For each option, what must be true of the buyer for it to pay off, and which of those assumptions can Hariyali test cheaply before the board meets on 30 October?
  4. If Manasi may recommend only one bet, which would you choose, and what evidence would make you change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A teardown asks what the product is, before asking what it should become. Each proposal answered a different product: a logistics promise, a credit line, a habit tool. Deconstruction showed Hariyali was already the third. Forty per cent of buyers produced 57.3 per cent of GMV through a feature the company had filed under convenience, so the user, job and metric all pointed at the list.

One defensible path. Choose Option C, with a guard and a sequence. The guard is the biggest assumption: before committing the full ₹60 lakh, run a four-week test in Hyderabad, where steady buyers are 62 per cent, comparing list nudges against a control group, and release money in stages. The sequence is to keep Mustafa's early slot as a pilot for the 450 search-first buyers in one city only, since lateness is the very claim that remains untested, and to leave credit until an NBFC partner can carry the float.

Why not the others. Option A spends ₹42 lakh a month on a problem the data has not located. Option B turns a habit business into a lender. Option C is the smallest, reversible bet and builds on the strongest behaviour in Exhibit 2. A strong answer also says what to do if the test fails: look at Bengaluru's 41 per cent, where onboarding, Mia's point, may be the weakness.
exp20v2-sense.critique:
Product critique: giving feedback that changes the product

1. A Friday review and a ₹62 lakh question

On Monday 12 October 2026, Eshani Wankhede, an associate product manager at Dastak Home Services, was handed an unusual assignment. Dastak is a Pune-based marketplace that sends trained technicians to Indian homes for bathroom cleaning, appliance servicing and pest control. Its head of product, Devraj Kolhe, had a proposal on his desk: a ten-week rebuild of the booking flow, staffed by nine engineers and designers, costing ₹62 lakh. The design lead, Firdaus Mulla, favoured it. The proposal would be decided at a review on Friday 16 October, and Kolhe wanted a written critique of the current flow before anyone voted.

Wankhede's first draft, written on Monday evening, ran to two pages and contained sentences such as "the slot screen feels cluttered" and "the payment step should be simpler". She showed it to Gunwant Patki, a senior PM, who read it in four minutes and asked one question: "If I forwarded this to Firdaus, what would he do on Tuesday morning?" She had to admit he would not know. Her draft recorded how she felt about the flow. It did not say who the flow was for, what it was meant to achieve, where it failed that person, or what Dastak should try first.

The stakes were concrete. If the committee approved ₹62 lakh on the strength of taste, the team would spend a quarter polishing screens that might not be the bottleneck. If it rejected the rebuild on equally vague grounds, a real leak would stay open. The week's figures, from 28 September to 4 October, showed 2,40,000 customers starting a booking and 1,00,800 completing one. Wankhede's task was to turn an opinion into a critique, and this page follows what that means.

2. The idea: a teardown that ends in a recommendation

A product critique is a structured judgement of a product against its own purpose, ending in a ranked set of proposed actions and the evidence that would confirm or refute each. The word "structured" separates it from a review. A review reports whether the reviewer liked the thing. A critique asks whether the thing does what it was built to do, for whom, and at what cost to that person. It sits one step beyond a product deconstruction (a teardown), which merely lays out the parts: the user, the job they hire the product to do, its promise, its business model, its key metric and its biggest assumption. A critique takes that inventory and adds a verdict and a recommendation.

The practice descends from the studio "crit" of architecture and art schools, and from formal feedback protocols such as Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process, devised for dance in the 1990s, which makes the maker's intent the starting point and puts questions before opinions.

The problem it solves is that preference does not travel. "I don't like it" cannot be argued with, tested or prioritised. Wankhede settled on one sentence she could say in the room without sounding glib:

"Here is what this was meant to do, for whom; here is where it stops doing that; here are the options, ranked by what they would recover; and here is the cheapest test of the top one."

3. How it works: five moves, two of them usually implicit

Intent. Before judging anything, state what the product or feature is trying to do, in terms the team would accept. For Dastak's booking flow the intent is that a customer with a household problem should reach a confirmed, correctly timed technician visit quickly and without doubt. Practitioners usually leave this implicit and then critique against their own private intent. If Wankhede assumed the flow existed to upsell add-on services while Kolhe assumed it existed to maximise completions, every later remark would talk past the other.

User. Name the person, not the segment. Dastak's heaviest booker is a working household in Pune, Hyderabad or Gurugram, booking from a phone during a commute, often in a hurry, and often for a visit the same weekend. The user matters because friction is relative: a six-field form is trivial for someone at a desk and punishing for someone standing in a Metro coach.

Friction. Friction means any point where the user's effort rises or their confidence falls enough that they stop. It is found by walking the flow as that user and, where data exists, by reading the funnel. A funnel is the sequence of steps a user must complete, with a count of how many reach each one. Friction is an observation; it is not yet a diagnosis.

Alternatives. List at least three genuinely different responses, including doing nothing, and estimate what each might recover. What to test. For the leading alternative, name the cheapest experiment that could prove the critique wrong. A critique with no test is a belief.

4. A worked example, line by line

Fergus Tulloch, Dastak's analyst in Edinburgh, pulled the booking funnel for the week of 28 September to 4 October. Each step's conversion is the share of the previous step's users who reach the next.

Chose a service2,40,000n/a100.0%

The table shows 1,39,200 users lost in total (2,40,000 minus 1,00,800), split as 72,000 at the slot step, 42,000 at payment and 25,200 at confirmation. The largest absolute leak is the slot step, which is why the design lead blames the screens. But a leak's size does not decide what to fix; what can be recovered does. Wankhede wrote three alternatives, each with an assumed recovery share, then worked out the extra bookings. Dastak's average order is ₹600 and it keeps 25 per cent, so contribution is ₹150 per booking. Recovered users must still pass the later steps: after the slot step, 75% × 80% = 60% of users complete; after payment, 80% do.

AlternativeUsers lost at stepAssumed recoveredExtra bookings per weekWeekly contribution (₹ lakh)
A. Show slots earlier, with live availability72,00010% = 7,2007,200 × 60% = 4,3206.48
B. Add UPI retry and saved payment method42,00015% = 6,3006,300 × 80% = 5,0407.56
C. Fix the confirmation step25,20025% = 6,3006,300 directly9.45

On this first pass, C ranks first, then B, then A. The ₹62 lakh rebuild, which mostly redesigns the slot screens, would not be the best first move. Now change one input. Tulloch examined the 25,200 lost at confirmation and found that 9,000 were customers shown a "you already have a booking for this slot" warning, who abandoned on purpose. They were never recoverable. The addressable loss is 25,200 − 9,000 = 16,200, and 25% of that is 4,050 bookings, or 4,050 × ₹150 = ₹6.075 lakh a week. The ranking becomes B (₹7.56 lakh), A (₹6.48 lakh), C (₹6.075 lakh). One corrected input reversed the order of the whole list, which is why the critique must state its assumptions and not only its conclusion.

5. Nuances that separate users of the word from practitioners

Preference versus judgement

"I would prefer" is data about the critic. A judgement names a criterion drawn from the product's intent and shows the evidence. The test is whether a colleague who disagrees with your taste could still check your claim.

Observation versus inference

"Thirty per cent leave at the slot step" is observed. "Because the screen is cluttered" is an inference. Write them in separate sentences. Most arguments in design reviews are actually about the second, wearing the authority of the first.

Whose user?

Critiquing as yourself is the commonest bias. Wankhede books services on a laptop; Dastak's median booker does not. A critique is only as good as the portrait of the user it assumes, so say whom you imagined.

Friction is not always the enemy

Some steps are deliberate. The duplicate-booking warning cost Dastak 9,000 completions that week, yet it prevents technicians being sent twice to one address.

Critique is not usability testing

A critique is an expert reading of evidence you already have. A usability test puts real users in front of the product. The critique should end by deciding which test is worth running, since it cannot replace one.

Alternatives must include doing nothing

A recommendation compared only with another recommendation looks stronger than it is.

What it cannot tell you

A critique estimates; it does not measure. The recovery shares of 10, 15 and 25 per cent were judgement calls. They rank options but do not forecast results, and a reader who quotes ₹9.45 lakh as a promise has misread the page.

Questions to ask before relying on one

Who owns the intent, and did they agree to it? How old is the data? Which users are missing from it? What would the author have to see to change their mind?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In consumer products, critique concentrates on speed, clarity and trust in the first few sessions, and the funnel is long and cheap to measure. In B2B products, the person who buys is rarely the person who uses, so a critique must name both and judge the product against each. A procurement manager's intent (audit trail, price control) can sit directly against a clerk's intent (finish the invoice).

In a marketplace, there are two users, and a fix on one side moves the other. Dastak's alternative A, showing live availability earlier, would also expose how thin technician supply is on weekend evenings; customers who now leave at the slot step might leave faster, and technicians might see fewer idle gaps. The critique must therefore name the supply-side consequence of each alternative.

Scale changes the process. In an early-stage company a critique may be a conversation and a shared note, and the test may run by Thursday. A large company needs it written, because the reader will be a stakeholder who was absent from the walkthrough, and because a decision must survive being reviewed by a committee, as Dastak's did.

7. Common mistakes

The adjective critique. Symptom: feedback is full of "clunky", "premium" and "cluttered", and the maker asks "what exactly should I change?". Misunderstanding: describing a feeling instead of a failure. Diagnostic: delete every adjective and see whether a claim remains.

The solution-first critique. Symptom: the critic arrives with a redesign and works backward to find the problem. Misunderstanding: treating the first alternative as the only one. Diagnostic: ask for a second and third option, and for what the critic would do if the preferred one were ruled out.

The funnel-as-verdict critique. Symptom: the biggest percentage drop becomes the headline. Misunderstanding: confusing size of leak with size of recovery. Diagnostic: multiply each loss by a recoverable share and downstream conversion, as the table above does, and see if the order holds.

The untestable critique. Symptom: the meeting ends with agreement and no change in what anyone does. Misunderstanding: assuming the critique itself is the deliverable. Diagnostic: ask what result next week would show the critic was wrong.

8. What good looks like

Wankhede's second draft, delivered on Wednesday 14 October, ran to a page and a half. It opened with a two-line statement of intent, named the weekend-booking household as the user, and showed the funnel. It listed three alternatives and the status quo, gave the arithmetic with each assumption marked as judgement, and flagged the duplicate-warning finding as a correction to the first estimate. It ended with a single proposed test: ship UPI retry to 20 per cent of customers for a fortnight and compare payment-step conversion with the other 80 per cent.

9. The decision, and what to carry forward

At the Friday review, Kolhe did not approve the ₹62 lakh rebuild. He authorised the retry-and-saved-payment test for a fortnight, asked Tulloch to instrument the slot step so that the reasons users leave it were captured, and deferred the larger decision to the end of the experiment. His reasoning, recorded in the meeting note, was that the critique had made the cheapest uncertainty the first one to resolve, and that the rebuild, still plausible, now had a number it had to beat.

To go further, study design critique and collaboration, which covers how to deliver and receive a critique in a room with the maker present, since this page has dealt only with its logic.

Two questions to sit with. First, in Wankhede's second pass, one fact reordered the whole list; which assumption in your own last piece of feedback would do that if it proved wrong? Second, if a critique can never be proved correct in advance, what makes one better than another?
exp40v2-sense.critique:
Product critique

What separates a critique from a preference, where the arithmetic lives, and what the field has not settled.

1. Two rooms, one October

On Monday 5 October 2026 the product council of Sambhav Warehouse Systems, a Bengaluru firm whose software runs the picking operations of twenty-three Indian logistics companies and retailers across forty-one warehouses, received a proposal: ₹1.9 crore and two quarters to rebuild the picking module. Rituparna Sule, the staff design lead, had walked a customer floor in Bhiwandi and returned with eleven screenshots and one true sentence — the screens were a decade old and looked it. Shalaka Tulpule, director of product, was to critique them before the council voted on Thursday 29 October.

Tulpule agreed with Sule. Her difficulty was that agreement of that kind cannot be priced. Sambhav sells per named user per month; its annual recurring revenue was ₹21.4 crore, of which the Bhiwandi customer, Taqseem Distribution Network, was ₹38 lakh, or 1.8 per cent. Every hour the rebuild saved a picker landed in Taqseem's accounts, not Sambhav's.

Fifteen days later, on Tuesday 20 October, Taruni Sheth circulated a memo at Riyaaz Voice Labs in Chennai. Riyaaz makes a voice-practice app for Hindustani and Carnatic students: the learner sings into a phone, and the app returns pitch and tala feedback. Since Monday 3 August 2026 a randomly assigned quarter of its learners had been receiving Riyaaz Guru, a spoken critique generated by a language model from the audio and pitch trace. Quasim Rizvi, the founder, wanted Guru on every account by Diwali; the decision was set for Monday 26 October. Sheth's memo said nobody had written down what Guru was for, or the cost of being wrong in front of a teacher.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about what

A product critique is a structured judgement of a product against its own stated purpose, terminating in a ranked set of candidate actions, an estimate of what each would recover, a statement of the pool into which that recovery falls, and the cheapest observation that would falsify the leading claim. That third clause is the one most often missing, and the one on which Tulpule's case turns.

The practice has three ancestries, and today's schools correspond to which one a practitioner absorbed: the studio crit of art and architecture schools, formalised by Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process in the 1990s, where the maker states intent before responders offer opinions; engineering design review, which treats a product as a mechanism with enumerable failure modes, each carrying a frequency and a consequence; and the econometric tradition that reached product work through growth analytics. All three exist because preference does not travel.

Each would and would not sign specific propositions. The studio school signs the maker's intent is the only legitimate yardstick and refuses a critique is incomplete without a quantified estimate, because premature numbers anchor a room on the measurable. The mechanism school signs a critique is an incomplete hazard analysis until each friction carries a frequency and a consequence and refuses intent is the yardstick, since a product can do what its makers intended and still be the wrong product. The measurement school signs any claim that cannot become a comparison between treated and untreated groups is a hypothesis; its weakness is that it under-weights harms too rare to surface in a two-week test.

No synthesis commands assent; the working compromise is sequential — studio school for the yardstick, mechanism school to price, measurement school to decide.

3. Mechanics in depth: the steps left implicit

The method has five published moves — establish intent, name the user, locate friction, generate alternatives, choose a test — plus three that rarely appear in the write-up. The first is sourcing the intent — finding the sentence somebody with budget authority actually wrote, and dating it. Tulpule found two. The 2019 requirements document said the picking module existed "to let a supervisor verify that the right unit left the right bay"; the 2026 sales deck said it "cuts picking labour by a fifth". A critique against the first scores the module well, against the second badly, so Tulpule put both at the top of her memo.

The second is instrumenting the task before judging it. Tulpule asked Sofia Radulescu, the analytics lead in Cluj, to log every interaction at Taqseem's Bhiwandi facility for the week of Monday 7 to Sunday 13 September 2026 and decompose a pick line into steps, each with its incidence and its median duration. A step's weighted contribution is incidence times duration; the sum is the time cost of one pick line.

Step in a pick lineIncidence (share of lines)Median seconds when it occursWeighted seconds per line

Bhiwandi runs 36,000 pick lines a day, so 28.49 seconds a line is 1,025,640 picker-seconds — 284.9 picker-hours — every day. At Taqseem's loaded cost of ₹120 a picker-hour that is ₹34,188 a day and, over a 300-day operating year, ₹102.56 lakh. Only now can the alternatives be priced.
