The rebuild saves the most time — 4.80 seconds a line against 1.98 for the cheapest fix — but at ₹1.9 crore it pays back in eleven years against seven months for option A. And every rupee in the fourth column belongs to Taqseem.

The third implicit move is therefore naming the pool: for each action, whose profit and loss account the recovery lands in. Sambhav's revenue is seats, not hours, so picker-hours reach it only through renewal and new deals.

Options A and B together remove 5.10 seconds a line, worth ₹18.36 lakh a year to Taqseem, and cost Sambhav ₹22 lakh of engineering. But four accounts were flagged amber for renewal, carrying ₹5.6 crore of recurring revenue between them, the session timeout and mismatch dialog being their two most-cited support items. If fixing both lifts renewal probability on that ₹5.6 crore from 0.70 to 0.85, expected recurring revenue retained rises by ₹84 lakh a year for ₹22 lakh of work. Separately, Sujay Thatte in sales could show that 3 of 11 deals lost in FY26, that is 27 per cent, named the picking interface; at an average contract of ₹44 lakh, three a year is ₹1.32 crore of new recurring revenue, or ₹102.96 lakh of contribution at a 78 per cent gross margin — a payback on ₹1.9 crore of about 22 months. The rebuild is a sales-capacity investment argued as a usability repair, and the eleven-year payback is a category error.

4. When the method applies, as testable claims

One: a purpose exists that someone with authority will own in writing. False at Sambhav, where two incompatible purposes circulated; false differently at Riyaaz, where Guru was built in nine days as a demonstration and never acquired a specification. Two: the friction can be observed for less than the value of knowing. True at Sambhav, where a week of logs cost days of Radulescu's time; partly true at Riyaaz, where grading needs an expert per instance and the sample took eleven paid teacher-hours.

Three: the actions differ enough that ranking them changes behaviour. True at Sambhav, where options A and D differ by a factor of nearly fifty in cost; weak at Riyaaz, where every option ran through the same model. Four: a cheap falsifying observation exists. True at Riyaaz, where a holdout was available and unused; weak at Sambhav, because a picking module cannot be half-shipped, so the test is a pilot at one site.

Critique is actively misleading when the product has no users, when the dominant uncertainty is demand rather than execution, and when its object is a distribution rather than an artefact.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Probabilistic output. Guru has no screen that is good or bad; it has a distribution of responses whose mean is nearly irrelevant. Sheth engaged three vocal teachers, including Sarala Qadri, to grade 400 critiques drawn at random from the 69,750 recordings the beta arm submitted between Monday 21 and Friday 25 September 2026 — the beta being a quarter of Riyaaz's 1,86,000 monthly active learners, or 46,500 learners submitting a mean of 9.0 recordings a month, 13,950 a day.

Grade assigned by the panelCritiquesShare of sample
Specific and correct — names a bar and a fix14837.0%
Correct but generic — true of any performance12631.5%
Vague or empty8220.5%
Specifically wrong — a fault that is not there4411.0%
Total sample400100.0%

Read as a mean this is passable: 148 of 400 critiques, 37.0 per cent, were useful. Read as a distribution it holds a liability, because a specifically wrong critique is not a missing benefit but a positive harm: a student told their third beat is flat when it is not will distrust the app. Rukhsar Talegaonkar, the machine-learning lead, split the 44 wrong answers by what the microphone heard.

The failure is concentrated in one input condition, and the sample mis-weights it. Backing-track recordings were 80 of the 400 rated, 20.0 per cent, but 31 per cent of all submissions in September. Re-weighting the conditional rates to real usage — 49 per cent solo, 20 per cent drone, 31 per cent backing track — gives 0.49 × 5.71 + 0.20 × 8.18 + 0.31 × 28.75, which is 13.35 per cent, not 11.0 per cent. Against 16,74,000 recordings a month that is roughly 2,23,000 wrong critiques, in the register of a teacher.

Structural seams. On a marketplace the critique must name the other side's consequence: Satrangi Craft Exchange found that each buyer-side friction removed from checkout raised orders faster than artisan supply could absorb. In regulated products the seam is legal: at Tahsil Credit Services, Tanveer Tolani's team critiqued a four-screen disclosure sequence as redundant, but three of the four exist because a regulator requires a separately timed consent.

Mature companies run two tiers. The written critique is reserved for decisions above a threshold — at Sambhav, ₹25 lakh; below it, critique is a thirty-minute conversation, because the full method costs more than it would improve. The failure mode is that nobody notices when sub-threshold decisions add up to a strategic one.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The intent has an author and a date

A competent practitioner states the purpose; an expert states who wrote it and when, because purposes drift and the drift is where disagreement lives. The tell-tale sign is two people agreeing on "improve the picking experience" and disagreeing about every consequence. The obvious reading — align on priorities — is wrong: two dated sentences compete.

The recovery lands in somebody's account

Every quantified benefit belongs to a specific profit and loss account, and in business software rarely the one paying for the work. The tell-tale sign is a value estimate in hours or errors with no sentence on how it becomes revenue; that customer value eventually becomes vendor value will not rank a quarter.

Your denominator has a door on it

Experts ask who is missing from the data before asking what it says. The tell-tale sign is a rate computed over users who already passed an unmeasured gate — an installation, a pairing, an eligibility check. The gate looks like somebody else's problem; it is not, because a critique run on survivors improves only survivors.

For probabilistic products, the tail is the product

When output is generated rather than designed, mean and perceived quality diverge, because one confidently wrong answer costs more trust than several good ones build. The tell-tale sign is a team quoting an average while users call the feature unreliable: they integrate over a tail the average smooths.

Some friction is load-bearing

Steps that cost conversion sometimes prevent a worse outcome, so removing them transfers cost rather than eliminating it. The tell-tale sign is a step whose history nobody can explain. At Sambhav an unchallenged mismatch becomes an inventory write-off, so option B cut the dialog from 38 seconds to 12 rather than deleting it.

Conditional rates are not causal rates

A table of outcomes by exposure invites the reader to move people between rows while holding each row's rate fixed — a selection assumption, not an arithmetic one. The sums check; the inference does not, because exposure may proxy for the kind of user. An expert runs it anyway, labels it an upper bound, and names the replacing experiment.

State the switching value, not just the order

A ranking is an artefact of its assumptions; the useful output is the value at which the order changes. The tell-tale sign is a list with no sensitivities. At Sambhav, option D overtakes A at any gain above 12.4 per cent of the 16.00 seconds of core steps, far below the 30 per cent claimed.

The artefact is rarely the system

Critique drifts towards screens because screens are visible, while the binding constraint often sits in a process no product person owns: an installer's job card or a call-centre script. The sign is a redesign that tests well and moves nothing.

7. Differences by product type and company stage

In consumer products the user is the buyer and the funnel is long and cheap to instrument, so the measurement school wins internal arguments and the risk is critique that optimises what is easy to count. In business and enterprise products buyer and user are different people with conflicting intents, the population is too small for a quarter's fix to reach significance, and the hardest paragraph is pool attribution. On a platform or marketplace the method is the same, but every action must carry the other side's consequence.

For hardware plus software the critique must include a physical installation step no analytics event covers, and the observable population is whoever completed it. For AI-native products the unit of critique is a distribution over outputs conditioned on input type, so the exhibit is a graded sample. By stage, what changes is what the critique must survive: a conversation at seed, the absence of its author at Series B, a committee with prior commitments at scale.

8. Three worked examples

One: the cohort exhibit at Riyaaz. Over August and September 2026, 31,000 learners in the Guru beta arm made a first recording, and 9,000 of them — 29.0 per cent — reached ten recordings within a fortnight. Ruben Tavares, the data scientist in Lisbon, tabulated their thirty-day retention against the wrong critiques each received in those ten recordings.

Wrong critiques in first ten recordingsLearnersRetained at day 30Retention rate
None4,2001,72241.0%
One2,80092433.0%
Two1,30031224.0%

Total / blended rate9,0003,06334.0%

Tavares then re-weighted the cohort as if the backing-track path performed like the drone path — 6,100 learners with no wrong critique, 2,100 with one, 600 with two and 200 with three or more, still 9,000 in all — holding each row's rate fixed. Retention becomes 2,501 plus 693 plus 144 plus 30, that is 3,368 of 9,000, or 37.4 per cent: 305 extra learners per 9,000, a gain of 3.39 percentage points. Applied to September's 62,000 first-recording learners, of whom the same 9,000-in-31,000 share, 18,000, cross the threshold, that is 610 extra retained learners a month; at Riyaaz's 13.0 per cent paid conversion, 79 subscribers at ₹249 a month, or ₹2.36 lakh a year. Guru's inference bill, at ₹0.42 a critique across 16,74,000 recordings a month, is ₹84.37 lakh a year — about thirty-six times that.

Two: the switching value at Sambhav. Tulpule computed what would have to be true for the rebuild to be the right first move on customer value alone, and found the threshold low: any gain above 12.4 per cent of the 16.00 seconds of core steps beats option A's 1.98 seconds. She priced the two pools in Figure 2 and recommended both — ₹22 lakh now against ₹84 lakh of expected recurring revenue retained, and the rebuild re-submitted as a sales investment. Tarique Surve noted that A and B shared no code with it.

Three: the critique that failed, at Sugandh Appliance Industries. Sugandh, in Rajkot, sells a ₹18,900 reverse-osmosis purifier whose app shows filter life and sells replacements. In 2025 its product head, Sulekha Tirodkar, ran a textbook critique of the reorder flow. Only 31 per cent of owners who had paired the device reordered through the app; the critique predicted 48 per cent, and the rebuild shipped after eleven weeks and ₹34 lakh. The share moved to 34 per cent — 2,736 extra reorders a year against the 15,504 predicted. The cause lay outside the app: 62 per cent of the 2,40,000 installed base had never completed pairing, because the purifier's module needed a 2.4 GHz network and the installer's job card did not mention it. The critique had been run on the 38 per cent who had paired, that is 91,200 owners. Sugandh rewrote the job card, retrained 1,400 technicians and added a pairing confirmation, for ₹6.2 lakh. Pairing rose from 38 to 79 per cent over two quarters, lifting paired owners to 1,89,600 and app-channel reorders from 31,008 a year to 64,464, a factor of 2.08. At a ₹330 margin advantage per kit over the call centre, the ₹34 lakh rebuild paid back in 3.77 years and the ₹6.2 lakh change in under three weeks.

9. Failure modes, warnings and the cost of catching them late

The adjective critique. Warning: the maker asks "so what should I change?" Diagnostic: delete every adjective and see whether a claim survives. Late: a quarter of polish aimed at the wrong constraint.

The unsourced intent. Warning: two people use the same phrase and disagree about every consequence. Diagnostic: ask whose sentence the purpose is, and when. Late: a feature satisfying an abandoned purpose.

The orphaned pool. Warning: the benefit is in hours with no route to revenue. Diagnostic: ask which account the money lands in, and how. Late: a successful project with no effect on results.

The gated denominator. Warning: a rate whose base is "users who have X". Diagnostic: ask what share of all customers reach X. Sugandh caught it late for ₹34 lakh and eleven weeks.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether expert critique is evidence at all. The measurement position at its strongest: across large catalogues of shipped changes, expert predictions of direction are barely better than chance, so a critique's output is a prioritised experiment queue and nothing more. For it to be wrong, the harms that matter most would have to be too rare to show in a powered test — precisely the mechanism school's claim. That school, steelmanned: the defects that destroy products are low-frequency and high-consequence, so a method that sees only what a two-week test measures is blind to them. For it to be wrong, expensive failures would have to be dominated by high-frequency causes, and nobody has counted.

Whether intent is a legitimate yardstick. The studio position holds that critiquing against anything but the maker's intent is really strategy, and that conflating the two is why design reviews become status contests. The counter holds that a product can achieve its intent perfectly and still be worthless. Settling it needs evidence on which error is commoner.

Whether quantification helps or anchors. Tulpule's tables are the case for; against is that the first number in a room becomes the frame, and the first to arrive are the measurable ones. Rizvi argued that the 2.0 percentage-point conversion gap between beta and control — 3,720 extra subscribers on 1,86,000 monthly actives, ₹1.11 crore a year at ₹249 each — was the only hard number anyone had, and that discarding it for an undemonstrated confound was motivated scepticism. Sheth argued that beta assignment depended on device tier and so correlated with willingness to pay, so the gap partly measured whose phone could upload clean audio. They differ on who bears the burden of proof — risk appetite, not data.

11. What mastery looks like

A student of critique produces the five moves and a tidy document. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They spend a disproportionate share of effort on the two sentences nobody asked for — whose purpose this is, and whose account the recovery lands in. They volunteer the switching value of their own ranking unprompted. They separate observation from inference in their grammar, so a colleague who distrusts their judgement can still use their facts. And they will recommend an action worth less than the one they argued against, as Tulpule did.

12. The decisions, and three questions

At the Sambhav product council on Thursday 29 October 2026, Tulpule asked the council to split the decision rather than reject the rebuild. It approved ₹22 lakh for options A and B against the ₹5.6 crore of amber renewals, told customer success to log renewal conversations against the two frictions so the 0.70-to-0.85 assumption could be tested, and sent the ₹1.9 crore rebuild back to Thatte and Sule as a sales-capacity case. Tausif Rangnekar, Taqseem's operations head, agreed to a four-week measurement at a second facility, so the pilot was not a sample of one.

At Riyaaz on Monday 26 October 2026, Sheth did not get the hold she had argued for, and did not lose either. Rizvi agreed to gate Guru to paying subscribers while the backing-track path was fixed, cutting monthly exposure by 87 per cent — from 16,74,000 recordings to the 2,17,620 that Riyaaz's 24,180 subscribers submit — and the inference bill from ₹84.37 lakh a year to ₹10.97 lakh. Sheth in turn accepted a randomised holdout on a tenth of new learners to test Rizvi's 2.0-point claim. Neither conceded; they converted the argument into a measurement, which is the most a critique can honestly do.

Three questions. First: when does fixing the small frictions first destroy the case for the rebuild that was actually needed? Second: Tavares labelled his 3.39-point gain an upper bound, because the exposure buckets may proxy for repertoire difficulty. Should a critique include a number its author believes is biased upward, and how should it be presented so a committee does not quote it as a forecast? Third: Rizvi's ₹1.11 crore conversion case rests on a comparison he did not randomise, and Sheth's ₹2.36 lakh retention case on a counterfactual she cannot identify. If both are inadmissible, on what grounds should the Riyaaz decision have been taken?

13. Going deeper

  1. Product deconstruction — the inventory a critique presupposes: user, job, promise, model, metric, biggest assumption.
  2. Design critique and collaboration — this page is the logic; that one is the room, with the maker present.
  3. B2B vs B2C — pool attribution follows from buyer and user being different people.
  4. Product sense and taste — taste generates the alternatives arithmetic ranks.
  5. Reasoning about trade-offs — report the assumption at which a recommendation flips.
  6. First-principles reasoning — how Radulescu reached 28.49 seconds: incidence times duration, step by step.
  7. Competitive teardown — the method aimed at a product you cannot instrument.
  8. Product vision and mission — when two purpose statements compete, the resolution is a vision decision, not a critique.
case20v1-sense.critique:
Gharkhata Systems: Critiquing the Family Pool Redesign

A decision case in product critique

1. Opening

At 9:40 on Monday 19 October 2026, Leena Purohit, head of product at Gharkhata Systems, sat in a glass meeting room at the company's Hinjewadi office in Pune with two phone screens propped in front of her. The left one ran the Family Pool flow users already knew. The right one ran its redesign, which the design team in Lisbon had spent eleven weeks building. At 8:15 that morning the chief executive had sent a one-line message: "Lucia's screens are lovely. Let's go."

Leena had until 6 p.m. on Friday 23 October to tell the marketing team which flow the Diwali campaign would send people into. Creative and ₹1.2 crore of ad buys would lock that evening, the campaign would start on Monday 26 October, and Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. Her September beta funnel did not match the chief executive's enthusiasm.

2. Company background

Gharkhata Systems was founded in Pune in 2019 by Lokanath Pandya, a former banker, to help Indian households run their money together. The app tracks shared expenses and pays electricity, gas, broadband, school fees and insurance premiums through Bharat BillPay, using UPI as the rail. It has 38 lakh monthly active users and a team of 210, with design and customer success run remotely from Lisbon and Johannesburg.

PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm and CRED all offer bill payment inside much larger apps. Gharkhata's wedge is the household, not the individual. Its newest product, Family Pool, makes that explicit: an organiser names a pool, sets a monthly budget, invites relatives, and the family pays shared bills together. A pool is a ledger over each member's own UPI account; Gharkhata holds no balances. Members' numbers are used only after consent, as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires.

Finance estimates each active pool earns about ₹1,800 a year in biller commissions and paid reminders. Marketing expects the campaign to bring 3,00,000 people to the Create button over its 14 days.

3. The situation

In September a beta split people who tapped Create Family Pool between the current flow and the redesign, with 12,000 on each. Exhibit 1 shows what happened to them. The redesign did better at the start: 80.0 per cent named a pool against 75.0, and 65 per cent of those invited someone, against 60. But at acceptance it fell to 50 per cent from 60, and at the first bill paid from 70 per cent to 60. Compounded, the redesign produced 1,872 active pools from its 12,000 users (15.6 per cent) and the current flow 2,268 (18.9 per cent).

The numbers showed where the loss occurred, not why. Lwazi Phiri, who leads customer success from Johannesburg, had read the beta's support tickets. Of 214 tickets about invitations, 131 (61 per cent of those tickets) said that the one-time password never arrived, and 94 of those 131 (72 per cent) came from invitees with a non-Indian mobile number, typically a son or daughter working abroad. Tickets come only from people who complain, so Leena treated this as a lead, not proof.

The invitations differed too. The current flow opens a WhatsApp share sheet pre-filled with a link. The redesign, sends a six-digit code that the invitee types into the app after verification. Lucia Pinto, the design lead, argued that a code feels safer to older relatives; nobody had tested it.

4. The people

Lokanath Pandya, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. He wants momentum and a launch that looks as good as PhonePe's. He will read a funnel table, but has said critique is often "taste with spreadsheets".

Lucia Pinto, design lead, Lisbon, four and a half hours behind Pune until the European clocks change on 25 October. She wants the redesign to survive; her usability sessions showed organisers found it clearer, and steps two and three did improve.

Lakshit Parikh, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He wants no heroic week. The invitation service supports both a link and a code, so he estimates three working days for each of two variants, if scope is fixed by Wednesday.

Lwazi Phiri, customer success, Johannesburg, three and a half hours behind Pune. He speaks for invitees, who are in no meeting, and wants verification for family members outside India repaired before a campaign sends them more of it.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 puts the funnel in rupees. If all 3,00,000 campaign taps reach one flow, the current flow yields 56,700 active pools and the redesign 46,800, a gap of 9,900 pools. At ₹1,800 a pool that is ₹178.2 lakh of annual revenue run-rate, and it moves the campaign's cost per active pool from ₹211.6 to ₹256.4 (₹1.2 crore divided by the pools produced).

Exhibit 3 shows the calendar. The critique would take the five working days from 19 to 23 October, a test would run for seven days from 26 October to 1 November, and the winner would take the remaining seven days to Diwali on 8 November.

Exhibit 3: Calendar for the decision. Dates only; no scaled quantities.

6. The options

Option 1: Ship the redesign as built. It has the chief executive's backing and eleven weeks of design work. Its cost is in Exhibit 2: on beta rates, 9,900 fewer active pools than the current flow, or ₹178.2 lakh of annual run-rate.

Option 2: Spend the week on a structured critique, build two repaired variants and test them in the campaign. The critique would take the redesign apart by intent, user, friction and alternatives, and the first week of the campaign would split 1,50,000 taps three ways: the current flow, the redesign with a link restored (Variant A), and the redesign with a code that works for numbers outside India (Variant B), with 50,000 taps in each arm. The winner would take the second week's 1,50,000 taps. The cost is a week of Lakshit's team and a worst case in which both variants perform like the unrepaired redesign. Then week one yields 9,450 pools from the current-flow arm and 15,600 from the two redesign arms, and week two on the current flow yields 28,350, a total of 53,400 pools, ₹961.2 lakh of run-rate and ₹224.7 per pool. That is 3,300 pools, or ₹59.4 lakh, below Option 3. Each percentage point gained on the second week's taps is worth 1,500 pools, or ₹27 lakh a year.

Option 3: Revert to the current flow for Diwali and revisit the redesign in January. It is the safest, at 56,700 pools on beta rates. But it discards what the redesign did better at steps two and three, and teaches nothing about why invitees leave.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What was the redesign for, and who is the user at each step? Which funnel step best measures that intent, and why is "invitation sent" the wrong place to stop counting?

2. Using Exhibit 1, where did the redesign gain and where did it lose? What would you need to know about the 131 password tickets before treating them as the cause?

3. Which parts of the chief executive's reaction and Lucia's defence are preference, and which evidence? How would you restate each as a testable claim?

4. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, what is the most each option can lose, and what would you tell marketing at 6 p.m. on Friday?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A critique is a teardown that ends in a recommendation, in five moves: intent, user, friction, alternatives and what to test. They separate "I prefer the old one" from "invitees outside India do not receive the password, which costs us X".

One defensible path: Option 2. Intent: the redesign exists to get a family to pay a shared bill together, so the measure is the active pool, not the invitation. User: the invitee, often abroad and not in the room, is the person the redesign hurt. Friction: the accept step (60 to 50 per cent) and the first bill (70 to 60 per cent) carry the loss, while the steps the designers cared most about improved, so the critique keeps what worked. Alternatives: restore the link, or fix the code for foreign numbers. What to test: both variants against the current flow, with the current flow as the control.

Option 1 gambles ₹178.2 lakh on an untested design; Option 3 wastes the learning. Option 2 caps the downside at ₹59.4 lakh in a worst case that assumes both fixes fail, buys an answer inside the campaign window, and gives each arm 50,000 taps, enough to resolve about two-thirds of a percentage point at a rate near 18 per cent, well under the 3.3-point beta gap. Caveats: the 214 tickets are a lead, not a census; ₹1,800 is an assumption; two variants must be built in five working days. The message to Lokanath is a method: what Lucia got right, what the funnel shows, what we will know by 1 November.
case40v1-sense.critique:
Parikshan Health Services: Reading the Redesign

An ambiguous case set in Hyderabad, December 2026

1. The night before

At twenty past eleven on Sunday night, 6 December 2026, Avantika Ekbote sat on the floor of her flat in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with two phones and a printed exhibit pack. One ran the Parikshan Health Services app as a customer in Lucknow would have used it in August; the other tonight’s build. Senior vice-president for product since February, she had opened both thirty times that weekend and could no longer tell whether she was evaluating them or just looking.

Three things were due. At 9.30 on Monday 7 December the product review wanted a recommendation on the autumn release: keep, pull, or hold. On Thursday 10 December the board met: Ayesha Elavia of Prayukt Growth Partners, which led the ₹86 crore Series B in February 2025, had asked for “the honest read on self-serve, not the slide”. On Friday 11 December the first invitations for the Pushti Foods Industries contract had to leave: Pushti’s 42,000 employees had ninety days from that date — to Thursday 11 March 2027 — to complete their annual health check, and it paid in full only if 85 per cent of them did.

The pack said the release was working. It also said the company was smaller than in August. Both statements came out of one database.

2. The company, and a signature that still binds

Parikshan Health Services was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 by Ashwath Elangovan, who had run retail operations for a listed hospital chain, and Agastya Ekande, a pathologist. It owns no laboratory; it owns demand: an app and a call centre selling blood tests and panels, 1,480 phlebotomists who collect samples at home, and NABL-accredited laboratories that process them. By December 2026 it worked in eleven cities, from Hyderabad to Indore, Nagpur and Bhubaneswar.

In March 2025, a month after the Series B closed, Ekande signed the agreement that shapes every product conversation the company now has: exclusive processing rights for Pratyay Pathology Partners in six of those cities to March 2030, at rates roughly 14 per cent below market. Two clauses matter. Take-or-pay: a minimum of 1,20,000 samples a month across the six cities, the shortfall billed at ₹310 a sample. And a presentational clause: there the app must display Pratyay’s own catalogue names for every panel and show no comparison across laboratories. The renegotiation window opens on 31 March 2027.

The second constraining decision is in no contract. In June 2025, reorganising into outcome squads, the company retired its weekly design review, where anyone could take a live screen apart in front of its author. Elangovan had thought it decorative: “Nine people arguing about a button, and nobody owned the number.”

3. The industry

Indian diagnostics is a volume business with a trust problem. Dr Lal PathLabs and Metropolis Healthcare hold the confidence of referring physicians; Thyrocare set a price floor through scale; Redcliffe Labs pushed into smaller cities. Apollo 24|7, Tata 1mg and PharmEasy bundle tests into wider journeys and can subsidise one to win a pharmacy order. Parikshan owns neither laboratory nor pharmacy, so it has nothing to defend but the experience of booking a test and reading the result.

Regulation bears on the product directly. Diagnostic services are GST-exempt, while the wellness consultation added in 2026 attracts GST at 18 per cent. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs result-sharing, which is why Pushti receives only aggregate reporting. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission requires reports against an ABHA number, and ICMR guidance on direct-to-consumer marketing has made the company wary of anything resembling a screening programme.

One revenue line is foreign: since February 2026 Parikshan has licensed its report-reading module, white-labelled, to Panah Medical Services LLC, a four-clinic group in Muscat, for ₹96 lakh a year. It renews on 31 January 2027, and Panah’s medical director has twice written that his clinicians prefer the old layout.

4. What happened, and what was believed

In June 2026 Parikshan hired Anvita Elhence, from Pune, as its first director of design. Her brief, agreed with Elangovan, was to raise the share of orders customers place themselves: every agent-taken order carries about ₹95 of call-centre cost. She diagnosed two problems: customers could not choose a panel, and could not understand the result.

Her team shipped four changes in five weeks (Exhibit 1). A Panel Builder, which asks three questions about symptoms and age and proposes panels, went live in all eleven cities on Monday 14 September. A redesigned Result Card, putting each marker on a coloured band with a plain-language note, followed on 28 September; a slot picker on Monday 5 October; a UPI autopay prompt at the payment step on Monday 19 October. None went to a holdback group: the release note argued that the four reinforced one another.

Two events in that window were not the design team’s. On Saturday 12 September the platform was re-instrumented: the schema changed, and a reason code for re-collections — a second visit, the sample unusable or the wrong tube drawn — was created for the first time. On Tuesday 15 September, to fund phlebotomists, Amrita Eswaran cut the call centre from 180 seats to 120, a third of its capacity.

Exhibit 1: Sequence of events, August to December 2026. Dates only; no scaled quantity. Releases: 14 September (Panel Builder), 28 September (Result Card), 5 October (slot picker), 19 October (UPI autopay), the last live for 13 of October’s 31 days. Not caused by the release: the 12 September re-instrumentation, the 15 September seat cut, Dussehra on 20 October.

By mid-November the squad had a story: self-serve bookings sharply up, more customers finishing the flow, the new card understood. Aaron Ellery mailed the Pushti pilot plan on that basis on Wednesday 2 December. Next day Anneke Esselink sent two pages that refused to confirm it. August is the only clean month for the old build, but predates the re-instrumentation, and one funnel step was redefined in it. October carries all four releases, the last for 13 of its 31 days, and contains Dussehra, when fasting tests are postponed; the staffing cut falls between the windows.

5. The people

Avantika Ekbote, product, Hyderabad, sponsored the release at the August roadmap review and wants a defensible answer by Thursday. She has told nobody that in ten months she has never taken a shipped screen apart in front of its author.

Ashwath Elangovan, co-founder and chief executive, is raising a Series C and needs self-serve share as the headline; the deck, he says, cannot carry “a slide about things we are still thinking about”. He is not saying that Prayukt’s discussions assume call-centre cost keeps falling.

Anvita Elhence, design, Pune, thinks the release correct and under-measured, and is right that nobody tested the old flow as hard. She is not saying she opposed the holdback to keep her first release out of a test harness.

Aniketh Erady, engineering, Bengaluru, has fourteen of sixty-two engineers on the squad and needs eleven working days to restore August in all eleven cities, because autopay and the ABDM format were rewritten underneath. He is not saying he skipped the holdback to avoid two code paths in festival season.

Amrita Eswaran, operations, Chennai, owns the phlebotomists and the re-collection budget — ₹340 and a burnt slot each time — and wants the Panel Builder withdrawn. She is not volunteering that she cut 60 call-centre seats the week it shipped.

Anneke Esselink, data science, Amsterdam, four and a half hours behind, will not sign the self-serve claim and wants a city-level holdback. She is not saying she flagged the instrumentation gap in September and was told it could wait.

Amara Ekirapa, customer success, Nairobi, two and a half hours behind, speaks for customers in no meeting: older patients, and the adult children who book for them. She wants the card kept and the Builder fixed; her queue is also her case for more agents.

Aaron Ellery, enterprise and international accounts, Austin, eleven and a half hours behind, signed Pushti and renews Panah. He needs self-serve to work for one and the old layout to survive for the other, and has not said so.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 is the one everyone quotes. Against the entry step — sessions in which a customer opened “Book a test” — confirmed self-serve bookings rose from 14.7 per cent in August to 19.3 per cent in October, and from 70,560 to 1,00,386: a rise of 42.3 per cent on the August figure. Three of the four conversion steps improved, none more than step 2 (70.0 to 78.0 per cent of the prior step); step 5 is flat at 75.0 in both windows. Step 3, 40.0 to 44.0, is the gain whose definition changed on 12 September — the least comparable figure.

Exhibit 3 is the one nobody puts on a slide. Confirmed bookings across the three channels fell from 2,50,560 in August to 2,28,386 in October: down 22,174, or 8.9 per cent of the August total. But the response rate fell from 18.0 per cent of those shown to 13.0, and against everyone shown comprehension moved the other way: 10.8 per cent in May, 9.8 in October. The denominators differ.

7. Voices

“Forty-two per cent more self-serve bookings in two months. I am not apologising for that to a board.”

Ashwath Elangovan, product review, 23 November

“I can sign ‘app bookings rose while total bookings fell, across an instrumentation change, a staffing cut and a festival’. Nobody wants that sentence.”

Anneke Esselink, memo, 3 December

“Three phlebotomists in Indore now carry extra tubes at their own cost. That is not a design preference. That is ₹22 lakh a month.”

Amrita Eswaran, operations call, 27 November

“Nobody has said a word about what the Result Card fixed. Daughters in other cities stopped calling to ask what a result means. That is in no funnel.”

Amara Ekirapa, chat thread, 29 November

“Pushti’s HR head asked one question: can her supervisor in Nagpur book his own test at 6 a.m.? If we revert to August, I would rather she not ask.”

Aaron Ellery, email, 2 December

“If the only thing we measure is whether my work moved a number, I will design things that move numbers. You disbanded the room where somebody could have told me in week two.”

Anvita Elhence, 5 December

8. The options as Ekbote sees them

Option A — restore the August build in all eleven cities before the Pushti invitations. Eleven working days of fourteen engineers; autopay and the ABDM format rebuilt behind it; Panah pleased; Elhence probably gone. It treats four changes as one object and discards what the Result Card did.

Option B — roll forward, retire a further 60 call-centre seats, and run Pushti on self-serve. Elangovan’s preference and the Series C narrative. But on Exhibit 5 the app contributes ₹270 a completed order against the call centre’s ₹410, so moving volume to the app lowers contribution per order; and Exhibit 6 puts its re-collection rate at two and a half times the call centre’s.

Option C — freeze, hold two cities as a control for four weeks, and critique each of the four changes separately. It buys comparability and delays the Pushti invitations by about three weeks, pushing the ninety-day window past the end of Pushti’s financial year.

Ekbote is uneasy with her own page. Each option assumes the release is a single thing to keep or discard, when Exhibit 1 shows four changes on four dates. None touches the panel-naming clause that Eswaran’s diagnosis points at and that no testing will move before 31 March 2027. None says what should be true of a screen before it ships. And all three accept Exhibit 2’s framing, in which the measure is who finishes the flow rather than whether the right test was ordered and understood.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday 7 December, 9.30 a.m.: a recommendation. Thursday 10 December: the board, with Elavia. Friday 11 December: Pushti’s first invitations, or the window to Thursday 11 March 2027 does not fit.

Pushti covers 42,000 employees at ₹1,250 each, a contract value of ₹525 lakh, payable in full only if 85 per cent of them — 35,700 people — complete a check inside ninety days. Esselink’s model compounds October’s own rates: 70 per cent of the 42,000 register, 80 per cent of those who register book, and 87.0 per cent of bookings complete, giving 29,400, then 23,520, then 20,462 completions — 48.7 per cent of the 42,000, little more than half the threshold. At per-completion rates that is ₹255.8 lakh, a shortfall of ₹269.2 lakh against ₹525 lakh. Ellery disputes the first rate, Elhence the third.

Pratyay’s take-or-pay is 1,20,000 samples a month across the six cities. October’s six-city volume was 1,12,300 samples, 54.3 per cent of all 2,06,860 completed collections, so Parikshan paid ₹23.9 lakh for 7,700 samples it did not send: a fall in bookings costs twice. The DPDP Act permits Pushti only aggregate reporting. The Panah licence of ₹96 lakh renews on 31 January 2027. Cash was ₹41 crore on Monday 30 November against net burn of ₹2.6 crore a month: 15.8 months, into March 2028. Elhence’s confirmation is on the December agenda.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What was each of the four changes in Exhibit 1 for, and for which user? Where intent and the measure used to judge it diverge, which should move?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 come from one database and point opposite ways. State what each permits you to conclude, naming the denominator of every percentage you use.
  3. Exhibit 4 has comprehension rising on one base and falling on another. Which base answers the question the Result Card was built to answer?
  4. Separate preference from evidence in Elangovan’s, Elhence’s and Eswaran’s positions. Restate each as a claim that could be shown false, and name the observation that would do it.
  5. Exhibit 6 blames panel naming, which the Pratyay contract fixes until 31 March 2027. If the friction you find is contractually immovable, what does a critique produce instead of a fix?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Ekbote recommend at 9.30, what does she say to the board, and what does she tell Pushti on Friday? What should change about how Parikshan decides a screen is finished, and would she still argue for it if Exhibit 2 had shown nothing?

11. Later that night

Ekbote put the two phones side by side one more time. On the left, eleven panels with names like “Lipid Profile, Extended, Serum”. On the right, three questions about how she had been feeling, then two cards, one recommending a panel she was sure she did not need. She thought about the phlebotomist in Indore buying his own tubes, and about the nine people who used to argue about a button on Thursdays.

Somewhere in the pack was the sentence she would say at 9.30. She had found four, they contradicted one another, and all were true.
